name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. Attorney General Sunday urges Congress to preserve ban on hemp product
description: Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday and a group of 34 bipartisan attorneys general wrote a letter to Congress asking them to preserve a ban on intoxicating hemp products.
text:
A bin of THC edible products from Virginia stores is displayed by the state attorney general. While states continue to expand access to legal marijuana, a separate market of hemp-derived intoxicants has blossomed. (Photo by Graham Moomaw/Virginia Mercury)Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday and a group of 34 bipartisan attorneys general signed a letter to Congress asking them to preserve a ban on intoxicating hemp products.
The ban was scheduled to go into effect November 12.
“Pennsylvanians have a right to know what they’re buying and confidence that products with intoxicating effects are being sold responsibly and not marketed to children,” Sunday said in a statement. “Closing these loopholes, and ensuring they stay closed, protects consumers, supports businesses that follow the law, and makes it harder for intoxicating products to end up in the hands of children.”
The letter was addressed to U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and the chairs of the House and Senate appropriations committees.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The availability of intoxicating hemp products, which are sold in gas stations and head shops across Pennsylvania and America, was the byproduct of the 2018 Farm Bill, which redefined hemp in an attempt to allow farmers to more easily grow the crop. The bill allowed the plants to be processed into products containing intoxicating products like delta-8 THC.
The so-called Hemp loophole was closed by Congress through a funding bill in November 2025, set to go into effect a year later.
The move comes as the Trump White House has reportedly lobbied senators to delay a ban on intoxicating hemp as they negotiate a spending bill for federal agencies.
“If the loophole is reopened or the new definition is weakened or repealed, States will face renewed litigation, inconsistent enforcement, regulatory uncertainty, increased youth access to intoxicating products, and disruption of lawful businesses that have already adjusted their operations to comply with the new federal framework,” the letter read.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: The 2026 midterms are heating up, but this election panel is focused on 2028
description: In 2028, as Georgia residents cast their ballots in the presidential primary, voters across the state will be using a brand new election system. At least, that’s the hope of a special committee dedicated to helping state officials make the switch.  The committee, which includes mostly Republican lawmakers from both chambers as well as current […]
text:
Members of Georgia's
Election Equipment Specifications and Standards Committee hold their first meeting in Atlanta on Aug. 7, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderIn 2028, as Georgia residents cast their ballots in the presidential primary, voters across the state will be using a brand new election system. At least, that’s the hope of a special committee dedicated to helping state officials make the switch. 
The committee, which includes mostly Republican lawmakers from both chambers as well as current and former election officials and other experts, held its first meeting Friday at the state Capitol. The panel was established under a new law passed in June during the state’s special legislative session. 
Ballot QR code bill headed to governor after Georgia lawmakers scale back hand-counting requirement

Lawmakers had been faced with a self-imposed deadline to end the use of ballot QR codes to tally votes last month. The measure passed earlier this summer extended that deadline out to 2028, when Georgia will be required to count ballots using text that can be deciphered by humans. A last-minute amendment to that law instructed the committee to focus solely on hand-marked paper ballot voting systems. 
Georgia’s current system uses machines to mark voters’ selections and then prints a completed paper ballot. The machines were purchased for $107 million from Dominion Voting Systems, which is now known as Liberty Vote, and used statewide in Georgia for the first time during the 2020 election.
Rep. Victor Anderson, a Cornelia Republican who co-chairs the committee alongside Sen. Max Burns of Sylvania, said he is concerned about the tight timeline to overhaul Georgia’s election system, but remains optimistic that the committee can deliver on its promises.
“We have buy-in from three of the legs of the stool in this state: The Senate, the House and the governor’s office,” he said. “Everybody understands the importance of this. Everybody understands the immediacy of us getting it done, and so I feel very confident that we can do that.”
Anderson added that the committee will be able to build on previous work from other legislative bodies, such as a “blue ribbon” committee on elections that met throughout last summer and fall.
Atlanta Rep. Scott Holcomb, the panel’s sole Democratic appointee, urged the committee to dedicate some of its time to cleaning up the state’s election code and removing references to old systems and technologies that are no longer in use, such as direct-recording electronic voting machines that were used statewide before 2020.
“Part of what we also should be doing is to identify where the code really needs some modernization and updating,” he said. “These things are not divorced from each other. In fact, they’re central and critical to the overall policies that we might implement going forward.”
The committee’s final report is due next year at the end of January to allow state lawmakers to begin the procurement process. The 2027 legislative session will start in January. 
Members of Georgia’s Election Equipment Specifications and Standards Committee. Pictured from left to right are Rep. Scott Holcomb, Deidre Holden and Chris Harvey. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
But Deidre Holden, a Paulding County elections director who was also appointed to the panel, urged her colleagues to try and submit it before the end of this year to ensure that local election workers have as much time as possible to implement the new equipment.
“There’s a lot that goes into the procurement process, and there’s also a lot that goes into public education and also into training our staff and our poll workers,” she said.
Procuring the new system is designed to be a multi-step, competitive process. Assuming everything goes smoothly, it could take between four and six months according to Georgia Department of Administrative Services Commissioner Rebecca Sullivan. 
The committee is scheduled to hold two additional meetings focused on gaining insight from a variety of experts, and another two meetings hearing from election equipment vendors and learning about their technical capabilities. The next meeting will be held on Thursday, Sept. 3 in Atlanta.

title: New DMACC President Lori Suddick starts path to understanding college’s core aim
description: With 26 years of service in community and technical colleges, Lori Suddick said there isn’t much she hasn’t seen already. The new president of Des Moines Area Community College is reminded of Wisconsin roads when traveling between different DMACC locations in Iowa, and she’s been responsible for a similar number of campuses in the past. […]
text:
Lori Suddick started her tenure as president of DMACC on June 15. (Photo courtesy of DMACC)With 26 years of service in community and technical colleges, Lori Suddick said there isn’t much she hasn’t seen already. The new president of Des Moines Area Community College is reminded of Wisconsin roads when traveling between different DMACC locations in Iowa, and she’s been responsible for a similar number of campuses in the past.
Prior to her selection as DMACC’s new president after Rob Denson’s retirement, Suddick held faculty and leadership roles at technical and community colleges in Wisconsin and Illinois. Suddick has spent the weeks since her June 15 start at DMACC getting to know the spaces and people that make up her new community and those who influence it, while “trying to enculturate” herself in all things Iowa and DMACC.
“The common fact is these are community colleges. We all have an open access mission, and we’re here to help our students succeed and make an impact on our community,” Suddick said. “The differences are learning, where are we making that impact, and where are opportunities?”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Establishing communication, priorities
As Suddick sets up meet-and-greets and prepares for the upcoming fall semester, she said she’s making early observations of where DMACC is succeeding and where it could grow.
DMACC is “thriving” in its concurrent enrollment opportunities for students still in high school, Suddick said. That’s important, she said, because she knows that students who have participated in those programs are more likely to complete their community college education, whether that leads to credentials or transfer to a four-year institution.
However, adult learning is one area where she believes DMACC could pay more “intentional attention to.” She said it’s important to take a diversified approach to ensuring Iowans already past their primary education have access to furthering their education, just like with student supports and other areas of college operation.
When it comes to business partnerships, Suddick said Iowa’s Industrial New Jobs Training (260E) Program is unlike any she’s seen in her career, and one she’s “been extremely impressed by.” She wants to expand 260E contracts, as well as business partnerships in general.
“I know it was a big point of debate in the last (legislative) session,” Suddick said, “but it is so important to the partnerships and local workforce needs, and community colleges and employers really have a great design, and so we want to make sure we’re continuing that.”
The new DMACC president gave kudos to Iowa Central Community College for its EMT program’s selection as the first in the U.S. to become eligible for Workforce Pell Grants, saying DMACC programs are in the process of seeking their own federal approval. Suddick said she sees Workforce Pell as a “specific program that taps a specific population” rather than a cure-all solution to improving access to training. She said DMACC will enact Workforce Pell once it has been approved for the college and measure its pros and cons.
DMACC also needs to take a look at community engagement beyond concurrent enrollment at all of its locations across central Iowa, she said, to make sure local workforce needs are being met and to create strategic partnerships that draw in and support targeted populations, like people aged 24-54 who need a college access point.
“I feel like we have good bones around it, but I feel like there’s some spots where we are needing to expand the reach of the pathways that we are offering at different locations,” Suddick said. “That’s top of mind eight weeks in.”
Anchored to mission
Suddick is also spending time learning more about one “stark difference” she’s identified between her job in Iowa and those in other states — state code, budgets and the Iowa Legislature. She said she’s leaning on other community college leaders in the state during this process, as she doesn’t want to “disrupt” but add to the good work they’re already doing.
Anchoring to DMACC’s mission is Suddick’s central approach to working with state government and she focuses her conversations with lawmakers on ways to positively impact communities, something she believes everyone wants but can differ in their opinions on how to fund those efforts.
“There’s a lot to do in terms of just building relationships and understanding where everyone’s at, so I can figure out … where my leadership can help plug DMACC in, whether that’s enhancing good things we’re already doing or taking a new look at how we approach some things.”
When Suddick spoke to DMACC community members in her candidate forum for the presidency, she told them “belonging is the key” to ensuring every student sees success in their goals. When asked how she would navigate this belief with laws passed by the Legislature banning diversity, equity and inclusion offices and activities in public higher education, Suddick said “nothing in law changed the mission of community colleges,” which is to serve everyone, regardless of demographics or background.
Lori Suddick speaks to DMACC stakeholders during a presidency candidate forum. (Photo courtesy of DMACC)
Suddick said she’s trying not to let words get in the way of good work occurring at DMACC. One challenge the community college and others face, however, is when funding changes have an impact on certain populations more than others, and the question they have to answer is how to “ensure we’re living to our purpose” and connecting students to the resources and opportunities they need amid funding and policy shifts.
“My job is to make sure that the institution I lead is prepared under its mission to meet every student where they are and get them where they want to go,” Suddick said. “And ideally, we know that people thrive best when they can be their own authentic selves and are in environments where they feel valued and respected and included.”
Looking to the fall
Before Suddick can really tackle the big goals of moving DMACC forward and showing the public its areas of impact, she said she still needs to “launch a college community,” which she plans to do this fall through a college community gathering. This will be a chance for Suddick to share back what she heard from the listening tour, she said.
“There’s a need for us to envision and co-create together, and that’s what I’ll be engaging the college community in,” Suddick said. “It is unclear to me what our core aim is right now, and I came to, like everyone else that’s here, to help support student outcomes, but we need to get some clarity on what that is, and so that is where we’ll begin as a team.”
In order to hear directly from other stakeholders and bring their voices to the institution’s strategic planning process, Suddick said she’ll undertake another listening tour during the fall and spring semesters for students, workforce partners and  K-12 school and university officials.
While DMACC will still keep its present focus on already-established priorities, like a visit from an accreditor scheduled for the spring, Suddick said she needs to better understand people’s perception of the college and where it can improve before she can move ahead with the college’s vision.
“We’re wrapping up on that 60th anniversary, so now we have a chance to question, how do we use this time to position this institution for its next 60-year climb,” Suddick said.

description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Gentner Drummond said he will release copies of his financial and health records to the public after being challenged to do so by a debate moderator. The Republican gubernatorial candidate, who serves as Oklahoma’s attorney general, also told Oklahoma Voice during an interview Thursday that he plans to go a step further […]
text:
Attorney General Gentner Drummond with his wife, Wendy, files to run as a Republican candidate for governor on April 1, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Gentner Drummond said he will release copies of his financial and health records to the public after being challenged to do so by a debate moderator.
The Republican gubernatorial candidate, who serves as Oklahoma’s attorney general, also told Oklahoma Voice during an interview Thursday that he plans to go a step further and also release results of a drug test. 
The 62-year-old Hominy resident said he felt the drug test is important because it illustrates if he was on any medications.
Drummond said he is not “suggesting one way or the other” if his opponent Mike Mazzei is physically able to perform the job.
“The results will be available in three days and we’ll publish those and we’ll see if the other candidate feels confident enough in his physical stature to do that,” Drummond said.
The two men are facing off in an increasingly contentious race to secure Republican gubernatorial nomination during Oklahoma’s Aug. 25 runoff election. 
The candidates were asked during a recent television debate if they would release their financial and health records, Drummond said.
Mazzei, 61, who is a financial planner, said he wouldn’t discuss releasing his financial and medical records when asked by Oklahoma Voice during an interview on Thursday.
Mike Mazzei addresses his supporters on Tuesday, June 16, 2026, during Maze’s watch party in Bixby, Okla. Supporters gathered to watch results in the Republican primary election.Photo by Ace Cuervo/Oklahoma Voice
“I’m not going to get into something like that,” Mazzei said.
Mazzei said his opponent’s campaign is suggesting that he is unfit to be governor and is “probably on some unhelpful medication.”
Mazzei, of Tulsa, said he has not been on any medication since the car accident in 2008.
“I am not on any pain medication now,” Mazzei said.
But he accused Drummond of using his 2008 car accident in which Mazzei sustained nerve damage to his back as “political ammunition.”
“I have been surprised and disappointed that Drummond and his team would stoop to that low,” Mazzei said.
Mazzei’s car accident resulted in significant missed votes in the Senate, where he began serving in 2004. 
He was elected again for a second term without opposition and reelected for a third term before facing term limits in 2016.
“I’m just grateful that the Lord helped me get my abilities back,” Mazzei said. “I’m fit as a fiddle and I’m a pretty lucky guy to be a candidate for governor.” 
Drummond and Mazzei were the top vote getters in the June 16 primary that featured nine Republicans. 
Drummond secured 26.25% of the vote while Mazzei landed 25.97%.

North Dakota National Guard soldiers and airmen work with the Department of Emergency Services to prevent the spread of a wildfire near Mandaree on Oct. 6, 2024. Gov. Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide fire emergency Aug. 7, 2026, due to drought conditions. (U.S. Army National Guard photo courtesy of Staff Sgt. Samuel J. Kroll)North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Friday declared a statewide fire emergency as drought conditions have spread across the state. 
North Dakota also is activating the State Emergency Operations Plan as the risk of wildfires has intensified during a hot, dry summer. 
The emergency declaration directs all state agencies, including the North Dakota Department of Emergency Services, North Dakota Forest Service and North Dakota National Guard, to maintain high levels of readiness to combat fires. The order is effective until Dec 1, unless extended.
“In just a few months, we’ve seen ground conditions shift from lush green to tinder dry across large portions of our state, and we need to be prepared for a potentially intense wildfire season this fall,” Armstrong said in a news release. 
More than half the state is in moderate or severe drought. Another 36% is rated abnormally dry. Officials are not expecting conditions to improve in the near future. 
In October 2024, wildfires burned more than 100,000 acres in North Dakota and claimed two lives.

name: VTDigger
title: UVM Health says big change is afoot — but is it enough to balance the budget?
description:
After years of pressure to cut its revenue, the hospital network now takes an axe to expenses.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM Health says big change is afoot — but is it enough to balance the budget?.
text:
The University of Vermont Medical Center complex. Photo courtesy of UVM Health Network
It’s been a long year for the University of Vermont Health network.
Last year, regulators took a particularly critical view of the network finances, which prompted a leadership change at the highest level of the organization, followed by significant slimming of its executive level positions. As it carried out those regulatory budget orders, charged less for certain pharmaceutical drugs and inked a 2026 contract with BlueCross BlueShield that cut what the insurer paid the hospital, the flagship medical center in Burlington found itself operating at a loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars a day. In May, an independent liaison found that the group needs to cut its expenses by $300 million in the next three years.
Then came large layoffs, cuts to employee benefits and a frantic push to see more patients.
And still, more change is in store, the state’s largest healthcare provider told regulators this week as part of its annual budget-setting process. 
Every summer, the Green Mountain Care Board reviews the budget of each of Vermont’s 14 hospitals and issues binding budget orders by the start of the Oct. 1 fiscal year.
This year, the network has struck a notably different tone across the budget hearings.
“It was the most transparent accounting of our current finances, our plans for the future and the really, really challenging and difficult decisions that we’re making right now,” Dr. Steve Leffler, who leads both the UVM Health network and its Burlington flagship hospital, UVM Medical Center, told VTDigger. 
It’s also the first time in recent memory that the hospital has submitted a budget with a negative operating margin.
The network expects to lose more than $14 million across the system in the coming fiscal year, even with an estimated $3.16 billion in network-wide revenue. It expects UVM Medical Center to operate at a $43 million loss.
That number, according to Leffler, “represents our best attempt to balance required expense reductions for affordability and our commitments to maintaining access to Vermonters,” he said in his opening remarks to the care board.
This year’s budget process notably prioritizes cuts to hospital expenses, while past years have focused on charging patients and insurers less — and thus, decreasing revenue. 
Cutting expenses 
Already, the network has proposed $140,000,000 in cuts to expenses such as administrative staff, clinician time and supply costs. Even with those aggressive cuts, the network still expects its spending to increase more than $97 million compared to this year.
One of the largest cuts to expenses comes from slashing non-clinical, administrative staff across the network — in areas like IT, human resources and legal departments. The network estimates the cuts will save $15 million.
The network also indicated it would use fewer traveling nurses — from 228 in 2025 and 173 this fiscal year to a proposed 114 for 2027. It’s a cut that is also expected to save nearly $15 million.
Similarly, the medical center said it’s trying to reduce overtime and urgent pay by better staffing departments according to patient volume, which should yield nearly $25 million in savings. 
Judy Peck-Lee, the medical center’s chief financial officer, told regulators that the hospital’s emphasis is on moving care to lower-cost sites and reducing length of patient stays in the hospital.

READ MORE

It’s all part of a larger push to increase clinician productivity, which the hospital hopes can bring in higher revenues while also trying to decrease wait times for patients.
The Medical Group — a separate UVM Health body of more than 1,500 doctors and other clinicians who work across the network’s hospitals and clinics —  is going through some of the biggest changes, Leffler told regulators.
As part of the new productivity focus, the network set a 36-hour standard minimum number of patient-facing hours per week. The network is also streamlining its scheduling processes and trying to better match patients’ needs with the right level of clinician, such as staffing an advanced practice nurse when one might be more appropriate than a doctor, Peck-Lee told regulators.
A spokesperson for the hospital said it’s “unclear at this time” if increasing productivity in this way will also result in higher revenues for the network, but it’s something they will continue to monitor.
Fine balance between revenue and expenses
Historically, the Green Mountain Care Board has focused primarily on how much money the hospital network makes, not how much it spends.
Last year’s intense focus on curbing hospital revenue pulled more than $200 million out of the networks’ hospitals’ budgets, according to a memo from an independent oversight group. The network did that by pulling down prices for commercial insurance payers and reducing the hospital price of drugs.
Those slashed costs meant that commercial insurers in Vermont — BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont and MVP — could keep their insurance premiums lower for consumers.
This coming year’s budget proposes no increase to what the hospital group charges commercial insurance — though the care board had originally asked them to reduce it by 1%.
Yet those cuts to revenue need to match cuts in the hospitals’ expenses in order for the network to break even. But neither the 2026 nor the proposed 2027 budgets strike that balance.  
“We anticipate that we’ll end the year significantly in the red at UVM Medical Center and at (Central Vermont Medical Center). The reason is fairly straightforward,” the network’s Chief Financial Officer Rick Vincent told regulators Monday. “The revenue reductions have happened very quickly, and by contrast, our expense efforts are taking longer to implement.”
The care board, in approving hospital budgets, has a tricky balance to strike — to keep healthcare prices affordable for consumers while also keeping the hospital solvent. 
“We want high quality and the best types of care, but that money comes from somewhere. The most clear (place) it comes from is either taxpayer dollars or paychecks,” Chris Whaley, a healthcare economist not connected to Vermont’s regulatory process, told VTDigger.
Still more reduction
The independent liaison group tracking UVM Health’s finances says that the hospital network still needs to cut an additional $50 million from its expenses this coming year to prevent the network from eating into reserves. Specifically, the liaison team suggested that those cuts come from supply chain costs, administrative costs and making its independent group of clinicians more efficient.
The spending proposed by the hospital group is still less aggressive than the goal of a 2.4% increase in expenses that the care board had set for UVMMC earlier this year, a number that aimed to set just enough room to keep pace with inflation.
Peck-Lee told regulators that UVMMC is trying to bring this figure down even further by negotiating cheaper contracts for medical and surgical supplies.  
But the hospital has said that it doesn’t know exactly where those cuts might come from. 
“We did not have those savings completely identified yet, which is why our budget has a negative margin,” Leffler told VTDigger. In the past, the hospital has patched budget holes like this with abstract, placeholder numbers, called “plugs.” This year, instead, its leaders wanted to wait to clarify the cuts more concretely.
“I really don’t like plugs because plugs don’t actually identify what you’re going to do,” Leffler said. “They just feel kind of like you’re kicking the can. So we were honest. We said we don’t have the full savings right now.”

READ MORE

Still, the network expects to have $136 million in reserves for 2027, enough for about 150 days cash on hand. UVM Medical Center maintains a stable A rating from Fitch.
Leffler acknowledged that a lot of that suggested $50 million in expense reductions comes down to staffing costs — which he said make up 65% of total expenses. Leffler said wants the hospital to “save every single dollar we can” from supply chain purchasing and clinician efficiency before resorting to layoffs, even if that means prolonged anxiety and uncertainty for many employees. 
Jacob Berkowitz, the president of the UVMMC support staff union, expressed frustration that workers have been bearing the brunt of the expense cuts. He worries about a “culture of fear” where managers assign fewer staff to their floors, even before official guidance, and about staffing reductions based purely on data, not staff experience. 
“If done correctly, it can be fine,” Berkowitz said. “But the issue comes … when staff input is not heeded.”
Yet, for all this change at the state’s largest healthcare provider, Vermonters still need to see change translate into tangible reductions in prices for services and insurance, Sam Peisch, who works for the Vermont Health Care Advocate, told VTDigger. He is still waiting to see those concrete figures.
“Sometimes the conversations around hospitals frame solvency as the be-all, end-all of sustainability,” he said. “Cutting expenses does not automatically make healthcare cheaper for Vermonters. It’s a starting line, but it’s not the finish. 
In the coming weeks, the Green Mountain Care Board will hear budget proposals for the state’s remaining hospitals, before turning to deliberations in September and issuing its budget orders by Sept. 15.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM Health says big change is afoot — but is it enough to balance the budget?.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: After Ogles’ primary defeat, Trump flips endorsement to Hatcher for Tennessee’s 5th District
description: After former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher emerged victorious in the Republican primary for the state’s 5th Congressional District, President Donald Trump explained away his endorsement of administration ally U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles. Trump endorsed a candidate in each of Tennessee’s nine congressional district primary races. Ogles is the on[...]
text:
Charlie Hatcher, in a surprise victory, defeated incumbent U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles to clinch the Republican primary for Tennessee's 5th House District on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)After former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher emerged victorious in the Republican primary for the state’s 5th Congressional District, President Donald Trump explained away his endorsement of administration ally U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles.
Trump endorsed a candidate in each of Tennessee’s nine congressional district primary races. Ogles is the only candidate carrying Trump’s flag that did not advance to the general election.
Hatcher won the race with 53.2% of the vote to Ogles’ 46.8%.
“Last night was another good night for Endorsements, 8-1, and the 1 was a person who I remained loyal to even though he had virtually no chance of winning, and was running against a Great ‘Trump’ Candidate, and former Agricultural Commissioner of Tennessee, named Charlie Hatcher,” Trump posted on his social media platform, Truth Social, Friday morning.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Trump then gave Hatcher his “complete and total endorsement” in the general race against Democratic challenger, Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, and independent candidates.
After withholding an endorsement in Tennessee’s gubernatorial primary, Trump on Friday also endorsed U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who won the Republican primary against U.S. Rep John Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts.
Ogles’ tenure and ties to Trump
Trump’s endorsement was a prominent feature of Ogles’ campaign in the newly drawn district, which stretches from Middle to West Tennessee. Tennessee’s legislature quickly redrew and passed a new congressional district map favoring Republican candidates in May at Trump’s urging after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Louisiana v. Callais struck down a portion of the 1965 Voting Rights Act allowing for the creation of majority minority districts.
The redrawn district meant Ogles, the incumbent, was vying for an almost entirely different constituency. 
Former Tennessee agriculture commissioner Charlie Hatcher knocks Andy Ogles out of 5th District race

Trump endorsed Ogles in October — before the district changed — and stumped for Ogles in a “tele-rally” in the waning days of early voting, praising Ogles’ loyalty to the administration.
Ogles defeated eight opponents to win the 2022 Republican primary just after the district was redrawn, cutting Democratic-leaning Davidson County in thirds to give Republicans the upper hand. He claimed the seat in the 2022 general election against state Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, and again cruised to victory in 2024, defeating Republican primary competitor Courtney Johnston, a Metro Nashville council member, and Democrat Maryam Abolfazli in the general election.
During Ogles’ two terms, he introduced multiple bills supporting the Trump administration’s agenda. In 2025, he proposed an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would allow a president to serve three terms. 
Ogles recently pushed for “millions” of people of Islamic faith to be “remigrated” from the country.
His time as a congressman has been marked by controversy, including a federal investigation into missing and incorrect campaign finance disclosures and accusations of inflating his resume.
Voting attendance records show Ogles at 91.8%, the 21st lowest attendance rate in Congress and the lowest of the Tennessee delegation.
Hatcher’s winning primary campaign
Hatcher’s campaign painted him as a hard-working farmer and former state veterinarian, referring to himself as a “work horse” to Ogles’ “show horse.”
He also aligned himself with Trump, saying Trump’s work ethic would make him a good farmer. Gov. Bill Lee endorsed Hatcher two days before the election.
Trump stumps for Andy Ogles’ reelection in tightening District 5 primary race

An outside political action committee targeting Ogles for his actions against renewable energy development poured $2 million into advertising supporting Hatcher or opposing Ogles since May 15. Ogles criticized the group, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, as “liberals” trying to “buy seats in Tennessee” before the election.
Ogles also got support from a political action committee. The Freedom Caucus Fund, which is affiliated with hard-right U.S. House Freedom Caucus, pumped more than $810,000 into media buys and robocalls supporting Ogles or opposing Hatcher since May 15, and helped pay for the Trump tele-rally.
Hatcher’s “Hire a Farmer” message resonated in several of the district’s most agricultural counties, earning him a 60% majority of votes in Dyer and Weakley counties. Ogles narrowly claimed Obion County.
Hatcher secured about 55% of the votes in Williamson County, the most populated county in the district and his home turf. Williamson gave Hatcher nearly one third of his winning 36,544 vote total.
But Hatcher also dominated in Maury County, where Ogles once served as mayor; granted, by a much narrower margin of just 207 votes.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: GOP Congressional hopefuls focus on issues, and campaign styles
description: Four CT Republicans, despite long odds, are fighting to win the GOP nominations in two Congressional Districts that are solidly blue.
text:
Four Connecticut Republicans, despite the long odds in November’s general election, are fighting to win the GOP nominations Tuesday in two Western Connecticut Congressional Districts that are solidly blue.
As in GOP primaries of the past, the candidates don’t have major differences on policies but are clashing over their approaches to the campaign. And some offered criticisms of both parties in addressing voters’ concerns around issues like affordability.
The Republican primaries are in the 4th Congressional District, which covers the southwestern corner of the state, and the sprawling 5th Congressional District, mostly in Northwestern Connecticut, considered the most competitive in the state.
Even for the winners of the primaries, the prospects of a victory in November look bleaker than in previous years. Democrats hold all five congressional seats in Connecticut. Republicans haven’t won the 4th District since 2006 or the 5th District since 2004. President Donald Trump lost both districts in his past three races but by a much smaller margin in the 5th District.
Trump remains a power broker in GOP primaries, but he hasn’t been involved in Connecticut since the 2022 Senate primary for Leora Levy.
Two of the candidates scored endorsements in their primaries at the nominating convention in May, but the state Republican Party doesn’t provide support until there’s a nominee. 
The primary winners will spend money on get-out-the-vote efforts to boost early and absentee voting that “helps the entire ticket,” Ben Proto, the state GOP chairman, said.
Proto said the candidates have “very different styles of campaigning.”
“I think in both districts you have very different types of candidates that have a very unique background to talk about. I don’t think there’s any one candidate who is more conservative or less conservative,” he said, adding that the four running in primaries are all supportive of Trump’s agenda.
He expects lower turnout for a midsummer primary with people on vacation and school starting back up in a few weeks, especially without a Republican primary in the governor’s race.
4th Congressional District: Michael Goldstein vs. Dan Miressi
The two-way GOP primary to take on Democratic U.S. Rep. Jim Himes features familiar faces.
It’s the third time Michael Goldstein, a doctor and attorney, has run for the congressional seat in the southwestern corner of the state. He lost the Republican primary in 2022 but became the GOP nominee in 2024, eventually losing to Himes. In this year’s primary, Goldstein is the party-endorsed candidate and faces Dan Miressi.
Miressi is a former professional hockey player who coaches youth hockey. He’s run for elected office before, including an unsuccessful race to unseat state Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, D-Norwalk, in 2022.
Miressi ran for Himes’ seat in 2024 but fell short during the nominating convention and didn’t make it onto the primary ballot. This time, he qualified for the Aug. 11 primary, but Goldstein secured the endorsement.

Michael Goldstein, a doctor and attorney, is running in the Republican primary for Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District. A Republican hasn’t won the district since 2006. Credit: Courtesy of Michael Goldstein

Goldstein decided to run again, despite the growing political divisions in the country.
“It’s become such a divisive time and our country has become so polarized that I felt compelled to actually stand up and advocate for things that I believe are important,” said Goldstein, who also pointed to the rise in antisemitism. “It was not an easy decision to do, knowing that the odds are well against anybody running against a longtime incumbent as a Republican in a predominantly Democratic state.”
He cited concerns over Democratic policy proposals like “Medicare for All,” arguing that health care needs more competition and choice. And as he has in past campaigns, he raised concerns about high energy prices amid debate over a natural gas pipeline that could serve the state and frustration over I-95 becoming a “parking lot.”
Miressi started to get more involved in politics in 2022 when he challenged Duff. Miressi said he’s been on the “Trump train” long before he ran for office, going back to 2010. Similar to Democrats running in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District, he wants to see “a new type of leadership” for Republicans.
He supports the tax breaks in Trump’s “big beautiful bill” but cautioned that Republicans need to be more mindful of pork-barrel spending that further drives up the deficit. He argued they should be “bolder” on tax policy, with flat taxes and an elimination of payroll taxes. He believes Connecticut should invest in chip manufacturing and that the government shouldn’t be involved in student loans and should “zero out interest rates.”

Dan Miressi is running for the GOP nomination in Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District. The primary is on Aug. 11, and the winner goes on to face U.S. Rep. Jim Himes. Credit: Courtesy of Dan Miressi

He also offered a blunt assessment of his own party, saying they need to do more outreach to younger constituents who are struggling to afford housing and other necessities in Connecticut. He believes both parties aren’t doing enough to address issues around affordability, including members of the state’s congressional delegation.
“Why I got into this whole mess to begin with was the Republican Party, especially in Fairfield County, overall in Connecticut, is either nonexistent, incompetent or apathetic,” Miressi said, arguing his party is more focused on people over 50 who are already homeowners and not on young voters who are struggling to buy a home, pay off student loan debt and afford groceries. “I love [Ronald] Reagan as much as the next person, but we’re stuck in 1986.”
“My generation, people under 40, really everyone now, we don’t have time anymore to stand on the sidelines,” he said. “We have to be cognizant of the fact that there’s more to Connecticut, there’s more to people’s lives than the coastline.”
Miressi said he wants Republicans in Fairfield County to look beyond Greenwich and “representing the country club” and that a new generation should be at the table.
Goldstein pushed back on Miressi’s characterization of the local and state GOP and the implication he can’t address issues because of an age difference. He has his own ideas on higher education, seeking an expansion of trade schools that could provide “AI-proof” jobs and a proposal that universities should disclose to applicants “what happened to students who graduated with the degree” and a salary range.
Goldstein said he has a “different skill set” than his opponent, noting his work leading medical societies and other organizations as well as balancing budgets in businesses.
Himes is seeking his 10th term to Congress. If he wins reelection and Democrats take back the House majority, he’d serve as the chairman of the House Intelligence Committee. Himes’ campaign declined to comment on the GOP primary for his seat.
The congressman has a major cash advantage over both of the Republican candidates, with $2.5 million in the bank. Goldstein has raised a total of about $46,000 since the start of the year, spent about $5,7000 and has $41,000 left to spend. Miressi brought in a total of about $10,700, spent a similar amount and his cash on hand is -$1,400.
5th Congressional District: Chris Shea vs. Jonathan De Barros
The 5th District remains the most competitive seat in the state, and the Republican primary has become particularly heated in recent weeks.
U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes faced Republican George Logan in her last two reelection races, but she will have a new opponent this year. Chris Shea and Jonathan De Barros are seeking the Republican nomination and both are running a different campaign than Logan, who kept Trump at arm’s length in his campaigns in 2022 and 2024.
Shea won the endorsement at the party’s nominating convention in the spring, but De Barros still comfortably qualified for the party even after some vote switching. Both are first-time candidates.

Chris Shea in his campaign video. Credit: Chris Shea campaign

Shea is a North Haven firefighter and retired Navy SEAL. He founded the nonprofit Hero to Hero, which encourages military veterans to consider a second career as first responders. He believes he can be more competitive than previous years because he’s from the 5th District and he doesn’t expect issues like abortion and reproductive rights to be as potent of an issue against Republicans.
He said his career in service and at the Pentagon prepared him for the job because he worked a lot with Congress and “got a chance to see how things work — or not.”
“I’m not running to be Trump,” Shea said, adding that he’s much more interested in the president’s policies, such as the tax breaks that passed Congress last summer over his rhetoric. He argued that the western part of the state “deserves different representation than Jahana Hayes.”
De Barros has described his campaign as untraditional. He’s talked a lot about redemption and second chances based on his past. He fatally shot a man in 1996 and was convicted of murder, but it was overturned on appeal. The court ruled that the original judge had erred in barring evidence relevant to De Barros’ claim that he shot the victims in self-defense. He was granted an “absolute pardon” in 2022. He’s been out of prison for over a decade, working as a mentor for at-risk youth.
“I decided to run in the 5th Congressional District after I just saw the failed policies that Jahana Hayes was voting for in Congress, how those policy decisions were affecting that community we both were born and raised in,” said De Barros, who pointed to Democrats’ opposition to Republicans’ major tax bill that also had incentives for more investment in economically distressed communities known as “opportunity zones” as well as the party’s bill related to immigration and the border.
He said Republicans were dismissive of him when he first broached the idea of running, arguing it’s part of a larger problem with the Republican Party. De Barros has aligned himself closely with Trump, calling himself a “MAGA patriot.”
“For the most part, Democrats and Republicans have been ignoring the urban communities, taking that vote for granted. Republicans don’t make an attempt,” he said. “I’m not a blind Republican. I’m not going to blindly support someone because I’m supposed to, because they belong to my party.”

Jonathan De Barros, center, at the 5th Congressional District nominating convention in May. Credit: Mark Pazniokas / CT Mirror

That has put him at odds with members of his own party, frequently calling out state lawmakers and leaders and dubbing some of them RINOs (Republicans In Name Only). “If I see something in my own party I don’t agree with, I point it out,” he said. One example he gave was a small group of Republican state senators who supported the creation of a state emergency relief fund in response to federal cutbacks.
On social media, he doesn’t mince words. But when asked if he regrets anything he’s posted, he’s a bit more reflective, but he said he stands behind the substance.
“Maybe the way I’ve said it, I probably could have said it differently in a way it didn’t sound as harsh,” De Barros said, while adding that he believes he’s “standing up for the truth. I don’t apologize for that at all.” He noted that he and Republican state Sen. Rob Sampson of Wolcott “buried our hatchet.”
That has led to a lot of finger pointing between the candidates in the final days.
Shea argues his opponent’s campaign tactics serve as a distraction and “become a spectacle of personal attacks, grudges and internal warfare that serves only one side — the Democrats.” To Shea, that includes “insulting” comments as well as posting a video of a flyer from Shea’s campaign that was lit on fire. De Barros said it was a video sent to him by supporters who were upset about the content and were exercising their First Amendment rights.
“It’s very juvenile. This isn’t a clown show,” Shea said, adding that the party needs to come together instead of “lashing out at everyone around you.”
“Our resumes should be closely examined,” he said later, adding that while De Barros received a pardon from the state Board of Pardons and Paroles, “I have a record of service, he has a record of serving.”
De Barros, who said he’s called for debates for months, has pushed back on Shea’s characterization, arguing that he and his allies are depicting him unfairly. He recently filed a defamation suit against a few convention delegates who supported his opponent, alleging they called him a murderer. Shea is not a defendant in the lawsuit.
“It’s being weaponized against me by my opponent. That was a low blow,” said De Barros, who said he’s focused on policy priorities like providing financial literacy training in urban communities to get people “off of government subsidies.”
But once they get past Tuesday’s primary, Shea said, he hopes that the party can ultimately come together to “build a big tent.”
Hayes is staying out of the fray while the Republican candidates battle it out for the nomination. But she said she’s aware of the posts on social media that she gets tagged in and the criticism that comes with it.
“These things have been tried before, and they haven’t worked,” Hayes said. “It feels like a recycled version of the campaign that was run the last two cycles.”
Hayes’ 2024 race against Logan was not as close as the one in 2022. This cycle, election analysts who rate competitive races moved Connecticut’s 5th District closer to Democrats. And historically, the party in power faces headwinds in a midterm election.
Hayes has so far raised less money than she did this time two years ago, but she has a significant amount in her campaign account: nearly $1.1 million. Shea has raised about $311,000 since the start of the year and spent $166,000, with about $145,000 in the bank. De Barros has brought in a total of nearly $25,000, spent about $17,500 and has about $7,000 in his campaign account.
But Hayes, who touted the federal funding she’s secured for Waterbury and other parts of the district as well as her office’s constituent services, said that doesn’t change her outlook or approach to running for a fifth term.
“The thing about having a competitive district is that you never take it for granted. I’m always preparing for attacks,” Hayes said. “I’m just ready to run a really strong campaign.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: As an American Jew, my first political loyalty is to American democracy
description: I’m an American Jew, and my political loyalty is not to Democrats or to Republicans.  It is to American democracy. Full stop. That shouldn’t be controversial, but for some people, a Jew saying that their first political loyalty is to American democracy will sound like a statement against Israel. They’ll assume I have rejected my […]
text:
Getty ImagesI’m an American Jew, and my political loyalty is not to Democrats or to Republicans. 
It is to American democracy. Full stop.
That shouldn’t be controversial, but for some people, a Jew saying that their first political loyalty is to American democracy will sound like a statement against Israel. They’ll assume I have rejected my Jewish upbringing or drifted away from it. 
In fact, the opposite is true.
I was raised in a Jewish household by Jewish parents who were seasonally Kosher, thanks in no small part to our neighbors the Bushnells who took in our leavened products every Passover, a holiday we marked each year with an interminable (to a kid at least) seder at home, presided over by my Syrian grandfather. 
Or Hanukkah celebrated each year with my non-Jewish friends imagining 8 nights of amazing gifts, not realizing the reality was one “big” gift and seven other nights of smaller gifts, which one year actually included a stapler. (Oh yes, that happened) And for good measure, I was bar mitzvahed at Temple Emmanuel in Oak Park by Rabbi Kauffman, who, just days before the big event, exasperatedly handed me a sheet with the phonetic pronunciations of the Hebrew I was expected to recite, a feeling with which my future high school Spanish teachers would surely commiserate.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And with that briefest of back stories (I’m Jewish. Believe me, I could go on forever), here’s the point:
My Jewish identity isn’t incidental to this argument. It’s precisely because I take that identity seriously that I believe my highest civic responsibility is to the democracy in which I actually live. Israel matters to millions of Jews for reasons that are deeply personal and entirely understandable. But the United States is the nation whose institutions protect my rights, my neighbors’ rights and my children’s future.
Which brings me to the aftermath of Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, in which the U.S. relationship with Israel and the war in Gaza took center stage. 
For some Jewish Democrats in Michigan, that line seems to be Abdul El-Sayed’s nomination for the U.S. Senate. Reports after Tuesday’s primary show that some lifelong Democrats now plan to vote for Republican Mike Rogers instead of supporting their party’s nominee solely because of El-Sayed’s views on Israel and the war in Gaza.
As someone who values both Jewish principles and American democracy, this leaves me scratching my head.
Jewish history is replete with examples of what happens when strongmen seize power and when minorities discover too late that the institutions they relied on not only can’t protect them, but are actively turned against them. That history should make us especially watchful against authoritarian tendencies, no matter which policies we prefer on any single issue.
My Jewishness lives in family stories, in humor and debate (with arms flailing no doubt) around the dinner table. But it mostly lives in the stubborn insistence on questioning everything — including our own assumptions. If nothing else, being Jewish (religiously or not) is the tradition of asking difficult questions, of wrestling with ideas, of valuing learning and debate. It is the inheritance of immigrant grandparents who arrived with little but language, recipes, and a determination that their children would have a better life. It is the sensibility that turns suffering into satire and survival into storytelling.
None of that, not one bit of it, should obligate Jewish Americans to feel loyalty to a country they likely never lived in and that increasingly may not represent the values they were raised with. 
I wish the people who live in Israel and the territories it occupies — Jews, Palestinians, Muslims, Christians, and everyone else — peace, safety, and dignity, just as I wish those things for people anywhere. But wishing human beings well is not the same as pledging blind allegiance to a nation-state.
Jewish ethics stress justice, protecting the vulnerable, pursuing peace, and upholding human dignity. They also teach us that we are responsible not only for ourselves but for the society in which we live. 
No candidate is entitled to anyone’s vote. Abdul El-Sayed certainly isn’t, nor is Mike Rogers.
Political disagreements come and go. Elections come and go.
The health of a democracy is much harder to restore once it’s lost.
That, more than any disagreement over foreign policy, is the lesson history urges us never to forget.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Sheehy seeks to extend nationwide concealed carry privileges to some veterans
description: Under new legislation proposed by Montana Sen. Tim Sheehy, veteran “qualified special operators” would be given the ability to conceal-carry firearms across state lines without a specific permit in the state, a privilege available to retired law enforcement officers since 2004. A press release from Sheehy’s office says it would build on that framework by […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.Under new legislation proposed by Montana Sen. Tim Sheehy, veteran “qualified special operators” would be given the ability to conceal-carry firearms across state lines without a specific permit in the state, a privilege available to retired law enforcement officers since 2004.
A press release from Sheehy’s office says it would build on that framework by extending carry privileges to a “narrowly defined group” of military veterans.
“Our Special Operations Forces spend their careers protecting the American people with unmatched discipline, judgment, and professionalism,” Sheehy said in a press release. “This bill honors that reality by giving qualified special operators the same nationwide concealed carry privileges already afforded to retired law enforcement officers.” 
Specifically, the bill would allow special operations veterans to concealed carry nationwide, with a requirement to have firearms qualification test and a federal Department of Justice course called, “Concealed Carry Use of Force in Society.”
Kevin Michalowski, a U.S. Navy veteran and a counselor with the U.S. Concealed Carry Association said he was in strong support of the legislation.
“I don’t see a downside for this this legislation because we’re talking about some of the most highly trained, most motivated, most effective people in the military, and they’ve gone through tons and tons of training, specifically about deadly force decision making,” Michalowski said in an interview.
The law currently allows “qualified” retired law enforcement officers to essentially have a nationwide concealed-carry permit. Michalowski said that in order to keep the nationwide permit, retired law enforcement officers have to recertify every year — it’s every five years for state concealed carry permits. He’s also in support of the legislation because moving a firearm across state lines without an ID card is a felony.
“This just continues to show that the these arbitrary boundaries that we call state lines, people shouldn’t be a criminal if they carry a gun from one state to the next,” Michalowski said.
He also urged anyone carrying a gun to get training around the weapon, including “deadly force decision making.”
The bill would also make the carry privilege contingent on, “honorable discharge (if applicable), continued status as a qualified special operator, sobriety, continued federal firearm eligibility, and current training.”
It adds the carry privilege ends “immediately” if any condition of the federal permit fails. 
“Our elite warfighters never stop serving, and this bill ensures the law reflects the trust they’ve earned through a lifetime of sacrifice,” Sheehy said in a press release.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Democratic House speaker pushes back at Republican leader over vacancy
description: New Mexico House of Representatives Speaker Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) on Friday publicly urged the Doña Ana County Commission to fill a vacant seat, and pushed back against the Republican minority leader’s call for the body to leave the position open until the general election.
text:
New Mexico House Speaker Javier Martinez (D-Albuquerque) on Aug. 7, 2026, urged the Doña Ana County Commission to name a replacement to House District 37 despite an election for the seat taking place in November. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico House of Representatives Speaker Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) on Friday publicly urged the Doña Ana County Commission to fill a vacant seat, and pushed back against the Republican minority leader’s call for the body to leave the position open until the general election.
The push-pull follows the July 27 retirement of state Rep. Joanne Ferrary (D-Las Cruces), leaving a vacancy in District 37. Ferrari, along with State Rep. Susan Herrera (D-Embudo), had previously announced she wouldn’t seek reelection, but their terms run through the end of the year.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As a result, county commissions in each House district will select replacements for their preferred candidates and send them to Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, for approval. 
Subsequently, House Republican Leader Rep. Gail Armstrong (R-Magdalena) issued a statement that criticized Ferrary for dropping out early and urged the Doña Ana County Commission to let the Nov. 3 general election between Democrat Lori Martinez and Republican Isabella Solis play out. 
The winner of that race will take office in January and serve a two-year term. 
“The Democratic nominee should have to earn this seat from the voters, not receive it through a political appointment designed to tip the scales in her favor,” Armstrong said in a statement. 
Martínez, on Friday, disputed Armstrong’s characterization of the process, writing to the commission that her letter “ letter fundamentally conflates two separate matters: the county commission filling an immediate vacancy within an unexpired legislative term and the voters of House District 37 duly electing their representative for the next two years. The Commission is in no way being asked to determine who will represent the district in the long term. That decision remains, as it always has, with voters this November.”
Moreover, he said, appointing a replacement still leaves the final decision with voters.
“Nothing currently before the Commission alters that fundamental democratic principle,” he wrote.
Members of the Doña Ana County Commission and officials at the county manager’s office did not return Source NM’s calls seeking comment on when the commission might take up the matter. Naming a replacement for Ferrary is not on the commission’s Aug. 11 meeting agenda.

name: VTDigger
title: New affordable multi-family housing opens in Rutland
description:
Developers are mulling investment strategies for affordable housing in Vermont as federal funding sources run dry.  
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New affordable multi-family housing opens in Rutland.
text:
Kathy Becker, senior vice president of real estate at Evernoth, Mary Cohen, executive director of Cornerstone Housing Partners, and Rutland City Mayor Tom Donahue cut ribbon at newly opened Maplewood Commons. Aug 6, 2026. Photo by Greta Solsaa
Rutland City — The Marble City gained a 30 unit housing complex near the downtown, including six units for people transitioning out of homelessness. The multi-family housing will remain affordable in perpetuity, said Kathy Beyer, senior vice president of real estate at Evernorth, a co-developer and owner of the project. 
“When we build new homes for all income levels, we know that we lift everyone’s boats,” Beyer said. “New housing is vital for the local economy, for employers trying to hire, and for neighborhoods to thrive.”
The other co-developer and owner, Cornerstone Housing Partners, and Evernorth broke ground on the property in May 2025, and finished the project within budget and on the planned timeline, said Cornerstone’s Chief Executive Officer Mary Cohen. The partners received $14.6 million in a mix of private and public funding to cover development costs. 
At the groundbreaking last year, housing advocates voiced worries that federal changes would stymie affordable housing projects going forward. At the time, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development had seen staffing cuts and funding freezes.
The Rutland project made it under the wire as the Office of Management and Budget proposed a rule that would change the review process for federal grants and could cause funding uncertainty for everything from housing development to rural hospitals to scientific research. 
The HUD cuts put the planned 10 HUD vouchers for Maplewood Commons in jeopardy, but the funds came through, Cohen said. HUD vouchers provide housing assistance to low-income families, the elderly and people with disabilities. 
Cohen said Vermont developers now have a better sense of what conditions and funding landscape they are working within. 
There is a glimmer of hope nationally, she added. The federal housing bill — with several provisions that help increase affordable home ownership and construction — passed Congress with bipartisan support in June and became law despite President Donald Trump’s veto. 

Mary Cohen, executive director of Cornerstone Housing Partners, speaking at Maplewood Commons ribbon cutting event. Aug 6, 2026. Photo by Greta Solsaa

There is also action on the local level to help streamline housing development going forward. Mayor Tom Donahue said that Rutland was the first municipality in Vermont to submit a land use exemption application for downtown centers through Act 181. This legislation received a lot of attention for its impact on rural conservation areas this past legislative session. 
If Rutland City gets the greenlight, it will mean that all housing, commercial and industrial development will go through local review and avoid the arduous Act 250 state land use review process, saving developers time and money for projects, Donahue said. He hopes that Rutland will be the first to receive this exemption. 
Gus Seelig, executive director of Vermont Housing and Conservation Board, said it will be harder to build housing without federal funding coming to the state as it once was, including American Rescue Plan Act dollars that funded public health and economic recovery initiatives during the COVID-19 pandemic era. 
The Vermont Housing and Conservation Board helped dedicate $4 million in ARPA funding to Maplewood Commons and has dedicated around $30 million to around 500 units in Rutland, Seelig said. One asset of the project is that large buildings in dense neighborhoods near downtowns help further the state’s environmental goals.
“The more we can build where there’s infrastructure, the more we can continue to enjoy the mountains that surround this community,” said Seelig.
Cornerstone also intends to secure funding next week for another project called East Creek Commons that includes a total of 36 units in the Rutland area, said Cohen. Another 31-unit property owned by Cornerstone called the Arlington Village Center is slated for rehabilitation work. Cornerstone also plans to revamp two projects in Brandon and Bennington as well, she said.  
One of the reasons Cornerstone Housing Partners has several projects in the pipeline currently is due to an influx of federal funds to the state several years ago, Cohen said. 
While working with less funding support, Cornerstone is zeroing in on rehabilitation of existing affordable housing properties as well, Cohen said. 
“It’s really important to reinvest in what we currently have,” Cohen said. “The focus has been really on new units over the last five years. Preservation projects are now coming to the forefront.”

title: North Dakota reports first case of West Nile virus in 2026
description: North Dakota has confirmed its first human case of West Nile virus this year, with health officials advising people to protect themselves from mosquitoes.  The North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services says a Cass County resident was hospitalized after contracting the mosquito-borne virus.  Five North Dakota counties have reported mosquito pools p[...]
text:
North Dakota reported its first human case of West Nile virus for 2026. (Photo courtesy of CDC)North Dakota has confirmed its first human case of West Nile virus this year, with health officials advising people to protect themselves from mosquitoes. 
The North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services says a Cass County resident was hospitalized after contracting the mosquito-borne virus. 
Five North Dakota counties have reported mosquito pools positive for West Nile virus: Cass, Grand Forks, Richland, Ward and Williams. Also, an animal in Sioux County and a bird in Richland County have tested positive for the virus.
Most people infected with West Nile virus experience no symptoms, according to the agency. Those who develop symptoms will commonly report fever, headache, body or joint aches, or rash. People who develop severe illness may experience stiff neck, altered mental status, paralysis, coma, or possibly death. 
People over 60 or those with underlying health issues are most at risk for getting ill from the virus. 
Health and Human Services recommends using an insect repellant, eliminating areas of stagnant water where mosquitoes breed and wearing protective clothing between dusk and dawn. 
Last year, 86 people in North Dakota were infected with West Nile, leading to 36 hospitalizations and two deaths, according to the agency’s annual report.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Cheers drown out Healey as she signs immigrant protection bill
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: The new law (H 5620), known as the PROTECT Act, arose as a top priority for lawmakers and the governor amid intensified immigration law enforcement efforts led by President Donald Trump.
text:
IT WAS HARD to tell whether Gov. Maura Healey hosted a party or bill signing ceremony when she signed legislation Wednesday that the governor and lawmakers say provides the strongest immigrant protections in the country.
A band played and while Healey gave her remarks, the governor’s voice repeatedly drowned out by the cheers of dozens of supporters who packed into a hot, crowded room.
The new law (H 5620), known as the PROTECT Act, arose as a top priority for lawmakers and the governor amid intensified immigration law enforcement efforts led by President Donald Trump. The law expands protections against warrantless civil immigration arrests at courthouses as well as public schools, child care centers and health care facilities. 
“I think we can agree that we need immigration reform in this country. We can agree we need controls at the border. We can also agree that ICE is so wrong in what it’s doing, and ICE needs to be stopped here in Massachusetts and around this country,” Healey said during a bill signing ceremony in Chelsea at La Colaborativa, a nonprofit focused on supporting immigrants.
Healey, a Democrat seeking reelection this year, called Trump’s immigration enforcement tactics “cruel, unconstitutional, un-American; It is so stupid.”
She also referenced Trump’s recent decision to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitian and Syrian immigrants.
By ramping up immigration enforcement actions, Trump is pursuing campaign promises he made to increase deportations as part of an effort to reduce crime and crack down on illegal immigration. Protests have unfolded across the country in response to the increasingly violent actions by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.
“Today in Massachusetts, we’re saying enough is enough. We’re standing up for what’s right, and we’re taking action to protect people’s safety,” Healey said. “The PROTECT Act is the strongest law in the country to protect people from ICE and to protect public safety.”
Fidel Maltez, Chelsea’s city manager, said the law offers relief to many in the community who have been afraid to go to work, school and other locations over fears of running into ICE agents. Chelsea has among the highest foreign-born populations in Massachusetts, with latest U.S. Census numbers showing about 46 percent of the city’s residents are immigrants.
“We in the city have seen the cost of that fear: empty classroom seats, neighbors who have left the state, businesses that have shuttered, and trust broken between residents and our institutions that are meant to protect them. But today, today that changes. Today our governor makes history. Today the PROTECT Act becomes the law of the land,” Maltez said to a roaring round of applause.
The sweeping legislation also codifies the Massachusetts’s Supreme Judicial Court 2017 Lunn v. Commonwealth decision that found there is “no authority for Massachusetts court officers to arrest and hold an individual solely on the basis of a Federal civil immigration detainer.” It prohibits new agreements allowing state and local officials to perform certain federal immigration enforcement actions while preserving the Department of Correction’s existing agreement with ICE. 
The law allows parents to arrange guardianship for their children in case they are detained, and creates a civil cause of action against federal law enforcement officers who violate a resident’s constitutional rights. 
Under an emergency preamble lawmakers attached to the bill, the sweeping law will go into effect immediately. 
While supporters celebrated the bill’s signing on Wednesday, opponents have raised concerns.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve issued a statement saying that by signing the bill, Healey “prioritizes politics over public safety,” as the law will limit cooperation between state and federal law enforcement officers. 
“Governor Healey’s decision to sign the PROTECT Act is driven by politics, not public safety,” Shortsleeve said. “There is no safer or more secure place for state authorities to transfer a criminal into federal custody than a courthouse and this law bars that from happening. Instead, this law creates new barriers to cooperation and sends the wrong message at the wrong time.”
Massachusetts Coalition for Immigration Reform said the law “is an ill-advised measure that assigns a higher priority to ideology than to public safety” and “by any measure illegal immigration is economically and socially harmful.”
“By preventing [law enforcement agencies] from communicating with ICE concerning persons in custody, the PROTECT law in effect protects criminal aliens who should otherwise be deported,” the group said in a press release issued Wednesday. “MCIR believes that ICE agents deserve our support in performing the critical, difficult, and often dangerous task of securing our borders and protecting Americans from terrorists and criminal aliens.”
The Asian Pacific Islanders Civic Action Network applauded the bill’s enactment and called for more protections for immigrants.
Among the group’s requests were: banning all 287(g) agreements in the state, including the DOC’s, and ending institutions that share information among different levels of law enforcement. Also, the group said immigrant communities, like Muslim and Asian American and Pacific Islanders, were left out of some conversations.
“For too long, we have seen how the voices and experiences of current and formerly incarcerated immigrants are erased from policy because of criminal carveouts and the PROTECT Act is no exception,” the group said in a July 31 press release. “This approach reinforces the very systems that have long placed immigrants at greater risk of detention and deportation.”
Healey emphasized the law as a public safety measure. The governor also said the conversation surrounding immigrant protections is not finished.
“There will be ugliness coming out of today. There will be ugly rhetoric. There will be meanness. There will be cruelty. There will be racist tirades. You see it online and elsewhere,” she said. “Okay, listen. We’ll be strong. We’ll be tough. We know what’s right. We know how to protect ourselves. We know how to protect public safety, and we know what we need to do because we know how terrible, terrible ICE has been in Massachusetts and around this country, and this is about stopping it.”
Before signing the law, Healey issued a statement Wednesday morning calling on ICE agents to keep their vehicles out of Boston in response to NBC 10 reporting that ICE was looking to lease 249 parking spots downtown.

name: VTDigger
title: Windsor County Sheriff candidate placed on administrative leave from Bellows Falls PD
description:
Joshua Lake is one of three Democrats seeking to replace embattled Sheriff Ryan Palmer, who himself is facing a raft of criminal charges stemming from his work as sheriff.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Windsor County Sheriff candidate placed on administrative leave from Bellows Falls PD.
text:
A Bellows Balls Police Department vehicle seen in 2020. YouTube photo

This story by Susan Smallheer was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Aug 6, 2026.BELLOWS FALLS — The village of Bellows Falls has placed one of its police officers running for Windsor County Sheriff in Tuesday’s Democratic primary on administrative leave in the wake of a letter from both the Windham County State’s Attorney and the Vermont attorney general’s office, raising questions about his credibility as a police officer.
Joshua Lake, 30, who has been a Bellows Falls officer for about two years, was placed on administrative leave on Wednesday, according to Bellows Falls Police Chief David Bemis.
Bemis said an “outside” law enforcement agency will conduct the investigation to look into the questions raised by Lake’s admission he “exaggerated” an incident involving his wife to a Walpole, N.H., police officer last December.
At the time, Lake said his wife — who at one time was an interim Windsor County deputy sheriff — had pulled a gun on him and had also abused their young daughter.
Since then, Lake has said both that the incident never happened and that he had exaggerated the incident.

Bellows Falls Police Officer Joshua Lake, who is a candidate in the democratic primary for sheriff in Windsor County. Provided photo

The Walpole officer, following police protocols, reported the incident to his superiors, which in turn triggered an investigation by both the Vermont State Police and Windsor County Sheriff Ryan Palmer.
On Monday, Windham County State’s Attorney Steven Brown and Domenica Padula from the Vermont Attorney General’s office issued a so-called Giglio letter, which is sometimes called a Brady letter, alerting defense attorneys that Lake’s credibility as a police officer had been called into question.
“The Vermont State Police conducted an investigation involving Bellows Falls Police Officer Joshua Lake involving statements he made while off duty during a conversation with an on-duty New Hampshire Police Officer, a person he considered to be a friend, regarding a crime he said he witnessed off duty. When asked by Vermont State Police investigators about the statement, Officer Lake stated he exaggerated what he told the New Hampshire Police Officer,” the joint letter from Brown and Padula, the chief of the criminal division of the Vermont Attorney General’s office, said.
Lake didn’t return a message seeking comment Thursday.
Brown, in a telephone interview Thursday, said that criminal cases from Bellows Falls involving Lake would still go forward, but would come under additional review and checks for credibility. Brown said he had never called Lake as a witness in a trial, but he said he does have pending cases with Lake, as both a witness and case officer.

READ MORE

He said the Giglio letter, and not an “alert,” as Lake has characterized it, is relatively rare, and he said he knew of only one other Windham County police officer “who had a letter.” Some Giglio letters are a death knell for a law enforcement career, depending on the severity of the misdeed. The other Windham County officer with a Giglio letter had misrepresented his timesheet, Brown said.
“We are going to evaluate on a case by case basis,” Brown said.
It was that letter, a short press release from Bemis, that prompted the action by the village manager Aaron Patt to place Lake on administrative leave, with pay. Patt couldn’t be reached Thursday.
Lake, although he’s been a Bellows Falls officer for only two years, has a long family history in law enforcement in Windham County. His father, Ron Lake, is the former Bellows Falls police chief who resigned in January 2020, citing medical problems. His grandfather, Sherwood Lake Sr., was a longtime officer in the Brattleboro Police Department, and both his father and his uncle, Sherwood Lake Jr., worked in the Windham County Sheriff’s Department.
Lake recently moved from Rockingham to Chester, which is in Windsor County, during the campaign. Lake is one of three Democrats seeking to replace Palmer, who himself is facing a raft of criminal charges stemming from his work as sheriff. Palmer has not resigned, despite being stripped of his certification as a Vermont law enforcement officer.
On Wednesday evening, the Windsor County Democratic Committee sent out a letter to its membership alerting them to the Lake development, and the Giglio letter.
