name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Homeownership preservation must be part of our housing strategy
description: There is a significant gap between making a homeowner and sustaining one.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS HOUSING POLICY echoes a familiar three-part refrain. We need to build more homes. We need to ensure that rental units are safe and affordable. And we need to make buying a home more accessible to low- and moderate-income households. All three are crucial moves for dealing with our sharpening supply and affordability crisis, but they often neglect a quieter, equally urgent crisis unfolding in thousands of Massachusetts households: Too many of our state’s homeowners are struggling to stay in their homes after they buy them. 
A coalition of partners, including the Boston Foundation, worked with The MassINC Polling Group on a recently released survey of 850 homeowners across Massachusetts. (The MassINC Polling Group is part of the nonprofit civic organization MassINC that publishes CommonWealth Beacon.) It asked households about the benefits and challenges of homeownership. It also inquired about the programs they participated in to become homeowners in the first place. 
Let’s start with an important finding: For those who decided to buy a home, homeownership created significant benefits. Nearly all the Massachusetts homeowners surveyed expressed satisfaction with owning their home, and 72 percent said that it had helped build their financial resilience. For those who used state or local down payment assistance, the results were even stronger. Ninety-three percent of those households reported never facing foreclosure risk, compared to 81 percent for those without such help. Similarly, households who completed a first-time homebuyer course said they were better off across virtually every measure of financial and housing stability. 
These data validate what the public and private actors in the housing ecosystem have bet on: Decreasing the cost and financial barriers to home buying gives homeowners greater stability and opportunities to build wealth. 
Yet while Massachusetts has done a great deal to help residents buy homes, families are facing challenges in keeping them. Almost half of homeowners in the survey reported that it has been at least somewhat difficult to afford their housing costs over the past year. Nearly a third say they have had to skip or delay paying for food, utilities, or medical bills to cover their mortgage. And more than a third have deferred urgent home repairs. 
These numbers are not evenly distributed. Black homeowners face particularly acute stress: 48 percent have skipped basic needs and 47 percent have delayed urgent repairs. For households earning under $50,000, the foreclosure risk rate climbs to nearly 30%. Gateway City residents say they face compounding hardship across nearly every indicator. 
And then there is a looming intergenerational threat: Only 21 percent of homeowners have any legal arrangement—a will, trust, or life estate deed—for what happens to their home when they die. Among non-White homeowners, that figure drops to just 12 percent. The top barriers to these arrangements are the cost of legal fees (40 percent), not knowing where to start (37 percent), and lack of awareness about the process (32 percent). Without these protections, a lifetime of wealth wrapped up in home equity can evaporate in probate court, over contested claims or the forced sale of a property by a family that never meant to let it go. 
It is time for Massachusetts to build and scale infrastructure to ensure homebuyers can become long-term homeowners. 
We need to broaden access to programs that offer homeowners funding support to help them absorb economic shocks. The Homeowner Assistance Fund, the most recent and significant state intervention to prevent foreclosure, was a federally funded program born of the COVID-19 pandemic, but it ended in 2024. Other mortgage assistance and home repair assistance programs exist but are often subject to eligibility or geographic restrictions and carry long waitlists. Without the provision of these resources to communities across the Commonwealth, too many households remain one emergency expense away from falling behind on their mortgage.  
We also need to expand the availability of post-purchase counseling. While first time homebuyer classes focus on the home buying process, post-purchase education helps homeowners learn how to navigate maintenance needs, build savings, and avoid predatory lending. Only 33 percent of homeowners surveyed have taken these courses, with participation dropping sharply among older and lower-income owners who are often the most vulnerable. 
Lastly, we must develop accessible and affordable estate planning resources. Black and Latino homeowners—the very households for whom a home represents the largest share of total family wealth—are least likely to have legal protections in place. A promising pilot is underway: Boston College Law School’s Initiative on Land, Housing & Property Rights has partnered with the Massachusetts Affordable Homeownership Alliance and Harvard Law School’s clinical programs to offer estate planning services to MAHA homebuyers after closing. This is exactly the kind of innovation the field needs—and it remains, for now, a pilot that is serving a fraction of those who need it. 
The survey confirms what we already know: there is a significant gap between making a homeowner and sustaining one. In our Commonwealth, a foreclosure, an inherited property tied up in probate, or a home that crumbles because repairs were put off each threatens the ability of a household to preserve its homeownership and build generational wealth. The Commonwealth’s housing sector has gotten good at opening doors. It is time for us to invest as much in keeping them open. 
Courtney Brunson is director of Economic Equity Initiatives at the Boston Foundation and director of the Racial Wealth Gap Partnership, a broad-based coalition of more than 40 organizations convened by the Boston Foundation to close racial wealth gaps through expanded homeownership opportunities in Greater Boston and beyond.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: During Operation Metro Surge, ICE arrested dozens of immigrant crime victims
description: Years ago, Rosa watched from inside the car as men robbed her husband at gunpoint, shortly after they’d arrived in Minnesota from Guatemala. The couple had a pending asylum case, but once they reported the crime to the police, they were eligible for a U visa, which provides a path to legal permanent residency for […]
text:
ICE agents search the passenger of a truck as they arrest both him and the driver during a traffic stop on Feb. 11, 2026 in Robbinsdale, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Years ago, Rosa watched from inside the car as men robbed her husband at gunpoint, shortly after they’d arrived in Minnesota from Guatemala.
The couple had a pending asylum case, but once they reported the crime to the police, they were eligible for a U visa, which provides a path to legal permanent residency for victims of, and witnesses to, serious crimes — and, in some cases, their immediate family members. At her request, the Reformer is using Rosa’s first name to protect her from government retribution. 
Rosa’s family is among the 75 Minnesotans identified by the Reformer who were detained by immigration authorities during Operation Metro Surge, despite having permission to live and work in the United States because they were victims of a crime and reported it to the police. 
One man survived a shooting in 2019 that took him out of work for six months and left him permanently disabled. Another was stabbed in the leg during a 2016 robbery in Minneapolis. Others survived human trafficking, felony assaults and armed robberies. 
In one case, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents broke down a family’s front door and arrested all three people inside — without a warrant, according to the lawsuit.
The Reformer analyzed more than 1,100 habeas corpus petitions — federal lawsuits challenging a person’s detention — filed in Minnesota between December and mid-March and identified at least 75 people who were detained by immigration agencies despite having been granted work permits and deportation protections allowed to crime victims. That number is likely an undercount; Many immigrants did not have access to attorneys for long stretches; couldn’t afford legal fees; or were shipped out-of-state before their lawyers could file the lawsuit in Minnesota. 
In May, a federal judge ordered ICE to revert back to its previous policy of not arresting crime victims, temporarily, while a lawsuit works its way through the courts. 
Many of the crime victims who filed lawsuits over their detention won and returned to their families in Minnesota, and are now fighting the deportation proceedings initiated by their arrest. 
Trump has remade the immigration court system to support his mass deportation campaign, however, so even people who have been issued work permits and deportation protections face an uphill battle to stay in the U.S. 
ICE did not respond to the Reformer’s emailed questions for this story. 
The arrest of immigrant crime victims undercuts a public safety tool created by Congress to combat crime and strengthen relationships between immigrants and law enforcement agencies. The shift in policy, however, fulfills a longstanding Republican goal to roll back the protections provided to immigrants under the program.
When Congress formalized the U visa program as part of a renewal of the Violence Against Women Act of 2000, members of both political parties agreed on the need for a law protecting undocumented victims of crimes. The U visa is an expanded version of the T visa, which offers protections for undocumented victims of human trafficking. 
Congress created the U visa “out of recognition that victims without legal status may otherwise be reluctant to help in the investigation or prosecution of criminal activity,” according to Department of Homeland Security guidance. 
Public safety and policing experts say the U visa program helps local police officers build trust with undocumented communities by assuring crime victims that they won’t be deported for seeking help from the police — the same logic that underlies many local police departments’ separation from immigration authorities.
A masked ICE agent stands guard outside as ICE and other law enforcement agents raid Las Cuatro Milpas in Minneapolis, Minnesota Tuesday, June 3, 2025. The incident led to a strengthening of the separation ordinance between immigration authorities and Minneapolis Police. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
A bona fide determination
Rosa and her family applied for a U visa in 2023, which required a certification document from local police confirming that Rosa’s husband had reported the robbery and cooperated with investigators. 
But there was one major issue: Congress had capped the number of U visas issued per year at 10,000. The year Rosa’s family submitted their application, the backlog of applications surpassed 344,000, or a 34 year waitlist.
In 2021, the administration of President Joe Biden found a way to help people waiting for their visas. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services would review the pending applications — running criminal background checks and checking law enforcement certifications — and issue a “bona fide determination” to immigrants whose applications met the U visa criteria, but for whom there were no available visas. 
Two years after Rosa and her husband applied for the visa, and one month into President Donald Trump’s second term, they received a letter in the mail from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. 
“The evidence demonstrates that … they warrant a favorable exercise of discretion to receive employment authorization and deferred action,” the letter read, meaning work permits and protection from deportation while they waited for the full visa, which would provide a path to permanent residency. In the meantime, they needed to stay in the country; not commit any crimes; and attend regular check-ins with ICE.
Rosa walked into the Whipple Federal Building, the headquarters of ICE in Minnesota, on Jan. 23 with her husband, their six-year-old daughter and the paperwork they needed for a routine check-in. Friends had warned Rosa not to go to the meeting because many people never returned, but Rosa’s husband reassured her: “We have paperwork,” she remembers him saying.
After sitting in a waiting room for eight hours, Rosa said, three agents entered. They placed handcuffs on her husband, informed the family they would be separated, and whisked her husband out the door. 
Then, the agents ushered Rosa and her daughter in and out of hallways and holding cells, on and off airplanes. They spent the night on the floor of a room. Rosa had no idea where they were. Her daughter kept asking where her dad was. Neither of them could stop crying. 
The hallway to immigration court in the Henry Whipple Federal Building in Minneapolis Thursday, April 9, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Operation Metro Surge and beyond
Ten days after Trump assumed the presidency for the second time, the acting director of ICE issued a memo to all agency employees, reversing decades of policies that instructed agents not to detain immigrants with pending U visas. 
Shortly after, immigration authorities began arresting people around the country who had been granted work permits and deportation protections under the program. The Trump administration has similarly rolled back protections for refugees, asylum seekers and other categories of immigrants. 
By the time ICE agents swarmed Minnesota this winter, the agency was treating people with pending U visas as fair game for deportation. 
Marcos Lopez Garcia arrived in Minnesota from his rural Mexican town as a teenager. He dropped out of school at 13 to help with his family’s farm, and crossed the U.S. border in search of better job opportunities than in his rural community. He met his wife, also a teenager at the time, at their job cleaning Minneapolis hotel rooms. They settled in Bloomington and had four children, all citizens, the oldest now in her mid-20s. Lopez Garcia worked his way into a management position at a commercial cleaning company. 
At one of his cleaning jobs, a coworker repeatedly came onto him, asking him to leave his family for her. Each time he refused, she grew angrier, until she threatened to report him and his wife to immigration authorities. In June of 2022, she showed up at his home uninvited. 
He called the police to report the crimes. The Bloomington Police Department certified on his U visa application that he had been a victim of blackmail and extortion and that he was cooperative. 
ICE arrested him on his way to work on Jan. 26, shipped him to Texas and held him for two weeks before his lawyer won his release.
Kevin Ramirez Mancia hitchhiked from Honduras to Minnesota with his father when he was 13. They settled in Willmar, a city of 20,000 people, 100 miles west of the Twin Cities. 
Ramirez Mancia attended Willmar Senior High School while his father worked in a nearby egg factory. In November of his sophomore year, he was at his desk singing a song and waving his hands to the music. Another classmate thought Ramirez Mancia was making signs at him, and flipped him off. Ramirez Mancia kept singing. 
The classmate took a knife out of his backpack and walked towards Ramirez Mancia, the knife pointing towards his neck. 
“I thought he was going to stab me,” Ramirez Mancia said.
Photo courtesy of Kevin Ramirez Mancia.
He got the attention of the teacher, who confiscated the knife and called the principal, who notified the police. Ramirez Mancia told the officer what happened, and that evening, police arrested the student who had threatened Ramirez Mancia, according to the incident report. 
In 2023, Ramirez Mancia applied for a U visa based on his status of a victim of second-degree assault and threats of violence, and received his work permit and deferred action — protection from deportation.
On April 4, police pulled over Ramirez Mancia, now 20, and arrested him on suspicion of driving under the influence of cannabis and possessing a pistol without a permit, resulting in three misdemeanor charges. As he was waiting for his release paperwork, an ICE officer approached and informed him he was being taken into immigration custody. 
He spent exactly four months in Freeborn County Jail, which holds immigrants on behalf of ICE. On Tuesday a judge ordered his release; he will remain free while he appeals his deportation order.
A politicized program
Republican politicians have long criticized the U visa program, arguing that the list of qualifying crimes — blackmail, domestic violence, obstruction of justice and felonious assault among them — is too broad. In 2012, when the Violence Against Women Act was up for renewal, GOP members of Congress soured on the legislation in part because of its protections for immigrant crime victims. 
“(Violence Against Women Act) is meant to protect victims of violence. It shouldn’t be an avenue to expand immigration law or to give additional benefits to people here unlawfully,” Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican, said in a 2012 Judiciary Committee hearing before Congress ultimately renewed the law without major changes to the U visa provisions.
Project 2025, the roadmap for President Donald Trump’s second term, called for the total elimination of U and T visas.
White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller listens as U.S. President Donald Trump addresses the media during a news conference at his Mar-a-Lago club on January 03, 2026, in Palm Beach, Florida. Miller is the architect of Trump’s immigration policies. Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
“Victimization should not be a basis for an immigration benefit…. Pending elimination of the T and U visas, the Secretary should significantly restrict eligibility for each visa to prevent fraud,” the document reads. 
Richard Hodsdon, general counsel for the Minnesota Sheriff’s Association and a former prosecutor, said U visas “certainly can support public safety from a victim perspective.” 
They can also be used for “manipulation and abuse,” he added. 
Defense attorneys, Hodsdon, said, sometimes asked for U visas for their clients as part of a plea negotiation, seeking compensation for flipping on co-conspirators. 
A handful of high-profile fraud cases have bolstered Republicans’ argument. In 2023, the U.S. Department of Justice announced charges against multiple men accused of staging armed robberies at convenience stores to create pathways for U visas for the “victims.” The ringleaders in that case pleaded guilty, and in March, the feds charged 11 additional people for their participation in the plot. 
And, in June 2025, the DOJ charged five Louisiana men in an alleged scheme to falsify police reports for U visa applications. 
“(Those cases) are symptomatic of a bigger problem, which is that desperate people do desperate things, and if we had an immigration system that worked in an effective and efficient way, you wouldn’t have desperate people doing desperate things,” said Rekha Sharma-Crawford, a Kansas City-based attorney who serves on the executive committee of the American Immigration Lawyers Association. 
Residents walk through the South Texas Family Detention Center in Dilley, Texas, on April 29, 2015. (Photo by Charles Reed/U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)
In limbo
A coalition of California-based immigrants and activist organizations sued ICE in October over its treatment of people with pending U and T — trafficking — visas. 
“ICE now routinely detains and deports people who have valid grants of deferred action from USCIS in connection with pending U or T visa petitions,” according to the lawsuit. 
The Trump administration has found other ways to slow down the process of obtaining the visas or associated work permits: delaying confirmation of receipt of applications, prolonging processing times and nitpicking applications, according to the lawsuit and interviews with immigration attorneys. 
“USCIS is (starting) with the idea that we are going to deny the application, and then if they can overcome that and somehow convince you, then maybe we will think it over. That’s the attitude of the agency right now,” Sharma-Crawford said.
In May, a federal judge temporarily voided the 2025 ICE memo that permitted agents to detain crime victims with pending U and T visas. Since then, the arrest of such people has slowed, Sharma-Crawford said. 
“But that doesn’t mean that they won’t try and either disregard a court order or appeal it,” she added. 
For many families, the damage is already done. 
After their series of flights and holding cells, Rosa and her six-year-old daughter arrived at the processing center of the South Texas Family Detention Center in Dilley, Texas. They spent 26 days in detention before a judge ordered their release. 
Every member of her family is still terrified. They’ve relied on support from staff at her daughters’ school to make ends meet. Her daughter complains of her chest hurting — possibly from anxiety, Rosa said — and can’t sleep. 
“My daughter still hasn’t recovered from this,” Rosa said, her voice shaking. She hasn’t recovered, either.

name: Nevada Current
title: Potential conflicts of interest cloud Metro probe of Hope for Prisoners founder
description: Jon Ponder, a three-time convicted bank robber who was pardoned by President Donald Trump, is under investigation by the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department – a scenario that raises questions about potential conflicts of interest, given Metro’s partnership with Ponder’s non-profit, Hope for Prisoners.  The Nevada Current reported in May that Ponder was[...]
text:
Hope for Prisoners founder Jon Ponder (Hope For Prisoners publicity photo)Jon Ponder, a three-time convicted bank robber who was pardoned by President Donald Trump, is under investigation by the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department – a scenario that raises questions about potential conflicts of interest, given Metro’s partnership with Ponder’s non-profit, Hope for Prisoners. 
The Nevada Current reported in May that Ponder was banned from the Nevada Department of Corrections pending an investigation into misconduct. Hope for Prisoners, which receives state funding, provides reentry services to Nevada inmates. 
Metro Undersheriff Andrew Walsh and Assistant Sheriff Michael Gennaro serve on HFP’s board of directors. Metro Sheriff Kevin McMahill, served as a board member while undersheriff during Gov. Joe Lombardo’s tenure as sheriff. The non-profit is featured on Metro’s website as a community partner and holds its monthly graduation ceremonies at police headquarters.
NDOC denied the Current’s request for public records related to the investigation of Ponder, citing his right to a fair trial. The records requested, NDOC wrote on May 15, “are part of an ongoing investigation and release would jeopardize law enforcement information” that “may be introduced as evidence.” Releasing the documents, NDOC wrote, would “undermine the constitutional rights of a defendant to a fair trial.”
NDOC also declined to reveal the nature of Ponder’s alleged infraction. 
Ponder has not been charged with any crimes. He did not respond to requests for comment.
The Office of Inspector General, which is under NDOC, turned the investigation over to Metro. It will not say why it chose Metro over the Attorney General, given Metro’s relationship with Ponder. 
“Simply because there is a relationship doesn’t negate Metro’s ability to investigate,” says retired Metro Lt. Randy Sutton, a frequent media commentator on police matters. 
Sutton says there’s “some merit” to questioning why another agency “like the Attorney General’s office, didn’t take that investigation forward. But I’m not saying that there’s anything untoward in Metro conducting the investigation because they investigate people they have relationships with all the time.” 
Attorney General Aaron Ford, a Democrat who is challenging Lombardo in the gubernatorial race, did not respond to questions about the investigation. 
Sutton says there’s a “strong possibility” that Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson, given his relationship with Ponder, would present the case to a grand jury or turn it over to a special prosecutor or the Nevada Attorney General. Wolfson did not respond to requests for comment. 
“Here’s the thing,” Sutton added. “The state of Nevada has a relationship with Ponder, too.” 
The state, during Lombardo’s tenure, has expanded its program with HFP. 
Ponder has long been the subject of allegations of sexual misconduct. 
A motion to compel the production of documents in a 2024 lawsuit against Ponder and the nonprofit sought a “letter written by Kristina Wildeveld to the Board in September 2020 informing the Board of allegations of sexual misconduct with clients, mentors, and/or employees of the Company by Jon Ponder, CEO of the Company.”
The letter from Wildeveld was sent in 2020 to McMahill, who was undersheriff to Lombardo at the time, and to Wolfson at their government email addresses. 
Metro and the DA’s office, which also has a partnership with Ponder, denied the Current’s public records request for Wildeveld’s letter. The agencies maintain the correspondence was sent to the officials in their private capacity, and their release is not required under the state’s public records law.  
Lombardo did not respond to requests for comment. He has long refused to say whether he, as sheriff, investigated the allegations against Ponder. 
Ponder was briefly suspended in 2020, however, the board, aware that Trump intended to expand Hope for Prisoners nationwide if re-elected, backed down after the pardon, according to a former HFP board member granted anonymity by the Current in order to share confidential information.
In June, Ponder’s wife, Jamie, filed for divorce in Clark County Family Court. On Monday, she requested a voluntary dismissal of the proceedings. She did not respond to the Current’s requests for comment. 
Ponder, who was previously listed on the Hope for Prisoner’s website as its CEO and founder is now listed only as its founder. The names of the nonprofit’s board of directors have been removed, as well.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Bloomberg gives $1.25M to Missouri abortion rights campaign as fundraising gap grows
description: The campaign opposing a November ballot measure that would reinstate Missouri’s abortion ban has raised more than $6.5 million — including a recent $1.25 million donation from former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg. Stop the Ban, formed last year to oppose Amendment 3 on November’s ballot, reported the Bloomberg donation Wednesday to the Missouri […]
text:
A campaign called Stop the Ban is focused on defeating a proposed amendment that would again ban nearly all abortions in Missouri. It will appear on the November 2026 ballot as Amendment 3 (photo submitted).The campaign opposing a November ballot measure that would reinstate Missouri’s abortion ban has raised more than $6.5 million — including a recent $1.25 million donation from former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg.
Stop the Ban, formed last year to oppose Amendment 3 on November’s ballot, reported the Bloomberg donation Wednesday to the Missouri Ethics Commission. Bloomberg also donated $1 million in 2024 to Missourians for Constitutional Freedom, the campaign that successfully placed an abortion rights amendment on the ballot and helped win its passage.
The leading political action committee on the other side, Her Health, Her Future PAC, has raised just over $1 million as of this week. The group is backed by Gov. Mike Kehoe and Missouri First Lady Claudia Kehoe, who serves as the PAC’s treasurer.
In November, Missourians will again be asked to decide on the fate of abortion rights. This time, lawmakers are asking voters to repeal the reproductive rights amendment approved in 2024 and reinstate a near-total ban on abortion.
The proposal, drafted and placed on the ballot by lawmakers in 2025, would ban abortions with exceptions for medical emergencies and pregnancies resulting from rape or incest during the first 12 weeks. It would also put a ban on gender-affirming care for minors into the state constitution.
That care is already prohibited under state law. In January, the Missouri Supreme Court upheld the law barring minors from receiving gender transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and puberty blockers, as well as a prohibition on Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming care for patients of all ages.
Other top donors to Stop the Ban include the members of the PAC’s coalition, including the ACLU of Missouri, the Fairness Project, Planned Parenthood Great Plains Votes, Planned Parenthood Great Rivers Action, Abortion Action Missouri, PROMO and Beacon Reproductive Health Network.
Missouri Right to Life PAC is also working to pass the new abortion restrictions. As of Tuesday, the group spent about $230,000 on the campaign, including yard signs, speaking engagements, and “Make Missouri Pro-Life Again” brochures, according to the latest finance reports. 
Missourians getting abortion pills by mail from out-of-state providers quadrupled since 2023

With Tuesday’s primary over, spending by both sides is expected to accelerate as the Nov. 3 election approaches.
In November 2024, with a near-total abortion ban in place, Missourians voted to amend the state constitution to guarantee the right to reproductive health care, including abortion up to the point of fetal viability. 
The campaign was expensive and the results were close, with about 52% of Missourians voting in favor of the amendment. Missourians for Constitutional Freedom, whose coalition included many of the same organizations behind Stop the Ban, raised more than $31.5 million in 2024. 
At the same time, a patchwork of half a dozen PACs trying to defeat the 2024 abortion rights amendment raised about $5 million. The largest single contribution was $1 million from a group tied to conservative activist Leonard Leo.
A lengthy court battle followed the 2024 election as Planned Parenthood and the ACLU of Missouri challenged dozens of abortion regulations still in state law that prevented providers from immediately offering abortion services again. 
In June, after about 18 months of litigation, a Jackson County judge overturned nearly all the challenged regulations on abortion providers. 
Planned Parenthood clinics in Kansas City, Columbia and St. Louis have been offering procedural abortion appointments since last year. Those clinics, along with clinics in Gladstone and Springfield, also began offering medication abortions following the court decision in June.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Rutgers dental school program brings free preventive care to classrooms
description: Rutgers' dental school now provides free dental sealants to children in low-income school districts, part of an effort to expand preventative care.
text:
A young patient at a Rutgers dental clinic in Newark during the Give Kids a Smile event, one of several programs the school runs to promote oral health in low-income communities. (Photo courtesy of Rutgers School of Dental Medicine.)It started in a classroom at Hillcrest Elementary School in Franklin Township with a team from Rutgers School of Dental Medicine armed with portable dental equipment, oral health props, and plenty of new toothbrushes.
Over multiple days starting in February, the Rutgers team visited all seven elementary schools in the Somerset County district, conducting cursory check-ups and applying dental sealants – plastic coatings that significantly reduce the chance of decay – to some 200 students who had signed up. About 2,000 kids took home oral-health goody bags.
The Rutgers program launched to provide these preventative oral health services for free to low-income schools throughout the state. The team is now planning visits in the fall to schools in Buena in Atlantic County, according to Dr. Mary Beth Giacona, a pediatric dentist and associate professor at Rutgers, who spearheaded the program and is eager to expand its reach.
“A lot of people put a lot of effort into making this happen and I think it’s going to be one of those true snowball situations where that first little gleam – that first little starter snowball, that took so much time and effort – then just kind of builds as it rolls along under its own momentum,” Giacona told the New Jersey Monitor.
Providing dental sealants in schools is nothing new, Giacona said, but she felt strongly that as New Jersey’s only dental school, Rutgers should be involved in this work. A 2012 report from the nonprofit Pew Research Center gave New Jersey an F for its lack of preventative pediatric dental programs, noting that between one-fourth and one-half of schools with the poorest students had access to sealants.
Sealants prevent decay by filling the crevices in the permanent molars where tartar and bacteria easily collect, Giacona said, areas that are the origin for 90% of all tooth decay. Children who are Black, Hispanic, or from low-income families are more likely to have decay, she added.
Giacona said failing to protect these permanent teeth, which emerge around age 6, is “almost a guarantee” that tooth decay will follow, “because the risk is so high for unsealed molars.”
New Jersey also has one of the nation’s lowest levels of fluoridated water, with roughly 16% of its water infused with the mineral that helps prevent tooth decay, versus the 72% average nationwide.
A 2025 report from the nonprofit New Jersey Health Care Quality Institute notes more than one-third of all third graders in New Jersey had untreated dental disease, compared to one-fifth nationwide, and on any given day 15% of Garden State kids this age had urgent oral health needs. The report was based on data collected by the Department of Health in 2023 as part of its work to create the state’s five-year oral health plan, following the 2019 hire of New Jersey’s first statewide dental director in decades.
Giacona said the state has supported the program and recently provided funding, a total of $55,000 in two grants it received early this year. She also credited Nashon Hornsby, the health department’s assistant commissioner of health promotion, as an “oral health champion” in Trenton.
Hornsby said the state is proud to support a program like this, which advances health equity and gives kids a chance to thrive on multiple levels.
“Oral health is not just about teeth; it’s about supporting overall health. When preventive oral health services are available in schools, families face fewer barriers to care, children receive services before small problems become bigger ones, and we can prevent dental disease before it starts, leading to improved health, lower absenteeism, and better learning outcomes,” Hornsby told the New Jersey Monitor by email.
The Rutgers dental school sealant program does not replace regular dental check-ups with X-rays that provide a fuller picture of potential decay, Giacona stressed. But she also knows that accessing care can be a challenge for busy families, even if they do have insurance.
Medicaid, the publicly funded insurance plan that covers 40% of New Jersey children, includes preventative dental benefits, but the Quality Institute report documented how it can be hard to find pediatric dentists who accept the plan.
In their classroom visits, the Rutgers team conducts a visual check of students’ teeth to fill out a “report card” that includes three checkboxes: no obvious problems, some obvious problems, and urgent needs. They also try to identify if the child has a dentist they see regularly and will try and connect them with services if needed, including at the college’s dental clinic in Newark, which welcomes Medicaid patients.
Students from the Crossroads School in Westfield, a Union County program for kids with autism, have been coming to the Rutgers clinic for several years, Giacona said. Her team is now working to include Crossroads in the school-based sealant program, along with the Douglas Development Disability Center, a similar school run by Rutgers in East Brunswick. Several charter schools in Newark are also interested in the sealant program, she said.
Rutgers dental students will also be visiting back-to-school events later this month in Buena and Franklin, Giacona said, to answer questions about the program and sign families up to participate. Securing the registration and consent forms from parents, and legal agreements with schools, takes significant time and effort, she said.
“That’s really the most labor-intensive part,” she said, adding, “We can’t just show up and pull kids out of classrooms.”


Giacona said the state funding will allow the team to expand the program further by purchasing a second portable dental chair, laptops, and other equipment. Rutgers covers the dentists’ salaries and some of the overhead and the team can bill Medicaid for students covered by the plan.
“I think the driving force behind those of us who want to do public health outreach, especially for the pediatric population, is that (tooth decay) is highly preventable, yet timing is everything,” Giacona said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Educators face off in GOP race for Oklahoma superintendent
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — The Republican nomination for Oklahoma state superintendent will go to one of two longtime educators — either an experienced school administrator who decries political partisanship or a high school teacher and Christian minister who says his insight from the classroom could benefit schools statewide. Robert Franklin and James Taylor advanced[...]
text:
James Taylor, left, and Robert Franklin, right, are seeking the Republican nomination for state superintendent in an Aug. 25 runoff election. (Provided photos)OKLAHOMA CITY — The Republican nomination for Oklahoma state superintendent will go to one of two longtime educators — either an experienced school administrator who decries political partisanship or a high school teacher and Christian minister who says his insight from the classroom could benefit schools statewide.
Robert Franklin and James Taylor advanced to the Aug. 25 runoff election as the top two vote earners from a crowded GOP primary. The winner will face Democrat Jennettie Marshall in the Nov. 3 General Election.
State superintendent, considered Oklahoma’s chief of public schools, leads the state Department of Education and the state Board of Education.
Franklin, an inductee in the Oklahoma Educators Hall of Fame, has promised to lean on his decades of experience in school and CareerTech administration, rather than party politics, if elected to the post. 
Taylor, an 18-year teacher and a pastor, has attracted comparisons to Oklahoma’s far-right-wing former state Superintendent Ryan Walters, but he insists he would bring a different leadership style, one more focused on children’s academic needs.
Both candidates said Oklahoma’s bottom-tier ranking in reading and math scores must improve.
Franklin, 66, of Sand Springs, said the state needs to attract more properly trained teachers to accomplish an academic turnaround.
Robert Franklin files to run as a Republican candidate for state superintendent on April 1 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
He pledged to collaborate with tribal nations, higher education institutions, state lawmakers and other stakeholders to tackle Oklahoma’s yearslong teacher shortage and to provide effective training in the science of reading.
He said the state also could redesign instruction and elective options in middle schools to expose students to job skills at a younger age, better preparing them for the future workforce.
Improving students’ academic outcomes, Franklin said, will take a “relentless effort.”
“It won’t be what we do on day one,” he said. “It’ll be what we do daily to get us to that place, and that means lots of helpful, thoughtful, seasoned, experienced teachers and reading specialists and job coaches, or what you consider to be instructional coaches, to work with our teachers so that we can begin to really put good practices to work.”
Taylor, 67, of Oklahoma City, said he would carry out new legislative mandates with fidelity by incorporating more reading specialists and phonics-based instruction. 
This year, the state Legislature required more comprehensive interventions for struggling readers, including a repeat of third grade for children who score below a basic literacy level.
“We are going to make sure that is going to be a successful program,” Taylor said.
James Taylor, a Republican candidate for state superintendent, sits in the sanctuary of First Christ’s Church of Norman on July 24. Taylor, a teacher and pastor, founded the church in 2013. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Both candidates point to behavioral disruptions in the classroom as another top issue facing public schools today. Their solutions to the problem differ. 
Franklin suggested bringing more behavioral health specialists and counselors into schools to assist teachers. 
Taylor said classroom discipline is a strength of his. His idea is to “reproduce myself” through technology, like an informational video, to explain how to handle behavioral issues.
He said his priority is that “our teachers are secure and safe in their classroom” and that students learn to read and do math.
Taylor also promoted on the campaign trail a controversial cost-saving plan to consolidate district superintendent positions from 500 to 100, but he told Oklahoma Voice the idea is now “off the table.” He said he prefers to focus instead on academic outcomes, teacher support and parent empowerment.
Both candidates face criticism as they step into spotlight
After surging to the front of the GOP primary field, Franklin has faced questions over his Republican credentials. He said he was a registered Democrat from 1978 until a few years ago.
Franklin said he changed his party affiliation after the 2022 elections, when key statewide races were effectively decided in the GOP primaries. The Democratic Party also had shifted “to a more liberal agenda that I didn’t align with,” he said.
“I think agendas have become really hardened, and I don’t see hardened positions, no matter what spectrum you’re on, as a really effective way of trying to do the school work,” Franklin said. “This particular position (of state superintendent) probably calls for the least amount of political ideation in that role.”
Taylor, who has called himself the race’s most conservative candidate, has received criticism over his qualifications for office because of his lack of experience in school administration. He said he is confident he is qualified to lead the large Education Department because he has administrative experience in churches.
If elected, Taylor pledged to surround himself with staff members who are strong in areas where he is weak. 
The fact that he chose to hire a former employee of Walters’ administration as his campaign communications director also has generated scrutiny. Taylor has since said in public appearances that the employee has been removed from that position.
Taylor told Oklahoma Voice that Walters isn’t someone he aims to emulate. He said he has a calmer temperament than the former state superintendent, whom he criticized for resorting to “name calling.”
“I don’t distance myself from him, and I don’t embrace him,” Taylor said of Walters. “He’s who he is, and he was who he was. That’s not me. I don’t make comparisons. That’s what other people do, is they make comparisons. I don’t make comparisons between he and I.”
Walters resigned in September to lead a nonprofit with more than a year left in his superintendent term. He did not file to run for any political office this year. 
Church-state separation a key focus in superintendent race
Taylor, the pastor of First Christ’s Church of Norman, said he wouldn’t repeat Walters’ push to place a Bible in every Oklahoma public school classroom, though he has been supportive of Walters’ pro-Bible social studies standards.
Walters attempted to mandate that all districts teach Bible stories to contextualize the religious beliefs of important figures in American history. 
State Superintendent Ryan Walters speaks during a meeting of the Oklahoma State Board of Education on Sept. 25 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Taylor agreed the country’s “foundation was on a Christian heritage,” but he said teachers don’t need to be required to have a copy of the Bible. State law already allows educators and students to bring their religious texts to school, if they wish.
“I think that you don’t have to have a Bible in the classroom,” he said. “I teach early U.S. history, and early U.S. history is about the Judeo-Christian heritage of our foundation of our country.”
Meanwhile, church-state separation has become a major talking point for Franklin. 
While leading the Statewide Virtual Charter School Board, he voted against opening a state-funded religious charter school. The Oklahoma Supreme Court later struck down the school’s concept, deeming it a violation of the state Constitution. The U.S. Supreme Court deadlocked 4-4 on the case, which upheld the state-level ruling.
A second attempt to open a religious charter school in Oklahoma has prompted a federal court case.
Franklin, a member of Life.Church in Jenks, said his Christian faith is a “very important” part of his life, but teaching religious beliefs is the job of faith leaders and families, not public schools. 
“There’s a lot of different faiths that are practiced in our schools, and I just think it’s far too slippery of a slope to simply say that this one particular faith is valued and supported by tax dollars more so than this one,” he said. “I don’t think our country was designed that way.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland reinvented how it pays hospitals. Primary care was left underfunded
description: Maryland's global payment system for hospitals took the financial incentive out of filling beds, writes Alexander Kaysin, but the state neglected the other half of the equation -- it hasn't built the primary care infrastructure that payment reform aimed to make possible.
text:
Maryland's global payment system for hospitals took the financial incentive out of filling beds, writes Alexander Kaysin, but the state neglected the other half of the equation -- it hasn't built the primary care infrastructure that payment reform aimed to make possible. (Photo by a href="https://stock.adobe.com/contributor/202762547/s-l?load_type=author&prev_url=detail"> s_l/Stock.adobe.com).Ask almost anyone in Maryland how long it takes to get a new primary care appointment, and you’ll hear the same answer. Months, if you can find a doctor taking patients at all. That’s a strange thing to be true in a state the rest of the country studies as a model for controlling health care costs.
Maryland really is different. Since 2014, our hospitals have been paid under global budgets, a fixed amount of revenue set each year by the Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) instead of a fee for every admission and test. The idea is elegant. If a hospital no longer profits from filling beds, it has reason to keep people healthy and out of the hospital in the first place.
By several measures it worked. Maryland holds down hospital spending, keeps employer premiums comparatively low and posts solid numbers on preventable admissions and emergency room visits. In the Commonwealth Fund’s 2025 scorecard, the state ranks seventh in overall health system performance.
This isn’t a story about failure. It’s a story about something we left half-finished.
Global budgets changed how hospitals get paid. They didn’t build the primary care system the whole design depends on. You can’t keep people out of the hospital without somewhere for them to go instead. That somewhere is primary care, and family medicine in particular, because they are far more likely to practice the kind of broad outpatient care that provides access to the whole family and keeps communities well.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Look at where the doctors come from, and the gap is hard to miss. Maryland trained 28 new family medicine residents in 2014; in 2024, it trained 27. During those same years, Virginia and Pennsylvania substantially grew their training pipelines, including new programs aimed at rural and underserved communities. Maryland rebuilt the way we pay for hospital care and never made the matching investment in the people who deliver care everywhere else.
The state’s own data tells the rest of the story. Maryland’s most recent primary care investment analysis found that primary care spending didn’t rise between 2021 and 2023. It fell for some Medicare populations and stayed flat for others. The analysis flagged a cluster of ZIP codes, concentrated in Baltimore City and parts of western and southeastern Maryland, where the most disadvantaged neighborhoods get less primary care investment.
Global budgets may not have caused this shortfall, but they didn’t help. Residency growth depends on federal Medicare funding caps, faculty, training sites and choices made by medical school leaders. The payment model, on its own, didn’t push hospitals to build family medicine capacity.
A global budget rewards a hospital for cutting avoidable admissions this year. A new residency or a community clinic takes years to pay off, and the savings leak out across other hospitals, other insurers, and the state’s overall cost calculation. For a safety-net hospital in a low-income community with little spare capital, the math rarely closes. The hospital gets told to reduce preventable hospital use while leaning on an insufficient workforce and a limited number of underfunded clinics.
On Jan. 1, Maryland moved from its Total Cost of Care model into the new federal AHEAD model. For the first time, the state has committed to setting annual primary care investment targets, beginning in 2027. It is an admission that the old model underdelivered on exactly this.
Public reporting alone won’t change a hospital’s spending. The state should tie targets to actual financing, and weight the money toward underserved communities, rather than letting a rising statewide average cover up local gaps.
It should set a specific goal for new family medicine residency positions, and protect that funding from the annual pressure to show a one-year drop in admissions, because training a family physician takes longer than a budget cycle.
It should give community health centers and independent practices a defined way to share in the savings their work creates under a hospital’s global budget. And it should measure what actually matters to a patient, which isn’t dollars spent but whether you can get an appointment, keep the same doctor, and find one in your ZIP code.
Maryland embarked on a bold experiment to reduce hospital spending, and it worked. We haven’t yet built the primary care infrastructure that payment reform was supposed to make possible.
As AHEAD takes shape, Maryland will need to decide whether to finish the job. For the Marylander still calling around for a doctor who will see them, that decision isn’t abstract. It’s the difference between a system that looks good on a national scorecard and one they can actually feel is working.

name: WyoFile
title: Proposed changes to federal oil and gas provisions are bad for public land, private property owners and democracy
authors: Shelly Fyant, Don Schreiber and Kim Pexton
description:
But it's not too late, write guest columnists Shelly Fyant, Don Schreiber and Kim Pexton. The Bureau of Land Management is taking public comment on the proposed revisions till Aug. 24.
The post Proposed changes to federal oil and gas provisions are bad for public land, private property owners and democracy appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
As leaders and advocates, we know that public participation is essential to transparent decision-making, and it’s what builds trust. Public process — especially when it comes to decisions affecting our public lands and property rights — is not bureaucracy for its own sake, but something that helps catch mistakes, improves terms in lease agreements, protects water supplies and cultural sites, and avoids conflict. 

Opinion

Under newly proposed revisions to the federal onshore oil and gas program, the Bureau of Land Management intends to hollow out this process, defying the centuries-old values that make our government one of, by and for the people.
To start with the most shocking example, BLM would no longer be required to notify landowners of plans to offer natural resources beneath their land for development. The agency manages some 57 million acres of these “split estate” lands, which means a private landowner holds the rights to the surface property while BLM controls the minerals beneath it.
The notification process has always been imperfect, but under current rules, landowners can generally see what’s coming and receive notice at the leasing stage, when they can still protest the sale, ask questions and potentially negotiate surface protections. With notification requirements gone, the first a surface owner may hear about a project could be much later in the process, maybe even when a company is already applying for a permit or when a survey crew shows up. In our states — Montana, New Mexico and Wyoming, which have the most split estate acreage in the country — that is unacceptable. 
The proposal also significantly shortens the overall comment and protest period, despite the fact that agency director Steve Pearce recently said “a lot of public input” is the answer to balancing the many uses of BLM lands. Currently, the public has 90 days total to weigh in on a proposed lease sale: a 30-day scoping period, a 30-day comment period on the environmental review and a 30-day protest window once a sale is announced. BLM’s proposal eliminates the first two and cuts the third to just 10 days, while adding a new processing fee of $1 per page for protest filings over 50 pages.
Sidestepping landowner notification, combined with fewer and shortened comment windows, means drastically fewer opportunities to raise concerns before decisions are locked in. These are not just procedural adjustments; they’re silencing mechanisms that degrade public trust and government accountability.  
This loss of accountability also shows up in how the proposal treats cleanup, forcing liability onto taxpayers by slashing minimum bonding rates, or the amount an operator must set aside for cleanup once a well’s productive life ends. Even though reclaiming a single well can cost tens of thousands of dollars or more, the proposed rule would reduce bonding requirements to levels set as far back as the 1950s.  
It is fundamentally un-American to undermine basic property rights, reduce public comment periods to mere days, hand corporate responsibility off to taxpayers and impose fees on using your voice. If this rule is finalized, it will cost us not just access to and protections for our lands, but a vital stone in the foundation of our democracy. 
The concept of public process is as old as this country’s founding and was codified in 1946 under the Administrative Procedure Act, giving the public a formalized say in government decisions that affect and directly shape our communities. It makes sense that this idea would and should apply to the agency that oversees 245 million acres of surface land and 700 million acres of subsurface mineral estate — more than any other federal government entity. 
In the American West, one of the most powerful means of democratic participation is weighing in on decisions that affect the lands where we live, work and recreate. BLM’s proposed rule is a chance to defend our democratic rights by exercising them, and the agency is legally required to respond to public comments during its planning and rulemaking processes. For those who care about our shared land, the right to protect private property, and a participatory democracy, you can ask your local or tribal government to pass a resolution, contact your Congress members, and share your concerns before BLM’s comment period ends Aug. 24.

name: WyoFile
title: Massive Pacific Northwest fires pump smoke into Wyoming
description:
With hot and dry weather in the forecast, hazy skies and potential for health advisories are likely to linger. 
The post Massive Pacific Northwest fires pump smoke into Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
When meteorologist Adam Dziewaltowski drove to work around sunrise, he could see the telltale sign on the horizon.
“I kind of describe it as a highlighter orange,” he said Thursday of the vivid display. 
As smoke rolls into Wyoming, the ashy air puts on a show of burnt orange sunrises and salmon-colored sunsets. While pretty for a picture, dawn and dusk can be some of the worst times for air quality as the ashy air sinks with cooling temperatures.
Cool temperatures are what caused smoky air to blanket Wyoming this week, said Dziewaltowski, a National Weather Service meteorologist based in Riverton.
Wildfires burning across the Pacific Northwest — destroying more than 800 buildings around Spokane, Washington, and creating some of the worst air quality in the world in Portland, Oregon — are putting up a steady supply of soot-filled air. 
“The majority of the smoke is coming from Washington and Oregon,” Dziewaltowski said. Satellite images show the feathery plumes drifting across the state. “Everything’s kind of being funneled across the north of us and then kind of swooping back in.” 
Then a cold front moved through Wyoming on Monday, he said. “As that cold front came through, the smoke behind it sunk down into the basins.” 
The mountains surrounding the basins act like a bowl, holding the smoke in place. “It will just kind of stagnate and stay there,” he said. “So that’s what’s kind of happened the whole week.”
Wildfire smoke obscures the view of Casper Mountain from the north end of the city on Aug. 3, 2026. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
In northwestern Wyoming, smoke crept into the Tetons by early Sunday morning, prompting residents to shut windows and start recirculating indoor air. In addition to bigger fires burning across the Pacific Northwest, the Big Rock Fire, discovered July 31 in eastern Idaho, has consumed more than 2,000 acres and forced the temporary closure of Heise Hot Springs resort, about an hour’s drive west of Victor, Idaho.
Wildfire also forced the weekend closure of Devils Tower National Monument in eastern Wyoming. After the Left Creek Fire flared up Saturday morning about a mile from the monument, the park ordered visitors and employees to evacuate, the Gillette News Record reported. On Sunday afternoon, a second fire, the Newton Fire, started less than 3 miles southeast of Devils Tower. But crews got the fires under control, and Devils Tower reopened Monday.
On Tuesday, firefighters on the other side of the state began battling a new fire burning on the Bridger-Teton National Forest, Bureau of Land Management land and private property in Sublette County. The Bare Fire has grown to about 800 acres, torching in heavy timber northwest of Big Piney. The fire’s cause is undetermined. People can track air quality related to the Bare Fire and get smoke outlook reports for the Pacific Northwest on the federal government’s AirNow fire and smoke map. 
The public also can see near real-time monitoring for Wyoming at wyvisnet.com, which is maintained by the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality’s Air Quality Division. The division issued an air quality alert for Wednesday and Thursday. The alert recommended older adults, young children and people with respiratory problems minimize outdoor activities, including exercise. The Wyoming Department of Health also advises everyone to avoid prolonged exposure to poor air quality, the alert said.
Smoke can be tricky to forecast because it depends on how the fires behave, and air quality can fluctuate, Dziewaltowski said. But based on what he can forecast — it’s looking like a rerun of July’s hot and dry weather — hazy skies are likely to persist through the weekend.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming shows that small libraries can do big things
description:
Guest columnist Marion Yoder celebrates a big national award for Ten Sleep's tiny library. 
The post Wyoming shows that small libraries can do big things appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Karen Funk, director of the Washakie County Library and its tiny Ten Sleep branch, lives by the credo that being small is no deterrent to doing something big. The Ten Sleep library, which serves a town of 226 people, was recently recognized as exceptional by the Institute of Museum and Library Services. 

Opinion

For 30 years, that federal agency has been rewarding particularly notable museums and libraries for their efforts, giving them medals and substantial checks to support continued good work. On July 21, 2026, Ms. Funk’s library and four others from across the country were presented with  $10,000 checks and awards at the George Washington Masonic National Memorial in Alexandria, Virginia, near Washington, D.C.
Other 2025 winners include public libraries serving Haines Borough, Alaska, Brockway, Pennsylvania, Waxahachie, Texas and Terrabonne, Louisiana. Of these small places, Ten Sleep is by far the smallest.
Quite a feat for such a small library to be singled out for such recognition. The United States is home to nearly 125,000 libraries, according to the National Library Association. Of these, some 98,500 are school libraries and about 17,600 are public libraries, including bookmobiles. 
The Institute of Museum and Library Services’ mission has long been to advance, support and empower America’s museums, libraries and related organizations. In 2024, the institute awarded $266.7 million via grantmaking, research and policy development. 
Beginning in April, 2025, however, the institute began issuing grant cancellation notices citing changing agency priorities. Nonetheless, the 2025 awards were issued and Wyoming’s Ms. Funk and her colleagues were there to receive theirs. 
The Ten Sleep branch library is unique, too, for simultaneously serving as both a public and a school library. It also hosts many tourists, including rock climbers, seeking high-speed internet access during the summer. The Ten Sleep branch previously distinguished itself among Wyoming libraries by suggesting an idea — that the Wyoming State Library provide databases making it possible for students and adults alike to look up information about the 19 prisoner of war camps maintained in Wyoming during World War II. The suggestion has since become a reality.  
Washakie County Library Director Karen Funk has been saying for years that small libraries can do big things. The Institute of Museum and Library Services award validates that statement. She says her team in Ten Sleep has “consistently tried to give some large library experiences in a small rural town setting” and, along the way, provided good customer experience with small-town hospitality. “I think that’s what stands out about us.”
To get an idea of just how important the Ten Sleep branch library is to the community, a quick glance at its Facebook page says a lot. This summer, the library is all over celebrating America’s 250th birthday. Look, too, at the Ten Sleep page maintained by the Washakie County Library system to see the wide array of services and activities on offer. 
Many people remember growing up around a Carnegie library, one of hundreds funded by industrial philanthropist Andrew Carnegie over 100 years ago. Washakie County’s is not among them. It came about as a matter of state law, now codified at WY Stat § 18-7-101, et seq. Wyoming statute has long required that each county levy a tax to support a public library. 
Cheyenne’s is the oldest, having been established in 1886, before statehood in 1890. Laramie County holds the distinction of having the oldest continually operating county library system in the United States. Cheyenne citizens spent five years raising funds before the first library opened.
Andrew Carnegie donated the whopping sum of $50,000 to open Laramie County’s first dedicated library building in 1902. It was the first Carnegie library built in Wyoming. Nationwide, Carnegie fostered over 1,600 libraries. 
For anyone who grew up making regular trips to the public library and respecting librarians, it comes as no surprise that people love their libraries. They do, but that has never meant that it is “easy” to be a library worker. Book banning and other censorship attempts have made lives difficult for library workers since at least the McCarthy era of the 1950s. 
In recent years, “LGBTQ-friendly” library programs and materials have attracted public attention and, sometimes, attack. Former Campbell County Librarian Terri Lesley’s successful civil rights case for her dismissal is but one ignominious example. The American Library Association tracks book banning efforts around the country and reported that 2024 and 2025 saw big surges. Each year, more than 4,000 unique book titles are challenged across the country. 
Recognizing the need for mutual professional support and the potential for isolation among rural librarians, the Association for Rural and Small Libraries got its start back in 1982. It aims to “build strong communities through advocacy, professional development and elevating the impact of rural and small libraries.” It seeks to be the voice of libraries that serve communities of 25,000 or less.
The Association for Rural and Small Libraries’ annual conference this September will showcase Amanda Jones, a small-town Louisiana school librarian who fought book banning at her school and got death threats in return. She wrote That Librarian and continues with her anti-censorship work today. 
Teton County Library Director Kip Roberson has long been active with the association, and has worked in small libraries around the country. He is happy to live now in Jackson, a place he calls an “extremely library positive” community, and to work with a library board he describes as “fantastic.” Roberson has been in the library business since 1989. In July, he marked five years as director of the Teton County Library. With a staff of 43, the main library is open seven days a week in winter and six in summer. 
Roberson serves as the Association for Rural and Small Libraries’ representative for the West region, which includes Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, Nevada, California, Oregon, Washington, Alaska and Hawaii. 
Roberson’s library is not experiencing book banning efforts, but during quarterly Zoom calls with library workers in his region, he hears about it happening elsewhere.
Roberson’s county library board is so opposed to censorship that it successfully opposed a book-ban bill in the Wyoming Legislature this year and, in May, went on record opposing a similar federal effort, House Resolution 7661. A story about The Teton County Library Board’s action and the importance of speaking out even appeared in Book Riot, an independent literary website. 
Outstanding library workers love the places they live and the communities they serve. It’s a good thing they do, because they’re not in it for the money. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the median pay for librarians and library media specialists in 2024 was about $31 an hour, or $64,320 annually. The typical entry-level education requirement is a master’s degree. Compare that to the median U.S. household income of $83,730 in 2024 as reported by the Census Bureau. Then, consider thanking a library worker for what they do every day for the public they serve.
One wonders what America would look like, or how it would function, in the absence of public libraries and the people who make them work so well. As the American Library Association says of library workers, “Libraries work because we do.” 
National Library Week is an annual tradition that began in the 1950s when reading was declining as the use of radio and TV grew. This year, National Library Workers Day was April 21. That day recognizes the critical role all library workers play in providing education, lifelong learning and community engagement. Who among us does not want and need all of those things now and in the future?

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Just after statehood in 1876, two gamblers’ deaths evoked Colorado’s Wild West history
description: The shooting deaths of two different gamblers made headlines in the brand-new state of Colorado in early August 1876, though only one would still be the stuff of legend 150 years later. James Butler “Wild Bill” Hickok was killed in the boomtown of Deadwood in the Dakota Territory on Aug. 2, though it was more […]
text:
An 1874 photograph shows J.B. "Wild Bill" Hickok, second from left, alongside other famous frontier figures, including William "Buffalo Bill" Cody, center. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, Z-6084)The shooting deaths of two different gamblers made headlines in the brand-new state of Colorado in early August 1876, though only one would still be the stuff of legend 150 years later.



← July 30–Aug. 5
Aug. 6–12 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

James Butler “Wild Bill” Hickok was killed in the boomtown of Deadwood in the Dakota Territory on Aug. 2, though it was more than a week before the first reports of his death were published in the Rocky Mountain News.
“Everybody in this country has heard of ‘Wild Bill,’ a noted scout, buffalo-hunter, and plainsman, and who on account of his reckless bravery was made marshal at different times of several frontier towns when it was necessary, because of the lawlessness that prevailed in their early settlement, to have peace officers who would kill in order to uphold their authority,” wrote the News.
Earlier in 1876, Hickok, then living in Cheyenne, had joined up with his friend Charles “Colorado Charlie” Utter, as he led a wagon train from Georgetown, Colorado, to the Black Hills. They were among the thousands of residents of Colorado and neighboring territories who flocked to the Dakota Territory during the gold rush there.
The Wild Bill legend had its origins in an 1867 Harper’s magazine article, which wildly exaggerated his history as a frontier gunslinger, claiming that Hickock “with his own hands has killed hundreds of men.” (At the time of his death, newspapers reported the figure at 36.) A more grounded portrayal of Hickok, and dramatization of his death, would come nearly 130 years later in HBO’s “Deadwood” TV series.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The News lumped Hickok in with other larger-than-life characters already famous throughout the West, like John “Texas Jack” Omohundro and William Frederick “Buffalo Bill” Cody, who would remain a popular local figure until his death in Denver in 1917.
Days after Hickok’s murder in Deadwood, another gambler met his end in southern Colorado after a dispute involving a poker game. Like Hickok, Tim Shay had made a living in storied Wild West cattle towns like Dodge City, Kansas, which recorded some of the highest homicide rates in U.S. history during the 1870s. Both men, in the expression of the day, “died with their boots on.”
Colorado in 1876 wasn’t immune from the Wild West’s plague of deadly gun violence

In contrast to the mythic figure of Wild Bill, however, Shay “bore an exceedingly bad reputation,” reported the Pueblo Chieftain on Aug. 8, the day after he was shot by Rufus Edwards, proprietor of a dance hall in the newly founded town of La Junta.
“When sober he was known as a peaceable and generous-hearted comrade, willing to give his last meal ticket to a hungry man, but intoxicated, his first impulse was war with his fellows,” said the Las Animas Leader.
A coroner dispatched from Las Animas empaneled a jury of six men, who collected testimony from Edwards and a handful of witnesses, who said they’d heard Shay threaten Edwards’ life over a dispute involving a $20 sum Shay was alleged to have stolen during a poker game. The jurors signed a verdict declaring that Edwards had acted “in defense of his own life.”
“He said that he was going to kill me,” Edwards told the jury. “He had his pistol half drawn when I shot. He killed one man in Dodge.”
With Colorado having achieved statehood at last, the Pueblo Chieftain expressed hope that this frontier violence would soon become a thing of the past.
“Shay was about the last of a crowd of roughs who have infested southern Colorado and western Kansas for several years,” the Chieftain said. “Most of these men have died with their boots on, after killing several men each, and Shay has been no exception to the rule.”



Selected sources

The Pueblo Chieftain, Aug. 2, 1876
