title: Wilderness in Idaho, the West is subject to review by Trump administration, Wilderness Society says
description: Officials at the nonprofit Wilderness Society say more than 1 million acres of wilderness and wild lands in Idaho could be affected by a federal policy review being undertaken by U.S. Department of Interior officials.  In June, officials with the Department of Interior announced they were beginning a nationwide review of rock climbing management, as […]
text:
Officials with the nonprofit organization The Wilderness Society published a map depicting wilderness and wilderness study areas to show what public land could be affected by a U.S. Department of Interior policy review. (Map provided courtesy of The Wilderness Society)Officials at the nonprofit Wilderness Society say more than 1 million acres of wilderness and wild lands in Idaho could be affected by a federal policy review being undertaken by U.S. Department of Interior officials. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In June, officials with the Department of Interior announced they were beginning a nationwide review of rock climbing management, as well as policies governing wilderness study areas and land that has wilderness-like qualities. 
In response, officials with the Wilderness Society published a map of wilderness and wilderness study areas – including in Idaho – that the nonprofit organization says could be affected by the review. (Click here to open the map in a new window)
Idaho includes 41 designated wilderness study areas that cover more than 544,000 acres, according to the Wilderness Society. Idaho’s wilderness study areas include Eighteen Mile Wilderness Study Area, situated along the Continental Divide Trail, the Borah Peak Wilderness Study Area that includes that state’s highest mountain and the Marshall Mountain Wilderness Study Area, located next to the more well-known Frank Church- River of No Return Wilderness.
The organization says more than 200 million acres of land across the country could be affected, and the existing policies provide valuable protection for some of the last wild places in the U.S.
 



 How to make a public comment on the U.S. Department of Interior’s review of wilderness management policies

Members of the public may make written public comments online at regulations.gov by entering the relevant docket number for the review. The comments will be published publicly. 

BLM-2026-0067 is the docket number for the Bureau of Land Management’s potential update to management of designated wilderness areas.
FWS-HQ-NWRS-2026-2575 is the docket number related to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife’s potential update to its wilderness stewardship manual. 
NPS-2026-0100 is the docket number for the National Park Service’s review of wilderness stewardship policies. 

The public comment period is open through Aug. 14. 
 



Michael Carroll, BLM campaign director with the Wilderness Society, said current wilderness policies prevent development, oil and gas drilling and motorized use in wilderness areas. They also preserve the natural and primitive qualities of wilderness land. Carroll also said the existing policies and management practices provide clarity for outfitters and guides, agriculture users who graze animals in wilderness areas and the public at large.
“They are dependent on management by federal land management agencies that is outlined in all those policies the current administration is reviewing and potentially rolling back,” Carroll said in a phone interview. “Without those management practices in place, or with significant rollback of those management policies, you could see wilderness across the West be under threat from potential development, potential road building and the potential handing over to the private sector.”
“There are a lot of things to be concerned with overall within the review,” Carroll added.  
Carrol said the Wilderness Society chose to develop and publish a map because the U.S. Department of Interior did not include a map or specify how many acres or which exact parcels of land could be affected when it announced the federal policy review. 
The map shows congressionally designated wilderness areas managed by the Department of Interior as well as land identified by federal agencies as having wilderness-like qualities, according to the Wilderness Society. 
This isn’t the first time the Wilderness Society has published a map to generate awareness about public lands and policy issues. 
In 2025, the Wilderness Society published a different map of U.S. public lands that would have been in jeopardy of being sold under an unsuccessful proposal from U.S. Sen. Mike Lee, a Republican of Utah. 
 Why is the Trump administration reviewing wilderness policies?

In June, officials with the U.S. Department of Interior announced they were undertaking the review and launching a 60-day public comment period. 
“The Department is seeking public input on two important efforts: First, establishing a consistent approach to recreational rock climbing management across designated wilderness areas and second, evaluating whether existing wilderness study areas and lands with wilderness characteristics policies should be updated, clarified or revised to improve management and use of some of America’s most treasured landscapes,” the U.S. Department of Interior wrote in its June 10 announcement. 
According to the Department of Interior, “The review will help determine whether existing policy documents should be updated or clarified to improve consistency, increase transparency and ensure public lands continue to be managed effectively in accordance with applicable laws.”
Efforts to reach U.S. Sens. Mike Crapo and Jim Risch and U.S. Reps. Mike Simpson and Russ Fulcher – all R-Idaho – were unsuccessful. 
U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum issued a statement saying public comment would guide the policy review. 
U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum testifies during a House Appropriations Committee hearing on April 20, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images)
“America’s public lands are meant to be experienced and enjoyed by the American people,” Burgum said in a written statement. “At the same time, we have a responsibility to be good stewards of these lands. By seeking public input on both recreational climbing guidance and wilderness stewardship and access policies, we are taking a thoughtful approach that supports recreation, improves management and helps ensure these iconic landscapes remain available for future generations. Under President Trump’s leadership, Interior is focused on expanding outdoor recreation opportunities, removing unnecessary barriers to access and use and managing public lands in a way that benefits the American people.”
Carroll, from the Wilderness Society, said he is concerned the review and changes will go farther.
“The review of those policies seems very open-ended, but it includes language we have already seen very clearly from this administration when it wants to eliminate policies, rollback protection or outright eliminate designations. By that I mean ‘streamlining,’ ‘removing barriers’ and ‘looking for efficiencies in management.’”
Carroll encouraged Idahoans to make public comments that support keeping public lands public and oppose rolling back protections and policies governing wilderness areas.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Health officials report record-breaking 50 heat-related deaths this summer
description: The 2026 heat season is now the deadliest in known history, as new data from the Maryland Department of Health reports a total of 50 heat-related fatalities since May, surpassing the previous record set of 46 in 2012.
text:
The 50 heat-related deaths recorded so far this summer -- with a month left in the "heat season" -- makes it the deadliest in state history, health department officials said. (Photo by Andrey Sayfutdinov/Getty Stock image)The 2026 heat season is now the deadliest in known history, as new data from the Maryland Department of Health reports a total of 50 heat-related fatalities since May, surpassing the previous record set of 46 in 2012.
The number of heat-related deaths soared in July, with 43 deaths reported just last month, according to a Wednesday update to the state’s weather-related illness dashboard. Fatalities could continue to climb with weeks remaining in the 2026 heat season that runs from May through September.
Maryland Health Secretary Meena Seshamani and the health department urge Marylanders to check in on vulnerable neighbors and loved ones for the remainder of the summer, while staying cool and hydrating to avoid future health emergencies.


“With each tragic loss, the Secretary and Department extend our condolences to the loved ones of these individuals,” Seshamani said in a written statement Thursday. “We continue to work with Marylanders on steps they can take to guard against overheating, including visiting a local cooling center and checking on older individuals and people with chronic diseases who are particularly vulnerable to heat.”
The Wednesday update to the state’s data dashboard shows that along with the 50 fatalities, there have been 1,300 trips taken to urgent care or the emergency room for heat-related illnesses and around 1,260 calls for emergency medical services.
The 50 fatalities reported so far surpasses the previous record from 2012, when 46 people died due to heat-related illness. That year, a July storm disrupted the power and air conditioning to many Maryland homes for days just as a heat wave hit. Some of those outages lasted more than a week, according to state documents.
Heat-related deaths have been on an upward trend in Maryland since 2022, when five heat-related deaths were reported for the summer.
Certain populations, such as elderly residents, are vulnerable to heat-related illness and fatalities. Among the 50 people who died this summer, 62% were aged 65 and older. Meanwhile, people aged 45 to 64 account for 28% of heat-related deaths. The department reports at least one child aged 4 or younger also died due to heat-related illness this year.
State health officials urge Marylanders to check on their elderly neighbors as the summer continues. Drivers should also check to make sure that children and pets are not left in the car during the summer, as temperatures inside vehicles can climb quickly and become dangerous or fatal.
On hot days, the department reminds Marylanders to drink plenty of fluids and urges folks to avoid alcohol, caffeine and overly sweetened beverages. Those in need of a cool location can contact their local health departments or call 211 to find the nearest cooling center.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: As federal protections fade, Americans with disabilities fear a return to institutions
description: When Rob Stone finished high school in Bethesda, Maryland, in 2018, he was asked to identify three goals for his life. Stone loves art and baseball. He’s cheerful, sports a cheeky mustache, and he’s always up for an adventure. Stone has a rare genetic movement disorder, dystonia-parkinsonism, that limits his mobility and speech. Setting specific […]
text:
Rob Stone, pictured with his mother, Jeneva, has a rare genetic movement disorder, dystonia-parkinsonism, that limits his mobility and speech. He has advocated for the preservation of state-funded services that allow him to live in his community, rather than in an institution. Federal and state policy changes and budget cuts could make it harder for many people with disabilities to get home- and community-based care. (Photo courtesy of Jeneva Stone)When Rob Stone finished high school in Bethesda, Maryland, in 2018, he was asked to identify three goals for his life. Stone loves art and baseball. He’s cheerful, sports a cheeky mustache, and he’s always up for an adventure.
Stone has a rare genetic movement disorder, dystonia-parkinsonism, that limits his mobility and speech. Setting specific goals would help him construct the life he wanted, and help his family identify the services he would need to live it to the fullest.
His parents suggested goals like “going on lots of walks” or “visiting state parks.” Stone just looked at them like they were ridiculous, said his mom, Jeneva Stone.
“We eventually discovered, through the right series of questions, that Robert wanted to protest,” she said. He’d watched disabled protesters dragged out of their wheelchairs from then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s office at the U.S. Capitol the year before, as they demanded the preservation of the Affordable Care Act.
Now 29, Rob has been a fixture on Capitol Hill and at the Maryland State House ever since, advocating alongside his parents for disability rights and healthcare. Earlier this year, he joined with other advocates to lobby the state legislature not to cut funding for services that help him and others live in their communities.
They weren’t able to prevent the cuts, but they did succeed in limiting them.
Disability advocates around the country are fighting a surge of federal and state actions that have eroded protections meant to keep people with disabilities living and working in their communities, rather than in institutions.
The federal government has walked away from decades-old requirements that states deliver disability services to people where they live. At the same time, state leaders, citing budget shortfalls, have rolled back community services the feds don’t require them to fund.
“It’s really hard,” said Rob Gorski, an Ohio father of three sons with autism who runs a popular social media account called TheAutismDad. “You try to wrap your head around one thing, and by the time you even figure out a path forward from there, they’ve thrown more stuff at you.”
 Navigating One Big Beautiful Bill Act cuts to Medicaid, independent living services

In Maryland, state lawmakers were weighing cuts to Medicaid, the joint federal-state program that covers much of Rob’s care, which he receives at home. The federal government will be reducing its share of Medicaid funding as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the broad tax and spending measure President Donald Trump signed last summer.
Maryland ended up cutting $126 million from the agency that administers Medicaid for people with developmental disabilities — but that was less than the $150 million reduction that Democratic Gov. Wes Moore originally proposed. The final budget also scrapped a proposed cap on how much state funding a person in the program could receive per year.
Idaho governor approves $22M in Medicaid disability budget cuts

“Medicaid itself isn’t just a budget line item,” Jeneva said. “It’s the mechanism through which the federal government ensures that people with disabilities have the civil right to live in their communities.”
Other threats to community-based disability services have emerged in Washington, D.C., and across the nation.
In June, the U.S. Department of Justice issued an opinion memo that says states don’t have to fund in-home or community-based services for people with disabilities who don’t want to live in institutions. The memo is a significant reinterpretation of federal law and represents a shift away from decades of civil rights protection.
The memo doesn’t change federal law, but it does signal a new focus for the DOJ, which is the primary enforcer of disability rights. Without enforcement, advocates worry, the civil rights protections they rely on could become moot.
In July, the DOJ published another notice saying it would no longer enforce its longstanding guidance on how to implement a landmark U.S. Supreme Court decision, Olmstead v. L.C., that requires public entities to provide community-based services, rather than institutional care, to people with disabilities whenever possible.
The federal spending reductions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act are likely to spur more cash-strapped states to cut home- and community-based services, since the federal Medicaid law only requires them to provide institutional care. More than half a dozen states have already moved to limit such services for people with disabilities, according to an analysis of state actions by researchers at George Washington University.
And at least three states are suing to dismantle a section of disability law that requires states to provide community-based services.
Defenders of the changes say they will allow states to refocus their limited dollars on people with the most serious medical needs.
New Medicaid work requirements in the Trump law, which are expected to drop between 3 million and 7 million people from the rolls, “will free up more state funding for (home- and community-based services) recipients,” said Rachel Barkley, director of the Able Americans disability policy think tank, which is housed inside the conservative National Center for Public Policy Research.
But Jeneva Stone says the cuts in Maryland threaten her son’s ability to get the nursing and other services he needs to be able to live at home. She worries families like hers will be the first to face forced institutionalization.
“More and more burden falls on family caregivers to fill in the gaps, and that leads to unsustainable economic situations for families,” she said. “Once your job situation falls apart, your savings are gone, you’re faced with this ugly choice: I believe strongly in my son’s civil right to stay in his community, but I can’t keep a roof over his head.”
Everything feels uncertain, she said, as longstanding protections seem to be dissolving for her son and others like him.
“They’re happy, they’re living great lives,” she said. “Are they medically complicated? Yeah. But do they deserve to spend the rest of their lives lying in a bed in a facility just because it’s easier to care for them in a congregate setting?”
 Shifting resources away from institutional care because ‘that’s what people want’

In the middle of the 20th century, disabled activists and their family members demanded an end to systemic abuses suffered by many of the hundreds of thousands of disabled people who were hidden away in sprawling state institutions around the country.
In the following decades, presidents and lawmakers of both parties championed a national shift away from segregating disabled people in huge facilities and toward the provision of services — such as home health nurses, physical therapy or adaptive tools — that would enable them to live at home or in their communities.
The two most consequential landmark federal disability rights laws were signed by Republican presidents: Richard Nixon signed the Rehabilitation Act in 1973, and George H.W. Bush signed the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990. Then, in its 1999 Olmstead ruling, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the unjustified institutionalization of people with disabilities was a form of discrimination.
Idaho families can’t find caregivers for kids with disabilities. Lawmakers won’t consider a fix.

“For decades we have very intentionally been shifting resources away from institutional care and into the community, because that’s what people want, and it’s more cost effective,” said Alison Barkoff, a health law and policy professor and director of the Hirsh Health Law & Policy Program at George Washington University.
“We can serve, generally, three people in the community for every one person in an institution. And it leads to better outcomes.”
More than 8 million Medicaid users receive such home- and community-based services across the country, while 1.5 million get services in institutions, such as nursing homes. Federal law requires state Medicaid programs to provide medical care and other support for people with disabilities.
People who live in institutions cost Medicaid an average of $54,462 per year, compared with $17,298 for people who get home and community services, according to the most recent Medicaid data.
State investments in home- and community-based services often result in short-term spending increases, but over time lead to long-term cost savings and a reduction in institutional spending, according to research from Brandeis University’s Community Living Policy Center.
The national shift to community-based services has been overwhelmingly popular. About 82% of people who receive community-based services prefer to live at home rather than in an institution, according to the most recent survey by the Medicaid and CHIP Payment and Access Commission.
That’s why, Barkoff said, “it is incredibly shocking, the approach that this administration is taking to something that has been so bipartisan and so much a part of American culture for decades.”
Some Republican-led states now want courts to adopt the Trump administration’s new interpretation of the Olmstead decision. Texas has already used the June DOJ memo in its lawsuit challenging federal requirements to provide community-based services. Florida also has used the memo as part of its appeal of a case involving medically complex children who were forced into nursing homes because the state refused to pay for in-home services.
Conservative state leaders say the federal government shouldn’t dictate how states offer support for people with disabilities, and argue that nursing shortages and other issues make it too difficult for states to care for some people outside of institutions.
 What about adequate support for community settings?

Barkley of Able Americans supports the shift away from institutionalization, but she says there should be more public investment in group homes or smaller facilities that can provide 24/7 oversight for people with more complex needs who can’t live safely at home.
“Unfortunately, it’s only when somebody with a serious mental illness hits the criminal justice system that they’re able to receive care,” she said. “And so for this sliver of the serious mental illness population, this movement has left them behind.”
VOR, a national disability rights nonprofit that supports “a full continuum of care options” for people with disabilities, argues that overly aggressive enforcement of the Olmstead decision and related federal law has, in some cases, resulted in people with disabilities being moved into community settings without adequate support. That broad-strokes application has contributed to poor outcomes, including homelessness, for some people.
The DOJ memo and other federal actions reducing community care have been driven in part by the Trump administration’s push to address homelessness, said Barkoff. Trump issued an executive order last July giving states a green light to commit people experiencing homelessness to treatment centers or hospitals, whether they want to go or not.
In Idaho, a public transit program can take you to the doctor. If it has enough funding.

“They have created this narrative that Olmstead created this problem” of not enough beds for people who need higher levels of care, said Barkoff. But without Olmstead, “there was just a hollow promise to close institutions,” she said.
“What Olmstead did was create a tool to require states to follow through on that commitment.”
Gorski said it’s been more apparent this year than ever that there are people and families, particularly those with complex care needs, who feel that the shift away from institutional care hasn’t helped them.
Recent efforts by the Trump administration to roll back protections are “exploiting where we’ve failed to ensure that we’re taking care of our own people,” he said. “Everyone in this community should feel seen and heard and like they have a place at the table.”
But even VOR warned in a June statement that the DOJ memo “substantially weakens” protections and federal pressure on states to fund the community-based services many people with intellectual or developmental disabilities depend on.
 States on their own

In June, Republican lawmakers in Ohio swiftly backtracked on a proposal that would have barred Medicaid recipients’ family members from being paid as caregivers. They pulled the controversial portion of the bill after backlash from residents who said it would hurt people with developmental disabilities whose caregivers are often relatives whose caregiving duties prevent them from taking other jobs.



Quotation







They’re happy, they’re living great lives. Are they medically complicated? Yeah. But do they deserve to spend the rest of their lives lying in a bed in a facility just because it’s easier to care for them in a congregate setting?


– – Jeneva Stone, Maryland mother of a son with complex medical needs


Some states have recently expanded home and community-based services, including Georgia, Illinois, Ohio and Wyoming, according to George Washington University’s analysis. Others, including California, Idaho, Indiana, Maryland, Minnesota and Nebraska, have limited services.
Some, like Kansas and Virginia, have done both.
Ultimately, as the feds back away from enforcing civil rights protections, states are left to figure out how to offer services for people with disabilities in a way that balances civil rights with budget realities.
“At this point it’s kind of a state-by-state effort,” said Illinois state Sen. Julie Morrison, a Democrat who sponsored a bill this year, now law, that turned Illinois’s state disability commission into a cabinet-level agency.
“But at the end of the day we are obligated, morally I believe, to make sure we are taking care of people who need these services and who want to live in an independent environment.”
Rob Stone and his parents plan to continue meeting with state legislators in Maryland to push back against deeper cuts to services that help him remain with his family. His mother said she’s been doing a lot of explaining to lawmakers about how civil rights for people with disabilities fit into existing law.
“There’s a tremendous need for advocates to educate legislators at the state level about this because they’ve never had to think about these things before,” she said.
“It’s always been something the federal government takes care of.”
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Democrats to choose party chair at potentially contentious meeting
description: Alabama Democrats will gather in Montgomery Saturday to pick party leadership for the next four years.  Current Alabama Democratic Party Chair Randy Kelley; Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton of Greensboro and Robert Hunter, the party’s nominee for a Gadsden-area House seat, were declared candidates for the position as of Thursday.  Republicans maintain[...]
text:
Alabama Democratic Party Chair Randy Kelley (left, in light blue jacket) listens to Alabama Democratic Party Vice Chair for Minority Affairs Joe Reed (right, in beige jacket) during a rally against redistricting at the Alabama Statehouse on May 4, 2026 in Montgomery, Alabama. The State Democratic Executive Committee will meet on Saturday in Montgomery to elect a leader for the next four years. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

At least three Democrats — incumbent Chair Randy Kelley; Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton of Greensboro and Robert Hunter, a nominee for a Gadsden-area House seat — will run to lead the state party at a meeting on Saturday.
Alabama Democrats saw improved turnout in May and appear to be competitive in Huntsville-area legislative seats, but there have been major disputes within the state organization over leadership.
Similar disputes have led to intervention by the Democratic National Committee (DNC) in the past. A DNC representative will observe Saturday’s meeting.




Alabama Democrats will gather in Montgomery Saturday to pick party leadership for the next four years. 
Current Alabama Democratic Party Chair Randy Kelley; Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton of Greensboro and Robert Hunter, the party’s nominee for a Gadsden-area House seat, were declared candidates for the position as of Thursday. 
Republicans maintain control of Alabama politics, but Democrats in the state are carrying momentum into November. The minority party had higher turnout than Republicans in the May 19 primary election, and has the largest slate of midterm candidates since 2018. Some of those candidates are in competitive races in and around Huntsville, but other statewide candidates remain underdogs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the middle of an election year, the party is also dealing with internal discord. Many members of the State Democratic Executive Committee (SDEC) have expressed their displeasure with the party on social media ahead of the committee’s meeting on Saturday. The posts range from complaints of a lack of election education to accusations of illegal campaign finance practices from former candidates.
A new direction?
Randy Kelley, the chair of the Alabama Democratic Party, stands during a rally against redistricting at the Alabama Statehouse on May 4, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama.  (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
Kelley, long aligned with Vice-Chair of Minority Affairs Joe Reed, a major power in the party, said in a phone interview Thursday that he inherited a “poor administration” from his predecessor Rep. Chris England of Tuscaloosa, but the party has had some “great victories” under his leadership. England declined to comment in a phone interview Thursday afternoon.
“If we’re gonna give the people of Alabama the best that politics has to offer for them, then we’re going to have to pull together and organize around our common issues and values,” he said. “If you look at much of what is affecting the people most in Alabama, the Democratic Party has fought for them.”
He touted the flipping of a Huntsville-area House seat by Rep. Marilyn Lands in a 2024 special election, and the election of U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, later that year after a federal court approved a new redistricting plan for the state. The U.S. Supreme Court in June allowed the Republican-controlled Legislature to use a map it previously deemed racially discriminatory.
“We’ve got to unite the party. The party hasn’t been united, and we have much more in common than we have differences. And we have to put aside these superficial differences in order to focus on what we ought to be about, so we can best serve the people of the state of Alabama,” Kelley said. 
Hunter said in a phone interview Thursday morning that he is generally frustrated with the party and its lack of action outside of SDEC meetings, like the one on Saturday.
Alabama House Democrats’ bill to end straight-ticket voting draws ire of Democratic leader

“I don’t like the fact that the party is not very useful when it comes to material action, both for the candidates, but also specifically for general community members,” Hunter said. “What I worry is, it got better in the last year and a half in part because we had this upcoming meeting where it’s report card time and you have to show improvement if you want to keep your job for the chair and the vice chair of minority affairs.”
Should Hunter be elected, he wants to “change everything.” 
“I want to make sure that we actually are reaching out to every single person possible, and we are trying to bring people into the fold that are not currently there. That includes showing that the party is the state party, not the Montgomery party,” he said.
Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, standing at a lecturn on the floor of the Alabama Senate on March 11, 2026, in the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
A message seeking comment from Singleton was left Thursday. Singleton said in an interview on Capitol Journal last week that he has “never felt supported by the party” during his time in the Senate. Singleton was elected in 2005. 
“All those things that Democrats support, but we just never got that support from the party,” he said. “If I can’t get someone else to get the job done, I don’t mind stepping up and doing the job myself. I can’t criticize someone else for something I’m not willing to do.” 
Tabitha Isner, vice chair of the party, said in a phone interview that having a legislator as party chair could be very helpful, and it would be difficult for other members to argue that Singleton is not qualified.
“We should be talking about policies that we’re passing, so it’s healthy to have a closer relationship between the policymakers and the folks who are recruiting candidates,” Isner said. “They’ve run elections and won elections. Granted, in safely Democratic districts generally, but those are folks who know the game, and we should be taking advantage of their expertise.”
Just because Singleton has policymaking experience, does not guarantee him as a viable candidate, she said. 
Isner has been active on social media recently, posting about her experience as vice chair under Kelley. Her posts have largely claimed that Kelley and Reed do not follow the party’s bylaws and there needs to be change. She said Thursday that she will not be running for chair. 
“Joe L. Reed will be the downfall of the Alabama Democratic Party if we don’t do something about it,” she said on a recent episode of “He’s Not Wrong,” a podcast hosted by Chad DuBois.
A message seeking comment was left with Reed Thursday morning.
Kelley said that social media posts from Isner and other members of the party come from people who have lost against him. 
“I do know that we have a lot of toxicity from some of our people, and some of that dissonance has to do with some people who lost the election last round,” Kelley said.
Isner said the contest “still comes down to issues of loyalty.”
Alabama Democrats restore most diversity caucuses after DNC order

 “The folks who are loyal to Joe Reed will likely vote for whoever Joe Reed tells them to vote for, even if that’s someone who you know has not done a good job,” she said. “The coach usually gets replaced when the team doesn’t win any games.”
Prior to the main business meeting, each minority caucus will meet. Isner said that these meetings are generally to discuss who the caucus will vote for in the chair election. The Black Caucus, which is chaired by Reed, is the largest and is loyal to him. In 2023, the SDEC passed bylaws that eliminated youth, LGBTQ+ and disabled caucuses and reduced the powers of affirmative action; Asian and Pacific Islander; Hispanic; and Native American caucuses “to monitor the affairs of the groups listed.”
Most of the minority caucuses were restored in 2024 by order of the Democratic National Committee (DNC). 
Isner said she expects the meeting to be long and contentious.
“I expect that Dr. Reed will make a motion to limit debate on everything, and that will be a fight,” Isner said. “People want to be heard. This is their only opportunity to be heard and to talk about these big important decisions.”
DNC delegates under supervision
Randy Kelley, chair of the Alabama Democratic Party, speaks to members of the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee in St. Louis on Oct. 6, 2023. Left to right: Ben Harris, an attorney for the party; Randy Kelley, and Vice Chair for Minority Affairs Joe Reed. (Screenshot/Alabama Reflector)
The SDEC will also elect three delegates for the DNC, an overdue vote from 2024. Reed in 2024 accused then-President Joe Biden’s campaign of “handpicking” delegates.
A representative from the DNC will be at the meeting to observe, according to Isner, but not to intervene. Kelley said the delegate vote would be “typical” but did not expand.
“The DNC will not intervene; they’ll only observe. I think that will frustrate people to know that there isn’t any intervention,” Isner said.
The DNC instructed the SDEC to do the delegate election via paper ballot, Isner said, but she is not aware of any nominees or processes in place to allow that to happen. 
The main question for SDEC members, she said, is deciding whether the current leadership has done a good job and what steps the party needs to take.
“I do think it falls largely on generational lines, also racial lines. But younger folks are saying we’ve got to do something different,” she said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Tennessee senators blame dehydration in botched execution
description: Dehydration was a primary factor in a botched execution that forced Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to call off and postpone a man’s death penalty for a year, a state senator told the Lookout. Republican Sen. Ferrell Haile of Gallatin, who signed a letter seeking an investigation of the failed execution of Tony Carruthers and postponement […]
text:
Sen. Ferrell Haile, a Gallatin Republican, said he is comfortable with the state of Tennessee proceeding with death penalty executions after a failed one due to what he says was the "dehydration" of the condemned man. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Dehydration was a primary factor in a botched execution that forced Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to call off and postpone a man’s death penalty for a year, a state senator told the Lookout.
Republican Sen. Ferrell Haile of Gallatin, who signed a letter seeking an investigation of the failed execution of Tony Carruthers and postponement of executions, said this week after receiving more information about Carruthers’ physical state he is satisfied with the governor’s plan to move ahead with an Aug. 13 execution of Darrell Hines and others scheduled this year.
Haile and seven other Republican senators sent Lee the letter in July amid questions about the qualifications of the physician overseeing the state’s executions after the Department of Correction’s death penalty team poked and prodded Carruthers for roughly an hour, creating what witnesses called a bloody mess as they tried to find veins to insert IVs to administer lethal drugs.
In spite of continued questions about the physician’s qualifications and whether he should be performing executions at all, Haile said he agrees the state should go ahead, using its protocol.
“We have found out more information since then. It wasn’t the protocol as much as it was other factors that came into play, that the inmate was dehydrated and … wasn’t in a position to deal with that in that point in time. I feel pretty comfortable with where we’ve gotten to,” Haile said.
Asked if the Department of Correction’s death penalty team will have to ensure the next person up for execution is properly hydrated, Haile said, “I assume so, yes.”
Tennessee GOP senators seek review of botched execution

Public Defender Kit Thomas, the federally-appointed attorney for Hines, told the Lookout this week there is no “public proof” that Carruthers was dehydrated. The state refused to allow a physician to examine Carruthers immediately after the botched execution, she said, and efforts in court to have him checked have been fruitless.
“There is no transparency around whether Mr. Carruthers was dehydrated,” Thomas said.
Thomas added that dehydration doesn’t explain the failure of the execution team to insert a central line, calling that “the failure of an unqualified, underskilled physician” and saying it’s “ingenuous” to compare the possible dehydration of Carruthers to the physical ailments of Hines.
The Tennessee Supreme Court Thursday denied Hines’ request for an order requiring the state to reveal whether it plans to use Dr. Mark Fowler for his execution and refused to appoint a special master to consider his Eighth Amendment claim against cruel and unusual punishment and postpone the execution.
Hines’ attorneys responded by sending a letter to the state attorney general, the governor and warden of Riverbend Maximum Security Facility asking the Department of Correction to disclose test results of the drugs is plans to use for his execution.
The state has declined to say whether Fowler will oversee the Hines execution even though a Davidson County Chancery Court ordered the state to make its plans clear. Hines, convicted of first-degree murder in 1985, is partially blind, extremely thin and paralyzed on his left side after suffering two strokes, raising concerns that the execution will have trouble accessing a central line, his attorneys with the federal Public Defenders Office say.
Tennessee governor gives reprieve to inmate after botched execution 

Yet Lee, who called off and postponed Carruthers’ execution as he lay on the gurney, said this week he is confident in the state’s lethal injection process and denied a request by Republican senators to independently investigate the circumstances surrounding the failed execution and postpone lethal injections until problems are resolved. Lee said he is committed to making sure “the law is carried out justly and legally.”
“I take it very seriously and have in every case and will in every case going forward,” Lee said this week. “I discussed that with Senate leadership as a result of their letter, and they’re in agreement.”
Stating the obvious, Lee said the Department of Correction is responsible for executing people on death row. Yet Correction Commissioner Frank Strada came to Tennessee from Arizona in 2022, shortly after overseeing three executions there that had IV access problems similar to Tennessee’s.
Thomas said the Arizona and Tennessee protocols contain “virtually identical provisions” on IV access, including allowing the execution team to practice without performing an IV catheterization. Previous protocol allowed a team of emergency medical technicians to handle IV access.
Lee, who previously put executions on hold because the state failed to follow its lethal drug protocol, said it is “legally crucial” that the state abide by its guidelines. He pointed out that the Carruthers execution wasn’t botched because of protocol, only because the doctor couldn’t establish IV access. He did not mention dehydration when questioned by reporters this week.
Considering Carruthers had been on death row for decades for a 1994 kidnapping and triple murder, it seems they would have had time to make sure his water level was up to par, raising further questions about the state’s ability to carry out an execution.
Raising other questions 
Other than the failure to make sure Carruthers had been drinking enough water, a major part of the state’s protocol falls short, mainly because it requires a doctor to participate in the execution, potentially violating the Hippocratic Oath to do no harm, according to Sen. Richard Briggs, one of eight Republicans who signed the letter to Lee.
Briggs wasn’t consulted by the governor but said it is clear the physician in charge of overseeing the execution should have been able to handle the IV. Briggs, a retired U.S. Army physician, said he’s established thousands of IVs in difficult situations and pointed out that the doctor in charge of the team hadn’t inserted an IV in more than a decade and had done it only a few times. 
“Ethically physicians aren’t even supposed to be involved in executions other than to declare someone’s dead,” said Sen. Richard Briggs, a physician, of doctors administering lethal injections.
“I don’t know how you can fix that because ethically physicians aren’t even supposed to be involved in executions other than to declare someone’s dead,” Briggs said. He said he favors coming up with another way to carry out the death penalty.
The governor didn’t talk to Briggs or to several of the senators who sought the investigation, only to some members in leadership positions.
Sen. Tom Hatcher of Maryville, chairman of a Senate corrections subcommittee, said Lee didn’t talk to him but that he was satisfied with the governor’s efforts to look into the situation after talking to Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson, who told him that Carruthers was dehydrated. Johnson didn’t respond to questions from the Lookout.
That leads us to believe the governor’s ultimate decision is based almost entirely on hydration, not on the ability of the execution team. 
We understand the concept of delivering justice for the families who were victimized by heinous crimes.
But another factor that has to be taken into consideration is the idea that people have been put to death for crimes they didn’t commit. One study finds that if all death row inmates remained sentenced indefinitely, at least 4.1% would be exonerated.
More than 200 people who were sentenced to death since 1973 have been exonerated, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which also has plenty of stories about people who were executed before people started changing their stories and evidence started falling apart. Official misconduct and perjury or false accusations are the most common causes for wrongful death penalty convictions.
Three people in Tennessee have been exonerated after being convicted of capital crimes and sentenced to death.
The missing “stones”
Campaign TV ads are the highlight of nearly every election, and this year’s are no exception, with one group identifying congressional candidate state Rep. Johnny Garrett as pro-LGBTQ+ pride and using artificial intelligence to put him in a rainbow shirt and U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn sending a cease-and-desist letter to the American Exceptionalism Institute for “defaming” her. Garrett and Blackburn both handily won their primaries Thursday.
But this year’s winner is Rep. Todd Warner, who came up with a “stones” ad at the tail end of this year’s primary. And we’re not talking about the Rolling Stones.
“Do you know what’s missing in Washington? Stones,” Warner says in the ad, in which he contends “it shouldn’t take stones this size to do the right thing.”
The ad shows Warner operating a backhoe to move large chunks of limestone as he talks about deporting “every illegal alien” and passing the SAVE America Act in his race against state Sen. Brent Taylor, who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement.

Warner, who was soundly beaten by state Sen. Brent Taylor in Thursday’s primary, told the Lookout the ad was shot on his farm but said he hasn’t broken any law, even though his mining operation is caught up in a quarrel with neighbors and the Marshall County Board of Zoning Appeals, which said he can’t operate a quarry on his farm. The state also sent Warner a violation notice after finding he was running a mining operation without a permit required by the Clean Water Act. That was contradicted by another inspection in which the state said it didn’t understand the nature of the operation and was uncertain about whether a federal permit was necessary.
Warner said the stones in the campaign ad were dumped there by Marshall County, which is building a water treatment plant across the road.
“We have no issues at all. We’ve done nothing wrong. There’s a lot of garbage out there this fake news puts out there on social media,” he said.
Warner contends he never asked for a quarry but rather dug a lake to water crops.
Gone but not forgotten
House Majority Leader William Lamberth hired former state Rep. Matthew Hill’s Birchwood Consulting to handle text messaging polls in state races, the Tennessee Journal reported. Republicans doled out $37,500 for the work.
Lamberth told the Journal Hill was able to do the quickest turnaround for the best price.
Hill, who lost in the 2020 primary but still has a brother, Rep. Timothy Hill, in the legislature, was a supporter of former House Speaker Glen Casada before his speakership crashed and burned.
Hill also boasted six years ago about netting $400,000 for a nonprofit organization to help children that came from a $4 million slush fund Casada put in the budget to dole out favors. That caught people’s attention, but Casada defended the fund at the time, saying it was a line item in the legislative budget that anyone could see. He was absolutely correct. It just didn’t pass the smell test as he tried to shore up support to stay in the speaker’s seat.
“Life is so strange when it’s changin’, yes indeed / I’ve seen the hard times and pressure’s been on me.” *
*”Gimme Back My Bullets”, Lynyrd Skynyrd

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Department of Human Services hasn’t implemented lawmakers’ key childcare bill by deadline
description: Senate Majority Whip Ben Queen, father of a young child, stood on the Senate floor in March to celebrate the Legislature’s first-ever hallmark childcare bill. “If we want people to go to work in this state, then we have to make sure they have somewhere safe and reliable for their kids to go during the […]
text:
Children join childcare advocates and lawmakers at the State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, on Feb. 2, 2026, to celebrate Child Care Day in the House of Delegates chamber. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Senate Majority Whip Ben Queen, father of a young child, stood on the Senate floor in March to celebrate the Legislature’s first-ever hallmark childcare bill.
“If we want people to go to work in this state, then we have to make sure they have somewhere safe and reliable for their kids to go during the day,” said Queen, R-Harrison. He smiled as he talked about his son’s childcare provider. 
“If we want to keep young families in West Virginia and attract new ones, childcare has to be part of that conversation,” Queen said.
Sen. Ben Queen, R-Harrison, supported a key child care measure during the 2026 legislative session. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
This month, the West Virginia Department of Human Services — the agency overseeing the childcare assistance program — has yet to implement the bill’s requirements after it went into effect July 1.
“We didn’t create a new system or a new program. We were just changing the system that we have, and obviously, there was a lot of attention towards it,” Queen said on Thursday. “Hopefully, we can put it into implementation soon.”
The childcare legislation, House Bill 4191, overwhelmingly passed the Senate and House with bipartisan support. Gov. Patrick Morrisey declined to sign the measure, and it became law without his public support.
Sen. Joey Garcia, D-Marion. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“This is a real issue where childcare providers have closed and are continuing to close across the state. This bill is supposed to be a lifeline for them,” said Sen. Joey Garcia, D-Marion. “It’s disheartening that we have a lot longer path to fix our childcare system, and if we can’t even take one step forward together, it’s not going to be a great collaboration.”
More than 260 childcare facilities have closed since 2024, often citing the state’s childcare assistance program as reason for financial instability.
Lisa Carpenter (left) and Alicia Brennian (right). (Courtesy photos)
The bill’s delayed implementation is worrisome for childcare providers, since the measure mandated changes meant to stabilize childcare services in West Virginia. Those changes are urgently needed, according to providers. 
“We’re still struggling. We’re still having these issues, but nothing’s getting fixed,” said Alicia Brennian, assistant director of Step Ahead Preschool in Martinsburg.
The facility serves around 40 children, many of whom rely on the childcare subsidy to access care. 
“Most of the people out there think that childcare centers are charging too much because they think that we make a lot of money, and I don’t know why,” said Lisa Carpenter, owner and director of Step Ahead Preschool. “Until you break down the bills that you have and just trying to keep your staff to want to stay with you is hard.”
The Department of Human Services did not respond to an inquiry from West Virginia Watch for this story.
“I have heard from the agency that they’re working on it — that they just need more time,” said Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha. “I don’t think the agency is purposefully stalling on this … but it’s unfortunate that this legislation passed in (March), and it hasn’t been implemented. They are breaking the law at this point.”
Del. Bob Fehrenbacher, speaking before a House committee Feb. 4, 2026, sponsored the landmark childcare legislation. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
West Virginia woefully short on childcare spots
More than 28,000 West Virginia children currently lack access to childcare because providers don’t have enough available slots, according to state estimates. The number of kids in need has grown since lawmakers adjourned in March.
West Virginia offers a childcare subsidy program to low-income parents who are employed or in school. 
“I don’t see it as a subsidy. I see it as a workforce tool to hopefully get people off the system,” Queen said.
Del. Bob Fehrenbacher, R-Wood, sponsor of the childcare legislation, hoped to eliminate what he called burdensome requirements for providers and boost industry stability. He sees it as essential to boosting the state’s low workforce participation.
“I have been informed that aspects of the bill were not implemented yet,” Fehrenbacher said. “You just have to collaborate and continue to ideally work together as opposed to, frankly, be at conflict and be working against each other. … At the end of the day, we have our respective roles, and hopefully, we can work in a respectful, purposeful manner to make progress and look out for the well-being of our citizens.”
The state uses federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families dollars to help pay for the child care subsidy program. That source of federal funding faces a multi-million dollar deficit, according to Morrisey, and his spending review has prompted current issues with the state’s school clothing allowance program.
Queen wondered if the governor’s ongoing review of TANF funds could have impacted implementation of the childcare bill.
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, speaks on the House of Delegates floor on March 5, 2026.(Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Childcare bill requirements 
The lengthy childcare bill expanded the state’s childcare tax credit for businesses and codified that the state — regardless of fluctuating federal guidance — reimburse childcare providers who serve kids using the state’s childcare subsidy by the total child enrollment rather than daily attendance in an effort to stabilize finances. 
The measure also required DoHS to make several changes to how the state manages the childcare subsidy program. 
DoHS must implement an electronic filing system for providers needing department verifications for reimbursement purposes. The state reimburses child care centers serving kids using the childcare assistance program.
Young explained that the online system will cut down on bureaucracy and required paperwork for providers.
“It would also really clear up any potential fraud because of the sheer volume of data that has to be submitted from the providers,” she said. “That portion of the bill is about reform and accountability and cutting down on red tape to make government work better. It’s a shame that it hasn’t been implemented.”
The legislation also changed how the state calculates the length of a childcare day for purposes of providers’ billing. 
“If we have a child that comes here (for) one hour and 55 minutes and doesn’t make that two hours, we’re put into another you know bracket of what we get paid,” Carpenter explained. “So when you have so many children that fluctuate, you can’t depend on how much money you’re making and if you’re going to have enough money to pay your bills or your staff.”
Lawmakers also asked DoHS to address what’s known as the “childcare subsidy cliff,” where a parent’s income increase abruptly ends their assistance. This specific part of the legislation is due by Jan. 1, 2027.
The average cost of childcare in West Virginia is about $800 per month for one child, according to research from the West Virginia Chamber of Commerce.
Young said it was important to note this year’s childcare legislation still didn’t focus on growing available childcare in West Virginia. 
“This bill was a good step towards stabilizing childcare facilities, not ensuring that we are growing the capacity,” Young said. “We as a Legislature haven’t done anything to address the larger childcare economic development problems that we’re seeing around the state.”
Step Ahead Preschool is closing down its two-year-old classroom this month despite growing population and childcare needs in the Eastern Panhandle.
Carpenter said it has been a struggle to retain staff. 
“I wish the legislators would understand that if you want a good workforce, you have to provide more money in education and childcare. It’s just what you have to do,” she said.

title: North Carolina high schoolers show improvements in mental health
description: One of the most vexing problems caused by the pandemic was the toll it took on the mental health of young people. Students struggled with school closures, isolation from their friends, and the difficulties of remote learning. But after years of focus on behavioral health, it appears that North Carolina high school students are doing […]
text:
A new survey shows the mental health of North Carolina's high school students is improving, but experts say more investments are needed in school psychologists and social workers. (Photo: iStock/Getty Photo) One of the most vexing problems caused by the pandemic was the toll it took on the mental health of young people. Students struggled with school closures, isolation from their friends, and the difficulties of remote learning.
But after years of focus on behavioral health, it appears that North Carolina high school students are doing better. That’s according to the 2025 North Carolina High School Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which was presented to the State Board of Education this week.
Researchers examined the responses from 1,692 students from 25 traditional public and charter high schools who voluntarily participated in the survey during the spring of 2025.
Dr. Ellen Essick, section chief for N.C. Healthy Schools in the state Department of Public Instruction, said the percentage of high schoolers who said they felt so sad or hopeless they stopped doing their normal activities for at least two weeks dropped to 29.7%.
“We’ve still got work to do, but it was good to see that drop from that high of 43% in 2021,” said Essick.
Dr. Ellen Essick, Section Chief for NC Healthy Schools, Department of Public Instruction (Photo: NCDPI)
North Carolina also saw a double-digit decline in the percent of high schoolers who said they had seriously considered attempting suicide. In 2021, 22.3% of students said they had considered ending their life. In 2025, that number fell to 11.4%.
“This is the lowest it’s been in a 20-year period,” said Essick. “If we can address some of the needs before they get to a place of contemplating suicide, then I think that totally helps us in terms of how we support students.”
Fourteen percent of the students in this latest survey acknowledged needing mental health counseling, but did not get it.
Taking a deeper dive into the data, 56% of high schoolers who self-reported making Ds and Fs in school felt sad or hopeless, compared to 22% of their counterparts who said they made mostly As in school.
“We don’t know if poor grades came first and then the mental health issues came, or mental health issues contributed to poor grades,” said Essick.
Jill Camnitz, who represents northeastern North Carolina on the State Board of Education, said it was “heartbreaking” that almost two in 10 high-school students say they have poor mental health most of the time, with one in 10 considering suicide.
One in four NC teens experience depression. Can peer-to-peer support improve their mental health? 

 Social media and addictive substance use decline 
“But I also put a lot of hope in the fact that we’re seeing a decrease in the use of social media, because we know that those are very deeply connected,” said Camnitz.
In the behavioral survey, the share of students who said they used social media more than once an hour or several times a day declined 4.5% over the last two years.
In January, a new law took effect restricting cell phones in the classroom. Educators say it has had a positive impact in reducing social media use during the school day and improving emotional well-being.
Alcohol use among North Carolina high schoolers who self-reported declined more than 26% since 2005. Marijuana use also declined more than 10% in the same period.
The state has also made headway in discouraging teen tobacco use and vaping. Only 3.5% say they currently smoke cigarettes. Nearly 13% of high schoolers routinely used vaping products, down from 21% in 2023.
 Improving school-based mental health services 
On the whole, students who were surveyed reported lower substance use and lower rates of fighting and safety-related absences than in the past. But Essick said the state must continue to invest in training support personnel, who may be the first to identify a problem and then serve as a bridge in making a referral.
School psychologists and psychiatrists have been in short supply in North Carolina for years. According to the N.C. School Psychology Association, 23 school districts in North Carolina have zero full-time school psychologists.
Essick is hopeful that will change.
In the past two years, North Carolina has received four mental health grants from the U.S. Department of Education totaling $29 million to help recruit more school social workers and counselors.
Earlier this year, the Department of Public Instruction announced a $4.8 million grant to fund salary and housing stipends for school psychologist interns to serve in high-need and rural districts. The grant supports supervision for those interns and practicing school psychologists.
“We have 10 interns already placed for this coming year. Some of those are from out of state, which is what we need because we don’t have enough [psychologists] produced in North Carolina,” said Essick. “If we can get somebody to come from out of state, then that’s one more professional we get in our schools.”

title: No silver bullet, no single fuel: What Texas can teach the Carolinas about energy resilience
description: What do record-setting heat waves, hurricane season, and severe droughts all have in common? They all create strain on the power grid, threaten reliability, and drive up costs. Duke Energy, which serves customers throughout the Carolinas, forecasts a demand increase eight times the pace of the prior 15 years due to economic development, population growth, […[...]
text:
Solar panels and wind turbines. (Photo: Marga Buschbell-Steeger/Getty Images)What do record-setting heat waves, hurricane season, and severe droughts all have in common? They all create strain on the power grid, threaten reliability, and drive up costs.
Duke Energy, which serves customers throughout the Carolinas, forecasts a demand increase eight times the pace of the prior 15 years due to economic development, population growth, and electrification. Managing energy affordability and reliability will be a balancing act, and energy experts across the political spectrum recognize that no single resource will be a silver bullet. What we do need is an “all of the above” energy approach.
A state that has fully embraced that approach is one you may not at first expect, yet it should get a gold (lone) star for its balanced generation mix. Texas has always been a major energy producer, but over the last decade it has invested in enough renewable energy to produce almost half of its total energy supply. This growth in renewable energy is not attributed to climate goals. It is driven by lower costs and long-term planning.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Wind and solar are among the cheapest and fastest forms of new energy generation. Texas has taken advantage of these low-cost resources and emerged as a clean energy leader by adding roughly 14,000 MW of wind and 19,000 MW of solar in five years. As a result, renewables generate 30% of the state’s electricity — enough to power nearly 10 million homes.
In North Carolina, renewables provide about 15% of electricity generation, while South Carolina remains closer to 8%. While both states have made progress in solar expansion in recent years, and North Carolina has two utility-scale wind projects online, the pace of development is much slower.
When it comes to energy, Texas and the Carolinas do have a few things in common. First, they both need affordable energy that is not affected by fluctuating fuel prices, and second, they need a reliable system during times of peak demand. Wind and solar check both of these boxes. They are quick-to-deploy resources that prove valuable during extreme weather and peak demand periods. They also apply downward pressure on energy costs by allowing utilities to use free renewable energy first, reducing the need to run more expensive resources.
History shows us that natural gas prices spike dramatically during severe weather events, which ultimately impacts ratepayers. By investing in fuel-free resources like wind and solar, Texas has built a more diversified resource mix that protects customers from sudden swings in fuel costs. During extreme conditions, such as hurricanes and winter storms, wind, solar, and battery storage help keep electricity affordable by stabilizing prices and reducing reliance on expensive fuel purchases.
People often criticize wind and solar because they aren’t considered baseload generation, but this overlooks the fact that grid operators can predict how much energy they will produce days in advance. Fossil fuels have reliability challenges too. Fuel supplies and prices can be disrupted by extreme weather or global events, often with little warning. Extreme weather can compromise gas infrastructure just as demand peaks, creating reliability challenges and price spikes. Unlike renewable variability, these problems are hard to predict and difficult for grid operators to control.
The July 4th weekend was one of the hottest stretch of the summer so far, and electricity demand climbed with the heat. Off the coast of New York, South Fork Wind ran at an average capacity factor of 74.7%. That included a capacity factor of nearly 90% on July 2, the day that the New York Independent System Operator issued an energy watch due to a decline in operating margins.
While summer loads remain critical, planning forecasts project that the combined winter peak demand for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress will grow by more than 6,000 megawatts over the next 25 years—an increase of more than 20% over today’s system. Wind energy tends to produce strongly during winter peak periods, making it well-positioned to help meet growing winter demand, strengthen grid resilience, and diversify the Carolinas’ energy mix against future extreme weather events.
The Carolinas are staring at a future of growth and pressure on an aging system. As we plan for tomorrow’s energy needs, we can’t pretend that every resource does the same job. Texas has recognized the economic and energy security benefits of an “all of the above” strategy. It’s time for the Carolinas to build a portfolio that is less fragile, less exposed to fuel shocks, and more predictable over time. A resilient grid.
Jocelyn Juliano is program manager at the Southeastern Wind Coalition in Chapel Hill, N.C.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: July heat produces ‘flash drought’ with more than half of North Dakota affected
description: More than half of North Dakota is now in a drought, with blistering July heat shriveling crops and taking a toll on pastures.  The U.S. Drought Monitor, which is updated weekly on Thursdays, shows a third of the state in moderate drought and more than 23% in extreme drought. The extreme drought area increased dramatically […]
text:
A soybean plant suffers from a lack of moisture in a sandy area of field in Griggs County, North Dakota, on July 31, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Jeff Stachler/NDSU Extension)More than half of North Dakota is now in a drought, with blistering July heat shriveling crops and taking a toll on pastures. 
The U.S. Drought Monitor, which is updated weekly on Thursdays, shows a third of the state in moderate drought and more than 23% in extreme drought. The extreme drought area increased dramatically from the previous week, when less than 9% of the state was in that category. 
“July was one of the warmest and driest on record, and so in turn we had some very rapid shift into dry conditions across the state,” Daryl Ritchison, state climatologist for North Dakota, said Thursday. 
The severe drought areas include a pocket in central North Dakota, much of the southwest corner and Cass, Traill and Steele counties in the east. 
The U.S. Drought Monitor map updated on Aug. 6, 2026, with more than half of North Dakota in a drought stage. (Screenshot from U.S. Drought Monitor)
Ritchison helps prepare weekly recommendations for changes in the U.S. Drought Monitor, and this week recommend the Sheridan County area in central North Dakota jump up two categories, from abnormally dry to severe drought. 
Miranda Meehan of North Dakota State University Extension helps facilitate reporting of pasture and crop conditions around the state. Unlike some years of prolonged dry weather, she said conditions have changed quickly this year, with several days of 100-plus degree heat in July. 
“This is almost like a flash drought,” Meehan said. “It was dry, but then with the heat, it just really intensified things.”
None of North Dakota is in the extreme or exceptional drought categories, which can be found in other areas of the western United States
Ritchison submits recommendations for which areas of the state fall into drought categories. He relies in part on a system called CMOR — Condition Monitoring Observations and Reports. People can submit photos, comments and anecdotal information through the nationwide system. 
There has been a spike in the number of comments submitted from North Dakota in the last week, with reports of lost crop yields, dried up watering holes for livestock and pastures that can’t be grazed. 
“Our alfalfa dried up, as we could not take a second cutting and our first cutting was only 40 bales compared to 60 last year,” Angie Johnson reported from northern Cass and southern Traill and Steele counties. “In many areas, the corn crop is completely fried and will have no yield. Soybeans and edible beans have aborted pods.”  
Cattle kick up dust in a dry pasture in Golden Valley County in western North Dakota in July 2026. (Photo courtesy of NDSU Extension)
Ranchers are having to pull livestock off of pastures early, instead using what feed they may have on hand. Some producers are baling crops to use as livestock feed instead of trying to sell  poor quality grain at the elevator. 
Ed Kessel farms near Dickinson in western North Dakota. He said farmers bale crops every year in his area where more producers also have livestock to feed, but he is seeing more of it this year. He is concerned that his wheat crop yield will be down and that it won’t meet milling quality standards, which could mean a steep price discount when he sells. 
An annual mid-July wheat tour to estimate yields put the North Dakota crop at a respectable 48 bushels per acre. But Kessel said the prolonged hot and dry weather means the yields will not be as good as projected.
“The heat took a lot of bushels away from us,” Kessel said. 
NDSU Extension provides recommendations to producers for managing a drought. 
Meehan said producers need to be careful about alternative feed sources. She said some baled crops can be high in nitrates and can be potentially fatal to an animal or an unborn calf. Similarly, shrunken watering holes can have poor water quality and should be tested. 
Meehan encouraged people to keep submitting reports through CMOR to create an accurate drought picture. Some U.S. Department of Agriculture drought relief programs are triggered by an area being in a severe drought and the reports can be helpful when applying for federal disaster assistance. 
Ritchison said he tries to read every comment. “Citizen science can very much help,” he said.
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska education commissioner says 5% spending cut won’t apply to school funding formula
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s education commissioner said a 5% spending cut Gov. Jim Pillen requested from all state agencies won’t apply to the state’s school funding formula. Commissioner Brian Maher provided an update on the Nebraska Department of Education’s response to the governor’s spending memo at a State Board of Education meeting Thursday. While portions of[...]
text:
Nebraska Education Commissioner Brian Maher of Lincoln talks to reporters after the first meeting of the School Financing Review Commission. Aug. 12, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s education commissioner said a 5% spending cut Gov. Jim Pillen requested from all state agencies won’t apply to the state’s school funding formula.
Commissioner Brian Maher provided an update on the Nebraska Department of Education’s response to the governor’s spending memo at a State Board of Education meeting Thursday. While portions of the memo will not impact the department, he said, it will require them to cut roughly $2.3 million in the agency’s current budget.
Pillen issued the memo in July, asking state agencies to immediately cut spending by a minimum of 5% on a month-to-month basis, which is expected to be in effect for both the current budget and the next biennium starting July 1, 2027. Maher noted the memo does not have the enforcement power that a statute or executive order holds, but it does signal the state’s long-term budget woes with multiple projected deficits on the horizon.
After meeting with members of the governor’s office, Maher said department officials learned that the 5% cut would not apply to the more than $2 billion in state aid going to schools, including Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act (TEEOSA) funds. It also would not apply to roughly $93 million in federal funding allocated to the department.
What’s left over is about $46.5 million in general fund dollars going to the department. Finance Officer Bryce Wilson said about $21 million of that amount is fixed costs that cannot be pulled, and parts of the remaining $25 million are also earmarked for specific purposes.
“Once we start throwing all those things together, it is not an easy task to come up with a 5% reduction for the department,” Wilson said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
There are five different “buckets” of legislative funding that could be pulled from, Wilson said. The largest is administrative costs, which was appropriated roughly $36.5 million between the state’s general fund and various cash funds. Others include the state’s vocational rehabilitation program and services for the deaf, blind and visually impaired.
No decisions about the cuts were made at the meeting. Maher said in addition to examining the funding buckets, department officials are following the governor’s advice to increase scrutiny on travel expenses and eliminate “nonessential activities.”
“I would tell you I don’t have any (activities) to say,” Maher told the board. “But we’re having some conversations on some things that we’re looking at, saying ‘Does that really help further the cause of the Nebraska Department of Education?’ And I think that’s probably a good conversation that you should have.”
Pillen’s memo also requested a hiring freeze across state agencies, but Maher said the governor’s representatives told them that order likely doesn’t apply to the Education Department. However, Maher said he intends to follow the request through a “measured approach.”
This means department officials will be looking at every vacant position and determining whether it should be filled or whether positions could be combined.
“While we may not have to do those things right now, I think it’s more a matter of should we do those things right now,” Maher said.
