name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Cassandra Sanchez came to NH to bring change. She’s leaving concerned for children’s future.
description: In 2021, Cassandra Sanchez was working for the Massachusetts Department for Children and Families in Lowell and growing frustrated with red tape and ineffective bureaucracies. She decided she needed to find a new role — one where she could enact systemic change. “I felt at a certain point that I wasn’t helping families by doing […]
text:
Cassandra Sanchez left her role as New Hampshire's child advocate last month. She had served in the role since 2022. (Photo by Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe)In 2021, Cassandra Sanchez was working for the Massachusetts Department for Children and Families in Lowell and growing frustrated with red tape and ineffective bureaucracies. She decided she needed to find a new role — one where she could enact systemic change.
“I felt at a certain point that I wasn’t helping families by doing that work,” Sanchez said. “I was actually harming them at times.”
Across the state line, the kind of role Sanchez was looking for opened up. New Hampshire had established the Office of the Child Advocate in 2018 to oversee youth-focused state systems like foster care, juvenile justice, and child welfare, and to advocate for the best interests of children in the state. The idea was to have an independent watchdog working to ensure vulnerable children are protected. When the first person to lead the office, Moira O’Neill, announced she planned to step down at the end of her term in 2022, the state put out a call for applications.
“It was almost like the perfect timing where I was getting burnt out in doing that work and feeling like it wasn’t beneficial in the way that I wanted it to,” Sanchez said, “that this posting came out.”
Fast-forward to 2026, and the optimism she felt while filling out that job application has evaporated. Last month, Sanchez was forced out of the role. She’s leaving office frazzled, disillusioned, and fearful for the future of the independent agency she’s spent the last four years leading.
In January, Gov. Kelly Ayotte had nominated Diana Fenton, a former prosecutor and lawyer for the Education Department, to replace Sanchez. However, after Fenton withdrew from consideration following accusations she held a conflict of interest in her personal life as a foster parent, Sanchez remained in the role on holdover status while a messy succession saga took place. In late July, the six months Sanchez was allowed to serve in holdover status expired, and former Manchester Police Chief Allen Aldenberg took over as acting child advocate. The search for a permanent replacement continues.
Sanchez fears for the future of the office amid this chaotic leadership transition, but she’s proud of what she accomplished over the last four years — work that, from the beginning, centered on tragedies and a belief that systems can do better to prevent them.
Entering office amid tragedy
In late 2021, 5-year-old Harmony Montgomery was reported missing in Manchester. A few years prior, a Massachusetts judge ruled the young girl would no longer live with her mother, Crystal Sorey, in Massachusetts and that her estranged father, Adam Montgomery, would have full custody in New Hampshire. Adam Montgomery was later convicted of assaulting and murdering the young girl in his Manchester home. The murder conviction was recently overturned, and a retrial is expected. Harmony’s body still hasn’t been found.
The high-profile case shocked New England and led to calls for reform, particularly after officials concluded Massachusetts failed to properly vet Adam Montgomery.
Those reform efforts were underway when Sanchez applied to be the next child advocate in New Hampshire. Her experience in Massachusetts, she said, primed her to examine interstate breakdowns in communications and other failures.
“I worked on the border of New Hampshire and Mass.,” she said. “And so having observed cross-border cases, how things could fall in between the gaps … I was like, ‘I want to be part of that. I want to be part of the solution. I want to be part of doing better by children.’”
Sanchez, who was nominated by then-Gov. Chris Sununu, took over the Office of the Child Advocate in April 2022 and continued the work of O’Neill’s team.
Sanchez said the Montgomery tragedy taught her the state needs to strengthen statutory language around what’s considered child abuse. In her view, Massachusetts was able to send Harmony to live with her father without proper vetting because of gaps in New Hampshire law that weren’t present in Massachusetts law. Sanchez worked with lawmakers for four years to attempt those changes, without success. Most recently, 2025’s House Bill 553 died on the table in the House.
Jason Taylor, an assistant child advocate who worked under both O’Neill and Sanchez, is proud to have worked with Sanchez.
“The relationships that we built with people in the state,” he said, “whether it be with group homes, whether it be with the agencies themselves, we have come miles forward during Cassandra’s time.”
A crisis in Tennessee
Another watershed event in Sanchez’s tenure as child advocate came in 2023, when she visited two New Hampshire boys sent to a care facility in Tennessee. What she saw horrified her.
At Bledsoe Youth Academy, she discovered children with rug burns on their face from aggressive restraints; unsanitary conditions; children being told “you are here because your mamas don’t love you”; children being dressed in a color-coded jumpers meant to designate them as suicidal, dangerous, or facing disciplinary measures; and “a culture of shame, humiliation, and inhumane punishment.”
“That is something that I don’t think will ever leave me in life,” she said. “I don’t. That situation is the real impactful type of situation where it’s almost like a piece of me walked away with some of their trauma.”
She promptly reported the abuse and was proud of how her office was able to force action on the issue.
Legislation was passed to enhance oversight of residential facilities by the Bureau of Children’s Behavioral Health and require visits from the Division for Children, Youth, and Families.
“That is the one area we were able to gain the most traction and impact change rather quickly,” she said, “because I do understand that change takes time and it’s often a slow process. But that one, there was a really swift response to.”
Friction with the Legislature
In March 2025, Sanchez was at a juvenile justice conference in Boston when she got a call from a colleague: A state lawmaker on the House Finance Committee had just proposed eliminating the Office of the Child Advocate as a cost-saving measure.
“We had no prior warning,” Sanchez said. “It completely blindsided us.”
Indeed, state Rep. Dan McGuire, an Epsom Republican, introduced the measure during the state budgeting process, launching a monthslong negotiation between lawmakers.
During that negotiation, what was pitched as a cost-cutting measure morphed into attacks on the office’s advocacy work. Notably, in April 2024, Sanchez appeared at a rally where she publicly advocated against a slate of legislation to ban transgender girls from playing in girls’ sports, require public school teachers and staff to reveal a child’s gender identity or sexual orientation if asked, and allow businesses to designate bathrooms and locker rooms based on biological sex. Several lawmakers, including Republican Sens. Victoria Sullivan and Tim Lang, criticized her advocacy in 2025 amid discussions to cut the office.
Sullivan told New Hampshire Public Radio at the time, the advocacy was “distracting from the actual good work that’s happening with the children, with the systems.”
After months of back-and-forth, a compromise struck by Senate President Sharon Carson saved the office, but instituted major cuts. In July 2025, when the new budget took effect, the Office of the Child Advocate’s staff went from nine employees to five. Sanchez said it’s been tough ever since. The team had to pull back on oversight measures and slow down their response times.
Taylor, the assistant child advocate, was frustrated with the way his boss was targeted for her LGBTQ+ advocacy.
“People have used the word ‘activist’ several times with me,” he said. “That Cassandra was some sort of activist, because we had one press conference that we participated in as an office, right? That’s like 1% of what took place during her tenure, and that’s what folks are talking about.”
The two are convinced that Republicans’ anger over her LGBTQ advocacy — which she still stands by — was always the deciding factor in their cuts. Sanchez said the dynamic undermines a core tenet of the office: It was designed to be independent.
“An independent agency that’s intertwined in statute the way that we are is not truly independent when the Legislature could remove your entire budget because they don’t like your advocacy,” she said. “Where is that independence truly?”
A degradation of trust and communication
When Sanchez entered office, Joe Ribsam was executive director at DCYF.
“He was very much, I will say in his time working for the agency, a visionary,” Sanchez said. “Very much looking to the future and how to expand and do better for children across the state.”
She said what made Ribsam stand out was his willingness to work with external partners. She said when crises occur in child welfare, agencies too often “shut everybody else out to say we need to figure this out on our own.”
“In those moments what’s actually far more impactful,” she said, “and has the ability to have greater system reform, is working with communities, other folks that are doing this work, getting their perspective.”
Joe Ribsam, then the director of the New Hampshire Division for Youth, Children, and Families, testifies before the House Finance Committee in March 2023. (Screenshot)
Sanchez said Ribsam did that.
In an interview with the Bulletin, Ribsam said he was fond of Sanchez as a colleague. 
“She understood the importance of being able to understand systemic challenges that systems face and that families face,” he said. “And how to make sure that when we’re making recommendations about improving things that we’re doing it from this broader systemic lens, and not just looking to, say, blame a caseworker for a bad decision when that might not have been the cause of the underlying challenge.”
He particularly appreciated the way Sanchez included frontline DCYF staff in conversations about systemic change.
“It wasn’t somebody from the outside saying, ‘I know what’s right and I’m telling you what to do,’” Ribsam said. “But rather working with people who actually do the work to understand what are all the problems that you’re seeing, and what’s the context in which you’re working trying to solve these problems for kids and families.”
Ribsam left the role in 2023 to work in the nonprofit sector before accepting a position as acting commissioner of the New Jersey Department of Children and Families. He was replaced by Jeff Fleischer, who left the role after less than a year “to pursue other interests closer to family out of state.” Marie Noonan replaced him in 2024, and still leads the division today. Sanchez has been disappointed with DCYF, which is part of the Department of Health and Human Services, since Noonan took over.
“I don’t believe there’s any partnership with the OCA and DHHS at this point,” Sanchez said. “… We make recommendations, and they say ‘thank you,’ and they move on, and they go do what they want to do.”
Sanchez doesn’t expect DCYF to take all their recommendations, but she doesn’t believe they’re being considered anymore. 
“They are failing our state’s children, and I have seen it,” she said. “I have tried not to say it, and I have tried to push behind the scenes to say things aren’t working. We, as a state, can do better.”
She acknowledges the tough job frontline social workers have and said they aren’t to blame, but added: “I really struggle with where I see leadership right now. And I don’t see the support for change, and I don’t see even just the acknowledgement of: ‘We’re not doing what we should be doing. We can do better.’”
In response to the Bulletin’s request for comment, Jake Leon, spokesperson for DHHS and DCYF, wrote in an email: “DHHS and DCYF believe that meaningful partnership with the Office of the Child Advocate is essential to protecting vulnerable children in New Hampshire. DCYF leadership has met weekly with the OCA for the past several years to hear concerns regarding children and youth in the child protection system, discuss with the OCA solutions to those concerns, and provide updates on our work responsive to OCA concerns. We have already met with Interim Child Advocate Allen Aldenberg and will continue to regularly meet with him.”
Sanchez said the change in the State House’s corner office has seen a similar dynamic. When Sununu was governor, lines of communication were open and he respected her efforts at advocacy, including the pro-LGBTQ rally she participated in, she said.
“He might not have agreed,” she said. “But I think what I felt the most from his office is the respect that we are an independent agency.”
Sanchez had “a lot of respect for” the line Sununu walked between respecting the office’s independence and engaging with it as the state’s chief executive.
“He was always a phone call away if I needed to bring something to his attention,’” she said. “But he was not calling me and saying, ‘I need you to tell me what you’re doing.’”
When Ayotte was inaugurated in January 2025 following Sununu’s retirement, Sanchez said that communication disappeared.
“She’s not engaged with the office,” she said. “I do not have a direct line to her in any way.”
Sanchez said she requested a meeting with the new governor following the inauguration but did not get it until 10 months later. Her staff formerly had communications with Ayotte’s staff, she said, but that ceased in January when Ayotte announced she wouldn’t be reappointing her.
Sanchez believes Ayotte decided to move on from her because of her LGBTQ+ advocacy. However, the governor has denied the charge, telling the Bulletin in January following Fenton’s nomination: “I have a responsibility to say who’s the best person for the job. And so I believe that the person I just nominated is going to do an excellent job, and she’s the best person for the job.”
Last month, after the Executive Council confirmed Aldenberg, Ayotte said “we’re continuing to search for the permanent child advocate to really make sure that we are acting as quickly as we can.”
Ayotte’s office did not respond to repeated questions about a lack of communication with the Office of the Child Advocate.
The Sununu Youth Services Center in Manchester. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Ongoing investigations at SYSC
Sanchez is leaving office in the middle of one of the biggest investigations of her tenure.
In late March, Sanchez and her team sent a letter to lawmakers and other elected officials alleging that staff at the state’s biggest juvenile detention center, the Sununu Youth Services Center, had been potentially abusive to and neglectful of the facility’s child inmates. They reported an overly restrictive lockdown that denied children access to the outdoors and an adequate education. And they said they reviewed security camera footage showing a staff member employing an illegal restraint on a child, resulting in a broken bone. 
The Office of the Child Advocate is continuing its investigation and monitoring of the facility. The Disability Rights Center-NH subsequently announced it had done its own investigation and reported more troubling accusations. The Attorney General’s Office and a state Senate subcommittee are also doing parallel investigations. More allegations, including children being forced to urinate on the floor of their cells, unnecessary strip searches, and dried blood found on the walls, have emerged as a result of the investigations.
The Sununu Youth Services Center, formerly known as the Youth Detention Center or YDC, has a long history of abuse. Even before this year’s allegations, hundreds of victims have come forward with allegations spanning decades and the state has paid millions in legal settlements.
Sanchez is “extremely frustrated” she’s being forced to leave in the middle of the new investigation and before the office drafts its final report. She worries that, in her absence, there could be outside pressure to downplay certain elements of the report, which is no longer in her control.
“These are children, and they may have made poor decisions, but they are children who need help,” Sanchez said. “And the system and the way it’s working right now is not helping them. It’s harming them further, and I do worry that that aspect is going to be either not allowed to get out public or downplayed completely.”
The Attorney General’s Office’s final report found leadership issues and staffing shortages, but no evidence of physical abuse by staff. Sanchez has publicly criticized the findings, telling the Bulletin the report “put the blame on the children almost completely” and “very minimal blame elsewhere,” which is “just not accurate.” 
Sanchez said staff experiences are important but should be balanced with children’s testimony. She hopes the Office of the Child Advocate’s final report centers the children’s experience more. However, she’s concerned the office will be pressured to be “more aligned with” the attorney general “because I’ve seen the governor’s coverage of supporting that report and I am not sure that the state wants the facts to show otherwise.”
Leon, the DHHS spokesperson, wrote in his email to the Bulletin: “We are actively addressing the long-standing operational challenges at the Sununu Youth Services Center identified in recent reports and have taken immediate steps to implement recommendations provided to us by several stakeholders, including the DOJ and the OCA. … We remain firmly committed to providing trauma-informed care for youth and working with the Office of the Child Advocate and other stakeholders to improve the operations and culture at SYSC.”
An uncertain future
Sanchez was prepared to serve on holdover status until a permanent replacement was found. However, the state’s human resources department informed her in late June that state law forbade her from serving in holdover status longer than six months.
At that point, she believed that Taylor, her deputy, would be offered the interim position. Taylor said human resources told him to prepare to take the role. However, earlier this month, Taylor said human resources reversed course and informed him he would not be given the interim position. He said the team only learned that Aldenberg would become the acting child advocate when they read it in the New Hampshire Union Leader.
While Sanchez is proud of the work the office has done, what she’s left with is uncertainty.
“I have more questions than I have answers at this point for the future of the office,” she said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: NIPSCO seeks $38M from customers for first 3 months of forced coal plant run
description: Separately, state regulators denied a $741 million, five-year transmission improvement plan NIPSCO submitted.
text:
Federal orders have kept coal-powered units at NIPSCO's R.M. Schahfer Generating Station in Wheatfield, Indiana open past a scheduled retirement date at the end of 2025. (Stock photo by Monty Rakusen via Getty Images)The Northern Indiana Public Service Co. spent $116.7 million from January through March to comply with Trump administration orders forcing the operation of two Jasper County coal units scheduled for retirement at the end of last year.
Coal units at the R.M. Schahfer Generating Station earned $33.5 million in coal-generated electricity sale revenue over that period, according to a Tuesday filing with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
Utilities warn of soaring costs related to Trump order for Indiana coal plants to stay open

NIPSCO is asking federal regulators to let it collect $38 million in quarterly costs from customers in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s 15-state footprint, which includes Indiana. The figure includes $2.8 million in profits for the utility company.
“We recognize that customers are focused on their energy bills and understand the importance of keeping energy affordable,” the company said in a statement to the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “… FERC has established a process that allows utilities to seek recovery of costs to comply with these federal orders, subject to FERC review and approval.”
“As this process moves forward, NIPSCO remains committed to managing costs responsibly to comply with this order, while providing safe, reliable service for our customers and supporting electric reliability across the region,” the statement said.
Federal orders’ price tag
Schahfer’s two remaining coal units, Nos. 17 and 18, were set to retire Dec. 31 after four decades in operation in the northwest Indiana town of Wheatfield.
But on Dec. 23, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued emergency orders to NIPSCO, CenterPoint Energy and MISO, directing them to “take all measures necessary to ensure” units at Schahfer and the F.B. Culley Generating Station in southern Indiana’s Warrick County were operational for 90 more days.
Subsequent 90-day directives in March and June have extended the forced operations at both facilities through Sept. 19. The Department of Energy orders were made under the Federal Power Act.
NIPSCO will charge customers through a tariff placed on the energy markets operated by MISO — after a 60-day notice period initiated with Tuesday’s filing and once the regional transmission operator submits and obtains federal approval for a separate compliance filing.
Meanwhile, the costs incurred on Schahfer’s coal units continue to stack up — even as both units have stopped bringing in revenue, amid extended outages.
‘Significant’ costs expected going forward
Unit 17 was available for coal-generated energy sales through February despite being derated from a capacity of 424 megawatts to 325 megawatts. In March, NIPSCO placed it in a planned outage for repairs and maintenance, with the outage scheduled to end in October.
Unit 18, meanwhile, has been in forced outage for more than a year, since last July, when a low-pressure rotator blade failed.
Story continues below.
20260804-5179_Transmittal Letter 202(c) Cost Recovery (final) (1)
 
Restoring the unit will require work on the turbine, generator, coal-handling system, mill, cooling tower and more, according to the filing.
“NIPSCO will need to incur significant expenses to bring Unit 18 up to operational capability consistent with the DOE Orders,” the company wrote. “… DOE is aware of the investments that have been, and will be, necessary to comply.”
The unit is expected to go back online in mid-December.
NIPSCO will make similar filings to recover costs incurred under the two later federal orders, as well as any future ones. The utility is preparing to keep the coal units operational “through late 2028 or early 2029” if required to do so, according to its filing.
State-level denial of hike for infrastructure work
Also this week, state regulators dealt NIPSCO a blow when they rejected the utility’s $741 million, five-year plan for natural gas transmission, distribution and storage infrastructure improvements and charges.
Indiana’s TDSIC statute lets utilities, with Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approval, recover 80% of costs incurred through a tracker. The remaining 20% is recovered through the next rate case.
Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission Chair Anthony Swinger speaks during a hearing on March 24, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The utility said the plan would “support continued improvements focused on modernizing and strengthening NIPSCO’s natural gas system, including investments intended to enhance system safety, reliability and resiliency.”
But in a scathing 3-0 denial issued Wednesday, the IURC said  that NIPSCO “failed to provide sufficient evidence for the Commission to determine that each proposed eligible improvement is cost-justified.”
“We decline to accept NIPSCO’s suggestion that cost-justification can be inferred because the projects were selected by internal subject-matter experts,” Commissioners Bob Deig, Anthony Swinger and David Veleta wrote.
The regulators cited a 2024 state Supreme Court opinion dealing with Duke Energy Indiana, arguing that the decision set a higher standard for the burden of proof utilities face on their infrastructure plans.
NIPSCO’s is the first plan to be considered since then, according to a concurring opinion authored by Swinger, the IURC’s chair.
“Although NIPSCO did provide more information for some projects as compared to others in its attempt to provide cost-justification, such as the rural extensions, we decline to sift through the proposed projects to create a reasonable TDSIC plan,” the regulators wrote in their joint order.
In order to try again, NIPSCO will have to file a new case with “the sufficient evidentiary foundation” for regulators to consider each proposed project.
“We appreciate the Commission’s review of our filing,” the utility said. “… We are reviewing the Commission’s order to assess its impact on the proposed investments and determine next steps. NIPSCO remains focused on delivering safe and reliable service and meeting the energy needs of the customers and communities we serve.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont sticks to a fiscal discipline not always applauded by labor
description: Unions support Gov. Ned Lamont, even if they remain unenthused about his hostility to committing to new things that have a recurring cost.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont stood in dappled sunlight on College Street in New Haven on Tuesday, basking in the praise of labor and community leaders at a rally outside the red-brick headquarters of Unite Here, one of the unions often at odds with one of the Democratic governor’s alma maters, Harvard and Yale.
“As you’re going to hear from my union brothers and sisters, it’s not complicated why labor is supporting our governor, Ned Lamont,” said Josh Stanley, the secretary-treasurer of Unite Here Local 217, whose members include cafeteria workers at Yale. “Can I get a woo-woo?”
Arms tightly by his side and hands folded at the belt, the wealthy businessman-turned-governor, whose family tree includes a capitalist great-grandfather made rich by J.P. Morgan and a socialist grand-uncle made famous fighting McCarthyism, gamely accepted the proffered woo-woo.
Lamont, 72, a Democrat elected in 2018 and reelected in 2022, is the first Connecticut governor in 48 years to face a primary. His challenger, state Rep. Josh Elliott, 41, is hitting him from the left, claiming a man of wealth from Greenwich is tone-deaf to the economic inequities and the needs of working families.
Most unions beg to differ, even if they remain unenthused about the governor’s central political brand — a hostility about committing to new things that come with a recurring cost and no commensurate source of revenue. While Elliott insists Lamont is trying to rebrand himself as a lefty-come-lately on issues of the moment such as Trump and ICE, his essential approach to money is little changed.
Initiatives Lamont promises to pursue in a third term, notably the state expanding healthcare options and taking on greater responsibility for special education, is more about finding efficiencies than writing big checks.
The “Connecticut Option” the governor is pursuing with Comptroller Sean Scanlon  would be a public-private partnership giving the state greater influence in the cost and delivery of healthcare without assuming the costs of a true public option.
Elements would include lowering  premiums by driving patients toward a designated network of high-quality, lower-cost healthcare facilities and using the state’s buying power to negotiate caps on costs. Similarly, his ideas about providing relief to municipalities on special education involve finding efficiencies and negotiating lower costs on expensive out-of-district placements.
“Everybody I’m around in the legislature, both sides of the aisle, ‘More, more, more, more!’ And I go, ‘Better, better, better, better!’ You know, it’s a slightly different mindset,” Lamont said in an interview. “I’m an entrepreneur, that’s what I am. I think that’s what a progressive is. Progressives are not just about more, they’re about better.”

Gov. Ned Lamont, center, gestures toward U.S. Rep. John Larson, D-Conn., during a campaign event, Saturday, July 25, 2026, in Bristol, Conn. Credit: Jessica Hill / AP

That’s not the reason why most unions are siding with Lamont in the Democratic primary on Tuesday. On money, they agree to disagree.
The governor’s eight years in office have been good ones for labor’s agenda: Passage of individual laws assuring, among other things, one of the nation’s highest minimum wages, a near-universal mandate on private employers to provide sick days, and protections aimed at Amazon warehouse workers.
He vetoed one high-priority labor bill, a measure that would have provided jobless benefits for strikers. But Sen. Julie Kushner, D-Danbury, co-chair of the Labor and Public Employees Committee, said she and the governor are negotiating a compromise to be considered in 2027. She has endorsed him for reelection.
“Obviously, I was a little reticent,” she said. “You can’t be the chair of the labor committee and have a veto by the governor on your priority bill and just say, ‘Oh, well.’ And I will say to the governor, to his credit, before he vetoed the bill last year, he called me and said we need to work on a compromise.”
And on May 11, Lamont signed into law an omnibus workforce development and worker protection bill packed with disparate labor goodies, including enhanced benefits for teachers and health workers assaulted on the job and making contractors liable for subcontractors who stiff workers on wages.
All those things were dutifully noted this week outside Unite Here by speakers representing the AFL-CIO, the Connecticut Education Association and the building trades, the latter represented by Joe Toner, an ebullient and white-haired trade unionist with a habit of going to topics that others might avoid. 
Lamont was pleasantly surprised when Toner expanded the list of accolades by mentioning a trait that more often than not inspires reactions ranging from anger to eye-rolling among labor leaders: His reluctance to take on new spending without a steady source of matching revenue — or to sign off on sharply higher taxes on the rich.
“Fiscal responsibility means a lot, and I know I’m a Democrat. I’ve been a lifelong Democrat, and I will say sometimes there’s not enough money to go around to be responsible and still run the state of Connecticut, right?” Toner said. “Think about the responsibility that has been displayed over the last eight years. What Gov. Lamont’s doing right now is he’s paying for the pensions that weren’t paid for the predecessors before him.”
There were no woo-woos. 
But no boos, either.
Paying down pension debt is not the best talking point in a Democratic primary, but Lamont rarely misses a chance to talk about it. When he took office, Connecticut had one of the worst unfunded pension liabilities in the U.S., a consequence of generous benefits and a failure over multiple generations of politicians to invest in a pension fund.
“We were 35% funded. Now we’re 70%. We’ll fall back 10% because the market will do something bad,” Lamont said.

Gov. Ned Lamont speaks during a news conference celebrating NSF Quantum Technologies Engine being awarded a National Science Foundation federal award at UConn Hartford’s campus on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

But a string of budget surpluses that have left Connecticut with a full rainy day fund and allowed Lamont to pay down pension debt is not a reason to loosen fiscal guardrails set in 2017 that require revenues gains from historically volatile sources to be held in reserve or reduce debt, Lamont said.
Elliott complains that Lamont is the beneficiary of luck — being in office when the state economy has improved and the Wall Street profits important to Connecticut’s income have boomed.
“We’ve had a pretty good economy, no question about it. And Trump and Biden threw a lot of money at us during COVID,” Lamont said. “We’ve also gone from being one of the worst-performing economies in the country to the 12th-best, or whatever you want to argue about. That makes a big frigging difference. Look at the pension. We finally got a good guy in there as chairman of the IAC.”
The IAC is the Investment Advisory Council that advises the state treasurer on investment policies. 
“We’ve gone from a chronic under-performer for 40 years to outperforming where we were before by about 1.5%. You go 1.5%, it’s $60 billion. One and a half percent of $60 billion was worth $900 million to our pension last year. So, I pay down a billion. We get $900 million,” Lamont said. “Pretty soon, you’re talking about real money.”
One of those earlier chairmen of the Investment Advisory Council was a fellow named Ned Lamont. He was installed there by Gov. Lowell P. Weicker Jr. and served throughout the entirety of Weicker’s eventful single term.
“It was insane when I was there,” Lamont said. “I couldn’t invest in international stocks, because of, you know, Mandela and South Africa. And I said, ‘Apartheid is over. Mandela’s in office.’ If you say I can’t invest in one third of the economy or the world economy, you’re holding us back.”
Lamont said Weicker, who took office looking at the worst budget shortfall in the U.S., understandably was more concerned about keeping government going.
“Weicker, I love Weicker, but he couldn’t give a shit about the pension funds either,” Lamont said. “You know, he just said, ‘I’m cutting support for Sonny, and you’re telling me about the pension fund?’ ”
Weicker’s son, Sonny, had intellectual disabilities, and he came to symbolize a broader population that relied on important state services.
Lamont’s predecessor, Dannel P. Malloy, was the first governor to make the actuarially required contributions to the state pension fund, even though he, too, faced a severe budget crisis.
Deferring pension contributions remains a crutch for state and local governments when a chief elected official is faced with immediate service cuts and tax increases — or pushing off pension investments.
“Guess who’s doing that now? Mamdani,” Lamont said.
Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York City and was quickly confronted with a projected budget shortfall of more than $5 billion. With help from the state, he managed to balance the budget.
“Want to know where he got that extra dough? Defer some payments, stretch them out,” Lamont said. He laughed and added, “Believe it or not, his pension’s in better shape than Connecticut, though. So I can’t be too harsh.”
The pension gimmick comes at a cost. By pushing back a pension debt repayment plan five years to 2037, it will cost New York about $7 billion in long-term interest.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire’s childcare crisis does not end when a child turns 5
description: Every time I read an article about New Hampshire’s childcare crisis, I notice the same thing. The conversation almost always focuses on infants, toddlers, and preschool-aged children. Those concerns are real and deserve attention. Families need affordable early care and education, providers need sustainable funding, and educators deserve wages that reflect t[...]
text:
"Many elementary schools dismiss students between 2:30 and 3 p.m., while parents may not leave work until 5 p.m. or later." (Photo by Dave Cummings/New Hampshire Bulletin)Every time I read an article about New Hampshire’s childcare crisis, I notice the same thing. The conversation almost always focuses on infants, toddlers, and preschool-aged children. Those concerns are real and deserve attention. Families need affordable early care and education, providers need sustainable funding, and educators deserve wages that reflect the importance of their work. 
But when I scroll through the comments on these articles, parents are often talking about something else entirely. They are asking where they can find an afterschool program, what they are supposed to do during the summer, and how they can keep working when school ends hours before their workday does.
Those comments point to a gap between the childcare conversation happening at the policy level and the reality families are experiencing. Children do not stop needing care when they enter kindergarten, and parents do not stop working when their child turns 5. The challenge simply changes. Instead of searching for infant care or full-day preschool, families begin piecing together before-school care, afterschool programs, school vacations, teacher workshop days, unexpected closures, snow days, and summer care.
As the network lead for the New Hampshire Afterschool Network, I spend a lot of time speaking with out-of-school time programs across the state. I hear from directors with limited staffing. I hear from programs trying to keep tuition affordable while also paying qualified staff, purchasing supplies, providing food, and covering transportation. I also hear from families who have called every program in their area and still cannot find an opening.
Somewhere along the way, school-age care became separated from the larger child care conversation. We use the terms early childhood education, child care, school-age care, and afterschool as though families experience each of them as a completely separate system. They do not. A parent is simply trying to make sure their child has somewhere safe, supportive, and engaging to be while they work.
The need does not disappear when the school day begins because the school day and the workday do not operate on the same schedule. Many elementary schools dismiss students between 2:30 and 3 p.m., while parents may not leave work until 5 p.m. or later. School is also closed during vacations, holidays, professional development days, and much of the summer. Families are left trying to fill those hours through a combination of relatives, neighbors, flexible work arrangements, paid programs, and, sometimes, no care at all.
This is not an argument for taking attention or resources away from early childhood education. It is an argument for looking at how children are cared for across the full continuum. A family with a preschooler and an elementary school student is not experiencing two unrelated systems. They are trying to meet the needs of both children while maintaining employment and managing the cost of living. When care is unavailable for either child, the entire family feels the impact.
Employers feel it, too. Child care is regularly described as a workforce issue, but school-age care is rarely included in that discussion. If a parent cannot return to work because they cannot find infant care, we recognize that as a child care and workforce problem. If a parent has to leave work every afternoon because there is no afterschool option available, the effect is the same. The employee loses hours or may leave the workforce altogether, while the employer loses a reliable worker. The child’s age changes, but the workforce problem does not.
School-age programs also provide far more than supervision. They offer opportunities for children to build friendships, explore STEM, participate in the arts, receive homework support, stay physically active, and develop relationships with caring adults. They can provide meals, mentoring, leadership opportunities, mental health support, and a sense of belonging. For some children, an afterschool or summer program is one of the most consistent places in their lives.
School-age programs are part of the child care system, yet they are often overlooked in policy conversations and public messaging. Even the language we use can make them seem optional. The word “afterschool” may sound like a club or extracurricular activity, but for many families, it is the only thing making a full workday possible.
New Hampshire needs to begin asking a broader question. Instead of only asking how we address the childcare shortage for children from birth to age 5, we should ask how children are cared for across the continuum. That includes infancy and preschool, but it also includes elementary and middle school, before and after school, school vacations, and summer.
Families have already been telling us what they need. Their comments appear beneath nearly every article about the childcare crisis: What about my school-age child? Where can I find afterschool care? What am I supposed to do all summer? We should start listening.
The childcare crisis does not end when a child enters kindergarten. It simply changes shape. If New Hampshire wants to create meaningful childcare solutions for families and strengthen its workforce, school-age care and out-of-school time programs must be included from the beginning — not added later as an afterthought.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansans’ right to know about criminal complaints at stake in Linn County case over sealed records
description: The First Amendment protects the public’s right of access to criminal complaints filed in court against adult defendants. A law sealing such records is unconstitutional in large part because public access to the criminal complaint “reflects the importance of its role in the criminal trial process and the public’s interest in knowing its contents.” But in 202[...]
text:
Kansans have a right to know, writes KPA Executive Director Emily Bradbury. But a law passed last year has hidden adult criminal cases. (Getty Images)The First Amendment protects the public’s right of access to criminal complaints filed in court against adult defendants. A law sealing such records is unconstitutional in large part because public access to the criminal complaint “reflects the importance of its role in the criminal trial process and the public’s interest in knowing its contents.”
But in 2025, the Kansas Legislature amended a statute to seal all criminal cases filed in Kansas courts that involve arrest warrants. Under that statute and a corresponding policy developed and implemented by the state’s Office of Judicial Administration, court clerks are not authorized to unseal such cases until proof that the warrant was served is filed in court. Until then, adult criminal cases proceed in secret.
Denied access to criminal records in Kansas boy’s death sparks First Amendment lawsuit

The state defends this practice by claiming that sealing criminal complaints in cases where an arrest warrant has not yet been served promotes public safety. But that rationale falls particularly flat in a Linn County District Court criminal case filed last year in connection with the death of a 13-year-old boy.
That case, which names Linn County resident Damon Leonard as the defendant, has been sealed for months even though Leonard has been in custody since law enforcement issued press releases about the charges in December, he was convicted of a related felony in Missouri and given a four-year prison sentence there in May, and the Kansas attorney general’s office announced murder charges against him in June.
Yet the case has remained sealed, presumably either because the arrest warrant has not been served or because proof of such service has not been filed with the court. Making matters worse, the same state law authorizing the seal also requires court clerks to deny the case’s very existence.
The local newspaper of record, the Linn County News, filed a civil lawsuit to resolve this legal limbo, arguing that sealing the case against Leonard violates the paper’s First Amendment right of public access to the complaint. The News’ right of access is based largely on the fact that in the United States, there is a “historic tradition of public access to the charging document in a criminal case.” Rulings on the News’s motion to temporarily void the statute and policy, as well as the state’s motion to dismiss, are pending.
Remarkably, the state’s central defense is that the News has no right to the complaint because the state claims the “historic tradition” of public access to court records does not exist in Kansas.
In support, the state revealed in its filings that when the state’s court system first adopted an electronic case management system in the early 2000s, “criminal cases filed in the district courts in which an arrest warrant was issued or applied for were sealed” in their entirety “until the arrest warrant was executed (or the application for the warrant was denied).”
The KPA’s members, and I daresay the public at large, were unaware of this policy to keep criminal cases secret.
The News’ lawsuit has revealed that the policy went unchecked until 2019, when the Kansas Supreme Court adopted a new case management system and implemented new court rules expressly establishing that criminal cases were not to be automatically sealed. The state even sent an email to attorneys licensed to practice law in the state in 2024 admitting that the rules had to change “due to our evolving understanding of the legal propriety of keeping cases presumptively sealed without a particularized rationale for sealing them.”
Still, the officials who are defendants in the News’s case claim that denying public access — not only to criminal complaints but also to the entire criminal case file — is justifiable because the Legislature’s 2025 statute merely restored the state’s authority to categorically seal criminal cases. In other words, the state argues that because criminal cases were routinely sealed in the past, the challenged law is constitutional and the News’s case should be dismissed.
But as the News put it in its filings, a policy authorizing the seal of court records for the better part of 20 years is “irrelevant to the inescapable legal conclusion that adult criminal complaints in courts throughout this country are among the types of court records that are historically and traditionally open.”
Moreover, a state law cannot trump the First Amendment, particularly if its existence is predicated on restoring a policy that, itself, was unconstitutional. As explained by the News in its case, “it is foundational to our democracy that constitutional rights cannot be legislatively abdicated.”
Still, unless and until the challenged statute is struck down, criminal cases in Kansas will continue to be automatically sealed.  But for now, the News’s lawsuit has shown that the state’s court administrators, many of them lawyers, appear to struggle with accepting the existence, let alone the necessity, of constitutional guardrails for handling court records.
In a democracy, the public has every reason to expect better from its courts.
Emily Bradbury is the executive director of the Kansas Press Association and Kansas Newspaper Foundation. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. title: Wisconsin critics say proposed federal changes would roll back Head Start standards
description: The federal government announced a proposed federal rule Thursday that rewrites or eliminates many regulations for Head Start early education programs nationwide. The Administration for Children and Families in the Department of Health and Human Services said the proposed change would provide more flexibility and help expand Head Start enrollment. Wisconsin[...]
text:
Children at a Sun Prairie Head Start center operated by Reach Dane gather in a circle with their teachers for a story. (Photo courtesy of Reach Dane)The federal government announced a proposed federal rule Thursday that rewrites or eliminates many regulations for Head Start early education programs nationwide.
The Administration for Children and Families in the Department of Health and Human Services said the proposed change would provide more flexibility and help expand Head Start enrollment.
Wisconsin providers and childcare experts, however, say the proposed rule would roll back standards for classroom quality, teacher qualifications and health services.
The new rule would end supports for children with disabilities and children who speak languages other than English, as well as requirements that Head Start providers work closely with the families of children enrolled in the early education program, advocates say.
https://wisconsinexaminer.com/2026/08/07/repub/trump-administration-threatens-to-gut-head-start-rules/
“The term ‘flexibility’ is being used to make it sound friendly,” said Jen Bailey, executive director of Reach Dane, which operates Head Start programs in 13 locations in Dane County and Green County. “We all like flexibility in our work.”
Bailey, who is president of the Wisconsin Head Start Association, spoke in an interview earlier this week, before the notice of proposed rulemaking was posted Thursday.
Bailey said existing rules already give Head Start programs flexibility to operate. “We’re designed to meet the needs of our local communities and kids and families,” she said. “I see this as a means to not fund the program, because if you eliminate many of the standards, then you can justify the flat funding we’ve been under the last couple of years. Flat funding is really a funding cut.”
Providers have been bracing for the rule change for several months following published reports from the Associated Press and other news outlets about early drafts of the document.
“Headstart, like childcare, is not just about making sure children are physically safe from dramatic harm,” said Jennie Mauer, executive director for the Wisconsin Head Start Association, which represents 39 Head Start programs across the state. “It’s really about nurturing their growth and development, so they come to the K-3 to 12 system prepared and ready to participate.”
About 12,000 children in Wisconsin are enrolled in Head Start, Mauer said this week.
School readiness for children in poverty
Head Start was launched in 1965 to help children from low-income families become ready for school and currently serves about 670,000 children in the U.S., according to a new report from the Children’s Equity Project at Arizona State University.
The report, a response to concerns about the program’s future that have been circulating since President Donald Trump took office, analyzes the potential impact of changes along the lines of those the federal government announced Thursday.
“Decades of research have found that children who attend Head Start show improved language, literacy, and social emotional outcomes after program participation and even improved rates of educational attainment and some intergenerational effects,” the ASU report states.
The report attributes those gains to national standards that Head Start has established for local providers to follow, drawn up to ensure higher quality early education,
Quality is important for all children in early education, the ASU report states, but “it is especially important to children who may have higher needs, such as children living in poverty, children with disabilities, children experiencing homelessness, and children involved in the child welfare system — the very children Head Start prioritizes in its services and those who demonstrate the most benefit from these services.”
Some of the performance standards that the proposed new rule eliminates were updated in 2016 and 2024.  
In some instances, the rule would replace Head Start standards with the standards set by childcare regulators in the Head Start provider’s state.
For example, the new rule eliminates a Head Start standard for the ratio between the number of children and the number of childcare teachers, deferring instead to the ratios prescribed in state regulations.
The current rule requires one adult caregiver or teacher for every four infants in a Head Start center. That aligns with Wisconsin state regulations and those of 34 other states and the District of Columbia, according to the ASU report.
But 15 states’ current regulations allow for more infants, and changing the Head Start standard would mean increasing the number of infants per adult in those states.
Head Start also requires one teacher for four 2-year-old children. Only three states also require that ratio, according to the ASU report. In 47 states — including Wisconsin — and D.C., local rules allow for a larger number of 2-year-olds.
“Changing the staff-to-child ratios is dangerous and a health and safety hazard,” said Bailey of Reach Dane. “We enroll many children with disabilities such as autism that need a lot of support to keep them safe.”
Because children growing up in poverty face additional adversities that require greater support, “It would be categorically unsafe to shift to different ratios in the name of flexibility,” Bailey said. “Children will be harmed.
Ending duplication — or lowering standards?
The notice of the proposed new rule states that the agency is eliminating a number of provisions in the current standards because they’re already specified in the federal law that governs the Head Start program.
For example, the new rule eliminates requirements in the current standards for Head Start programs to evaluate children’s health, help families navigate the healthcare system, help pregnant women get access to healthcare and insurance, teach children about brushing their teeth and provide mental health supports for children and families.
“Head Start programs remain responsible for ensuring the provision of health, mental health, and related services per the Act and must also continue to comply with applicable state and local requirements,” the notice states.
Mauer said the standards are supposed to help local programs carry out the federal law’s requirements, however.
“I think it leaves a large set of unanswered questions about what some of the components mean if there’s no explanation of how to implement them,” Mauer said. “There’s a lot of missing detail.”
The Administration for Children and Families said in its announcement Thursday that the new rule “restores flexibility to programs to meet local needs, reduces regulatory burden and administrative costs, and aims to increase available slots and services for families. It is projected to preserve or expand as many as 236,000 Head Start slots nationwide and save $2.2 billion .”
Mauer said that the proposal to serve some 200,000 more children nationwide “leaves a big unanswered question of how do they intend to get there.”
While the rule appears to give Head Start programs permission to continue to offer the comprehensive services that are outlined in the current standards, there’s no new money being allocated for Head Start, Mauer said.
“The math doesn’t math to me,” Mauer said. “It demonstrates to me a fundamental misunderstanding of what it takes to operate a classroom with small children.”
The federal proposal announced Thursday drew protests from a range of Head Start advocates and supporters. Some linked it to the Trump administrations’ past actions that delayed Head Start funding, closed federal offices that served local Head Start programs and at one point proposed zeroing out Head Start funding in the next budget year. The program was subsequently added back in.
The Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025, drawn up prior to Trump’s election in 2024 as a proposed blueprint for the next president, called for eliminating the program.
The new proposal amounts to “undoing the safeguards that have helped make Head Start one of the nation’s most effective public investments in young children and families,” the Wisconsin Early Childhood Association said in a statement.
Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) condemned the proposal, saying it “puts kids’ wellbeing and safety on the line and is all part of the President’s plan to shut down Head Start entirely, and it’s shameful.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Butter, baseball and a brand-new train: Indiana State Fair returns Friday
description: If there was any question whether Hoosier cuisine could find new uses for butter, deep fryers and over-the-top fixings, this year’s Indiana State Fair sets the record straight. Consider the butter-dipped ice cream: vanilla soft serve coated in melted butter, which hardens into a golden shell finished with flaky sea salt. Or the deep-fried Lindor […]
text:
A 4-H vegetable display is prepared for the 2026 Indiana State Fair at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)If there was any question whether Hoosier cuisine could find new uses for butter, deep fryers and over-the-top fixings, this year’s Indiana State Fair sets the record straight.
Consider the butter-dipped ice cream: vanilla soft serve coated in melted butter, which hardens into a golden shell finished with flaky sea salt.
Or the deep-fried Lindor Dubai chocolate truffles, skewered three at a time, dunked in funnel cake batter and fried until golden.
For fairgoers who consider a plain fried Oreo merely a starting point, there’s also a Hot Cheeto fried Oreo rolled in spicy red dust, drizzled with nacho cheese and crowned with more Cheeto crumbles.
They’re just a few of the nearly 50 new foods awaiting visitors when the 169th Indiana State Fair opens Friday at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis.
The fair runs through Aug. 23 and will be closed on Mondays. Organizers expect more than 850,000 guests over its 15-day run.
This year’s “Always a Hit” theme, presented in partnership with the Indianapolis Indians, carries baseball into attractions, food and entertainment across the fairgrounds. It also dovetails with celebrations of the nation’s 250th anniversary by pairing two long-standing American summer traditions — baseball and fairs.
Visitors can play Wiffle Ball at a miniature stadium, watch baseball movies in a throwback video store, attend concerts at a newly expanded free stage and ride a new train around the north side of the fairgrounds.
And because no fair theme is complete until it reaches the concession stand, the 2026 menu is loaded with dishes swinging for the fences.
Butter, batter and ballpark bites
The Taste of the Fair competition includes 48 new creations from vendors across the fairgrounds.
Among them is the Grand Slam Mary, a Bloody Mary garnished with a burger slider, hot dog slider, waffle fries, soft pretzel stick, Cracker Jacks, celery and lemon.
The Junkyard Spam Dog piles macaroni and cheese, coleslaw, potato chips, barbecue sauce and sliced jalapeños onto a Spam-brand hot dog. The “S’Mork” combines slow-smoked pulled pork and the flavors of a s’more on a fried sugar biscuit.
The World’s Tallest Fry, an extra-tall spiral-cut potato, on display during a Taste of the Fair preview at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Bacon Jalapeño HoneyBun Burger is one of dozens of new concessions on sale at the Indiana State Fair in 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Sweet and Salty Spiral, a stack of spiral potatoes topped with bacon and chocolate syrup.  (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The "Junkyard Spam Dog" twist on the classic hot dog is made with 100% Spam, topped with jalapeños, crispy onions, macaroni and cheese, chips and barbecue sauce. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Nitro Hog BBQ’s S’MORK combines smoked pulled pork and s’more flavors on a fried sugar biscuit and was featured at a Taste of the Fair preview at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Deep Fried Lindor Dubai Chocolate Truffles on display during a Taste of the Fair preview at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A Cookie Butter Biscoff Funnel Cake on display during a Taste of the Fair preview at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Cosmic Mango Coconut Dirty Soda is a lemon-lime soda  mixed with mango puree and coconut cream. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Dirty sodas like the Dirty Slime Licker are popular at the Indiana State Fair this year. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)Samples of strawberry shortcake on display at the Indiana State Fair Preview Day on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Samples of the Bacon Jalapeño HoneyBun Burger in the works during a Taste of the Fair preview in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)LeRoy Lewis III, director of community and media engagement for the Indiana State Fair, speaks during a media preview at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana State Fair is channeling nostalgia this year with a VHS revival on display at the Harvest Pavilion on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Nostalgic artwork on display at the Indiana State Fair. Pictured is Jim Carrey from the 1994 movie "The Mask." (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Pictured is the entrance to the Indiana State Fair Midway on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Other new dishes include a bacon-jalapeño HoneyBun burger; buffalo chicken dip pizza; pork rind nachos; Nashville hot fried pickles; a grilled cheese sandwich stuffed with Havarti, cheddar and dill pickles; and General Tso fries topped with ground bison.
The sweet side of the lineup includes a cookie butter Biscoff funnel cake, a blue raspberry milkshake, a lemon shake-up float and a fresh brownie topped with high-butterfat ice cream, homemade whipped cream and hot fudge.
Even the drinks carry the theme. 
Sun King Brewery created a beer brewed with corn and smoked malt to evoke the flavor of a State Fair corn dog. The Great American Shake layers vanilla ice cream with red and blue syrup, whipped cream, patriotic sprinkles and a cherry.
Fairgoers can vote for their favorite new dish by scanning QR codes posted at participating concession stands. The top three will be announced during the fair’s final week.
For visitors pacing their spending along with their appetites, the fair is again offering a $5 value menu with affordable options available at concession stands throughout the fairgrounds.
Baseball takes the field
The Indianapolis Indians partnership gets a home field of its own at Schumacher Stadium, a Wiffle Ball diamond in the Meijer Family Fun Park named for longtime Indians executive Max Schumacher.
The field will host free play, community games, tournaments and appearances throughout the fair, too.
A second-weekend “Hot Diggity Dog Games” celebration will extend the ballpark theme beyond the diamond. The Oscar Mayer Wienermobile is scheduled to visit Aug. 15 and 16, when fairgoers can expect hot dog-themed games and activities.
“What’s baseball without hot dogs,” LeRoy Lewis III, the fair’s director of community and media engagement, said during a Thursday media preview.
Corn Dog Beer, brewed with corn and smoked malt, on display during a Taste of the Fair preview at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Events are expected to include a hot dog toss, a corn dog eating contest, a hot dog assembly relay and what Lewis called the “inflatable Glizzy 500,” in which competitors dress as hot dogs and race.
The baseball theme also figures prominently in “REWIND: A VHS Revival,” a new immersive exhibit built around the video-store era of the 1980s through the early 2000s.
The exhibit features vintage movie-poster art, a baseball movie theater, an Indianapolis Indians gift shop, a “Moulin Rouge” speakeasy and the return of the Indy CD & Vinyl pop-up store. It is open daily and included with fair admission.
Lewis said movies shown throughout the fair will include baseball favorites from past decades.
All aboard
One of the fair’s largest physical additions is the Indiana State Fair Train, a new family ride that will carry passengers on a one-mile loop around the north side of the grounds.
Two trains, each capable of holding about 90 passengers, will depart from a newly constructed depot. Each narrated round trip will last approximately 15 minutes.
The ride costs $5, and visitors can also pay with midway tickets.
“REWIND: A VHS Revival” recreates the video-store era at the Indiana State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“You will not find another state fair that has an amazing train like this,” Lewis said.
Fair officials said the ride is a nod to the trains that historically carried generations of guests to the fairgrounds.
The new attraction is one of several upgrades intended to handle the large crowds expected this year. A redesigned Gate 6 is intended to improve traffic flow into infield parking, Lewis said, following similar work at Gate 5 last year.
The fair has also expanded and renovated the Hoosier Lottery Free Stage. The venue now has a 60-by-40-foot main stage, two wings, a taller roof, dual LED video walls and flexible configurations capable of holding between 5,000 and 7,500 people.
All concerts are included with paid admission, although premium reserved areas are available for some performances.
The lineup includes the Beach Boys on opening day, TUSK on Saturday, Josiah Queen on Sunday, Bret Michaels on Aug. 12, Busta Rhymes on Aug. 13, Grand Funk Railroad on Aug. 14 and Trace Adkins on Aug. 16.
Later performers include Gene Simmons, Sammy Kershaw and Craig Morgan, Don McLean and gospel singer Tasha Cobbs Leonard.
Animals, acrobats and agriculture
The fair’s Big Top Circus also returns with eight new acts inside an air-conditioned tent. Free, 45-minute performances are scheduled three times daily, with optional premium seating upgrades.
Other additions include daily calf cuddling in the Meijer Family Fun Park and tortoise feeding near Goat Mountain. A youth division is also being added to the fair’s mullet competition.
The Indiana State Fair runs through Aug. 23 and will be closed on Mondays. Organizers expect more than 850,000 guests over its 15-day run. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Still, organizers emphasize that agriculture and 4-H remain at the center of the event.
Nearly 10,000 people participated in fair competitions last year, submitting more than 50,000 entries. This year, 4-H projects will be displayed at expanded locations around the grounds.
The Featured Farmers program will recognize 15 Indiana farm families, one for each day of the fair. Visitors can meet the featured family and learn about its operation during daily conversations in the Glass Barn.
The farms represent products ranging from corn, soybeans, pork and dairy to maple syrup, flowers, leafy greens and lavender.
Last year’s fair attracted 854,977 visitors, slightly more than the 854,236 who attended in 2024, despite six days when temperatures topped 90 degrees.
Its other numbers were similarly outsized: the winning giant pumpkin weighed 1,323 pounds, an artist carved 1,600 pounds of Indiana cheese and more than 32,000 cans were used to construct sculptures that were later donated to Gleaners Food Bank of Indiana.
Plan before heading out
The fairgrounds are located at 1202 E. 38th St. in Indianapolis. Gates open daily at 8 a.m.
On-site parking costs $10 per vehicle. IndyGo Routes 4 and 39 and the Purple Line stop near the fairgrounds. The designated rideshare pickup and drop-off area is at 3773 Woodland Ave., accessible through Gate 7.
Free bicycle parking is available near the Monon Trail north of 38th Street, and cyclists receive $1 off admission. Children age 5 and younger are admitted free.
Advance discounts on admission, parking, family packages and ride wristbands remain available at IndianaStateFair.com through 11:59 p.m. Thursday.
The fair’s $2 Tuesdays return Aug. 11 and 18, with $2 admission, $2 midway rides and $2 food specials at every concession stand.
Military members, veterans, first responders and their immediate families receive free admission with valid identification Aug. 12. Other promotions include Indianapolis Indians Family Day on Aug. 13, IndyStar Free Ticket Day on Aug. 19 and free admission for AAA members on Aug. 20.
Lewis said security remains a top priority, pointing to metal detectors at every entrance and coordination with law enforcement, medical personnel and weather-monitoring teams.
After 6 p.m. Tuesdays through Thursdays and after 4 p.m. Fridays through Sundays, visitors younger than 18 must be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or chaperone age 25 or older.
Full schedules, maps, ticket information and policies are available at IndianaStateFair.com.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Building a better politics after Wisconsin’s messy primary
description: It’s hard not to get caught up in the increasingly contentious Democratic primary battle that’s mostly being waged online this week. But outside of the social media echo chambers, people who are taking the brunt of a vicious, authoritarian regime are asking deeper questions about how to build political power.   Union and immigrant-rights organizers in […]
text:
Hundreds of people came to the Capitol on Thursday, Oct. 28, 2021, to testify against the new voting maps drawn by Republican legislative leaders which advocates characterized as 'gerrymandering 2.0.' (Wisconsin Examiner photo)It’s hard not to get caught up in the increasingly contentious Democratic primary battle that’s mostly being waged online this week. But outside of the social media echo chambers, people who are taking the brunt of a vicious, authoritarian regime are asking deeper questions about how to build political power.  
Union and immigrant-rights organizers in Wisconsin held a joint press conference Thursday to talk about their efforts to get Latinos, newly naturalized citizens and struggling workers to the polls to elect people who will take a stand against the Trump administration’s terrifying crackdown on immigrants as well as Trump administration policies driving the crushing cost of living.
Roselia Navarro, a naturalized citizen who leads Voces de la Frontera’s New American program, helps guide other immigrants through the process of becoming citizens. She gave a touching account of how much citizenship and participating in American democracy means to her. She described it as a privilege to help other immigrants, many of whom have waited as long  as 20 years to obtain their naturalization papers and become eligible to vote. 
“I’m very proud to say I’m the first person that is able to vote within my family,” she said. “And that feels rewarding because when I vote, I feel that I’m not only making decisions for something that would benefit my kids, but it also inspires my family to see that I’m motivated and I’m involved.”
“I want to also invite the people in our community, especially the Hispanic community, that we can come together and we need to vote,” she added. “It’s extremely important for us to be part of the decisions that are being made in our state.”
First-time voter Yondo Borrera, who sat next to Navarro on the panel at the Voces office in Milwaukee, told reporters, “I will be voting to make a change in my community. I don’t like how everything is super expensive right now — gas, food, housing, rent. And I don’t like how ICE is in the community snatching people up, deporting people, taking people away from their families, and that’s something that I’m trying to change.”
Christine Neumann-Ortiz, Voces’ executive director, described the power of Latino voters in Wisconsin, a tippy purple state where elections are often decided by razor-thin margins. Over the last decade, “the Latino population, including the Latino voting population, has continued to grow in force statewide,” she said. She cited data from the 2024 election that showed high turnout among registered Latino voters about 84.9%  of whom voted, “yet this only represents 63% of the estimated eligible Latino citizen voting age population statewide,” she said. 
Immigrant rights’ organizers aim to drive the participation rate higher.
There is something poignant about that aim, which, in other election years, would seem like a run-of-the-mill exercise in civics. This is no ordinary election year, however. 
Armed federal agents have been dragging people out of their cars in Milwaukee. A young mother with no criminal record who fled violence in Colombia and was going through the U.S. asylum process, checking in with the government regularly as her case progressed, was grabbed along with her 8-year-old son out of their home in the Wisconsin Dells and is now incarcerated along with her little boy in an ICE detention facility in South Texas. 
This is just one case of the thousands across the country. Neumann-Ortiz described a few more in Wisconsin. “We’ve seen mothers and fathers and children and the larger community traumatized by the violence and the persecution and the racism, which is completely unchecked right now,” she said.
People who have full legal status are wary of being grabbed by rogue ICE agents looking to fill quotas in the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. Going to the polls in this environment is fraught. And yet, advocates say, it’s more important than ever. 
“We are in an unprecedented time of income inequality, with unwanted wars in the Middle East, and a quarter of a trillion of our national budget being used for the violent persecution and racial profiling of Black and brown people, Asian people, and shifting away these critical resources from healthcare and public schools and childcare and things that people need,” Neumann-Ortiz said. 
The only way to change all that is for people who are suffering under this terrible regime to grab control of their government.
Adrian Bracy, a worksite representative for the Service Employees International Union, spoke on the panel to people who feel that their vote doesn’t matter, that the system is too broken to be fixed at the ballot box. 
“Working for a union for 20 years, I know that uniting and standing strong and fighting firmly for what we believe in, it can make the difference,” she said. “It can definitely change things.” She urged people to encourage their friends and neighbors to vote.  “Let them know how important it really is, and that they do matter,” she said. “It does matter. It makes a difference …  in spite of the tactics they may use to intimidate or discourage or discredit our voters.”
As it happens, the effort to discourage and discredit voters is led by Wisconsin’s representatives in Congress. U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil (R-Janesville), who chairs the House Committee on Administration, is demanding information from the state Department of Corrections on voting by felons. The case that prompted Steil’s letter to DOC Secretary Jared Hoy involves a man convicted of theft who was one day shy of having served his full sentence on community release. Had he voted the following day, his ballot would have been legal. This single case, which did not affect the outcome of any election, is fodder for a campaign Steil is spearheading to cast doubt on the legitimacy of elections and disenfranchise likely Democratic voters by making them jump through hoops before they can vote, all in the name of rooting out exceedingly rare cases of voter fraud.
The main targets of this campaign are, of course, the supposed masses of noncitizens casting ballots and tilting elections to Democrats. 
U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden, like Steil an enabler of election conspiracy theories, also took a big stand this week, demanding that Gov. Tony Evers turn over the personal data of FoodShare recipients in an effort to root out “fraud.” People who get food assistance in Wisconsin are already seeing their benefits cut, just as grocery prices skyrocket, under the massive tax cut and spending bill both Van Orden and Steil supported.
These attacks are related. After voting for policies that make life much worse for the people they represent, our Republican members of Congress are trying to make sure voters can’t hold them accountable. 
“The challenges facing our economy and our democracy are inseparable,” says Taifa Smith Butler, president of Demos, a nonprofit progressive public policy organization. Demos rolled out its 2026 national policy agenda this week:  “Power Policies: How to Get and Keep People Power in the United States.” 
“For too long, public debate has centered on short term wins, but the more important question is what happens after power shifts,” Smith Butler said at a press conference announcing the new report. “History shows that periods of political upheaval can also create opportunities for transformative change. Previous generations have used these moments to advance civil rights, expand democracy, and build economic security.”
Rising authoritarianism is linked to the erosion of both economic and political power for most people, Alix Gould-Werth, Demos’ chief of programs and strategy, said at the same event. It’s important to stop that erosion in order to fight back.
The solutions the group lays out in its progressive policy plan include affordable housing, universal childcare and a robust national wealth tax, as well as nonpartisan redistricting and automatic voter registration.
Rebuilding democratic institutions in the current environment seems like a huge hill to climb. But starting on the state and local level, it’s possible to protect “laboratories of democracy” that will serve as models for a larger shift, Gould-Werth said. 
Community housing grants and low-cost loans are one example Demos offers.
Here in Wisconsin, which long ago served as the laboratory for New Deal programs and progressive reforms that grew into lasting federal institutions, there is an opportunity to stand up and defend a better vision of society. 
It’s scary. And it’s challenging. But it’s a relief to see advocates at both the local and national level light a torch and keep us focused not just on the short-term crisis we are enduring, but how it fits into the long-term fight for a better world.
