name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. state police are covering more municipalities than ever. Can recruitment and funding keep up?
description: Funding public safety has remained a priority in Harrisburg as the Pennsylvania State Police expands its coverage to more municipalities.
text:
A state trooper makes a traffic stop along the Pennsylvania Turnpike between Pittsburgh and Harrisburg on October 14, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star.
The state legislature has trimmed Gov. Josh Shapiro’s proposed spending plans each year since he took office. But funding public safety has remained a priority in Harrisburg as the Pennsylvania State Police undertakes more full-time coverage across the commonwealth. 
Public safety and law enforcement spending has increased by more than $1.3 billion since 2020, and Shapiro has dedicated $63 million to training new cadet classes during his term as governor. The administration also nearly doubled funding for municipal police training in the 2024-25 budget. 
But the overall number of police employees has fallen during the same time period, which a recent report from the Joint State Government Commission partially attributes to “highly publicized events,” including the death of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, that have “created a nationwide negative perception of police.” 
“The movement following George Floyd’s death appears to have created a broader socio-political effect than other police incidents,” the report said. “A study of several police agencies across the country found that most recorded a significant increase in resignations and retirements in the two years after George Floyd’s death.”  
Pennsylvania’s funding for public safety and law enforcement has increased by more than $1.3 billion since 2020. (Chart from the Joint State Government Commission)
Police departments nationwide have been “working to overcome a five percent deficit in staffing levels” since 2020, according to the report.
At the same time, a greater number of municipalities across Pennsylvania are shuttering their own police departments, largely due to financial constraints, requiring the state police to expand coverage to more communities. 
“With municipal police departments closing, the PSP is responsible for patrolling larger geographic areas and staff can frequently be spread thin or have longer response times due to the availability of officers,” the report reads. 
The commission recommended continuous funding for the state police agency and the repeal of the statutory cap on the number of troopers it can employ — a proposal that the Shapiro administration supports. 
The number of employed police officers in Pennsylvania has fallen since 2018. (Chart from the Joint State Government Commission)
Cap on number of troopers limits hiring, agency says 
The statewide law enforcement agency currently employs more than 4,200 troopers out of 4,410 available positions, according to a department spokesperson. 
And the cap “impacts the ability of the PSP to recruit and train new officers, as PSP must wait for vacancies to occur in order to hire additional officers,” the report states. 
In a statement, Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky urged the legislature to pass a bill repealing the cap. 
The state police has begun providing full-time coverage to 21 more municipalities since 2023, bringing its statewide total to 1,325 municipalities that comprise over 80% of Pennsylvania. An additional 408 municipalities partner with the state police for part-time coverage. 
Sweden Township in Potter County eliminated its local police force in 2024 after its police chief took another position, according to Debra Dehn, the township secretary. 
“When he left there was him and two part-time officers. … the Supervisors decided that we would be fine without a Police department,” she wrote in an email. “Not to mention, a Police department in any township is extremely expensive.”
The township is located “less than a quarter mile” from state police barracks and now relies on state troopers, she wrote, adding that “it is working out great.” 
“The municipalities that shut down their police departments, they always said it was a cost consideration,” said former state Rep. Mike Sturla, a Democrat who represented Lancaster County for 34 years. “They couldn’t afford to do it without raising taxes.”
A state trooper makes a traffic stop along the Pennsylvania Turnpike on October 14, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Should municipalities be charged?
Some state legislators are continuing to weigh if and how to charge municipalities for their increasing reliance on state police coverage — a debate that spans more than 30 years. 
Rep. Justin Fleming (D-Dauphin) represents several districts that all have their own police forces. His constituents pay taxes to fund those departments and the state’s Motor License Fund, which supports the state police. 
“It’s just patently unfair that the folks I represent are paying twice when others are getting a free ride,” he said. “It really is a fundamental issue of fairness.” 
In March, Fleming introduced legislation to charge municipalities an annual fee for state police coverage. Under his proposal, municipalities that require full-time state police coverage would be charged more than those that require part-time coverage, and municipalities that independently support local or regional police forces would be exempt. 
Fleming is not the first lawmaker to pursue a municipal police service fee. Republican Gov. Tom Ridge first introduced a municipality police fee in 1995, and Democratic Gov. Tom Wolf included similar language in three of his four proposed state budgets. The fee never made it into any of the final spending plans. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sturla also championed a service fee during his time in office. 
“I was not against the police, I was just saying somebody needed to pay for it other than the people that were already paying for their own police protection,” he said. “It never quite got as far as I wanted it to because members were afraid to tell municipalities that they needed to pay for it.” 
Fleming specified that any revenue from a municipality fee would go directly back to the state police, allowing them to investigate more cases, hire more troopers, and meet their financial priorities. However, he said the proposal hasn’t garnered much support from the agency or other lawmakers, and “proposing a new fee or tax on folks is not generally popular.”   
Shapiro’s office did not comment on whether he supports the initiative, writing that it will monitor the proposal as it moves through the legislature. 
“My intention is not to make the state police a political football,” Fleming said. “It’s really just to carve out a fair solution to all parties involved. Sometimes you have to do unpopular things to stand on principle.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: English literacy center serves Detroit immigrants despite climate of fear
description: At a historic Lithuanian church in Detroit’s Mexicantown neighborhood, All Saints Literacy Center is working to open doors for community members who are not literate in English — whether that be parents who need to meet with their child’s teachers, workers looking to advance in their careers, or someone who needs to understand what a doctor […]
text:
A student works one-on-one with a tutor at All Saints Literacy Center. July 15, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. At a historic Lithuanian church in Detroit’s Mexicantown neighborhood, All Saints Literacy Center is working to open doors for community members who are not literate in English — whether that be parents who need to meet with their child’s teachers, workers looking to advance in their careers, or someone who needs to understand what a doctor is saying at an appointment. 
Founded in 2015 by the Adrian Dominican Sisters, the center provides one-on-one, individualized tutoring sessions to adults seeking English literacy skills, all for free. Currently, there are 36 learners at All Saints, all English-language students.
Grace Irwin, who was named the executive director of the center in May, said that the center’s home in Mexicantown, on the city’s Southwest side, is and always has been a strategic location — All Saints is not the only adult literacy center in Detroit, but it is the one that caters most to ESL students. 
Many of the learners are immigrants, and all but one are native Spanish speakers. In a time when fear of deportation has been weaponized against immigrant communities nationwide, Irwin emphasized that even given the fear and uncertainty that ICE creates in the community, they work hard to create a safe and welcoming space for everyone there. 
All Saints Literacy Center in Detroit’s Mexicantown neighborhood is a home for English language learners in the city. July 15, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Steve Ragan, who chairs the board of All Saints Literacy Center, said that though ICE has never come inside All Saints or attempted to, they have had incidents where agents are parked outside their gates or down the street from the center. 
“This is a community where literacy is critically important. In every community, literacy is important, but especially here,” Ragan said. “I just want to be clear: most of these are legal immigrants. While we don’t screen them, we do know that most of the people we serve are legal immigrants, and the immigrant community is incredibly important.”
Immigrants have become very concerned about going to any institution, including schools — though Irwin noted that the option of remote classes, a remnant of the COVID-19 pandemic, has helped to mitigate those concerns for some students at a time of heightened concern. 
“We can’t even discuss it anymore, and so people are scared. I’d say the biggest thing I’ve seen is just fear, that a lot of people are afraid to come here,” Ragan, who said he considers himself a Republican, continued. “We don’t ask people to prove their citizenship. That’s not our business. But you know we also help people learn the skills so they can become citizens, and I think that’s really important.”
Grace Irwin, the executive director of All Saints Literacy Center. July 15, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
All of the tutors at the center are volunteers — currently, there are 29. One of them, David Rubenstein, who has been volunteering at All Saints for around a year and was doing literacy tutoring at a different location for years before then, said that he has gotten so much personal satisfaction and growth from doing this volunteer work. 
“I get the satisfaction of somebody improving their lives,” he said. “There’s nothing hard about it, and the easiest thing is doing it.”
Rubenstein now lives in Royal Oak and spent a number of years tutoring at the Siena Literacy Center in northwest Detroit, but he spent a period of his life living in Mexico and Panama, so he felt a particular connection to teaching Spanish-speaking learners, which All Saints caters to. He’s taught students from around the world — including from Vietnam, Jordan and Thailand. Now, he has two students at All Saints — one from Mexico and one from Iran. 
Beyond teaching them the fundamentals of English, Rubenstein said that he finds it meaningful to have his clients encounter different accents and cultural contexts — so he has them speak with each other in English, since he sees them on the same day.
But his involvement with his students also stretches beyond the bounds of classwork. 
“I also get involved with the ones that I like, which is all of them so far, in a way that we’ve become family,” Rubenstein said. “They’ve never been to a baseball game, so I took the Iranian guy and his wife to the Tigers game. I love Detroit, so I try to introduce them to new things.”
It’s also made it harder for him to feel the pain of the learners he works with as they deal with the immigration system. He recalled feeling the pain of one of his clients, who works at Henry Ford Hospital and whose wife is a post-doctoral researcher in Parkinson’s Disease, when they were denied a green card, even after putting in hours of work and even having a child. 
Learning materials at All Saints Literacy Center. July 15, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“It’s very disturbing. It’s costing the government nothing for us to teach these people,” Rubenstein said. “I’m sick to my stomach about what our government’s doing.”
Irwin, who previously worked with ACCESS, or the Arab Community Center for Economic and Social Services, in Dearborn, emphasized the real-life impacts of literacy work, giving the example of a client who was beginning to work towards her GED after developing her English skills. 
Those stories have stuck with the leadership of All Saints — including Ragan, who has been involved with the center for a decade.
“I think about the first person I tutored. I know that after we helped him improve his English skills, he got a promotion. He went to a manager level position that he never would have had if he hadn’t improved his English skills,” Ragan said. “So yeah, I think the work we do is life changing sometimes.”
And he remains close with another of his earliest tutees, a man from Sri Lanka whose wife was in the United States to do her Ph.D., and who himself had a medical tech degree from his home country. He asked Ragan for help studying for the TOEFL exam in order to apply for his master’s degree, a type of lesson that All Saints generally does not do. But Ragan knew he could help, and so he took it on.  
“I got some books, I tutored him, and a year later, we got him his score up, and he got into his master’s program, got his certification. He’s now working for Northwestern University,” Ragan said, adding that whenever he visits Chicago, he still makes a point to see his old friend. 
Approximately 75% of the learners are women, and most are between the ages of 25 and 44, according to statistics provided by the center. 
The future of the All Saints Literacy Center is bright — the Adrian Dominican Sisters, who founded the center, are shifting from literacy as a priority, Irwin explained, but are providing a $1.5 million transfer to the center as they become an independent nonprofit. That money, for a center with a relatively small annual budget, will make a big difference. 
All Saints Literacy Center calls a historic Lithuanian church home. July 15, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“One of the things we’ve done with their $1.5 million dollars is we’ve taken part of it and we’ve put it in reserve for growth, and we’ve taken part of it and focused it on capacity building,” Ragan explained. “Those are the three outcomes that we’re measuring. We want to grow fundraising, tutors, and students. And you know, because we know that there’s need in this community.”
He noted, however, that an administrative error by the IRS has delayed their ability to receive that transfer of funding in a timely fashion — an issue that he calls the agency every day to try to resolve. 
But the center continues to grow, with both staff like Irwin and volunteers like Rubenstein expressing interest in restarting group literacy classes that the center had previously held. 
Rubenstein also emphasized the cycle that he hopes to create by helping people develop their English skills and by giving back to the Detroit community.
“One of the things I hope is that these people, once they have sufficient English knowledge, will give back,” he said. “Not necessarily teaching, but will become part of their community, of our community, and participate.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: JobsOhio chairman lobbies for Intel, a company that got millions from JobsOhio
description: JobsOhio says that it’s been transparent and that its board has been free of conflicts as it has handed out $2 billion in what used to be public money to private corporations.  But the chairman of its board is a lobbyist who represented Intel just as the board of which he was a member disbursed […]
text:
A massive Intel chip plant near New Albany, Ohio is years behind schedule. (Photo by Marty Schladen, Ohio Capital Journal.)JobsOhio says that it’s been transparent and that its board has been free of conflicts as it has handed out $2 billion in what used to be public money to private corporations. 
But the chairman of its board is a lobbyist who represented Intel just as the board of which he was a member disbursed more than $2 million to the company as part of a package of grants for what is now a severely delayed megaproject.
The lobbyist, Josh Rubin, was being paid to promote Intel’s agenda to the governor’s office in September 2023 when Gov. Mike DeWine appointed him to the JobsOhio board, which he had also actively lobbied on Intel’s behalf as recently as a year earlier.
Earlier that year, JobsOhio had awarded the chipmaker a $25 million workforce-development grant before DeWine gave Rubin the top spot at Ohio’s controversial, quasi-private economic-development agency.
The workforce-development and other grants were part of a $150 million package JobsOhio pledged toward the Intel job. For its part, the state pledged more than $2 billion for the chip-making project.
Even after Rubin joined the JobsOhio board in September 2023, he and other members of his firm were paid by Intel to lobby DeWine, then-Lieutenant governor Jon Husted, and other executive agencies on the $20 billion project near New Albany, state lobbying disclosures show. 
That’s an arrangement that Paul Nick, executive director of the Ohio Ethics Commission, said appeared to violate assurances that Rubin gave DeWine’s office before his appointment that his lobby firm would cease services for any clients on matters in front of JobsOhio. 
Nick said that if Rubin were a state employee, it would be illegal for him to lobby for a company with business before the state. But because of JobsOhio’s legal status as a private nonprofit corporation, it’s exempt from Ohio ethics law, he said. 
Despite assuring DeWine that he and his firm would avoid all conflicts, Rubin and several partners renewed their annual registrations to lobby JobsOhio for Intel and other clients until the start of this year, when the registrations were terminated. 
All except one. In December, that partner renewed her registration to lobby JobsOhio through 2026.
Suspicions that Rubin’s lobbying might conflict with his role on the JobsOhio board have already been raised. Last month, John Kulewicz, the Democratic nominee for Ohio attorney general, asked the state inspector general to investigate whether Rubin’s representation of utility giant AEP conflicted with the fact that JobsOhio will soon be handing out $100 million to develop small-modular nuclear reactors.
JobsOhio denied that it did. Rubin didn’t respond to calls and emails for this story or a Capital Journal story about Kulewicz’s request.
JobsOhio also said that it has strong policies in place to ensure that board members recuse themselves from matters in which they might have a conflict.
A JobsOhio spokesperson said, “Any board member with an actual or possible conflict of interest on specific grant or loan proposals for a company must disclose it and… will recuse themselves from discussions and voting on such proposal.”
 Questions of conflict




Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The revelations about dual roles come in a scandal-plagued state where megabusinesses have paid Capital Square insiders and then have gotten large sums from taxpayers and electricity ratepayers. 
Catherine Turcer, executive director of Common Cause Ohio, said Rubin’s presence atop JobsOhio only deepens suspicions about the organization’s transparency and freedom from conflict. 
Lobbyists are paid by corporate clients to help them get contracts and other considerations from the government. As chairman of the JobsOhio board, Rubin has a top decision-making role in an organization whose job is to distribute billions of what used to be taxpayer dollars to such businesses.
“Because JobsOhio is being run by a lobbyist, we have to question everything,” Turcer said. “I’m sure some of those development dollars were reasonably spent. But we have to question everything. And because there’s such a lack of transparency, we are left imagining the absolute worst.”
 Promises made

On July 26, 2023, a lawyer in the governor’s office wrote to the Ohio Ethics Commission seeking guidance.
“Mr. Rubin is a registered lobbyist in the State of Ohio and has, to date, regularly lobbied the executive branch, the legislative branch, and JobsOhio,” it said. “If appointed he has affirmed to me that both he and (Rubin’s firm) The CJR Group would cease services for any clients on matters in front of JobsOhio and would fully comply with the separate JobsOhio conflicts policy as to any current or past clients.”
State lobbying disclosures show that at that time Rubin was registered to lobby the governor’s office and JobsOhio on behalf of Intel. 
Activity and expense reports also show he was actively lobbying the governor on the company’s behalf. As recently as April this year, Rubin still was, according to his state disclosures.
Despite filing annual registrations to lobby JobsOhio through 2025, Rubin hasn’t filed any “activity and expense reports” saying he was actively lobbying the agency for Intel since 2022 — a year before he joined the board.
He has continued to lobby the government for the company, and Intel has continued to receive money from the state and from JobsOhio.
Tax documents filed by JobsOhio for fiscal years 2023 and 2024 show that JobsOhio gave Intel more than $2 million during that period. 
Just before Rubin joined the board, JobsOhio gave Intel a $25 million workforce-development grant — part of $150 million JobsOhio has committed to the now-delayed project.
Asked about the grants, JobsOhio spokesman Matt Englehart said it wasn’t a conflict for Rubin because the board had already decided to award the funds before Rubin joined the board.
“JobsOhio’s offer of JobsOhio incentives to Intel were approved by the JobsOhio Board in December 2021 — before Mr. Rubin was appointed by Governor DeWine to the JobsOhio’s Board of Directors on Sept. 1, 2023,” Englehart said in an email. “Disbursement of funds is a staff function, based on 2021 approval by the JobsOhio Board.”
As chairman of the JobsOhio board, Rubin is in a position of authority over that staff. JobsOhio also places performance requirements on its grants and says it can claw the money back if they’re not met. That’s a process in which Rubin could have a say.
The massive Intel project was to receive more than $2 billion in state incentives, and factories were supposed to begin production last year. With the company facing economic hardship, production has been pushed back to at least 2030. 
The state has already given Intel a $600 million “onshoring” grant, and it’s unclear whether the state will claw any of that money back when the company misses a 2028 deadline.
As a member of the JobsOhio board, Rubin — whom Intel continues to pay to lobby DeWine — presumably could weigh in on whether to claw back any part of the more than $150 million JobsOhio committed to Intel. 
JobsOhio didn’t respond when asked whether its board has any say in decisions to recover money from companies that don’t deliver on their promises.
Intel didn’t respond to questions for this story — including how much it has paid Rubin and other members of his firm.
 Keeping his promise?

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to his state disclosures, Rubin continues to lobby the governor on the delayed Intel project, a matter that JobsOhio is also dealing with.
Is that consistent with what Rubin promised DeWine’s legal team — that “The CJR Group would cease services for any clients on matters in front of JobsOhio…”?
DeWine Press Secretary Dan Tierney said it was.
“Lobbying an agency that is not JobsOhio on behalf of Intel does not qualify as having business before JobsOhio on Intel,” he said in an email. “Our office is not JobsOhio. You are conflating two separate issues that produce different legal and ethical obligations.”
Paul Nick, the executive director of the Ohio Ethics Commission, had a different answer to the same question. He said the fact that Rubin and his partners kept registering to lobby JobsOhio after Rubin joined the board appeared to violate the lobbyist’s pledge.
And the fact that Rubin this year was still actively lobbying DeWine on the Intel project?
“That would also appear to contradict his representation to the Governor’s office,” Nick said in an email.
He explained that the Ethics Commission plays a role in helping identify potential conflicts of JobsOhio board members. But other than to compel complete financial disclosures, his office didn’t have power over Rubin and other members of the JobsOhio board, he said.
“Because Rubin is not subject to the Ethics Law, none of his actions could be potential violations of these laws,” Nick said. He later added that they would be if Rubin was a state employee.
In answer to the governor’s 2023 query, Nick encouraged Rubin to seek an advisory opinion of his own from the Ethics Commission to ensure he steered clear of conflicts. Rubin never did, Nick said.
 Rules of its own

SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The Ethics Commission advocated against exempting members of the JobsOhio board from ethics and transparency laws when then-Gov. John Kasich and his allies in 2011 said JobsOhio should be exempt so it could “move at the speed of business.”
“During the legislation that enacted JobsOhio, the Commission encouraged that all of the Ethics Laws should apply to JobsOhio and its board,” Nick said. “Instead, the final legislation required that JobsOhio create its own conflict of interest policy.”
Members of the JobsOhio board are subject to what Tierney, DeWine’s spokesman, called “a strong policy to ethically address conflicts.”
And Englehart, the JobsOhio spokesman said, “Any board member with an actual or possible conflict of interest on specific grant or loan proposals for a company must disclose it and… will recuse themselves from discussions and voting on such proposal.”
He added, “Yet this entire process is often unnecessary because a potentially conflicted member will typically recuse themselves from any discussion and voting by the Board on the matter involved.”
JobsOhio board meeting minutes going back to 2021 appear to contain no mention of the words “conflict” or “recuse.” They also show that on at least one occasion — June 13, 2024 — JobsOhio CEO J.P. Nauseef discussed how he wanted to “…capture the Intel supply chain” while Rubin was in the meeting.
A review of minutes going back to through Rubin’s tenure indicates that much of the sessions have been devoted to celebrating JobsOhio. But initial decisions about individual awards to companies are made in committee meetings which are not required to be open to the public. 
“Conflict acknowledgments from the prior year” are required to be made public. But records produced by the Ohio Department of Development in response to an open-records request appear only to contain documents in which officials acknowledged they were aware of JobsOhio’s ethics policy.
Englehart didn’t respond when asked if Rubin, a lobbyist with dozens of clients, had ever declared a conflict or recused himself since joining the JobsOhio board in 2023.
Possible conflicts for members of the JobsOhio board have been identified in the past.
In 2014, the Ohio Ethics Commission notified two Marathon Petroleum Corp. executives who sat on the JobsOhio board that they had potential conflicts because Marathon was receiving benefits from JobsOhio. Other corporations enjoying JobsOhio largesse who have had employees on the board include Sherwin-Williams, Bob Evans, and Procter & Gamble. 
Last year, Youngstown’s WFMJ reported that JobsOhio granted more than $2 million to a company run by a man who headed up a regional entity created by JobsOhio. 
 Private company?

Then-Gov. Kasich oversaw the birth of JobsOhio in 2011. Even then, it was controversial.
The legislature created it, the governor appoints the board, and it was allowed to make the sole bid to lease the state’s liquor franchise for much less than it was worth. It spends the difference on its large staff, marketing and making grants, and providing other things of value to businesses.
Despite the fact that it and its funding are rooted entirely in the state government, its supporters call JobsOhio a private nonprofit corporation that spends money from a private source. They say that rightly exempts JobsOhio from the ethics and transparency rules state employees were subject to when the Ohio Department of Commerce controlled the liquor franchise. 
JobsOhio has since disbursed just over $2 billion in grants, loans, and other incentives, Englehart, the JobsOhio spokesman, said.
As critics warned, in some cases that money has appeared to go to the well-connected for questionable economic-development reasons.
A university president, an inappropriate relationship, $60K podcasts, and another scandal in Ohio

For example, Ohio State fired then-President Ted Carter in March. When it did, the public learned that JobsOhio paid a woman with whom Carter had an “inappropriate relationship” $60,000 to make a podcast.
JobsOhio justified the spending on economic-development grounds, but it refused to say whether it had sponsored other podcasts or how much it had paid for them. A spokesman said he couldn’t answer because any podcast would be part of its “marketing playbook” and that “other states try to replicate what we do.”
In 2020, Ohioans were stunned by news of a dark-money scandal in which Akron-based FirstEnergy paid more than $60 million in bribes for a $1.3-billion bailout. FirstEnergy admitted to paying Sam Randazzo — DeWine’s pick to be the state’s top utility regulator — a $4.3 million bribe. Among other services, Randazzo helped write the corrupt legislation. He died by suicide after he was charged.
Rubin, who would within weeks become a FirstEnergy lobbyist, attended a December 2018 dinner with Gov.-elect DeWine, Lt. Gov.-elect Husted and FirstEnergy’s top executives. They discussed Randazzo’s suitability to be Ohio’s top utility regulator. 
Rubin advised the executives not to tell DeWine that they were going straight from the dinner to meet with Randazzo, the Associated Press reported in February. It was at that meeting that Randazzo’s bribe was negotiated, prosecutors said.
JobsOhio had already lent a hand to the struggling utility a few years before the bribes began to flow. In 2015, it forgave a $12 million loan to help FirstEnergy clean up one of its money-losing coal plants.
Before bribery scandal, JobsOhio forgave a $12m loan to FirstEnergy to clean up a coal plant

 Private money?

Good government advocates have also raised questions about how fair JobsOhio’s deal has been to taxpayers.
JobsOhio paid the state $1.4 billion for its initial lease of the state liquor franchise. Last year, a DeWine-controlled board extended that lease to 2053 without taxpayers getting any additional money.
Even though all that money used to flow into the state general fund, JobsOhio insists that “absolutely no tax dollars or other public dollars are used to support it.”
Turcer of Common Cause scoffs at the claim.
“Of course it’s taxpayer money,” she said.
DeWine himself didn’t dispute it being called taxpayer money in a TV appearance earlier this month, despite his spokesman’s insistence that JobsOhio and its funding are private.
CNBC had declared Ohio the Best State for Business — a designation about which JobsOhio is crowing.
During an interview with CNBC reporter Scott Cohn, DeWine quickly credited JobsOhio for the state’s success and touted data-center development as a big win for the Buckeye State.
“I think one thing we have is what we call JobsOhio,” he said. “We basically privatized a number of years ago under Gov. Kasich… we privatized our economic development… It gives us, I think, a strategic advantage.”
But Cohn pushed back on the governor’s praise of Ohio’s “privatized” economic development operation.
“You mentioned that you privatized the jobs agency and of all the economic development organizations that we deal with as we’re coming up with (state rankings), it is one of the most opaque,” Cohn said. 
“And it’s gotten a lot of criticism for that. I know there’s a bill pending to make JobsOhio more transparent, because this is taxpayer money ultimately. What do you do about that to keep the deals coming in, but also make sure the taxpayers are being looked out for?”
DeWine didn’t dispute Cohn’s description of JobsOhio as a nontransparent organization spending taxpayer dollars.
“I think there’s a happy medium that can be reached,” he said. “I think what JobsOhio has done is give us a competitive advantage.” 
 Still lobbying

Despite promises to avoid conflicts, Rubin and other members of his firm paid $25 each year to register to lobby JobsOhio even after he was on the board.
Then, according to documents obtained through an open-records request, Rubin on Jan. 27 emailed the Ohio Joint Legislative Ethics Committee, the agency that handles lobby disclosures. 
“Please find below my executive registrations for 2026,” it said. “We need to make sure JobsOhio is no longer listed in any of them.”
Controversial ‘private corporation’ JobsOhio gets billions more without paying more to state

He added that the commission should be receiving similar emails from other members of his firm, including Brittany Warner. But no such email ever came. 
Instead, Warner is currently registered to lobby JobsOhio on behalf of Intel and other clients.
“My quarterly activity and expenditure reports plainly show that I have not lobbied JobsOhio since 2023,” Warner said in an email to the Capital Journal. “The registration reports you are separately looking at are created at the beginning of an engagement with a new client, and those all pre-date September 2023. Those ‘initial filings’ you are referencing were all created in 2019-2022.”
Warner’s email did not address the fact that, according to the Ohio Lobbying Handbook, agents have to register each year and pay $25 for each client and name the agencies they might lobby on its behalf.
Warner filed her most recent annual registration saying she might lobby JobsOhio for Intel on Dec. 12, 2025.
As with Rubin, Warner’s activity-and-expense reports show she continued this year to lobby the governor and lieutenant governor for Intel. 
Tony Bledsoe, the Ohio Legislative inspector general, said that as with the state Ethics Commission, the JobsOhio board operates largely outside of his agency’s jurisdiction.
The Ohio Joint Legislative Ethics Committee “handles lobbying reporting (disclosure) relative to those lobbying JobsOhio as well as JobsOhio’s lobbying reporting relative to their legislative advocacy,” Bledsoe said in an email. “Beyond that, we have no jurisdiction concerning JobsOhio.”
Turcer of Common Cause Ohio said one doesn’t need the niceties of Ohio ethics law to see problems inherent in Rubin’s dual roles.
“One of the things we know is that you can’t serve two bosses well,” she said. “So Josh Rubin-lobbyist and Josh Rubin-the-chair-of-JobsOhio is only serving one of them.”

title: FIRE report gives 14 Ohio universities yellow light ratings for free speech policies
description: The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression gave 14 Ohio universities a “yellow light” rating for free speech policies in a new report, meaning that they operate under policies that could be too easily applied to suppress protected speech. The survey reviewed free speech policies at nearly 500 public and private colleges and universities nationwide [[...]
text:
Case Western Reserve University. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal.)The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression gave 14 Ohio universities a “yellow light” rating for free speech policies in a new report, meaning that they operate under policies that could be too easily applied to suppress protected speech.
The survey reviewed free speech policies at nearly 500 public and private colleges and universities nationwide and 13.2% of colleges and universities received a “red light” rating in FIRE’s 20th edition of the state of free speech on college campuses — an all-time low. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In FIRE’s first report back in 2006, 68.6% of all institutions earned a red light rating. 
“In general, private schools maintain more restrictive speech codes than their public counterparts: Private schools are significantly less likely to earn green light ratings and more likely to earn red light ratings than public schools,” FIRE said in their report. 
A “red light” rating means an institution has “at least one policy that both clearly and substantially restricts freedom of speech or bars public access to its speech-related policies by requiring a university login and password for access,” according to FIRE.
No Ohio universities received a “red light” rating. Nationally, 65 colleges and universities received a “red light” ranking. 
“This gulf widens at public schools, where the number of public schools earning a green light rating (68) eclipses the number of private schools earning a red light rating (37) by over 30,” according to the report. 
About 340 colleges and universities (69.4%) earned a “yellow light” rating, meaning a higher education institution has policies that “could too easily be applied to suppress protected speech or maintains policies that, while clearly restricting freedom of speech, restrict it in more narrow circumstances,” according to FIRE.
Bowling Green State University, Case Western Reserve University, Kent State University, Kenyon College, Miami University of Ohio, Oberlin College, Ohio University, Shawnee State University, Ohio State University, University of Akron, University of Cincinnati, University of Toledo, Wright State University, and Youngstown State University all received a “yellow light” ranking. 
FIRE gives a university a “green light” rating if the written policy does not “seriously threaten student expression,” according to FIRE. 76 universities received a “green light” rating. 
Cleveland State University was the only school in Ohio to receive a “green light” rating, according to the report. 
Ohio Senate Bill 1 took effect last summer that bans diversity efforts, regulates classroom discussion, prohibits faculty strikes, creates post-tenure reviews, puts diversity scholarships at risk, and creates a retrenchment provision that blocks unions from negotiating on tenure, among other things.

title: Ohio secretary of state sets sights on state auditor’s office
description: After leading the Ohio Secretary of State’s Office since 2019, Republican Frank LaRose is setting his sights on a new statewide executive office in the 2026 Election: Auditor of State. In announcing his campaign for state auditor, LaRose said that he plans to bring the same “focus on transparency, efficiency, and accountability” he says he […]
text:
An elections forecaster has moved three U.S. Senate races in the 2026 midterms in Democrats' favor, in Ohio, Alaska and North Carolina. (Getty Images)After leading the Ohio Secretary of State’s Office since 2019, Republican Frank LaRose is setting his sights on a new statewide executive office in the 2026 Election: Auditor of State.
In announcing his campaign for state auditor, LaRose said that he plans to bring the same “focus on transparency, efficiency, and accountability” he says he has as Secretary of State to the auditor’s office.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose. Official photo.
The Ohio Capital Journal made multiple requests for an interview with the Republican former state senator and current secretary of state. Requests made both through his campaign website and directly to a campaign communications representative went unanswered.
During campaigns for reelection to his secretary of state seat, LaRose touted the support of President Donald Trump, and he currently has the endorsement of the Ohio Republican Party in his bid for auditor of state.
LaRose attempted to gain a seat in the U.S. Senate in 2024, but came in third in a Republican primary, behind fellow former state senator Matt Dolan, and the winner, now-Ohio U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno.
The auditor of state is an elected statewide executive office that works as a check for local governments, like cities, schools, public libraries, and state boards and commissions.
Performance audits are regularly conducted by the auditor of state to ensure local entities are maintaining clean financial books, to investigate potential fraud, and to assist governments in coming back from financial issues.
The state auditor also sits on the Ohio Redistricting Commission alongside the governor and secretary of state, as well as four lawmakers including one member from each party from each chamber of the legislature.
Democratic candidate for Ohio Auditor continues a life of learning as she aims for top job

LaRose will face Maple Heights Mayor Annette Blackwell in the Nov. 3 general election. Blackwell had a career in banking before she became mayor in 2014. Amid her tenure as mayor, she helped bring the city out of fiscal emergency, working closely with the auditor’s office as she did so.
LaRose credits the leader of his Boy Scout troop as the first inspiration in his life of service, a military veteran who led LaRose to join the U.S. Army. Because of his military service, LaRose didn’t go to college until later in life, but he sees that as a positive.
“I guess I’m glad I knew myself well enough at that point to know that I maybe wouldn’t have been the most serious student at 18 years old, but I was a serious student when I did finally go to college in my late 20s,” LaRose told a gathering of the Akron Press Club in May.
His run for the auditor’s office comes at a time when he says government agencies and other entities need to work on regaining the public’s confidence.
“Trust is at an all-time low in institutions of all kinds: the government, the churches, the press, businesses, civic organizations,” LaRose said in his press club speech. “People are not as trusting of those institutions as they once were, and in some ways that’s well-founded.”
But in other ways, he said that lack of trust is held up by a “chaotic information ecosystem,” where access to information, true or false, good or bad, is always available in bulk.
“We’ve got more access to information than we’ve ever had … but in so many ways are more misinformed than we’ve ever been,” the secretary of state said in May.
The auditor’s role is to “make sure that taxpayers are empowered with accurate information about how their local, county, and state government entities are operating,” according to LaRose.
The secretary supports efforts to battle fraud, specifically pointing to allegations of Medicaid fraud and other topics that have come up in the headlines over the past year.
The auditor’s office wouldn’t be investigating individuals for certain fraud crimes, but instead is tasked with “going after public officials that are engaging in fraud,” as LaRose put it to the press club.
Other agencies like the Ohio Attorney General’s Office look into individual allegations of fraud, and the legislature and the governor’s office need to work together to maintain enforcement models that prevent fraud.
“There’s a whole-of-government approach, if you will, that needs to be taken as it relates to dealing with this,” LaRose said.

As secretary of state, LaRose made headlines as a member of the Ohio Redistricting Commission, which spent the better part of four years attempting to redraw Statehouse and congressional district lines, with multiple maps rejected by the Ohio Supreme Court as unconstitutional.
Part of his role as chief elections officer is to head up the Ohio Ballot Board, which saw contentious hearings and criticism over board-approved ballot language for a constitutional amendment on abortion rights, and a proposed amendment to reform the redistricting commission, with critics saying the ballot board was putting its thumb on the scale with biased and confusing language.
LaRose led the charge to attempt to change the threshold for voters to pass constitutional amendments from a simple majority to 60%, but the proposal was rejected by Ohio voters.
LaRose also supported legislation last year to remove the absentee ballot grace period in Ohio and invalidate ballots that arrive to their boards of election after Election Day.
As secretary of state, he has pledged to crack down on voter fraud, creating an “Election Integrity Unit.” At the same time, he has made it clear in various public comments and numbers from his office that even potential cases of voter fraud, let alone actual proven cases, are rare in Ohio. In 2024, an audit LaRose did of noncitizen voter registration rolled in naturalized citizens, causing confusion for those citizens who had taken the necessary steps to be registered.
Addressing the issue at the Akron Press Club, LaRose said voter fraud is “exceedingly rare, but it’s impactful when it does happen.”
The general election in Ohio is Nov. 3, with early voting scheduled from Oct. 6 and Nov. 1. The voter registration deadline for the November election is Oct. 5, and requests for absentee ballots must be received by the boards of elections by Oct. 27.
Absentee ballots must be postmarked by Nov. 2, received in a dropbox by Nov. 3, or received by the boards of elections by Nov. 7.

title: A wheelchair ride across Wisconsin calls attention to Medicaid cuts
description: After a 125-mile trip on his powered wheelchair, Carl Schulze rolled up just before noon Thursday to the Wisconsin Capitol. The resident of Fox Crossing, near Neenah, made the journey to make a point: How Medicaid has helped him and thousands of other Wisconsin residents with disabilities — and how that help is being threatened […]
text:
Joined by supporters and other people who need mobility assistance, Carl Schulze completes his journey to the state Capitol Thursday. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)After a 125-mile trip on his powered wheelchair, Carl Schulze rolled up just before noon Thursday to the Wisconsin Capitol.
The resident of Fox Crossing, near Neenah, made the journey to make a point: How Medicaid has helped him and thousands of other Wisconsin residents with disabilities — and how that help is being threatened in Washington, D.C.
Carl Schulze. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)
A fall from a porch 19 years ago broke Schulze’s neck. He survived, but the accident left him unable to use his arms or legs.
Medicaid coverage for home care makes it possible for Schulze to hire aides who help him with virtually every activity of daily living. But with cuts to Medicaid totaling more than $900 million in 10 years because of the tax cut and spending law that President Donald Trump signed in July 2025, he worries that it may be harder to maintain his coverage, or pay the healthcare workers who support him.
And another initiative from the administration has angered — and worried — Schulze as well.
Since 1999, the U.S. Supreme Court’s Olmstead ruling has been interpreted to say that people with disabilities have a fundamental right to get their care at home or in the community instead of having to live in a nursing home or other institution. In June, however, the Trump administration U.S. Department of Justice issued a legal memo rejecting that long-held assumption.
“Apparently, it’s not a violation of my civil rights to put me in an institution against my will,” Schulze said to a bank of TV microphones on the sidewalk in front of the state Capitol. “The federal government is openly telling states, there will be no consequences if they defund the very services that keep disabled people living at home. They have effectively given states a green light to warehouse us again.”
The looming Medicaid cuts could give states, which administer the health insurance program and cover some of its costs, “no choice but to cut programs,” Schulze said. “And when they decide on what’s cut, the programs that serve people with disabilities will be first up on the chopping block. That means people like me may soon be forced to choose between our physical health and even the rest of our life in the future.”
Other federal initiatives are cutting federal grants that “no longer align with the administration’s priorities,” Schulze said. “For Wisconsin, this means even more uncertainty and deeper potential cuts to independent living support.”
Schulze didn’t take his wheelchair ride alone. Starting in mid-July, he began the trip from his apartment in Fox Crossing, driving the chair until the battery needed charging, with drivers accompanying him in his van. With each successive day, they drove him and the chair to the point where he stopped previously and continued the trip. Along the way he recorded videos for social media.
Care in the community is first and foremost a human right, said Jenny Price, executive director of the Wisconsin Board for People with Developmental Disabilities, in an interview. But it’s also more economical than putting someone in an institution, she observed.
“When you look at these [home care] services on their own, they appear very expensive,” Price said. “What kind of gets lost when people look at that big dollar amount is what that dollar amount could be if it were provided in an institutional setting.”
The cuts’ impact doesn’t end with people who require Medicaid for their healthcare.
Jason Glozier, the co-chair of the Survival Coalition of Wisconsin Disability Organizations, is the executive director of the Wisconsin Coalition of Independent Living Centers, a network of agencies around the state that offer information resources, navigation assistance and advocacy for people with disabilities who want to remain in the community.
“Almost 50% of unpaid caregivers are providing as much or more care hours than a half-time job,” Glozier said, citing a survey that the Survival Coalition conducted last year. “And 31% of caregivers are providing care more than 60 hours per week. Under any sort of labor laws, that wouldn’t be fair treatment. It shouldn’t be fair to expect our families to provide that care unpaid.”
“Family members have been providing enormous amounts of uncompensated care, for decades in some cases, to keep people in their home,” Tami Jackson, a policy analyst for the Board for People with Developmental Disabilities and  the other Survival Coalition co-chair, told reporters. “Even small cuts to the number of hours [of healthcare coverage] that somebody like Carl and many others get can mean the difference between being in their home and being locked away in a nursing facility where you don’t have the freedom to decide what your hours are, when you eat, who you can see, whether or not you can commute to a job, and a thousand other daily things that most of us are not thinking about right now.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio government doesn’t have to ban speech on campus to silence it
description: Three years ago, I warned that Ohio lawmakers were trying to cure perceived ideological bias in higher education by handing government greater authority over universities. I argued that even well-intentioned attempts to regulate speech could create a chilling effect. I knew something about that risk. Before Ohio’s universities were navigating Senate Bill 1,[...]
text:
A university professor addressing his students during a lecture. (Getty Images file photo.)Three years ago, I warned that Ohio lawmakers were trying to cure perceived ideological bias in higher education by handing government greater authority over universities. I argued that even well-intentioned attempts to regulate speech could create a chilling effect.
I knew something about that risk.
Before Ohio’s universities were navigating Senate Bill 1, I spent eight years fighting the federal government over my band’s name. The issue was never whether officials liked the name. It was whether the government had the authority to decide what our words meant. In 2017, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that it did not.
Now, with S.B. 1 in effect, Ohio offers a real-world test of that same question — and the early results are telling.
Start with the sheer machinery.
Across the state, public universities have stood up implementation committees, compliance websites, complaint portals, and reporting forms to interpret a single statute.
Kent State estimates compliance will cost it between $1.5 and $2 million every year.
The University of Toledo created forms for reporting “intellectual diversity” complaints.
Bowling Green opened a new compliance office.
Before anyone asks whether a professor has crossed a line, universities first have to spend enormous energy (and real money) determining where the line even is.
This is the pattern emerging from Ohio’s early implementation of the law.
When the government claims the authority to decide what speech means — what it intends, what it implies — it doesn’t need to punish anyone. The uncertainty does the work.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The evidence is already visible in how faculty behave.
This spring, a Kent State journalism class surveyed 38 faculty members about the new law.
More than a third said they had already changed how they teach in order to comply. A quarter said they worried a student might report them for something said in class. One professor described taking long pauses mid-lecture and second-guessing his words.
At the University of Cincinnati, the faculty union has said some professors are now reluctant to teach courses like African American history, for fear the subject is too controversial to risk.
No one banned those lectures. No one had to. The law produced the result that censorship usually requires a prosecutor to achieve — and it did so without charging anyone at all.
This is the part we consistently misunderstand about free speech.
We imagine its violations as dramatic: a banned book, a fired professor, a courtroom. But the most durable restrictions on speech are quieter.
They show up as a syllabus revised out of caution, a topic skipped rather than defended, a sentence rephrased so it can’t be misread.
As one Cincinnati faculty leader put it, professors are now spending their time figuring out how to comply with state mandates rather than teaching and doing research.
The First Amendment isn’t tested only when someone is punished for speaking.
It’s tested when institutions grow so busy interpreting government language that the operative question in every classroom shifts from “Is this true?” or “Is this worth teaching?” to “Will this get me in trouble?”
Supporters of S.B. 1 say it protects open inquiry. But you cannot foster free expression by making educators afraid of their own words.
Ohio has created a system in which professors must constantly consider how the state may interpret the meaning of their teaching — and, understandably, many are flinching.
Legislatures across the country are watching Ohio, weighing versions of the same law. So this is worth stating plainly, before it spreads: a free society does not lose its liberties only when the government forbids speech outright.
Sometimes it loses them when the rules become so uncertain that people begin censoring themselves before anyone asks them to.
The question is not whether Ohio’s professors are still allowed to speak. The question is how many ideas disappear — not because someone banned them, but because no one wanted to be the person who tested the boundary.
Simon Tam is the founder of The Slants and the central figure in Matal v. Tam (2017), the unanimous Supreme Court decision addressing viewpoint discrimination in trademark law. He speaks nationally on First Amendment issues.

With final results in, Blackburn, Green set up all-woman gubernatorial contest


By J. Holly McCall - Friday August 7, 2026 12:09 am





Tennessee voters will select a woman as the state’s governor, as U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn and Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green clinched the Republican and Democratic gubernatorial nominations, respectively. 
Despite predictions of a close race, Blackburn fended off U.S. Rep. John Rose and state Rep. Monty Hatcher, winning by 11 percentage points. 
Green easily defeated four opponents, winning with 69% of the votes cast. 
Two-term 5th District U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles lost his primary to Williamson County farmer and former state agriculture commissioner Charlie Hatcher, a shocking setback for President Donald Trump, who endorsed Ogles in each of his three races. 
Columbia, Tennessee Mayor Chaz Molder will face Williamson County farmer Charlie Hatcher in November for the chance to represent Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District. (Photo: Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)
Hatcher will face Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder in the November general election. 
In other hotly-watched races: 
Congressional District 4
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Scott DesJarlais, a Republican, cruised to victory in his primary, while second-time Democratic candidate Victoria Broderick defeated Metro Nashville Councilmember Mike Cortese by nine percentage points.
 Congressional District 6
State Rep. Johnny Garrett foiled a comeback attempt for former U.S. Rep. Van Hilleary in the newly-drawn 6th Congressional District. Garrett, who allied his campaign with Blackburn, handily beat Hilleary by 14 percentage points.
Congressional District 7
Darden Copeland, founder of a Nashville-based land use consulting firm, defeated three challengers, including state Rep. Vincent Dixie, to clinch the Democratic nomination for the 7th Congressional District. He will face incumbent U.S. Rep. Matt Van Epps. 
 Congressional District 9
Two state lawmakers will face off for the opportunity to represent the 9th Congressional District in a campaign that will likely get national attention. The district, formerly encompassing Memphis, has been held by a Democrat for more than 50 years and was redrawn in a May special legislative session. 
Rep. Justin J. Pearson won the Democratic nomination, defeating his colleague, state Sen. London Lamar, while Sen. Brent Taylor bested three other Republicans, including state Rep. Todd Warner.

Blackburn, congressional candidate Garrett, speak to GOP faithful in Wilson County


By J. Holly McCall -  2:34 pm





U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, with her campaign treasurer, Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs standing behind her, speaks to supporters in Mt. Juliet, Tennessee on Aug.6, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
During a stop on a state fly-around Thursday, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, a leading Republican gubernatorial candidate, said she will halt alleged efforts to spread Communism if elected. 
Blackburn made the remarks in Mt. Juliet as part of her swing on Tennessee’s primary Election Day, in which Republican and Democratic candidates will be selected in the gubernatorial, U.S. Senate, all nine congressional seats and state House and Senate districts. 
She was joined by state Rep. Johnny Garrett, who is running for the 6th Congressional District, Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, Blackburn’s campaign treasurer, state Rep. Clark Boyd of Lebanon and anti-transgender activist Riley Gaines of Sumner County. 
When asked by the Lookout if she would continue to support keeping Tennessee National Guard troops in Memphis as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, Blackburn didn’t answer but did express her continued support for the collaboration of federal and state agencies created in September by President Donald Trump with the backing of Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee. 
Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, with state Rep. Johnny Garrett to the left and anti-transgender activist Riley Gaines, speaks to supporters at an Election Day event for Blackburn and Garrett. Jacobs is thought to be a leading contender to replace Blackburn int he U.S Senate should she win her race for governor. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“We started our morning in Memphis and people in Memphis are thrilled the city is safe,” Blackburn said. 
Lee told reporters this week crime in Memphis has dropped to its lowest point in decades, though he gave no specifics. 
Since May, agents with the task force have shot and killed four men in the city. All of the cases remain under investigation, but in at least one instance, the Drug Enforcement Agency officer involved in the shooting will not be prosecuted. 
Both Blackburn and Garrett mentioned Communism and threats to women’s sports by transgender athletes as their main concerns.
“We are truly sending a message that Tennessee is a conservative state and that all of these woke policies, all this move towards Communism, that ends at the Tennessee state line,” Blackburn said. 
Garrett, who faces former U.S. Rep. Van Hilleary and retired U.S. Marine Jon Henry, has made state efforts to crack down on transgender people central to his campaign, airing an ad featuring a drag queen playing basketball. 
“Did we ever think it would be an issue that we would have to fight the woke left to protect our daughters playing in volleyball, when they play in softball, when they play in basketball, that they are going to play against a full-grown man,” Garrett said, before introducing Gaines, who became a spokesperson for the anti-trans movement after tying for fifth place with a transwoman during a college swimming meet. 
Karen Harding, a gospel singer from Sumner County, said she believes Blackburn has been great as a senator and that she would do a “phenomenal job” as governor.
“And it’s pretty cool that she’s the first woman, too,” said Harding. “I got an invitation and thought, I have to be here and support her.”
If Blackburn wins the Republican nomination, she will be the first woman to do so. A win by Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis City councilmember thought to be the leading Democratic candidate in the gubernatorial race, would give Tennessee its first all-woman state election.

Ogles accompanies RFK, Jr. for proposed Head Start rule change announcement


By Cassandra Stephenson -  1:48 pm





U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles stands alongside U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. at Susan Gray Head Start in Nashville, Tennessee on Aug. 6, 2026. The secretary addressed proposed rule changes that would strip federal regulations for the Head Start program back to statutory requirements, putting further regulatory responsibilities on states. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)
U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles stood alongside U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams Thursday morning as the pair discussed the proposed rollback of federal regulations for Head Start, a program that provides education, nutrition and other supports for children from low-income families.
Ogles, who is on Tennessee’s ballot and faces a challenge in the Republican 5th Congressional District primary from former state agriculture commissioner Charlie Hatcher, did not take any election-related questions, but spoke briefly in support of the proposed changes.
Kennedy’s proposal would eliminate federal standards for the program beyond what is required by law, shifting regulatory decisions for things like staff-to-child ratios and education requirements to states. It would also reduce the amount of funding that Head Start programs can spend on administrative costs from 15% of the program’s total cost to 5%. Adams said the change could save around $2.2 billion, which could then be used to create more program spots for children.
Administrative costs can include everything from payroll to special support staff for children with disabilities. HHS later clarified in an email to the Lookout that teacher salaries and expenses related to educational facilities are not included in the administrative services category. ACF would continue to allow grantee agencies to apply for temporary waivers for the administrative cost cap.
Asked about stripping back mandates on salaries for Head Start employees, Kennedy asked if every Head Start should reflect the salary that someone may receive in New York, even if that program is located in Arkansas, Tennessee, or another state with an overall lower cost of living.
U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams deliver remarks on a proposed federal rule change for Head Start at Susan Gray Head Start in Nashville, Tennessee on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)
Kennedy and Adams pitched the regulation reduction as “cutting red tape” and opening “flexibility” for states and parents.
The proposed rule change would also require Head Start programs to provide nutrition in line with the Make America Healthy Again guidelines and establish a baseline requirement for physical activity. 
The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking will be published in the Federal Register on Friday and will accept public comments for 60 days.
