name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘Moms’ Equal Pay Day’ highlights the struggles faced by many Mississippians
description: Cassandra Welchin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable, speaks at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Feb. 13, 2025. Welchin emphasized the importance of the “Secure the Bag” initiative, which advocates for fair wages, paid leave and economic policies that support Black women and working families.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.   

Every day across Mississippi, mothers wake up early, get their children ready for school, go to work and do everything they can to provide for their families. Yet despite their hard work, far too many still face impossible choices: paying the rent or keeping the lights on, covering childcare or buying groceries, replacing a child’s school uniform or filling a prescription. No parent should have to make those decisions simply because her work is undervalued.
At Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable, we see these realities every day. The stories we hear from mothers across our state remind us that the wage gap isn’t an abstract policy debate. It’s a daily struggle that affects whether families can remain stable and whether children have the opportunity to thrive.
That is why Moms’ Equal Pay Day, which is recognized today, is more than a date on the calendar. It marks how far into the following year mothers must work – added with their pay from the previous year – to earn what fathers earned the previous year.
According to the National Women’s Law Center’s most recent Mothers’ Wage Gap report, last updated in May 2025, mothers working full-time, year-round earn approximately 74 cents for every dollar earned by fathers. In Mississippi, that figure drops to approximately 67 cents on the dollar, and the gap widens even further for mothers working part-time or part-year.
For many mothers – especially single mothers who are often their family’s sole provider – that gap translates into fewer opportunities to build savings, absorb unexpected expenses and create long-term financial stability.
Our mission at Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable is to build the political, economic and social power of Black women and girls throughout Mississippi. While we advocate for long-term policy solutions, we also recognize that families facing emergencies cannot wait for legislation to catch up. They need support today.
That understanding gave rise to our Community Outreach and Relief Resources Initiative, CORRI, which helps families weather unexpected hardship with dignity while we continue advocating for lasting economic opportunity.
One of CORRI’s signature efforts, Quarters Because We Care, began as a practical response to families facing extraordinary circumstances during the Jackson water crisis and has grown into a lifeline for parents struggling to keep their households together. Through CORRI, Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable provides emergency support – from laundry services to rent, utility and childcare assistance – that often determines whether a working parent can remain employed.
Clean clothes may seem like a small thing until you’re the parent trying to report to work or send your child to school with dignity. Economic justice is often built on meeting these everyday needs.
The impact of Quarters Because We Care is reflected in what participants tell us. One of the most common responses we hear is: “Thank you. I only came in to wash a couple of loads of laundry – whether it was my children’s school uniforms or my work clothes. Because your organization provided this service, I can now use those resources for other things my family needs.”
Many participants return later the same day or the following day to finish the rest of their laundry because they know they have a safe, welcoming place where they can meet an essential need without added financial stress.
Through the Quarters Because We Care program, the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable provides struggling families with help for basic needs like laundry services, rent, utility and childcare assistance. Credit: Courtesy photo
The families we serve come from every corner of Mississippi. They are teachers, restaurant workers, social workers, government employees and, at times, people experiencing homelessness. Their circumstances differ, but they all share the same determination: to provide for themselves and their families with dignity.
Programs like Quarters Because We Care give families room to breathe – allowing them to redirect scarce dollars toward groceries, gas, school supplies, utilities or rent while preserving dignity, restoring hope and reminding them they are not facing these challenges alone.
That program is just one example of how CORRI responds when families face immediate hardship. Our Emergency Assistance Program provides another critical safety net, helping parents bridge temporary financial crises before they become long-term setbacks.
We regularly hear from mothers whose financial stability has been disrupted almost overnight. One mother lost her childcare voucher, threatening her ability to continue working. Another welcomed a new baby while unpaid maternity leave reduced her household to a single income. In both cases, emergency assistance helped prevent temporary setbacks from becoming lasting financial crises by easing concerns about utility shutoffs, eviction and other immediate hardships, allowing parents to focus on caring for their families while regaining stability.
These stories remind us that the wage gap is not simply about unequal paychecks. It is about unequal opportunity. It is about whether families can build savings, purchase homes, afford healthcare, invest in education or recover when life inevitably brings unexpected challenges.
While Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable will continue meeting immediate needs through programs like CORRI, we know firsthand that emergency assistance alone cannot solve the structural inequities that leave too many working mothers one unexpected expense away from financial crisis.
When mothers are paid less than they have earned, the impact extends far beyond individual families. Employers lose valuable talent, local economies lose spending power and communities lose the stability that comes when working families have the opportunity to thrive.
That is why we continue advocating for policies that strengthen economic security for Mississippi’s families, including raising the state’s minimum wage, which has remained at $7.25 per hour for 17 years; strengthening equal pay protections by prohibiting employers from relying on salary history; expanding pay transparency and protecting workers who discuss wages from retaliation; strengthening protections against pay discrimination; and expanding access to affordable healthcare so mothers can remain healthy, employed and able to care for their families.
These are not partisan ideas. They are practical investments in Mississippi’s workforce, businesses, children and future.
Moms’ Equal Pay Day should challenge all of us – not simply to acknowledge the wage gap, but to ask what we are willing to do about it.
Every mother deserves the opportunity to provide for her family without having to work harder simply to earn less. Every child deserves the stability that comes when the youngster’s parent is paid fairly.
When we invest in mothers, we invest in stronger children, stronger communities and a stronger Mississippi. Closing the wage gap is about more than equal pay. It’s about ensuring every family has the opportunity not simply to survive, but to build a secure future for generations to come.

Cassandra Welchlin is executive director of the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable. A licensed social worker, advocate and mother, she has spent more than 20 years advancing policies that strengthen economic security and health for Mississippi women and families.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Questions arise about Pasco state Rep. Kevin Steele’s run for Congress in Hillsborough County
description: Pasco County Republican state lawmaker Kevin Steele has emphasized his Hillsborough County roots since entering the race for the Republican nomination for Congressional District 14. That’s because the newly redrawn congressional seat is set exclusively in Hillsborough, far from the area he now represents in the Florida House of Representatives. Federal law d[...]
text:
Pasco County state GOP Rep. Kevin Steele speaking in Plant City on Aug.t 4, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Pasco County Republican state lawmaker Kevin Steele has emphasized his Hillsborough County roots since entering the race for the Republican nomination for Congressional District 14. That’s because the newly redrawn congressional seat is set exclusively in Hillsborough, far from the area he now represents in the Florida House of Representatives.
Federal law does not require a member of Congress to live in the district he or she represents. However, state law says a state lawmaker must live in the district he or she represents.
The CD 14 seat has been held for the past 20 years by Tampa Democrat Kathy Castor. But after it was redistricted from an area she won by 15 points in 2024 to one that Donald Trump won by more than 10 points that same year, Steele and seven other Republicans filed to run for the seat.
When asked by the Phoenix Tuesday night whether he intended to move from Pasco to Hillsborough if elected to the seat in November, he said he already lived in and had voted in the district. He posted a photo on social media Monday with members of his family at the Jan Platt Library in South Tampa, the first day of early voting in the county.
Records show Steele is registered to vote in Hillsborough County. However, he still has a homestead exemption at his Dade City home in Pasco County, where he serves as a state representative in District 55.
According to his most recent Form 6 financial disclosure filed July 1, under the description of assets, he lists his “Residence and Land” as the street address of his home in Dade City, but instead of Dade City he lists the city as Tampa. However, the street he lists as his residence does not exist in Tampa.
State law says House candidates or incumbents must live and be registered to vote in the districts in which they were running at the time of the election and maintain a residence in the district for the entire term to which they are elected. Lawmakers are allowed to own multiple homes but can only have one principal, or legal, residence.
Florida House rules also say they consider a lawmaker’s legal residence to be the one listed on official documents or mentioned in statements to others, voter registration records, homestead exemption paperwork, and a driver’s license; where a lawmaker receives mail; or where a spouse and minor children live and attend school.
Steele did not respond to a request for comment.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Lawsuit seeks Missouri ballot spot for amendment limiting changes to voter-approved initiatives
description: A campaign seeking to make it harder for lawmakers to alter voter-approved initiatives sued Secretary of State Denny Hoskins on Thursday, asking a judge to overturn his decision blocking the proposed constitutional amendment from the November ballot. The lawsuit, filed in Cole County Circuit Court by three Missourians who signed the Respect Missouri Voters p[...]
text:
Volunteers with Respect Missouri Voters collect signatures during the No Kings demonstration at the Missouri State Capitol in Jefferson City in October 2025.  Respect Missouri Voters is the intiative petition campaign for a constitutional amendment that would make it harder for the General Assembly to overturn citizen-led ballot measures (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).A campaign seeking to make it harder for lawmakers to alter voter-approved initiatives sued Secretary of State Denny Hoskins on Thursday, asking a judge to overturn his decision blocking the proposed constitutional amendment from the November ballot.
The lawsuit, filed in Cole County Circuit Court by three Missourians who signed the Respect Missouri Voters petition, also challenges Hoskins’ attempt to withdraw and replace a ballot title his office certified nearly a year ago — before supporters collected hundreds of thousands of signatures.
It is the second lawsuit filed this week challenging Hoskins’ refusal to certify a citizen petition for the Nov. 3 ballot.
On Tuesday, Hoskins declared both the Respect Missouri Voters initiative and a referendum seeking to overturn Missouri’s new congressional map insufficient. People Not Politicians, the campaign behind the redistricting referendum, sued later that day.
Respect Missouri Voters filed its lawsuit Thursday morning.
“Hundreds of thousands of citizens, far more than required, signed to demand that the Respect Missouri Voters Amendment appear on the ballot,” Toni Easter, a volunteer and co-founder of the group, said after Hoskins announced his decision.
Hoskins could not immediately be reached for comment Thursday.
Referendum campaign asks court to block new Missouri map from November election

Respect Missouri Voters submitted its petition to Hoskins’ office May 3 after a yearlong campaign aimed at limiting lawmakers’ ability to change measures approved through the initiative process.
The campaign says it collected more than 367,000 signatures. Its lawsuit says more than 330,000 were submitted to the secretary of state.
A constitutional amendment requires signatures equal to 8% of the votes cast in the most recent gubernatorial election in six of Missouri’s eight congressional districts. The lawsuit says the petition needed 177,713 valid signatures across six districts.
Hoskins did not cite an insufficient number of valid signatures when he rejected the petition Tuesday.
Instead, he concluded the proposal violated constitutional requirements limiting initiative petitions to a single subject and changes to a single article of the Missouri Constitution.
His decision relied on a legal opinion from Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, who also argued parts of the proposal impermissibly restricted future legislatures and raised questions under the U.S. Constitution’s guarantee of a republican form of government.
The proposed amendment would declare initiative and referendum powers a fundamental right, preserve existing signature and statewide majority requirements and prevent lawmakers from weakening the initiative process.
It would also prohibit lawmakers from changing or repealing laws enacted through the initiative process, or passing laws similar to those rejected by referendum, without approval from at least 80% of both the Missouri House and Senate or a public vote.
The protections would apply to citizen-initiated laws and constitutional amendments approved after Jan. 1, 2010, as well as laws rejected by voters through referendum after that date. The restrictions would apply to legislative action taken after the amendment takes effect, meaning they would not automatically undo changes lawmakers made before then.
The lawsuit argues all of those provisions share one “reasonably narrow and identifiable central and controlling purpose” and amend only Article III of the Missouri Constitution.
But the dispute also centers on decisions Hoskins and the attorney general made before supporters ever began gathering signatures.
Former Attorney General Andrew Bailey, who held the office at the time, approved the petition as to form on July 31, 2025. Hoskins approved the petition’s form the same day and certified its official ballot title on Sept. 9.
No one challenged that ballot title during the 10-day period allowed under state law.
Supporters then circulated petitions bearing the title Hoskins had certified.
When Hoskins rejected the petition Tuesday, however, his certificate of insufficiency also purported to withdraw the September ballot title and certify a new one.
The lawsuit argues state law gives the secretary of state no authority to do that at the end of the petition process.
It points to a 2024 Missouri Supreme Court ruling arising from the abortion-rights amendment voters approved that year.
In that case, then-Secretary of State Jay Ashcroft attempted to reverse earlier decisions approving the form of the petition after a Cole County judge ordered the amendment removed from the ballot.
The Supreme Court said Ashcroft’s attempt was “a nullity and of no effect” and held that the secretary was not entitled to reassess matters he had previously approved.
The Respect Missouri Voters lawsuit argues Hoskins is bound by the same principle.
“The secretary is not entitled to re-assess matters of form that he [has] already approved,” the lawsuit states, quoting the 2024 decision.
The lawsuit asks a judge to reverse Hoskins’ certificate of insufficiency, order him to declare the petition sufficient and place it on the November ballot using the title certified last September.
The case comes days after Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected Amendment 4, a measure placed on Tuesday’s ballot by lawmakers that would have required citizen-led constitutional amendments to win a majority statewide and in each of Missouri’s eight congressional districts.
Respect Missouri Voters was among the groups campaigning against Amendment 4.
Tuesday was also the statutory deadline for Hoskins to decide whether citizen petitions had enough support and otherwise complied with state law to qualify for November.
Under state law, lawsuits challenging those decisions must be moved to the front of the court docket and decided “as quickly as possible.”
There is another deadline looming.
No court may order a measure added to the Nov. 3 ballot after Sept. 8, eight weeks before Election Day.
That leaves Respect Missouri Voters and People Not Politicians less than five weeks to win their cases if their proposals are to appear before voters this fall.

name: Delaware
title: First State Educate launches onboarding initiative for new school board members
description: Statewide program will provide governance training, mentoring and professional support as newly elected members begin making decisions affecting students, families and taxpayers By George D. Rotsch, Editor Delaware LIVE WILMINGTON, Del. — First State Educate has launched a statewide onboarding initiative that provides governance resources, professional learn[...]
text:
Statewide program will provide governance training, mentoring and professional support as newly elected members begin making decisions affecting students, families and taxpayers
By George D. Rotsch, Editor Delaware LIVE
WILMINGTON, Del. — First State Educate has launched a statewide onboarding initiative that provides governance resources, professional learning and ongoing support for Delaware’s newly elected school board members.
Julia Keleher, Executive Director of First State Educate, said the initiative is designed to help new members understand their responsibilities before they begin making decisions involving district budgets, superintendent leadership, student achievement, public policy and the use of taxpayer dollars.
School board members often take office only weeks after winning an election. Although they immediately assume responsibility for major policy and financial decisions, many begin their service with limited formal preparation for their governance role.
Keleher said the initiative will help new members begin their service with a clearer understanding of how an effective school board operates and how individual members can contribute to the board’s success.
Starting with governance
School boards establish district policies, approve budgets, hire and evaluate superintendents, and set the strategic direction of local school systems.
Board members are not responsible for managing the daily operations of schools. That work is generally handled by the superintendent and district administrators.
Understanding that distinction can help board members focus on long-term goals, student outcomes, financial oversight and accountability rather than becoming involved in routine management decisions.
Keleher said effective onboarding can also help new members understand meeting procedures, legal responsibilities, public accountability requirements and the importance of working collaboratively with other members of the board.
Resources, mentoring and professional learning
The First State Educate initiative includes a board onboarding framework, governance resources and continuing professional learning opportunities. The initiative is intended to provide support beyond a member’s first weeks in office. Keleher said ongoing professional learning can help board members respond to changing academic, financial and community challenges throughout their terms.
Keleher said the program also includes a partnership with Wilmington University and a governance credentialing pathway that allows board members to publicly demonstrate a commitment to effective school governance.
First State Educate also offers an opportunity to create a mentoring component that can connect newly elected members with experienced education and governance leaders.
Better preparation can also help members ask stronger questions, evaluate information more carefully and build productive relationships with superintendents, fellow board members and the public.
Why residents should care
Strong school boards benefit more than the people seated at the board table.
Board decisions influence classroom resources, academic programs, school safety, transportation, employee contracts, taxes and the long-term financial health of a district. Those decisions affect students, families, educators, property owners and businesses throughout the community.
Keleher said a well-prepared board is more likely to remain focused on measurable goals, responsible spending and student achievement.  Citizens can expect a more meaningful discussion at board meetings, more focus on the highest priorities and a better exchange of ideas between the community and leaders in the school.
Delaware residents also have a role in strengthening local school governance. Community members can learn who serves on their board, attend meetings, review agendas, follow budget discussions and communicate constructively with elected members.
Residents should not wait until a controversial vote or financial crisis to begin paying attention. Understanding how a board operates before disagreements arise can lead to better public discussions and more informed community participation.
Keleher said the initiative is intended to help board members start strong while giving Delaware residents additional opportunities to understand, follow and support the work of their local school boards.

What: First State Educate’s statewide school board onboarding initiative
Purpose: To provide newly elected Delaware school board members with governance resources, mentoring and continuing professional learning
Program components: A board onboarding framework, governance materials, a Wilmington University partnership, mentoring opportunities and a possible governance credentialing pathway
Who benefits: School board members, students, families, educators and taxpayers
Learn more: Visit First State Educate’s website for school board resources, educational programs and community discussion opportunities.

title: US Senate panel votes to hold Fauci in contempt for declining to answer COVID questions
text: WASHINGTON — Republicans on a U.S. Senate panel voted Thursday to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he declined to answer any questions at a hearing last week about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic.The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted along party lines to approve a resolution referring to the Justice Department charges that Fauci, a top public health official during the pandemic, violated a congressional subpoena when he repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and refused to answer any questions at a July 29 committee hearing.Fauci asserted his Fifth Amendment right 111 times, even in response to Republicans’ questions about his tie color or the day of the week meant to test his strategy.Chairman Rand Paul of Kentucky and other committee Republicans said Thursday that was a misuse of the privilege, in part because President Joe Biden issued a broad pardon to Fauci covering any conduct from 2014 to 2025.“We are voting on whether a witness who has received the benefit of a sweeping federal pardon can be ordered by this committee to answer questions and then defy that order without consequence,” Paul said.Walking into a ‘trap’?Democrats raised a host of objections to the contempt resolution.They said, as Fauci argued during the hearing, that Paul sought to trap Fauci. Biden’s pardon of Fauci would not cover new misstatements to Congress, Sen. Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat, said. “The goal was to wait for Dr. Fauci to make any kind of misstatement and then have a weaponized Department of Justice file criminal charges for that new statement that would not have been covered by the pardon, leaving Dr. Fauci little choice but to invoke his constitutional right to not walk directly into a trap,” Hassan said.Fauci said during an opening statement at last week’s hearing that he believed “any reasonable person” would conclude that Paul’s objective was to trip him up.“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something — anything — that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars,’” he said. Weakening future investigationsRanking Democrat Gary Peters of Michigan also said the partisan vote undermined the panel’s legitimacy.He took particular exception to Paul’s intention to send the resolution directly to federal prosecutors without gaining approval from the full Senate, which would require a bipartisan vote to meet the chamber’s 60-vote threshold.“No individual senator and no committee speaks for the entire Senate,” he said. “Institutional powers belong to the full body. Allowing one chairman to unilaterally assert those powers would invite future chairs in both parties to bypass the Senate whenever they cannot secure the support of their colleagues.”Future witnesses could use the vote to justify not appearing before congressional committees, Peters said.Highly public roleThe July 29 hearing was a departure for Fauci, who, as one of the nation’s most visible public health officials during the pandemic, spoke publicly about it on a daily basis for several months. He has testified before congressional committees two dozen times since January 2020 and had never declined to answer lawmaker questions before last week. Fauci was a member of the coronavirus task force during President Donald Trump’s first administration and a chief medical adviser on COVID-19 during Biden’s term. He headed the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases under presidents of both parties for nearly four decades.As the pandemic response turned increasingly political in the months following nationwide containment efforts in early 2020, Republicans became more critical of measures that caused significant economic problems.Sen. Ron Johnson, a Wisconsin Republican who chaired the panel in 2020, said Thursday that learning what officials like Fauci knew at the time was key to understanding what led to the response he considered an overreaction.“It's been six years since the pandemic began,” he said. “We have not had a reckoning of what happened.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Meet Iowa’s secretary of agriculture candidates
description: Water quality is shaping up to be a big issue in many of Iowa’s races for the Nov. 3 election but especially in Iowa’s race for secretary of agriculture, where Republican incumbent Mike Naig faces water quality advocate and Democratic candidate Chris Jones.  Iowa Capital Dispatch sat down with each candidate to talk about water […]
text:
Democrat Chris Jones, left, is running against Republican incumbent Mike Naig for Iowa secretary of agriculture. (Candidate photos by Zach Sommers for Iowa Capital Dispatch, wetland photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Water quality is shaping up to be a big issue in many of Iowa’s races for the Nov. 3 election but especially in Iowa’s race for secretary of agriculture, where Republican incumbent Mike Naig faces water quality advocate and Democratic candidate Chris Jones. 
Iowa Capital Dispatch sat down with each candidate to talk about water quality, a struggling farm economy, local food initiatives, conservation practices and foreign animal disease. 
As water quality issues hit urban areas like Des Moines and urban Iowans increasingly hold the agricultural industry responsible, the question of who leads the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship is interesting to more than just farmers. 
Meet Naig and Jones 

 Video filmed and edited by Zach Sommers for Iowa Capital Dispatch. 
Mike Naig grew up in the northwest region of Iowa near Cylinder, where he’s still part of the family century farm. He was elected Iowa secretary of agriculture in 2018 and reelected in 2022. 
Naig said in his time as secretary of agriculture, he has seen the impact the role can have on the people he has met across the state through the office. 
“Those businesses, those farms, you really can do things to help them,” Naig said. “You really can do things to make the situation better, and I love being able to do that. So that’s what I’ve enjoyed about the job, and certainly that’s why I’m hoping to be reelected again this year.” 

 Video filmed and edited by Zach Sommers for Iowa Capital Dispatch. 
Chris Jones is a researcher, author and water quality advocate. He previously worked at Des Moines Water Works, at Iowa Soybean Association and as a research engineer at the University of Iowa. Jones is also known for his book “Swine Republic” and his Substack of the same title, where he writes about agriculture and water quality in the state. 
Jones said he views his run for the office as a “referendum on the condition of Iowa’s water.” 
“If people think the water quality is what it should be, and they like what their drinking water is, and they like what the lakes and beaches are in Iowa and the conditions of the rivers, then, you know, I’m probably not the candidate for them,” Jones said. “If you think all these things are lacking and need improvement, and that we need some urgency in getting them improved, then I think my candidacy is worth consideration.” 
Water quality
Naig said he agrees with Jones that Iowa needs to improve the quality of its water.
“Clean water is non-negotiable – everybody, every Iowan, deserves access to clean water,” Naig said. “It’s not a debate as to whether or not we need to improve the situation … my opponent and I both agree on that, but the how is a completely different approach.” 
Naig’s approach in office has centered on incentive-based programs to increase adoption of conservation methods through Iowa’s Nutrient Reduction Strategy, a “batch-and-build” method of installing edge of field practices on cropland and most recently the state’s “Farm to Faucet” program, which increased conservation incentives and provided funding to water treatment facilities. 
Naig said rather than play the “blame game” between agriculture and downstream water users, the two should be working “in partnership.” 
“Let’s recognize that it is a farm to faucet approach that will actually deliver the results we need,” Naig said. “That means you have to, yes, have the water treatment infrastructure that’s required to serve not just Central Iowa but also communities all across the state, but we should also be working to make sure that pollutants don’t enter the streams to begin with.” 
IDALS and partners at Iowa State University have tracked an increase in the adoption of conservation practices like cover crops, and reduced tillage and nutrient reduction strategies like buffer strips and bioreactors, since the start of the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy.
Jones has criticized the industrial agriculture model in his writing, and in his campaign for secretary of agriculture he has called for taxpayer-funded offramps to help producers move away from the corn, soybean and ethanol dominated system. 
Jones argued that funding this transition would do more for water quality than the batch and build method and other edge of field incentives. 
“This edge of field approach to try to capture tile water off a few acres here and there is just this Band-aid and diaper approach,” Jones said. “I think that money could be much better spent on helping farmers transition to more sustainable production systems, ones where they’re integrating oats and small grains and forage crops.” 
Farm economy 
Jones argued that if the ethanol industry was built to create better markets for corn and soybeans, then markets for other crops, like oats, could also be developed for farmers. 
“If you’re a farmer, you just don’t wake up one morning and decide I’m going to grow oats, or you just don’t wake up one morning and decide I’m going to grow apples – that’s not the way it works,” Jones said. “You need to have infrastructure to support that activity.” 
He said taxpayer-supported programs could help to “indemnify those crops” as farmers transition from more traditional crops and learn what grows well on their land. 
“I think it’s entirely appropriate for the taxpayer to participate in this, and I think this is money that’s better spent than these diapers and Band-aids that we’re putting on the corn-soy system,” Jones said. 
Naig argued that approach would “gut” Iowa’s economy. 
“That’s actually a plan to shrink Iowa agriculture, not to grow it,” he said. 
He said Iowa grows corn and soybeans because of its soil and climate. Because it leads in those commodities, he said it also leads in livestock feeding and biofuel production — a way of “turning those row crops into something of higher value.” 
“If ag is strong in Iowa and growing, all Iowans benefit from that,” Naig said. “We shouldn’t be turning away from it, we should be thinking about how do we add even more value to what we do, but also creating opportunities for diversity and create opportunities for more food production in the state of Iowa.”
Naig said that as he visits with farmers, profitability is “at the center of everything.” It’s a combination, he said, of several years of low prices for corn and soybeans, high input costs and policy uncertainty as Congress has punted farm bill legislation for the past several years. 
Jones argued that if farmers transitioned to crops that required fewer inputs — like fertilizers, pesticides or machinery — it would help farmers financially and help the rest of the state because it “would reduce the amount of pollution in our streams and lakes.” 
Foreign animal disease 
Naig said the heart of the issue with agriculture is “making sure Iowans have access to safe, affordable food.” 
“We do this wrong — especially given Iowa’s outsized role in agriculture in this country — we do it wrong, consumers pay in the end for those things,” Naig said. 
The highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 outbreak has affected more than 208 million commercial and backyard birds since it began in 2022, which greatly affected consumer egg prices at the end of 2024 and in 2025. 
Naig said Iowa’s response to foreign animal diseases, including the highly pathogenic avian influenza, is one of the things he is most proud of over the past eight years. He said he has worked to build up partnerships, response teams and secure additional funding to make Iowa “if not the best, one of the best, in terms of our capabilities to respond.” 
“That didn’t happen by accident, that happened because it’s important,” he said. “That’s nothing short of protecting those family farms, which then, of course, it protects our Iowa economy as well.”
Jones said animal disease is a “huge issue” in Iowa, because of its large livestock operations. 
“Whenever you put this many animals under a roof, like we do with hogs and chickens, that’s the way nature works: you’re going to have disease,” Jones said. 
Rather than continue to fight off the diseases with antibiotics and other methods, Jones said he would push for alternative animal production means. 
“Let’s return some of these animals to pastoral systems, where they’re not eating commodity grains and they’re eating forage crops and they’re eliminating their waste in ways that’s not going to get into the streams,” he said.
Local food 
Iowans increasingly are looking to source food locally, according to a poll from Iowa Farm Bureau. 
Jones’ policy propositions to move away from a corn- and soybean-dominated ag economy include building better markets for farmers to grow and sell food crops. 

He proposed requiring schools to source 50% of their food from Iowa farms as a starting point. 
“Here in Iowa, we need to strategize about what comes after ethanol,” Jones said. “Let’s talk about it now, and let’s figure out what else we can do with this land to keep farmers in the state prosperous.”
Currently, more than half of the corn grown in Iowa is processed into ethanol, according to the Iowa Corn Growers Association.
Under Naig’s leadership, IDALS launched the Choose Iowa program, a marketing program to promote Iowa grown, raised and made products. The program has grants to help expand local food farm operations and funding matches for food banks and schools to purchase locally grown food. 
Naig said the program is only three years old, but it is growing in popularity as more Iowans support it. 
“We’re seeing a lot of growth in that area, and I’m really proud of that work that we’ve done to diversify agriculture,” Naig said. “That creates opportunities for the next generation of farmers, new farmers, actually get into it too.” 
Jones argued the program is underfunded to the point of being “almost trivial.” He said more money needs to be allocated to local food programs to make them effective. 
Iowans can vote for secretary of agriculture in the upcoming general election Nov. 3.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico delegation introduces bill to ban uranium mining in Chama Watershed
description: The Chama Basin Watershed Protection Act, sponsored by U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich and Ben Ray Luján and U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, all New Mexico Democrats, if enacted, would prohibit all forms of uranium mining through much of Rio Arriba County, including in the Santa Fe and Carson national forests.
text:
Members of New Mexico’s congressional delegation announced Aug. 6, 2026, that they were introducing a bill to ban uranium extraction in the Chama Watershed, including the area pictured above near Canjilon that a Canadian company is seeking to mine. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Members of New Mexico’s congressional delegation on Thursday announced they’d introduced a bill that would prohibit uranium mining throughout the Chama Basin Watershed, after a Canadian company earlier this year sought federal permits to conduct exploratory drilling.
The Chama Basin Watershed Protection Act, sponsored by U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich and Ben Ray Luján and U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, all New Mexico Democrats, if enacted, would prohibit all forms of uranium mining through much of Rio Arriba County, including in the Santa Fe and Carson national forests. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a statement, the three elected officials cited fears of potential impacts of uranium mining on the watershed and Chama River, which ultimately flows into the Rio Grande, along with concerns about uranium contamination on ranchers, tribes and acequias.
“These cherished lands and waters must be protected for future generations,” Luján said in a statement. “I will not stand by and allow a foreign mining company to threaten the communities of the Chama Valley and disregard the respect these communities deserve.”
The lawmakers said the legislation is in direct response to a proposal from Gamma Resources, Ltd. to drill up to 12 exploratory uranium boreholes up to 500 feet deep near Canjilon as part of its “Mesa Arc” project. The company told potential investors that it believes up to 3 million pounds of uranium exists in the area it seeks to drill.
The company has faced sustained backlash since Source NM first reported in March on its exploratory permit application to the Carson National Forest. Opponents include community groups, environmentalists and elected officials at the local, state and federal levels. 
Many of the critics cite the legacy of environmental and public health impacts due to uranium in New Mexico, particularly among Indigenous communities. Leger Fernández, in a statement Thursday, said abandoned uranium mines must be cleaned up before any new mines are approved. 
By the #s: More mining claims filed in New Mexico in last 4 years than previous century

“New Mexicans know the true cost of uranium mining,” Leger Fernández said. “Across our state, abandoned uranium mines have poisoned our land, threatened our water, and harmed generations of families. Before anyone talks about opening another uranium mine, we should finish cleaning up the mess that was left behind.”
A Carson National Forest spokesperson previously told Source NM the United States Forest Service is reviewing the company’s application. The company must also receive state approval from the New Mexico Mining and Minerals Division, but Gamma has not yet filed for a permit at the state level, according to a division database.
The Gamma proposal is just one of multiple examples of renewed global interest in extracting New Mexico’s uranium since President Donald Trump’s second term began. Heinrich, in his statement Thursday, said the legislation sends a clear message to the company:
“Back off,” he said. “The Chama Watershed belongs to the acequia parciantes, Tribal communities, ranchers, and rural families who care for and depend on this landscape and its water — not a foreign mining company looking to exploit it for profit.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: DCF changes detailed in response to CT child advocate concerns
description: DCF is hiring support staff and building up the foster family network, but disagreed with OCA on how to address girls' behavioral healthcare needs.
text:
A lengthy letter from the state Department of Children and Families released in response to concerns raised months ago by the state’s child advocate sheds light on actions the department is taking after a series of tragic child deaths. The letter also shows how the department is trying to address difficult conditions for employees, like high caseloads and overtime, that are leading to poor workforce retention.
In a 17-page letter addressed to Gov. Ned Lamont, DCF Commissioner Susan Hamilton said the department is hiring support staff positions, improving on how quickly visits to children and caregivers take place and hiring a nonprofit to improve its recruitment and retention of foster families. Hamilton noted the agency partly disagreed with Child Advocate Christina Ghio, however, on its efforts to address behavioral healthcare for youth, an issue that advocates say is in dire need of attention.
Hamilton’s memo is a response to one released by Ghio in April that outlined a series of issues within DCF and her office’s recommendations on how to address them.
Ghio said she wrote the public letter in part to ensure that another tragic death — the apparent suicide of a child who died within an hour of being told by a DCF worker that the youth’s request to be moved into foster care ‘was not an option’ — did not go unnoticed. Ghio’s letter also discussed extensive concerns at the department, including poor workforce retention and casework quality.
The child welfare agency’s response identifies and responds to each of Ghio’s 15 recommendations. In most cases, DCF details changes that are being made to comply with OCA’s suggestions. In a few instances, DCF disputes Ghio’s assertions. 
Ghio on Tuesday said that she was appreciative of DCF’s receptiveness to OCA’s criticisms. “There are some significant positives about their response,” she said, including an emphasis on in-person supervision of staff, a focus on safety practice and major hiring of support staff positions. “I think those are good things.”
Among the changes mentioned by Hamilton is her push to fill social work case aide positions. Those staffers assist social workers with a range of time-consuming tasks like driving children to appointments, so they can focus on their core work. In response to questions from the Connecticut Mirror, DCF said via email that 81 such positions are funded and 75 are currently filled, with two more candidates scheduled to begin employment this month.
DCF is also working with the Child Health and Development Institute to develop a statewide strategic plan to recruit and retain more foster parents, improve the process of managing placements and administer payments to cover services and supports for kids in foster care.
Responding to concerns about worker supervision, Hamilton wrote that new social workers are not allowed to telework within their first six months, which is part of the state’s telework agreement for all state employees. She reiterated previous assertions that in-person visitation and other mandatory case work is always done in person.
“However, we agree that in-person connection with supervisors, managers and other colleagues in accessible and meaningful ways is critical to our work,” Hamilton wrote, “and we will continue to prioritize those opportunities.”
One of Ghio’s strongest assertions in April was that many girls in DCF care with mental health needs are not receiving the care they need.
Ghio wrote that girls “wait twice as long as boys (about 80 days) for access” to psychiatric residential treatment facilities and when access to those is not available they are placed in STARR shelters, where they do not receive adequate treatment and often “lose hope, run away and/or fall prey to human trafficking.“
“DCF must take affirmative steps to develop a continuum of mental health treatment services, including out-patient, intensive in-home services for children and families, therapeutic group homes and residential treatment,” she wrote.
Hamilton wrote that while the agency doesn’t minimize the complex needs of such youth, “we respectfully disagree with the assertion that young women in need of treatment programs are routinely placed in Short-term Treatment STARR programs solely because appropriate treatment is unavailable.” She also said that they are “wary of assuming the solution to be ‘more beds.'”
Ghio said on Tuesday that she remains extremely concerned about the availability of not just any beds, but the ones girls need when they are in crisis. 
“Because there are open beds in some programs, that does not mean that all children who need to be in a certain level of care have access to that level of care,” she said.
Recently, DCF employees held a press conference to draw attention to the high number of workforce injuries at Solnit South, the state psychiatric institution for youth age 13 to 17. Workers argued many injuries were “preventable” and the result of a lack of resources, funding and appropriate staffing at the facility.
Hamilton’s response this week said the agency welcomes “the opportunity for ongoing collaboration with the OCA and other key stakeholders.”
Ghio in April had also recommended the creation of a public data dashboard with “real-time quantitative data,” including the number of reports received and accepted, the number of children in in-home and out-of-home care, worker caseloads and other information.
Hamilton’s response noted that  a public-facing dashboard was a priority but pointed out that a working group established by the Committee on Children “never completed its work and did not issue recommendations” regarding the dashboard.
The co-chairs of the Committee on Children, Rep. Corey Paris, D-Stamford, and Sen. Ceci Maher, D-Wilton, said they were surprised that DCF referenced the previous working group in the letter. Maher said the group was unable to complete the task of creating a dashboard because DCF’s information system at the time was not ready with sufficient pertinent data.
This year, Maher and Paris said, the working group is underway and has additional meetings planned. It expects to complete its work on time, they said.
A new oversight committee created by a bill passed this year will also be part of efforts to track the agency going forward. When the bill was proposed, DCF contended that no such committee was needed.

name: National
title: Trump administration threatens to gut Head Start rules
description: The Trump administration appears poised to gut the central policies that shape Head Start, a popular and long-established early childhood education program that serves the country’s neediest children. The Department of Health and Human Services announced the changes Thursday. The federal Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs posted a notice that it in[...]
text:
Preschool children line up to go outside at the Ralph Hawley Head Start Center in Emeryville, Calif., in December. The Trump administration has proposed major changes to the Head Start program. (Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters)The Trump administration appears poised to gut the central policies that shape Head Start, a popular and long-established early childhood education program that serves the country’s neediest children.
The Department of Health and Human Services announced the changes Thursday.
The federal Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs posted a notice that it intends to “significantly reduce regulatory requirements” for Head Start, effectively stripping the program of the unique features that have defined it since its creation in the mid 1960s.
That announcement came in late May and will likely go through a review process before becoming official in 2027.
The agency doesn’t specify what exactly it plans to cut, but reports indicate that it could be most of the program’s standards and guidelines. That may include low student-to-teacher ratios, minimum teacher qualifications, and stipulations that Head Start accept all income-eligible children regardless of whether they’re disabled or if their parents are citizens.
The agency also suggested it wants to shift Head Start funding to the states, although it didn’t specify how or when this would happen.
“The complete gutting of these goals ignores what we know really works in early childhood education,” said Deborah Stipek, a former dean of the Stanford School of Education who’s researched the topic. “If you’re going to spend money on something, wouldn’t you want it to have positive effects?”
The agency said in its announcement it expects the cuts to be “well-received by Head Start programs, since they will welcome reduced (administrative) burden and increased flexibility.”
It also said it would allow local Head Start programs to keep policies that “best address the needs of their communities.” But individual Head Start programs are unlikely to comply with standards that aren’t required, particularly if they’re facing pressure to serve more students, said Melanee Cottrill, executive director of Head Start California, a nonprofit that advocates for California’s 1,813 Head Start centers.
In the same announcement, the agency said it also planned to boost the nutrition and physical exercise components of Head Start, but didn’t offer further details.
‘It will be very different’
So far, Head Start has evaded major budget cuts, and the federal government doesn’t appear poised to slash funding now. A handful of California Head Start programs shuttered during the government shutdown last fall, but reopened when legislators returned to work.
But a reduction in standards would, eventually, have a significant impact, Cottrill said. It’s likely Head Start will have less qualified teachers, larger class sizes and fewer opportunities for parent involvement, she said.
“Those standards are what make Head Start a high quality program,” Cottrill said. “Head Start will still exist, but it will be very different from what it is today.”
Head Start, launched in 1965 as part of President Lyndon Johnson’s War on Poverty, is a federal childcare program that serves the country’s lowest-income families – those earning less than $33,000 a year for a family of four. The federal government issues grants directly to school districts, nonprofits or other organizations that run Head Start programs, sometimes in combination with other funding sources.
Head Start offers health screenings, meals, curriculum focused on literacy and math, and resources for parents such as parenting classes. Children who attend Head Start are more likely to go to college and hold professional jobs later in life, a 2022 study found.
In California, about 70,000 children are enrolled in Head Start. The number would be higher but programs have had to turn away families because they struggled to hire staff. Early childhood educators sometimes earn less than fast food workers and turnover is high, Cottrill noted.
Cost of losing disability screening
One Head Start standard that could be especially costly to eliminate is disability screening. Identifying and addressing disabilities such as dyslexia early can reduce the need for special education later on, potentially saving thousands of dollars, Stipek said.

Beth Meloy, an early childhood education consultant who worked on the federal government’s Head Start standards, said that simplifying and streamlining the standards is probably a good idea. Navigating too many standards may be overly burdensome for some local Head Start programs, she said.
But gutting them entirely would be a disaster, she said.
“Head Start is built around a mission of giving low-income children a path to sustained education and life outcomes,” Meloy said. “These changes lack the thoughtfulness that these children deserve.”
This story was originally published by CalMatters.

name: Source New Mexico
title: NM U.S. Sens. Luján and Heinrich lead Senate Democrats denouncing Utah national monument reductions
description: New Mexico’s two Democratic U.S. senators led a group of colleagues opposed to Trump’s reduction of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments.
text:
U.S. Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M) and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) led a group of 34 fellow Democratic senators in an Aug. 4, 2026, letter in opposition to President Donald Trump’s decision to shrink the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah. Pictured above: The Citadel, an Ancient Puebloan structure in Bears Ears National Monument (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)New Mexico’s two Democratic United States senators, along with U.S. Sen Dick Durban (D-Ill.) led a group of 34 senators in a letter Tuesday that expresses “strong opposition” to President Donald Trump’s recent decision to greatly reduce the footprints of two national monuments in Utah. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Trump on July 13 signed a pair of executive orders to shrink Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah by about 3 million acres or 90% of their original size. The decision drew outrage across the West from environmental advocates and Indigenous governments, including the Navajo Nation and Zuni Tribe, who said they were not consulted in the decision.
The leader of a New Mexico environmentalist group also said the move put him on “high alert” about similar national monuments in the state, including Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks, Río Grande del Norte and Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks.
In their letter to Trump, U.S. Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), along with 32 other Democratic senators, called the Utah monuments “national treasures” that also presented models of how tribes and the federal government can partner to protect nationally and culturally important sites. 
When Trump reduced the Bears Ears National Monument, he also disbanded the Bears Ears Commission, the senators noted, which they described as “a landmark model of collaborative management between sovereign Tribal Nations and the federal government.”
Beyond the impact on Indigenous people, the letter says shrinking the monuments leaves them vulnerable to “destruction and loss” and also economically harms communities adjacent to the monuments. 
“By attempting, yet again, to eliminate vast portions of these monuments, your Administration invites needless uncertainty to the stability that local communities, Tribes, land managers, scientists, recreation users, and businesses need. Not just in Utah, but for all local communities that rely on the stability of our national monuments,” the senators wrote.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump administration moves forward with Head Start overhaul, proposing to eliminate regulations
description: Franklin Head Start in Bude, Miss., Thursday, March 31, 2022.
text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s administration said Thursday it plans to overhaul Head Start, tossing out many of the regulations that are the hallmark of the early education program for the nation’s poorest children.
Officials from the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the federally funded preschool program, said the proposed changes would encourage more local decision-making. Early childhood policy experts argue the deregulation could undermine Head Start’s position as the gold standard in early education.
The Associated Press previously reported on the overhaul proposal, which became public Thursday when it was posted online. The public will have 60 days to weigh in on it before it goes into effect.
Head Start centers serve around 700,000 of the nation’s most vulnerable children, including those who are homeless, in foster care or disabled. That wouldn’t change under the overhaul.
But Alex J. Adams, an assistant secretary at Health and Human Services, said the department is hoping to give Head Start centers the flexibility to change the way they operate. That means eliminating most of Head Start’s regulations, such as standards for low staff-to-student ratios or requirements to provide services to preschoolers’ families.
“Federal mandates can certainly hinder local decision-making, drive up costs and limit the program’s reach,” Adams said on a call with reporters. He highlighted a decade-long decline in Head Start enrollment. “If we get this proposed rule right, we will grow the number of Head Start slots.”
On a call previewing the proposed changes, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy spoke reverently about Head Start, which was started by his uncle Sargent Shriver during the Lyndon B. Johnson administration.
“It’s a program that works for the most vulnerable of the poorest kids in our society, and it’s really important we protect it,” Kennedy said.
But the changes would undermine many of the things that make Head Start distinct from other early education programs, policy experts say.
“The model was created with intentionality,” said Khari Garvin, who oversaw Head Start under President Joe Biden, a Democrat. It was designed, he said, “as part of a strategy to move families out of poverty.”
What makes Head Start different
Head Start, which began in the 1960s as part of Johnson’s War on Poverty, is currently governed by more than 100 pages of regulations. Those regulations require centers to have low staff-to-student ratios and a research-backed curriculum, among other things, and they ensure centers are providing wraparound services that are critical to children in poverty, including medical and dental screenings and parent coaching.
The proposal would toss out nearly all of that rule book. Instead, Head Start’s 1,600 operators — which include nonprofits and school districts — would look to state and local childcare licensing requirements for guidance on many aspects of the program.
Once the proposed regulations are published online, the public will have 60 days to weigh in. The final rules could face legal scrutiny, further delaying their implementation.
While the proposed rules largely loosen requirements, Adams emphasized that centers have the option to continue to operate as they had in the past. He estimated the new rules could generate more than $2 billion in savings and potentially allow Head Start to serve more children.
The proposal adds in at least two new requirements, officials said. It includes a 5% cap on administrative expenses, down from 15% under current rules, and new nutrition provisions championed by Kennedy.
State rules are more lenient
Overall, experts emphasize, state childcare licensing requirements are far more lax than Head Start’s current regulations. State rules are largely focused on ensuring children are healthy and safe. Generally speaking, they do not require centers to provide things like medical or dental screenings, they don’t specify ways to engage with parents, and they don’t speak to what — if anything — should be taught in childcare settings.
Shantel Meek, who heads the Children’s Equity Project at Arizona State University, co-authored an analysis that compared state licensing requirements with Head Start standards and found massive gaps.
“Whereas licensing is, like, the bare minimum to keep kids safe, Head Start includes keeping kids safe but also ensuring that kids are developing, growing, learning well,” Meek said. “It’s a totally different purpose.”
Critically, states allow adults to care for far more children than is allowed under Head Start standards. In Mississippi, for example, one Head Start teacher is only allowed to teach up to four 2-year-olds. State childcare regulations would permit up to a dozen 2-year-olds to be supervised by one adult.
Head Start, which operates in all 50 states, has long had support from both Democrats and Republicans. But it has faced repeated threats under the Trump administration, whose budget chief, Russell Vought, had previously called for it to be eliminated. Not long after Trump, a Republican, took office again in early 2025, some Head Start programs had to briefly shutter because they had problems accessing their federal money. Later, a budget draft eliminated Head Start’s funding, but it was restored after widespread backlash.
In a call with reporters, Kennedy said he believes Head Start is effective. He cited research showing its graduates have fewer law enforcement encounters, do better in school and have better jobs than their peers. He added that he tried to shield Head Start from many of the cuts that hit the rest of his agency.
Still, the Trump administration succeeded last year in laying off much of Head Start’s support staff and closing half of its regional offices.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Democratic Progressive Caucus of FL endorses Dayna Marie Foster for governor in primary election
description: In a reflection that Florida progressives still aren’t comfortable with a former Republican as their standard bearer for governor this fall, the Democratic Progressive Caucus of Florida has endorsed educator Dayna Marie Foster for governor in the Aug. 18 primary election. The 32-year-old Foster resides in Fort Lauderdale and has never run for public office [[...]
text:
The Democratic Progressive Caucus of Florida isn't satisfied with former Republican David Jolly as the party's gubernatorial nominee, and instead has endorsed educator Dayna Marie Foster. (Getty Images)In a reflection that Florida progressives still aren’t comfortable with a former Republican as their standard bearer for governor this fall, the Democratic Progressive Caucus of Florida has endorsed educator Dayna Marie Foster for governor in the Aug. 18 primary election.
Dayna Marie Foster (from her campaign)
The 32-year-old Foster resides in Fort Lauderdale and has never run for public office before. She’s raised just over $30,000 in campaign contributions and has received virtually no media attention. She is running on a platform of expanding affordable housing, abolishing 287(g) immigration agreements across the state, and banning data centers.
“Dayna provides a positive vision, engrained in an idea that Floridians shouldn’t just be granted scraps, but the whole plate,” Matthew Grocholske, president of the Democratic Progressive Caucus, said Thursday.
“Over the past year, she has run a principled campaign that speaks to voters disappointed with the institutions of the Florida Democratic Party anointing a former Republican Congressman as the ‘presumptive nominee’ for Governor.”
That former Republican, of course, is David Jolly, who didn’t become a Democrat until April of last year. His selection of former North Florida U.S. Rep. Gwen Graham has solidified that the ticket is decidedly centrist. Whether that is the right strategy remains to be seen, but the fact is that there are now 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats in Florida.
“As a public-school teacher, I’ve seen the consequences of political failure up close,” Foster said in a written statement. “Working families deserve leaders who will lower the cost of living, expand healthcare, fully fund public education, protect our freedoms, and build an economy where everyone has the opportunity to succeed. I’m grateful for this endorsement because it reflects what this campaign has always been about: putting people first and moving Florida forward.”

name: Delaware
title: Wilmington Hospital Emergency Department earns second consecutive Lantern Award
description: International recognition highlights improvements in patient safety, emergency nursing, testing times and care for victims of violence and abuse WILMINGTON — ChristianaCare’s Wilmington Hospital Emergency Department has received the Emergency Nurses Association’s Lantern Award for a second consecutive cycle, recognizing the department for excellence in nursi[...]
text:
The Lantern Award recognizes emergency departments that demonstrate strong performance in leadership, nursing practice, education, advocacy and research. Photo created with AI on 8/6/26
International recognition highlights improvements in patient safety, emergency nursing, testing times and care for victims of violence and abuse
WILMINGTON — ChristianaCare’s Wilmington Hospital Emergency Department has received the Emergency Nurses Association’s Lantern Award for a second consecutive cycle, recognizing the department for excellence in nursing practice, patient safety and innovation.
The new designation covers 2026 through 2029. The emergency department previously received the award for the 2023-26 cycle.
Wilmington Hospital was one of 126 emergency departments recognized internationally this year.
“Earning the Lantern Award for a second consecutive cycle is a testament to the extraordinary skill and commitment of the Wilmington Hospital Emergency Department team,” said Danielle Weber, ChristianaCare’s chief nurse executive. “These caregivers have created an environment where nurses are empowered to identify opportunities, apply evidence and lead changes that result in safer, better care for patients.”
Recognition focuses on emergency nursing
The Lantern Award recognizes emergency departments that demonstrate strong performance in leadership, nursing practice, education, advocacy and research.
Named for Florence Nightingale, the award also considers an emergency department’s use of evidence-based practices, commitment to patient safety and efforts to create a healthy workplace.
Applicants undergo a blinded review that examines performance measures and detailed examples of the department’s work.
“The Lantern recognizes something incredibly special,” Emergency Nurses Association President Dustin Bass said. “It isn’t an award for an individual or an entire hospital — it’s a recognition earned by an emergency department and the team that powers it every day.”
Department cared for nearly 64,000 patients
During the one-year period included in its award application, the Wilmington Hospital Emergency Department cared for 63,765 patients.
ChristianaCare’s application highlighted several nurse-led and interdisciplinary projects designed to provide faster and safer care.
“What distinguishes this team is its ability to turn frontline insight into measurable improvements,” said Jennifer Moberg, ChristianaCare’s vice president of Emergency Services. “From reducing the time it takes patients to receive critical testing to redesigning triage so patients can begin care sooner, these caregivers work across disciplines to solve problems and improve patient outcomes and experience.”
Faster heart testing
One improvement involved the time required to provide electrocardiograms to patients experiencing chest pain or related symptoms.
The department created a dedicated ECG room in its triage area. By the end of 2025, the average time from a patient entering the department to receiving an ECG had fallen to about seven minutes, below the national benchmark of 10 minutes, according to ChristianaCare.
Nurses also created an “Idea Bin” that allows employees to submit suggestions by scanning QR codes placed throughout the department.
The first 42 submissions resulted in 26 projects or operational changes. Those changes included making point-of-care testing more accessible and placing commonly used supplies closer to caregivers.
Forensic nursing program expands
The award application also highlighted the growth of Wilmington Hospital’s forensic nurse examiner program, which provides specialized care to patients affected by violence, assault or abuse.
The program completed 158 in-person forensic examinations in 2023, 299 in 2024 and 386 in 2025.
ChristianaCare said the expansion has allowed more patients to receive specialized forensic care at Wilmington Hospital without being transferred to another facility.
Other initiatives included improvements in patient flow, pediatric emergency readiness and nursing education. Emergency department nurses also received specialized training to provide ultrasound-guided intravenous access.
“This recognition belongs to the entire emergency department team,” said Christina Hoddinott, who led the development of the department’s award application. “Nursing is a big puzzle, and each of us brings a piece. By working together, we keep finding better ways to care for our patients and support one another.”
