Award period: 2026 through 2029
Previous award: 2023 through 2026
Patients served during application period: 63,765
Learn more: Visit ChristianaCare’s website for information about Wilmington Hospital and its emergency services.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Republicans compete for Trump endorsement in Louisiana’s congressional elections
description: Republican candidates in Louisiana’s two competitive U.S. House elections are actively campaigning for President Donald Trump’s endorsement for the Nov. 3 primaries.
text:
Republican candidates in Louisiana’s two competitive U.S. House elections are actively campaigning for President Donald Trump’s endorsement for the Nov. 3 primaries. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Republican candidates in Louisiana’s two competitive U.S. House elections are actively campaigning for President Donald Trump’s endorsement for the Nov. 3 primaries.
State Sen. Stewart Cathey of Monroe, state Reps. Mike Echols of Monroe and Gabe Firment of Pollock all said they had talked to White House staff ahead of signing up to run for Louisiana’s 5th Congressional district Wednesday. Qualifying for the races continues Thursday and concludes at 4:30 p.m. Friday. 

State Sen. Rick Edmonds of Baton Rouge told reporters he also spoke with Trump’s staff and House Majority Leader Steven Scalise, R-Jefferson, about the president’s support before qualifying for the 6th District race. 
“We’ve spoken to the White House and we feel very confident that they are doing due diligence in this race,” Edmonds said after signing up to run for office this week. 
Trump’s backing is thought to carry a lot of weight, especially in districts like the 5th and 6th that lean Republican. His endorsement of U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, was considered key to her winning the GOP primary for Louisiana’s U.S. Senate seat over incumbent Bill Cassidy and state Treasurer John Fleming.

But Trump’s involvement in Louisiana’s races has a wrinkle: The president already endorsed state Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, in the 5th District race before May’s primaries were called off to allow legislators to redraw the boundaries for the state’s U.S. House seats.   
Heading into the second day of qualifying, Miguez hadn’t publicly announced his intention to run for Congress or whether he would seek the 5th or 6th District seat. He did not respond to phone calls and text messages Wednesday. 
Miguez’s public campaign website has also come down in the last few weeks, though his voicemail still indicates he is a candidate for Congress and his social media identifies him as a U.S. House candidate. 
“He’s playing it very close to the vest,” Sen. Alan Seabaugh, R-Shreveport, a colleague and friend of Miguez, said in an interview Wednesday. 
Louisiana’s congressional districts have changed dramatically since Miguez first decided to run for the 5th District.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

At the direction of Gov. Jeff Landry, Republican state lawmakers dramatically redrew Louisiana’s U.S. House map after the U.S. Supreme Court handed down a decision in late April permitting them to eliminate one of two majority-Black congressional districts in the state. 
The 6th District, held by U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, was changed from majority Black to majority white, and Fields declined to run for office again. It created a new opportunity for a Republican to win a congressional race in which Trump has not endorsed anyone.
In March, Miguez bought a house in Baton Rouge that was originally part of the 5th District but shifted to the 6th in the revisions to the congressional map. Before that, he lived in and represented New Iberia, which is no closer than 70 miles from the new 5th and 6th District lines. 

Members of Congress aren’t required to live in the districts they represent, but it is generally thought voters prefer them to be locals. If Miguez runs for either open congressional seat, other candidates are likely to criticize him as a carpetbagger. 
Since Trump’s endorsement, there have also been news stories about a 2007 rape allegation against Miguez made by a former girlfriend. He has denied the accusations, and some members of the former girlfriend’s family have seemingly sided with Miguez in the dispute. 
Edmonds said he’s confident Trump won’t back Miguez again. 

“What I do know is [Miguez] will not be getting the president’s endorsement in the 6th,” Edmonds said Wednesday after announcing his candidacy. 
Candidates who qualified for the 5th District race did not go as far as Edmonds but also seemed assured Trump would back a different Republican.

“I met with [Trump’s] political team. We’ve had numerous conversations over the last three months,” Echols said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska superintendents drill down on education policy with some gubernatorial candidates
description: Six candidates for Alaska governor from across the political spectrum appeared side-by-side in a room full of superintendents and school officials in Juneau and promised that boosting education funding would be a priority of their administration, if elected. Six candidates participated in the debate, out of 17 running for governor this year. Randy Hoffbeck,[...]
text:
Six candidates for Alaska governor and lieutenant governor participated in a debate on education hosted by the Alaska Superintendents Association in Juneau on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith)Six candidates for Alaska governor from across the political spectrum appeared side-by-side in a room full of superintendents and school officials in Juneau and promised that boosting education funding would be a priority of their administration, if elected.
Six candidates participated in the debate, out of 17 running for governor this year. Randy Hoffbeck, a candidate for Lieutenant Governor who stood in for his running mate, Bill Walker. They discussed their plans for education in a two-hour event hosted by the Alaska Superintendents’ Association on July 30. [Voter Guide: 2026 Voter Guide Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The gubernatorial candidates included Republican Click Bishop, Democrat Tom Begich, Republican Matt Heilala, Republican Lesil Maguire, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and Independent Hoffbeck.
The panel was moderated by Randy Trani, superintendent of the Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District, with questions organized by the board of the Alaska Superintendents Association. A group of roughly 50 superintendents and school administrators from across Alaska attended as part of the association’s summer conference event in Juneau.
All six candidates agreed Alaska education has been underfunded by the Dunleavy administration, with several candidates characterizing public education as “in crisis.” 
A record 12 schools were closed this year, amid millions in budget shortfalls, and others have cut teachers, programs and extracurricular activities. Districts reported funding has not kept pace with skyrocketing operating costs, amid declining enrollment as families leave the state or move to homeschool programs. 
Trani said afterward he found all the candidates “super impressive,” particularly their ideas for funding education. 
“They understand that there’s a fiscal reality problem in the state and it has to be addressed,” he said. “They all have different ideas of how they’re going to do it, but at least they’re leading with it as a top priority.”
 

Superintendents and school officials from across Alaska gathered for a summer conference in Juneau listen to a gubernatorial candidate debate on education on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Luke Meinert is superintendent of the Fairbanks North Star Borough School District, which has closed seven schools in the past five years due to budget shortfalls and declining enrollment. He said he was impressed with the candidates, their willingness to invest in education and their experience working on education issues in Alaska. 
“They’ve been in the game,” Meinert said. “I think maybe every one of them went to public schools here in Alaska, and so they had experienced public schools at a time where we were investing a lot in our school districts. And it was great to hear that they want to get back to those times because that can improve our retention and recruitment efforts for teachers, and then obviously student outcomes on the other end of that.”
Hoffbeck, who is running for Lieutenant Governor on Bill Walker’s ticket, did not go to Alaska public schools, but Walker did.
The candidates shared their plans for funding for Alaska districts, tackling billions of dollars in deferred maintenance, boosting recruitment and retention of teachers and staff, and providing them healthcare and retirement, as well as views on local control of school boards, fiscal plans for the state and other issues. 
Funding for education
Despite Alaska school districts reporting severe budget shortfalls and cutting teachers and programs, Gov. Mike Dunleavy has opposed sustained increases to per student funding, arguing against more funding without changes to policy. He has particularly sought changes related to charter schools and homeschool programs.     

Democrat Tom Begich discusses his education policy platform, with Independent Randy Hoffbeck (left) and Republican Click Bishop (right) at an education debate on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

But all six candidates agreed that schools have not been adequately funded under the Dunleavy administration, and that stable and reliable funding for districts is essential. They all said boosting investment in education is a priority of their campaigns.
Begich, Hoffbeck, Kreiss-Tomkins and McGuire said they support “forward funding” education and providing budgets to districts earlier in the year to provide more stability to districts. The state budget is currently finalized in June. 
Begich said he would advocate for an immediate boost to per student funding, known as the base student allocation — the core of the state’s funding formula — to account for rising inflation. He proposed increasing the figure by roughly 15% to $7,680 per child and tie increases with inflation each year. He said he would also support fully funding pre-K to be available in all school districts. 
Bishop said he would focus particularly on investing in career and technical education, referring to his experience growing up in a family of operating engineers and working in construction. “I’m going to push that till the day I die,” he said. “Nothing wrong with four-year degrees or higher. Career and tech ed needs to be improved upon in this state, and I’m the person that can do it working with you.” 
McGuire and Kreiss-Tomkins said they support reviewing and revising the state’s complex funding formula to ensure districts are adequately funded. Both McGuire and Kreiss-Tomkins as well as Heilala said education has become a politically divisive issue which has obstructed progress. Kreiss-Tomkins called education policy a “Pandora’s box” avoided by lawmakers not wanting to take political risks.     

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a candidate for governor, speaks at a debate on education on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Kreiss-Tomkins and Hoffbeck said they support a constitutional amendment to create a special fund for education separate from the state’s budget. “A constitutional amendment’s only way to dedicate funds in Alaska that can effectively politically de-risk education funding going forward, and also largely account for inflation,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. 
Hoffbeck agreed there is a lack of trust between districts and the state under Dunleavy, which he said must be repaired. He said he believes adequate funding varies by school district across the state, and he and Walker both support a review of state funding for education by an independent third party to study and assess how much funding is needed by each school. 
“Just throwing more money at it doesn’t fix the problem. We need to be surgical on how we add that money,” he said. “Yes, absolutely, we are underfunded. We need more funding, but we need to fund very surgically as we go forward.”
Teacher recruitment and retention
The candidates agreed investing in hiring and retaining teachers is a major priority, but diverged on the question of whether the state should revive a defined benefit retirement plan for educators. 
Bishop and Heilala said they would focus education investments on boosting teacher pay. Heilala said funding should be more focused and efficient, and directed to teachers. “I believe teachers need pay raises. I think they probably need 15 to 30% pay raises, and of course, that’ll happen with a booming economy,” he said.     

Independent Randy Hoffbeck, candidate for lieutenant governor running with Bill Waker, speaks at a debate on education on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Hoffbeck said teacher recruitment and retention should focus on training and hiring local teachers, particularly for rural Alaska. “The local teachers would stay in the rural communities,” he said, referring to his time working in the North Slope Borough. “And so I think we need to have a robust local recruitment process, including certification programs that make it possible for somebody in the village that may not have a four-year degree.”
Bishop, Begich and Kreiss-Tomkins support reviving the defined benefit retirement system for teachers, and said they believe offering that again would boost recruitment. 
The state defined benefit retirement system for public employees was ended in 2006, after the system accrued a multi-billion dollar shortfall. Lawmakers passed legislation to revive the program this year, but Dunleavy vetoed it. 
Begich said he would also want the state to provide medical benefits in a new defined benefit retirement plan, as well as grants for teacher housing. 
Heilala disagreed, and said the defined benefit system is the “biggest mistake.” He said a 401(k) retirement plan has greater certainty to create income.     

Republican Lesil McGuire speaks at a gubernatorial candidate debate on education on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

	 
Hoffbeck said he has concerns about a defined benefit retirement system as some districts would not be able to afford it.
McGuire said she does not support a defined benefit retirement plan, but supports a retirement system that the state can afford. She said she supports a student loan forgiveness program for teaching in Alaska, and low interest loans for housing to boost recruitment and retention. 
“I think housing is a huge issue. Let’s make Alaska the place you want to come teach,” she said.
School maintenance backlog
The candidates all agreed that addressing the state’s multi-billion dollar backlog in deferred maintenance in K-12 schools and the University of Alaska system would be a major priority of their administrations, and presented various ideas on how to fund it.     

Republican Click Bishop speaks at a gubernatorial candidate debate on education on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Bishop said part of his plan for funding education would be to levy an “education head tax,” a flat-rate tax per Alaskan regardless of income to pay for school maintenance. He said he’d introduced similar legislation when he was a member of the Alaska State Senate. 
“It’s ludicrous that we have this much of a deferred maintenance schedule,” he said. 
Begich said he supports the state paying to help boroughs and districts with school bond reimbursement, which is debt incurred by voter-approved bonds to fund school maintenance. He also supports the state backing a general obligation bond to generate hundreds of millions to address the existing maintenance backlog list. 
McGuire, Hoffbeck and Kreiss-Tomkins agreed issuing bonds was a good idea. Hoffbeck and Kreiss-Tomkins also said prioritizing hiring local contractors for construction and maintenance is important.
Kriess-Tomkins noted maintaining schools is an obligation under Alaska’s Constitution. He also cautioned that there will be changes to schools with declining numbers of students as a result of outward migration from the state and families having fewer children. He said he’d want to invest in a system to keep up with school repairs in order to avoid large costly repairs like roof replacements decades in the making.     

Republican Matt Heilala speaks at a gubernatorial candidate debate on education on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Heilala said the deferred maintenance backlog is a challenge, but sees opportunities for consolidating schools with “goodwill.” He said he believes “connectivity” will change infrastructure needs and said he sees artificial intelligence as a “supersonic tsunami” hitting American society now, and creating opportunities for education. “Education is going to be disrupted and changed. I believe in a good way,” he said. “There’s a lot of great opportunity, but we need to approach it with optimism.” 
McGuire said a variety of solutions are needed to address school maintenance and repairs. “We’re so far behind at this point. We’re actually bordering up against litigation,” she said.
She cited legislative hearings and public outcry around the state-run boarding school, Mt. Edgecumbe High School this year when a quarter of students disenrolled sparking public focus on deteriorating school facilities. 
“It was a stomach-turning event,” McGuire said. “So I think there are a variety of solutions. We need to be brave and bold, pull it out, assess what we need to do, and then look at solutions and address it immediately.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Nearly 1 in 5 Rhode Islanders is Latino. The voter rolls haven’t caught up.
description: Almost 1 in 5 Rhode Islanders is Latino now, roughly 220,000 people by the Census Bureau’s most recent count, up from 12.4% of the state in 2010. Central Falls is 69% Latino, and about 7 in 10 people who live there speak a language other than English at home. Pawtucket is roughly a quarter Latino. […]
text:
Four Rhode Island cities — Providence, Pawtucket, Central Falls and Woonsocket — are legally required to run bilingual elections under the Voting Rights Act.  (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Almost 1 in 5 Rhode Islanders is Latino now, roughly 220,000 people by the Census Bureau’s most recent count, up from 12.4% of the state in 2010. Central Falls is 69% Latino, and about 7 in 10 people who live there speak a language other than English at home. Pawtucket is roughly a quarter Latino. The voter rolls have not moved at anything close to that speed, and the distance between those two lines is where a surprising amount of Rhode Island policy gets settled without us.
Apathy is the easy explanation, partly because the real one takes longer to say out loud. Four cities in this state are legally required to run bilingual elections under the Voting Rights Act: Providence, Pawtucket, Central Falls, and Woonsocket. Whether it actually happens varies by city and by cycle. Federal filings estimate that nearly 3,000 voting-age citizens in Pawtucket alone have limited English proficiency, which means a translated mail ballot application and an untranslated one are the difference between a vote and a form that sits on the counter until it doesn’t matter anymore.
Then there is the part no law can fix. Voting is a habit, and habits get handed down. If your parents took you along to the school committee race, you know where your polling place is without looking it up. If your mother naturalized at 52, or came up somewhere elections decided very little, there is nobody at the kitchen table to tell you that Rhode Island closes registration a full 30 days out, that there is no same-day registration except in presidential years, or that this September the primary lands on a Wednesday because of Labor Day rather than the Tuesday every civics class promised. You find that out on your own, in your second language, off a state website, or you don’t find it out at all. Meanwhile the WhatsApp threads move faster than any correction, and families with mixed immigration status are weighing questions about visibility that most Rhode Islanders never have to think about once.
None of that is indifference. It’s an obstacle course, and it compounds. Campaigns work from lists of likely voters, so once a household falls off, the door knocks stop, the mail stops, and the information about what’s actually on the ballot stops arriving, which makes that household less likely to vote the next time, which pushes it further down the list. Legislators read the same data. A precinct that turns out gets its calls returned. A precinct that doesn’t, becomes a rounding error in somebody’s targeting spreadsheet.



Quotation







... when a fifth of the state participates below its own numbers, the whole state gets governed on incomplete information. Plenty of Rhode Islanders who have never once thought of Latino turnout as their concern are living with the results of it.


– Awilda Reinoso Lopez


That’s why this matters well beyond Latino families. School funding formulas, RIPTA routes, what rent does next year, how long you wait for a primary care appointment: those get decided by whoever showed up, and when a fifth of the state participates below its own numbers, the whole state gets governed on incomplete information. Plenty of Rhode Islanders who have never once thought of Latino turnout as their concern are living with the results of it.
We are not telling anyone how to vote. The Latino Policy Institute does not endorse candidates and has no plans to start. What we want is an electorate that looks like the state it lives in and that every eligible voter has the information and access to participate. 
So here is the ask, and it has a date attached. Tonight, go to vote.ri.gov and confirm you are registered at the address where you actually live. If you have moved since 2024, there is a good chance you are not. Monday, Aug. 10 is the last day to register, or to switch your party affiliation, before the Sept. 9 primary. Miss it and you are waiting until Nov. 3, and the deadline for that one is Sunday, Oct. 4. Mail ballot applications close Aug. 19 and Oct. 13. Early voting for the primary election runs Aug. 20 through Sept. 8, and then Oct. 14 through Nov. 2 for the general election. Polls open at 7 a.m. and stay open until 8 p.m.
Then check on one other person, because that is the part that actually moves the numbers. The cousin who naturalized last spring and never got around to registering. The neighbor who has moved twice and never updated her address. The nephew who turned 18 in March and assumes somebody handled it. One conversation each, and the rolls look different by October.
We are running voter education workshops in English and Spanish www.thelatinopolicy.org/vote-providence and www.thelatinopolicy.org/vote-pawtucket. Bring your questions and bring your mail. We will walk through the registration form, the mail ballot application, and what the offices on this year’s ballot actually control, and nobody gets talked down to for asking something basic.
Check your own registration tonight. Then call the person you thought of while reading this. Monday is the tenth, and nobody in this state should lose a vote to a deadline they never heard about.
The Latino Policy Institute (LPI) is a nonpartisan research and policy organization dedicated to advancing equity and opportunity for Latino communities in Rhode Island. LPI produces data-driven research, shapes state and local policy, and builds the power of Latino communities to advocate for themselves. LPI is a proud member of the Protect Our Healthcare Coalition. Learn more at thelatinopolicy.org.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: ‘It’s like the Hunger Games’: Quabbin Reservoir towns take funding fight to Beacon Hill amid extended drought
description: A perfect storm of long-held resentments, the well-known story of the financial crunch squeezing small towns across the state, and an act of blameless chance — weather — is raising the stakes and stoking new tensions between these sparse towns and the powers that be in state government.
text:
EMILY HILL works not from one town hall, but from what has become a collection of them. 
Along with the rest of the small municipal staff, Hill, the town coordinator of New Salem, a 1,000-person rural town in central Massachusetts, is operating out of multiple offices. Some of them are rented from a local church. 
The reason? The old well serving the original town hall building ran dry, rendering the building without water and workable restrooms.   
It’s all the more dissonant because a body of water spanning 39 square miles and holding 412 billion gallons of water laps against the town’s shores. 
The impossible decisions that Hill is faced with follow her whichever building she happens to call her workspace that day. The town tries to stretch its meager $3.7 million annual budget as far as it’ll go, but officials recently had to let go three elementary school classroom aides in just the latest instance of penny-pinching by necessity.  
New Salem is one of a handful of small towns that surround a giant reservoir of clean fresh water dug out a century ago in the middle of the nation’s worst-ever economic collapse in order to hydrate Greater Boston. 
The creation of the Quabbin Reservoir, as it’s called, is nothing short of an engineering marvel. Because of it, Boston has not, and likely will not, ever go thirsty.  
But, in the communities that are home to the Quabbin, there’s an undercurrent of anxiety and frustration.  
“There’s so much rage,” Hill said. “We sacrifice so much. And we are not getting compensated for it.” 
A perfect storm of long-held resentments, the well-known story of the financial crunch squeezing small towns across the state, and an act of blameless chance — weather — is raising the stakes and stoking new tensions between these sparse towns and the powers that be in state government. 
The Quabbin communities, despite protecting the water source, don’t drink from it themselves.  
That means that when water levels drop in their private wells or municipal sources due to drought, as much of the state has dealt with drier-than-normal conditions over the past two years, Quabbin-area residents can feel the impact of drought more than the 2.7 million residents to the east that drink water from the reservoir and are served by the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority. 
One glaring example: Recent rainfall notwithstanding, the first half of 2026 has been so dry that it won’t be safe for youth athletes in the Quabbin town of Belchertown to play soccer and football on their home fields this fall.  
At the same time, aid that the 29 towns across the watershed system receive as a form of compensation for state-owned land around the reservoir and the streams that feed it and the mandatory development bans that come with it has, for some, barely budged over the years — especially for the Quabbin’s seven “host communities.” 
Emily Hill is the town coordinator in New Salem, a rural community of about 1,000 people. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
With older dwindling populations and stagnant growth, some of the towns have had to consolidate resources, lay off municipal staff and teachers, and resort to asking their own residents to raise their property taxes, even though they are the guardians of Boston’s water and practically hold the keys to any housing or economic growth that’s to take place in the state’s eastern half.  
“It’s like the Hunger Games,” said Sen. Jo Comerford, a Democrat who represents towns around the Quabbin. “We’re starting to lose the ability to govern ourselves in this region. It’s as simple as that.”  
Exacerbating the tension is the ongoing drought, which has been afflicting most of the state with below-normal precipitation levels since 2024. 
Local officials around the Quabbin said they see it in reduced stream flows, drier soils, and more exposed chunks of shore at the reservoir itself.  
Because these residents drink from more fragile municipal sources and private wells, many of the towns have responded with bans on outdoor water use and other nonessential purposes — another layer of tightening the belt to keep life livable in these rural enclaves.  
In some Quabbin communities, in addition to others around the state, that means no watering the lawn, filling the swimming pool, or washing the car. 
That’s on top of perennial issues around contamination of “forever chemicals,” which have tainted some of the region’s wells and forced these towns to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars in remediation, along with regular enhanced testing of local streams that flow into the Quabbin.  
For communities so close to so much water, it’s a cruel irony. 
Yet MWRA customers aren’t generally under these same restrictions.  
Though customers living in a state-designed “critical” drought, like the state’s northeast region, are also supposed to stop nonessential outdoor water use, residents who are served by the MWRA and drink Quabbin water that is in some cases nearly 100 miles away aren’t at particular risk. 
The reason, said Stephen Estes-Smargiassi, MWRA’s interim executive director, is simple. 
The Quabbin, because of its sheer size, is hard to chip away at: It takes a lot longer for the water source to deplete in times of drought, insulating these consumers from more severe restrictions. It also, though, takes longer for the Quabbin to recover from drought, meaning the opposite could happen in the future, where communities in other parts of the state lift their drought restrictions sooner than the MWRA can based on conditions at the Quabbin. 
Right now, the Quabbin is about 82 percent full, said Estes-Smargiassi. The agency is asking customers to conserve water where possible on its website. 
The Quabbin is “able to capture water not over a period of a few months, but over multiple years,” he said. “So it takes a big, long drought to make the Quabbin go down. Whereas if you’ve got a small reservoir or a groundwater source, you’re likely to be affected if you’ve got three or four months of dry weather.” 
That doesn’t change the optics, though, for Quabbin communities, who live near water they can’t consume and watch Greater Boston seemingly drink freely despite the drought conditions on the ground.  
Now, in response to a range of apparent disparities, these communities have formed a loose coalition known as the Quabbin Stewards to coordinate in what they say is an unprecedented way to take their fight to the State House.  
Their legislative demands include a permanent seat on the MWRA board and a new trust fund to pay for municipal services like infrastructure and sewer improvements and public safety needs. They are also seeking increased payments in lieu of taxes from the state, or PILOTs, that they receive as compensation for playing home to state-owned land that can’t be developed. Lawmakers are considering these reforms in the environmental bond bill currently under negotiation.  
Those demands carry tradeoffs, argues the MWRA, a quasi-public state agency that provides water and sewer services for 61 municipalities, most of which are in the Boston area.  
“There’s no free money,” Estes-Smargiassi said in an interview. “That would mean a pretty substantial rate increase. It’s tough all around. It’s going to come from folks in Chelsea and Everett and folks here in the East, and many of them are having a hard time paying their bills.” 
The agency’s advisory board, in a 2025 letter, opposed the legislative reforms proposed by the Quabbin communities, though Estes-Smargiassi said the agency isn’t actively working against the measures in the Legislature and is merely “watching it play out.” 
Local officials, though, point to deep financial inequities in the PILOT payments they receive, which are calculated by a formula set by the state Department of Revenue and paid by the MWRA. 
Five of the seven Quabbin “host communities” have received the same amount in PILOT payments in each of the past five fiscal years – essentially a decrease when adjusted for inflation – laying bare a sizable difference between what these towns earn per acre through state aid and what they generate per acre through property taxes on developed non-Quabbin land. 
Last fiscal year, the Quabbin town of Hardwick received about $156,000 in PILOT payments, or $32 per acre, according to state records.  
That’s a slight increase to the $121,000, or $25 per acre, that Hardwick received five years ago in PILOT payments. 
On the other side of the reservoir, New Salem received around $722,000 in PILOT payments — 20 percent of its budget — to compensate for roughly 90 percent of its land falling within the watershed and owned by the state.  
That comes out to just $21 per acre, the exact same amount the town was receiving five years ago.  
The median PILOT payment for state-owned land across Massachusetts is $127 per acre, according to a 2025 report from Auditor Diana DiZoglio.  
PILOT payments alone aren’t necessarily intended to return all of the land’s value to the municipality. But Hill said that raising these payments closer to that statewide median would send a real signal about the land’s worth, doubling her town’s budget in what would amount to a “game changer.”  
Already, the town hires out emergency services from nearby Orange, shares a fire department with Wendell, and many municipal employees like the treasurer, library director, and police officers are only working 19 hours per week because New Salem can’t afford to pay their health insurance, she added. 
Given that her town is the one deploying scarce first responder resources to defend the water and sacrificing economic development and additional housing so that Greater Boston can grow, she wants to see the value of that land reflected in fairer state aid. 
“We choose protection over profit every single day, but locking away this land means we are left with a crippled local tax base and no way to grow,” reads a joint letter sent last month to the MWRA from Hill and the New Salem select board members. 
If the state doesn’t act, Hill said, expect more fights over raising property taxes on residents who already skew older and earn below the state median income.  
Nearby Belchertown, another Quabbin community, approved a $2.9 million Proposition 2 ½ override last fiscal year to fund municipal and school budgets. It passed by 21 votes. An override vote in New Salem earlier this year, meanwhile, failed by 19 votes, forcing the layoffs of classroom aides in its elementary school.  
Still, there are both macroeconomic issues and technicalities associated with the program at play. 
The Department of Revenue sets the value of the land, which guides the PILOT payment rate and can greatly vary between communities based on real estate prices and local tax rates. And, Estes-Smargiassi of the MWRA noted, property values in rural central Massachusetts aren’t as high as other communities near Boston or along the coast. 
If anything, he said, the MWRA is issuing PILOT payments at higher rates the agency otherwise might if not for a “hold harmless” clause that prohibits these payments from declining from year to year. Even if local land prices or tax rates decrease, these PILOT payments never will, though the average single-family tax bill in the Quabbin communities has generally gone up over the past decade, Department of Revenue data show. 
And other PILOT programs that rely on appropriations from the Legislature are underfunded compared to the payments issued by the MWRA, which fulfill 100 percent of the value as determined by the Department of Revenue, according to a 2020 report from then-Auditor Suzanne Bump.  
Land around the Quabbin Reservoir is owned by the state to protect the water source from development. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
The MWRA has paid about $200 million in PILOT payments since 1985 to 29 watershed communities, which stretch across the system from the Quabbin to the Sudbury Reservoir in and around Framingham.   
Those payments, though, have only increased by about $500,000 total between 2015 and 2025 and are shared across those 29 municipalities, according to state data.  
“We are not asking for charity,” said Matteo Pangallo, land use clerk in Shutesbury, a Quabbin town of 1,800. “We are asking for equity.” 
All of this collided at a rare MWRA board meeting at the Quabbin Visitor Center in Belchertown last month, where local officials and residents took Gov. Maura Healey’s top environmental official and the agency to task for the perceived disparities.  
William Tinker, vice chair of the Hardwick select board, said at the meeting that there are real economic choices facing Quabbin towns like his. With Hardwick’s hospital and ambulance now gone and its police station in another town, the municipality was recently offered $2 million annually for a regional landfill. 
Hardwick said no.  
It threatened the watershed, Tinker said. 
“What happens when the next offer is $5 million? Or $10 million?” Tinker told the MWRA board. “What happens when the weight of generations of neglect outweighs principle?”  
Some of the frustration reaches back nearly a century to the creation of the Quabbin in the 1930s as a water source for Boston, which literally flooded the region and forced four towns off the map.  
That’s not something easily forgotten here: The menu at the deli at the New Salem General Store, for instance, names different sandwiches after each of those four towns of Enfield, Prescott, Greenwich, and Dana. 
Farms, businesses, schools, homes, and properties were lost in the flood and taken through eminent domain; a crucial rail link connecting the Quabbin region was destroyed. Family cemeteries and burial points were moved, too. 
The history, like everything, is complicated. The project provided decent work during the Great Depression, when the towns were already declining, falling behind the nearby Connecticut River Valley. And there became some acceptance as the Quabbin inched closer to reality that this was a necessary sacrifice for the greater good. 
Still, “these were ordinary people living ordinary lives, whose familial and historical connections were all severed,” Elisabeth Rosenberg, author of “Before the Flood: Destruction, Community, and Survival in the Drowned Towns of the Quabbin,” said in an interview. “A lot of them did not have a lot of material things. What they had was land and community, and those were the two things that were taken away from them.” 
It’s against that backdrop that a new cry for help and a battle in the Legislature for money and relevance is being waged.  
And similar power imbalances persist in the current legislative fight, said Lexi Dewey, former head of the Water Supply Citizens Advisory Committee. The legislators representing the Quabbin towns are outnumbered by those representing the more populous Eastern Massachusetts. Much of that region is served water by the MWRA. 
Susan Cloutier (bottom right), member of the New Salem select board, Emily Hill (top left), town coordinator of New Salem, and Matteo Pangallo, land use clerk of Shutesbury, talk about issues facing their towns. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
Healey, meanwhile, is looking for a wider fix to the PILOT system, launching a special commission last year to probe “whether the allocation of PILOT funding is fair.” The commission has been meeting since May under the leadership of Healey’s budget chief Matthew Gorzkowicz and held four public listening sessions in July.   
It’s not clear when final recommendations will be issued, and any substantive changes would likely require legislation. But there seems to be some recognition that adjustments are in order.  
The current system, said Doug Howgate, president of the Massachusetts Taxpayer Foundation and a member of Healey’s special commission, is overdue for a review to ensure it “passes the commonsense test.” 
“Especially in the case of the Quabbin, this is land that we don’t want to be developed,” he said. “It leads to a different set of policy choices for how you want it to work.” 
For the Quabbin communities making an aggressive push on Beacon Hill, it comes down to what is land worth — and how much of that should fall on water customers in and around Boston. 
“The long story short of it is that we are running out of money,” said Hill, the New Salem town coordinator. “We have nowhere else to turn.”

Oh, the Ohio Ballot Board didn’t rewrite ballot language to confuse voters and make a mockery of themselves and democracy this time?The Statehouse News Bureau’s Sarah Donaldson reports, “Ohio Ballot Board OKs language that puts Issue 3, or photo ID, on ballot.”
Ohio voters will have a whole slate of statewide candidates to choose from this fall, but just one ballot issue is going before them.
Members of the Ohio Ballot Board have given the green light for the language for Issue 3, which asks voters whether they should have to show government-issued photo ID for any in-person voting. That’s already required to vote, before and on Election Day, and it has been since 2023.
Public schools levies and cuts. The Toledo Blade’s Mike Sigov reports, “Sylvania schools outlines $11.3M in cuts if earned-income tax levy fails.”Sylvania schools has detailed about $11.3 million in cuts it would need to make if a 1 percent earned-income tax levy fails to pass in November.
In a letter Tuesday to “Sylvania parents, guardians, and community,” Superintendent Tim Zieroff encouraged recipients to “carefully” review the positions, programs, curriculum, activities, and other expenses to be eliminated or reduced beginning with the 2027-28 school year if the Nov. 3 operating levy is not approved.
Public school teachers. Jessie Balmert reports in The Columbus Dispatch, “Ramaswamy revives debate over teacher merit pay in Ohio. Can it work?”Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy has proposed merit-based pay for Ohio’s public school teachers. The concept of performance-based pay for teachers has been debated for decades by both Republican and Democratic politicians.
Research shows merit pay can be effective, but success depends heavily on program design, teacher buy-in, and avoiding overreliance on test scores. Previous attempts to implement merit pay in Ohio, including in Cleveland, have ultimately failed due to various challenges.

title: Michiganders are going hungry in the wake of federal food assistance cuts
description: Just over a year after passage of the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA), Michigan families are feeling its harm. While good jobs remain hard to come by in Michigan and […]
text:
The entrance to a Big Lots store in Portland, Oregon. (Stock photo by hapabapa/Getty Images)Just over a year after passage of the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA), Michigan families are feeling its harm. The federal megabill cuts billions of dollars in food assistance and healthcare for struggling households to give further tax breaks to the ultrawealthy.
While good jobs remain hard to come by in Michigan and food prices continue to rise, the bill’s new layers of red tape have contributed to the loss of benefits under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) for more than 145,000 Michiganders.
As OBBBA strips grocery money from the families with the least, it will reduce the annual tax bills for the top 1% of Michigan households (those with incomes of at least $715,000 a year) by an average of $49,220.
Federal law limits adults without disabilities to three months of SNAP benefits every three years unless they prove they’re working at least 80 hours per month. Before OBBBA, people 55 and older and parents of minor children were exempt from the time limit. OBBBA increased the upper age threshold from 55 to 65 and narrowed the parental exemption to those with children under 14.
The result? One of every three Michiganders who have lost SNAP benefits following OBBBA’s passage is a child. Kids already face disproportionately high food insecurity rates, making the targeting of their families for cuts extra cruel.
The bill is also worsening the growing hunger crisis among older adults. From 2021 through 2024 (the most recent year for which data is available), the number of Michiganders ages 50 and older experiencing food insecurity increased by 59%.
And disabled people are losing vital food benefits, too. Although they’re exempt from the work requirement, SNAP’s definition of “disability” is one of the narrowest of any safety net program. It leaves out many with significant and long-term conditions and doesn’t acknowledge that disabled people often face the greatest challenges in proving they qualify for an exemption. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hunger was already rising, and we expect it to grow more rapidly as people lose their food and healthcare benefits altogether under OBBBA. It will be harder to measure, however, because in 2025 the federal government stopped comprehensive tracking and reporting of food insecurity rates.
The federal administration can try to hide evidence of the harm stemming from OBBBA and other recent policies. But they can’t hide the increases in need our local food pantries are seeing month after month or the soaring prices we feel on every trip to the grocery store. They can’t hide what we see happening to our families, friends and neighbors.
We applaud our state legislature and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer for continuing to support state-level programs that make it easier for Michiganders to get healthy food. These include Double Up Food Bucks, Ten Cents a Meal and funding for universal school breakfast and lunch.
But these initiatives are meant to complement SNAP, not replace it. And they could all be at risk in the coming years, too, as OBBBA shifts hundreds of millions of dollars in SNAP costs from the federal government to our state budget.
For many Americans, even full-time work doesn’t pay enough to cover basic needs. Seven in 10 workers using SNAP work at least 35 hours per week. The companies paying these workers poverty wages — like Walmart and Amazon — are some of the world’s largest and most profitable.
Those who already have more than they could spend in multiple lifetimes can’t continue taking from those who are struggling just to afford survival needs. It’s time for our lawmakers to put families over billionaires.

title: Missouri and Kansas can expect double-digit Obamacare premium hikes again
description: Kansas Citians who buy health insurance through hearthcare.gov can expect to pay much more for monthly premiums next year. According to preliminary rate filings submitted to state insurance regulators in Missouri and Kansas, every insurance company selling individual plans in the region through the Affordable Care Act marketplace wants to raise prices in 202[...]
text:
One Nation Overcharged, a national coalition working to raise awareness about health costs, invited people at the River Market Aug. 2 to take a free popsicle and answer the question, "What healthcare charges do you want to chill?" (Suzanne King/The Beacon).Kansas Citians who buy health insurance through hearthcare.gov can expect to pay much more for monthly premiums next year.
According to preliminary rate filings submitted to state insurance regulators in Missouri and Kansas, every insurance company selling individual plans in the region through the Affordable Care Act marketplace wants to raise prices in 2027.
Across both states, average premium increase requests range from 10% to 35% more than 2026 rates. And that follows a similar trend last year, when almost every carrier offering plans in the Kansas City area requested an increase.
The companies argue that health services and medications continue to cost more, while the volume of patient claims is rising. Both factors increase the insurance companies’ costs and eat away at profits, justifying a price hike, they said.

Nationally, a Peterson-KFF analysis found, individual marketplace insurers are requesting a median premium increase next year of 15%. Last year, the same analysis found the median national increase request was 18%, and it climbed to 20% once rates were finalized.
The combined two-year upswing is significant for people who rely on the government marketplace for health insurance. The KFF analysis notes that if regulators grant the 2027 premium requests, typical premiums on the marketplace will have jumped by more than one- third in two years.
Lacey Kennett of Alliance for a Healthy Kansas, a nonprofit that advocates for affordable healthcare, said the premium increases represent one on a long list of healthcare expenses people are having trouble affording.
At an Aug. 2 event put on by One Nation Overcharged, a national coalition working to raise awareness about health costs, Kennett said she heard from people who are putting off routine doctors’ visits and skipping medications in order to save money.
“Putting off care, waiting until it becomes more like an emergency, … then, of course, it’s even more expensive,” Kennett said. “Our goal is to make so much noise about the rising cost of healthcare that policymakers can’t ignore it anymore.”
Missouri and Kansas regulators are reviewing the ACA rate request filings to determine if the increases are justified and to ensure the plans comply with state and federal law.
States must publish insurance carriers’ premium increase requests along with justifications for them and give the public a chance to submit comments in response. In Kansas, people can submit comments with the insurance department. And in Missouri, people can go to the insurance department’s website to find more information about how to submit feedback.
The deadline for public comments in Missouri is Aug. 31. Final rates are expected by Oct. 31.
While fewer than one in 10 people buy insurance through the marketplace, according to the KFF report, the rate requests provide a window into how the industry is navigating the market, which could be a clue about how they may approach next year’s rates in other insurance sectors.
Last fall, many private employers struggled to afford the growing health insurance costs they were facing for 2026. And the situation is likely to be similar when it comes time to renew policies.
Missouri and Kansas’ small group markets, which sell insurance to businesses with between two and 50 employees, also project premium increases in 2027 of between 9% and 19%, according to state filings.

The largest premium increase request came from UnitedHealthcare in Kansas’ individual marketplace. The company, which reported profits of $12.8 billion last year, has asked the state for rates to jump between 29.68% and 36.48%.
In its filing with the state justifying the premium increase request, the company pointed to rising costs in U.S. healthcare spending. UnitedHealthcare said that in 2025 its “loss ratio,” the percentage of total premiums that go toward paying medical claims, was 95.85% on its Kansas individual plans. That is well over the loss ratio of 80%-85% required under the Affordable Care Act.
UnitedHealthcare’s Kansas filing listed specific healthcare trends driving up costs, including:

Increases in reimbursement rates the insurance company pays doctors, hospitals and drug companies.
A rise in claims due to patients going to the doctor more and receiving more expensive health services — surgery, for example, “versus simply monitoring or providing medications.”
“Deductible leveraging,” which the company said happens when healthcare costs rise but deductibles and copayments remain the same, forcing premiums to cover more.
New medical technology, which the company said can lead to more expensive services and increased healthcare spending.

In addition, the company pointed to the growing trend of healthier patients dropping out of the marketplace, leaving a more expensive patient pool behind, something other insurance carriers also called out as a reason for increasing 2027 premiums.
People dropping ACA coverage has become increasingly common since the end of last year, when federal lawmakers allowed enhanced premium tax credits, which subsidized ACA plans for a larger portion of the population, to expire.
By February, Missouri had already seen a 25% decline in ACA enrollment, to 260,999 from 347,424 a year earlier. In Kansas, enrollment had dropped about 20% to 143,880 from 179,920 a year earlier. Without the federal subsidies, many experts expect the departure of healthy people from the marketplace to continue, a trend insurers are anticipating as a reason to increase premiums for remaining policy holders.
On the Missouri side, the Oscar Insurance Co. also listed healthier patients leaving the market as one justification for its 15.9% increase in rates next year.
“Changes to the overall premium level are needed because of anticipated changes in the underlying health of the marketplace,” the company wrote.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Boston hosted the world. Let’s make it a habit.
description: Greater Boston can host the world. Now we need to make sure we are willing and able to do it again and again because doing so brings lasting economic and civic benefits to our region.
text:
FOR SEVERAL remarkable weeks this summer, the eyes of the world were on Boston and Massachusetts, and the city and Commonwealth were ready.  
From FIFA World Cup matches to the return of the Tall Ships/Sail Boston to the celebrations surrounding America’s 250th anniversary, Boston and the Commonwealth stepped confidently onto the global stage. Millions of people watched. Hundreds of thousands visited. We brought the world to our home, and that home sparkled.   
This period proved something important: Greater Boston can host the world. Now we need to make sure we are willing and able to do it again and again because doing so brings lasting economic and civic benefits to our region.  
The last two months demonstrated the case for hosting more major events. Economic activity was elevated, with marked boosts for the hospitality sector — bars, restaurants, and hotels — many of them small businesses. The full economic impact is still being calculated. For example, FIFA reports that Boston outdid all other World Cup host cities in the increase in spending in bars and restaurants during the first two weeks.  
We will also see long-term benefits: This summer did more for the state’s reputation than any marketing campaign could. Vibrancy, camaraderie, and fun dominated. Just as importantly, visitors had the opportunity to see the region anew, as a place to visit again, send their children to university, host global events, and even locate a business. Executives travelling overseas have been peppered with questions and comments about the region from their foreign counterparts.  
Throughout these events, visitors from around the world experienced Massachusetts at its best: a region that was welcoming, energetic, and capable of delivering events of international significance. They saw world class universities, hospitals, businesses, and research institutions all based here. They saw a place where ideas can become companies. For international companies considering where to establish or expand their US presence, the Commonwealth should be at the top of the list.  
These outcomes happened because the private sector, public officials, local communities, and civic organizations collaborated. Businesses contributed more than $25 million in direct sponsorships. Volunteers gave valuable time. Hospitality staff greeted visitors. Public safety personnel worked long hours to ensure events were safe and successful. Together, we showed what Greater Boston and the Commonwealth can accomplish when they rally around a common goal.  
At the same time, we should take away a deeper lesson. This region has always been global, a place that punches above its weight, while quietly changing the world. It helped launch a nation, fueled the Industrial Revolution, pioneered advances in medicine and education, and became one of the world’s leading centers of finance, technology, and innovation. Again and again, Greater Boston’s impact reaches far beyond its borders. This summer showed that we do not need to be quiet; we can bring the world to Boston and they’ll embrace it.   
Large-scale events are not just celebrations; they are an economic development strategy. The people who experienced Boston this summer are potential future residents and part of a future workforce. The businesses that watched from abroad are potential future employers. A region that can host the world signals to talent and capital alike that it is open, capable, and worth betting on.  
Policymakers can turn that initial interest into lasting investment by ensuring that the Commonwealth maintains a business climate as welcoming as the hospitality that greeted our visitors; competitiveness is won not in a single summer, but in the choices we make to keep the door open.   
Boston and Massachusetts shined this summer, and we should be proud of that. Importantly, we should treat it as the beginning of something larger: a shift to viewing ourselves as the impactful global destination that we are and something upon which we should capitalize.  
Ron O’Hanley is chairman and CEO of State Street Corp.

text:
A rendering of Morpheus, a micro nuclear reactor being developed by Nuclea Energy. (Courtesy of Nuclea Energy)A micro nuclear reactor may be coming to Utah as the state’s Office of Energy Development announced it signed an agreement with Nuclea Energy, a Canadian nuclear technology developer, to explore siting a test reactor in central Utah.
Morpheus, the microreactor Nuclea Energy is developing, is “designed to be factory-built, transportable and scalable from approximately 3.5 MWe to 50 MWe,” the company said in a news release.

The agreement aims to explore a site for the reactor at the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab, located in Orangeville, to advance the technology “toward demonstration and deployment.”
As Cox advances nuclear agreements, he says the cost to develop technology is nothing so far

“We are excited to be contributing to and benefitting from the nuclear innovation hub that Utah has fostered at (the San Rafael Energy Lab),” Josef Freundorfer, CEO of Nuclea Energy, said in the release. “We are confident that this partnership will help to prove the inherent advantages of our technology and accelerate our deployment schedule.” 
The agreement follows a series of similar actions Gov. Spencer Cox’s administration has taken toward bringing and developing nuclear developers in the state, including Valar Atomics, NuCube Energy, General Matter and TerraPower — all part of Cox’s efforts to make Utah a crucial part of the “nuclear renaissance” the Trump administration has called for in multiple executive orders.
With the memorandum of understanding signed in early June, Nuclea Energy said it hopes to advance research, development and commercialization of the Morpheus micro modular reactor, which is being promoted as a compact and transportable option for clean electrical power generation. 
The reactor also promises to operate at atmospheric pressure, “eliminating catastrophic failure risks associated with high-pressure nuclear systems,” according to the company’s website. The factory-built modules would allow them to be installed in months, not years.
With the agreement, Utah signed on to support the company as it engages with the U.S. Department of Energy and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, as well as exploring pathways to expand the company’s technology in the state.
“Utah is leading the nation in energy innovation, and our partnership with Nuclea is another step towards an abundant energy future that is reliable, secure and clean,” Emy Lesofski, Director of the Utah Office of Energy Development said in the release.

name: VTDigger
title: New details about proposed locked youth facility signals more disagreement over landmark ‘Raise the Age’ law
description:
Gov. Phil Scott has recently called on lawmakers to repeal part of Vermont’s landmark justice reform law. That push is bubbling up as the state plans its new locked youth facility.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New details about proposed locked youth facility signals more disagreement over landmark ‘Raise the Age’ law.
text:
Gov. Phil Scott in Montpelier in June 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
MONTPELIER — The Vermont Department for Children and Families says it does not plan to include 18-year-olds in its design for a locked juvenile facility, raising concern from lawmakers about how Gov. Phil Scott’s administration is rolling out Vermont’s landmark juvenile justice reform initiative. 
Officials with the Vermont Department for Children and Families said Wednesday that its new locked juvenile facility will only hold youths ages 12-17. Previous press statements from the department indicated that 18-year-olds would also be held at the facility. 
The 14-bed program, dubbed the Green Mountain Youth Center, has been criticized by youth advocates who say it’s too large and is an unnecessarily expensive investment. The state wants to build the facility in South Burlington after failed attempts to build it elsewhere in the state.
The new plan was explained Wednesday during a Joint Justice Oversight Committee meeting at the Statehouse, which convenes a group of mostly high-ranking lawmakers who focus on the criminal justice and child welfare systems.
Eight years ago, Vermont passed a first-of-its-kind law that allowed some 18-year-olds accused of crimes to have their cases tried in family court. That pathway, rather than criminal court, allows cases to move forward outside of public view, though there are exceptions for youth accused of committing the state’s most serious crimes. 
The initiative, called “Raise the Age,” was signed into law with support from Scott and was set to be implemented in stages, with older youth added to the family court system. But since 2022, lawmakers have continued to kick the can on its application to 19-year-olds. It’s most recently set to apply to the age group in July 2027. 
This year, in the governor’s annual budget address, Scott publicly changed his tune. Scott said that the initiative was a “mistake” and urged lawmakers to go further and repeal its provisions for those of age 19. 
As Scott has become increasingly skeptical of the law, legislators have accused him of refusing to enforce it. Now his administration is explicitly calling for the law to be repealed. 
“The Agency of Human Services (AHS) no longer supports expanding (Raise the Age) to include nineteen-year-olds charged with delinquent acts,” said an annual report released by the agency in June. 
The issue is coming to a head as the state plans to build a new locked facility for justice-involved youth. 
Just this June, the Department for Children and Families said in a press release that the facility would house youths ages 12 through 18. Then on Wednesday, Sandi Hoffman, the department’s commissioner, said the facility would only hold juveniles who are 17 or younger. 
The department denies, though, that it made any changes to its initial plan.
“When DCF previously described the population as ages 12-18, the intent was to describe youth through their 18th birthday,” said Hannah Marble, a spokesperson for the department, via email. 
The age distinction makes a critical difference because it means 18-year-olds would likely be held in a prison or facility out of state. Federal law does not prevent the state from holding 18 year olds among younger juveniles, including those in the Green Mountain Youth Center. 
During the commissioner’s update, Rep. Alice Emmons, D-Springfield, who chairs the joint committee, asked if the facility could hold 18 and 19 year olds.
“No. We’re not designing it for that,” Hoffman said. 
If the Legislature does decide to “move forward” with Raise the Age, Hoffman said, the state can discuss its plan down the line. In any case, the department would have to make sure that any adults in the locked facility would be out of sight or earshot of youth under the age of 18. 
Vermont’s Raise the Age law currently applies to 18-year-olds. And Rep. Martin LaLonde, D-South Burlington, pointed that out before making a distinction in response to Hoffman. 
The Legislature doesn’t have to move forward on Raise the Age, he said; rather, it’s already on track for Raise the Age to be implemented. 
Regarding Raise the Age, the Agency of Human Services wrote that some stakeholders “continue to express concern regarding the operational and systemic challenges associated with implementation (of the law).” 
In a statement Wednesday, the department’s spokesperson said the age of youth the state plans to hold at the new facility is a separate consideration from Raise the Age. 
“DCF does not believe that this decision should be interpreted as a position that Raise the Age should be repealed,” Marble said. 
Vermont hasn’t had a long-term locked facility for juveniles since it shuttered the scandal-plagued Woodside Youth Rehabilitation Center in Essex, which closed in 2020 amid allegations of staff abuse. In 2023, the state agreed to pay $4.5 million to settle a lawsuit brought on behalf of seven youth over use of force at the facility.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Farm Bills have been a farce for years. This one seems tragic
description: Lawmakers must stop pretending this Farm Bill works. As Charles Givens once said, “Doing more of what doesn’t work won’t make it work any better.” The U.S. Senate has released its version of the Farm Bill and lawmakers are already calling it “a strong safety net” and “support for producers.” But out here in rural […]
text:
(Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight).Lawmakers must stop pretending this Farm Bill works. As Charles Givens once said, “Doing more of what doesn’t work won’t make it work any better.”
The U.S. Senate has released its version of the Farm Bill and lawmakers are already calling it “a strong safety net” and “support for producers.” But out here in rural America, we can see plainly what Washington refuses to admit; this Farm Bill does not fix the problem. It doesn’t even try.
Facing challenges from loss of demand for our products through tariff trade wars, which has led to agriculture trade deficits since 2019, closing of USAID and cutting SNAP programs that undermine what farmers do, produce food for all. Congress doesn’t see this as a problem. It doesn’t try.
Instead, they left out mandatory country-of-origin labeling (mCOOL), year-round E15, meaningful antitrust enforcement, supply management, or any path back to parity pricing (cost of production plus a livable wage), the Senate bill protects corporate power leaving farmers exposed to the same broken system that has failed for decades. The loss of nearly 250,000 farms since 2014 bears this out.
Start with mCOOL. Lawmakers know exactly why cattle producers want it restored. Without mCOOL, beef imports are at record highs and increasing, but consumers have no way to know that it is imported. That omission benefits multinational packers, not American producers. Consumers want transparency. Farmers want fair competition. The Senate bill sides with neither. It instead supports the packers taking advantage in the middle.
But the most dangerous omission is the refusal to confront corporate concentration. Farmers cannot compete in markets that no longer function as markets. Four packers control more than 80 percent of beef processing. Two companies dominate seed sales. Fertilizer, chemical, and grain markets are vertically integrated to the point where farmers face monopoly power on both the buying and selling side. Yet the Senate bill contains no meaningful antitrust enforcement, no market transparency reforms, and no limits on abusive contracting or captive supply. Without structural competition, every other “support program” is just a subsidy for concentrated corporate power.
Then there is the foundation for any real farm policy: supply management and parity pricing. The Senate bill offers neither. Instead, it continues the same model that has failed, especially since 2014—encouraging overproduction, driving down farmgate prices, and then trying to backfill the damage with emergency payments.
Lawmakers know this model is broken. The evidence is overwhelming. Since the trade wars began farmers have received over $200 billion in emergency payments—ad hoc bailouts, disaster packages, market facilitation payments, pandemic aid, and “bridge payments.”
These payments were not signs of a healthy farm economy. They were proof that the Farm Bill as currently designed, cannot adjust to real-world shocks. When markets collapse, when corporate buyers squeeze prices, when global disruptions hit, the Farm Bill has no mechanism to stabilize farm income. Congress has had to invent emergency programs year after year because the underlying policy no longer works.
A Farm Bill that requires $200 billion in emergency patches is not a safety net. It is a failure of design.
The Senate bill does nothing to change that. It does not restore price floors tied to the cost of production. It does not manage supply to prevent overproduction and crashes. It does not rebuild competition. It does not give farmers the tools to earn a living from the marketplace instead of the federal treasury sending money to your mailbox.
What it does is preserve the status quo. A system where farmers take on more debt, rural communities lose population, land shifts to investors, and corporate buyers capture the value farmers create.
Lawmakers still have time to fix this. But you cannot fix it by pretending the current bill supports farmers. A Farm Bill without mCOOL, without year-round E15, without antitrust enforcement, without supply management, and without parity is not farm policy. It is a policy for corporations that profit from farmers’ losses.
Congress is writing a Farm Bill. Rural America needs a farm policy. Those are not the same thing. This moment is a chance to rebuild the system, not repeat it.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Group demands NJ yank school guidance on transgender students as feds cut protections
description: A conservative law firm is targeting state guidance on parental notification if their child attempts to change gender at school.
text:
A conservative law firm is targeting state guidance on parental notification if their child attempts to change gender at school. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A conservative law firm is calling on New Jersey officials to repeal state guidance on parental notification when students question or attempt to change their gender at school.
The Liberty Justice Center, a Texas-based nonprofit that has waged such battles for free around the country, warned New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport in a letter Tuesday that keeping the guidance, known as Policy 5756, in place will lead to “federal investigations or lawsuits for the violation of federal civil rights.”
The center also sent letters to attorneys general in New York, Illinois, and Washington, where similar policies are in place. The effort comes a week after the Trump administration threatened two school districts in Maryland and Michigan with sanctions, including pulling their federal funding, if they don’t repeal their policies.
“By withholding information from parents regarding their children, these school districts are violating federal law, not to mention basic morality,” Timothy Snowball, a senior attorney at the center, said in a statement. “Parents have the fundamental right to direct their children’s upbringing, and these attorneys general must comply with federal law or face possible legal action.”
New Jersey’s policy, which the state Department of Education issued in 2018, prohibits the disclosure of a student’s gender identity without their consent unless “a specific and compelling need” obligates school officials to alert parents, such as health and safety concerns or a bias incident.
Several school districts and parents have challenged the policy in court, arguing it interferes with parents’ constitutional right to raise their children as they want. The state’s attorneys have countered that students have a constitutional right to privacy, disclosure risks harm to students whose parents aren’t supportive, and the policy is voluntary guidance districts don’t have to follow. Judges so far have let it stand.
It’s unclear how many of the state’s 600 districts have adopted the state guidance. The group Defending Education, which opposes such policies, estimates 130 districts have done so, but local advocates suspect that’s an undercount, as school boards typically act on state guidance.
Snowball said the U.S. Supreme Court’s March order in a California case known as Mirabelli v. Bonta should spur states with similar policies to reexamine and revoke them.
California’s law requires schools to support a child’s social transitioning and bars alerting parents without the child’s consent. After it was challenged, a trial court issued an injunction that blocked enforcement of the law, an appeals court stayed that injunction, and a split Supreme Court vacated the stay and returned the case to circuit court, saying parents claiming religious exemptions likely will prevail.
The Liberty Justice Center filed a brief supporting parents in the California case.
“The constitutional questions have now been squarely presented, and the legal issues are no longer theoretical. Your office should reevaluate the state’s current position to ensure that New Jersey’s policies and enforcement actions comply with parents’ federally protected rights before further litigation compels that result,” Snowball wrote to Davenport.
Spokespeople for Davenport and the New Jersey Department of Education did not respond to requests for comment.
But Robert Kim, executive director of the Education Law Center, said Davenport and the other attorneys general shouldn’t change course because of the California decision, which was not a final ruling on the case’s merits but instead just a preliminary order issued in response to an emergency application — meaning there were no oral arguments, briefs filed, or extended opinion written.
“It is a very limited window into this emerging area of law,” Kim said.
The Liberty Justice Center’s letter-writing campaign adds “fuel to the fire that’s stemming from this pattern of disturbing behavior by the Trump administration, this fixation to aggressively target a small portion of the student population, the transgender community, for disfavored treatment by the federal government,” Kim said.
Michael Gottesman, founder of the New Jersey Public Education Coalition, also doesn’t think the California decision should sway policymakers here, noting that California’s policy is mandatory while New Jersey’s is voluntary.
The policy’s critics also ignore that the state’s Law Against Discrimination protects people from being forcibly outed, Gottesman added.
“The policy basically sets up a process which recognizes the fact that parents have rights, but students do too,” Gottesman said. “There’s a whole line of cases in the Supreme Court on parents’ rights, but there’s also a whole line of cases in the Supreme Court about students’ privacy rights.”
Opponents have mischaracterized the policy, which balances parental notification with student privacy, said Dillon Reisman, a staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey.
“Our state’s policies have never required schools to lie to parents when a parent asks about their student’s gender identity. The policy already recognizes that health and safety concerns or harassment, intimidation, and bullying laws might require schools to affirmatively notify parents of a student’s gender identity if it’s relevant,” Reisman said. “Those are two things that already meet the U.S. Supreme Court standard from Mirabelli v. Bonta.”

Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, right, orders cupcakes at Good Cakes and Bakes in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 5, 2026. Benson joined Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear for a small business roundtable to kick off the general election campaign. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson embraced Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed’s message of affordability during her first campaign stop of the general election.
Benson told reporters Wednesday morning that her focus as the party’s nominee for governor is delivering a victory not just for herself, but for the entire ticket of Democrats, who she said largely agree on key issues.
“We’re all committed to driving down costs, to ensure healthcare is accessible to all, to ending corruption, to growing our economy and increasing our wages,” Benson said. “You’ll see us as Democrats all working together with that same message, and a motivation to not just talk the talk, but walk the walk and deliver results.”
Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson kicks off her general election campaign for governor in a roundtable with small business owners at Good Cakes and Bakes in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Benson referenced El-Sayed’s catchphrase of “money out of politics, money in your politics, Medicare for All,” but only directly quoted the first two, instead referring generally to making healthcare more accessible and affordable for the final calling card.
Benson said affordability doesn’t end at driving down costs of things like healthcare and housing. She said it also needs to include increasing wages, which she said have stagnated in Michigan.
“In this economy, with costs skyrocketing, we cannot make it work on one job, which you need to be able to do,” Benson said.
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the chair of the Democratic Governors Association, joined Benson at a Detroit bakery Wednesday morning for a roundtable with small business owners.
Supporting small businesses is one way to grow the middle class and begin building generational wealth, Benson said.
She said states like Michigan need to address wealth inequality.
“There should be no ceiling the wealthy can create,” Benson said. “And I particularly want to invest in generational wealth opportunities, of which small business growth is a critical piece, so that we can ensure we’re investing in our families, investing in growth, and not just saying we want to get to this ceiling, but actually creating that floor so that people can just grow and thrive.”

“Being governor means no matter what’s going on at the federal level, that you can fight your hardest for the people of your state,” Beshear said.

He shared an anecdote about a police officer whose child went from going to therapy twice a week to five days a week.
