name: Connecticut Mirror
title: One field, many uses: A mowing question in Durham
description: Bobolinks migrate to CT in the spring and nest in public fields marked for mowing, putting farmers at odds with bird watchers.
text:
On a recent hot July evening, residents from Durham and nearby towns settled into folding chairs, clutching letters as they gathered to propose an answer to a seemingly simple question that had divided the rural community: When should a town-owned field be mowed?
What began as a outdoor meeting of the local conservation commission at Curtis Woodlands was soon overtaken by public concerns about another parcel of land.
Last month, the town of Durham mowed one of the fields it owns at Frederick White Farm weeks earlier than many had hoped, prompting criticism that the decision destroyed nesting habitats for bobolinks, a bird species that migrates to the area in the spring.
Others at the meeting, however, believed the farm should return to its original agricultural roots — hay production.
At the heart of the debate lay a deeper question: Who gets to decide how public land should be used?

Residents gather outside at Curtis Woodlands before the Durham Conservation Commission meeting on July 14 to comment on town’s early mowing of a field at White Farm. Credit: Tran Chau / CT Mirror

For Sue White, whose father owned the property for many years, watching the once-vibrant fields grow into unmanaged plots of grass and fallen trees has been disheartening. At the meeting, she urged the town to abandon the practice of delayed mowing. 
“The idea that we can’t mow until after July 15, at which point the hay is worthless — it’s not surprising no one wants it anymore,” she said.
The July 15 mowing guideline is part of a wildlife conservation effort that allows time for grassland bird species to nest and raise their young before fields are cut.

A bobolink perches on plants at White Farm on July 23. Credit: Courtesy of Christopher Grice

White added that the town is “worshiping a little black and white bird that isn’t native to our area.”

Resident Russell Robinson echoed that message: “Durham’s crest is not a bird; it’s a cow, and agriculture is deeply rooted in this community.”
Both Robinson and White argued that regular mowing would benefit the town by reducing maintenance costs and producing high-quality hay for farmers, which they described as a “win-win” situation.
However, for birders like Annyta Vizard, who spent years organizing bird walks at White Farm, the property means more than just agriculture. It serves as a home for abundant wildlife and a source of joy where she watches bobolinks — songbirds that travel thousands of miles between South and North America each year — return to the farm during nesting season. 
Over the years, Vizard has watched visitors come to the farm to admire the birds, reinforcing her belief that the farm should continue to be used as an open space.
“We’re only talking about town-owned land. We’re not talking about land that’s owned by the farmer,” she emphasized. “This is town-owned land that’s also for recreation.”
Durham resident Susan Lundgren said, “Our public lands should be a sanctuary for wildlife, not a casualty for bureaucratic deadlines.”
The issue drew concerns from more than just birders, with other longtime users of the farm weighing in.

Goldfinches build nests in the grassy fields at Frederick White Farm.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Stevan Akerley, a member of the model airplane club, who has flown model planes over White Farm for 35 years, pushed back against the idea that the club’s activities disturbed wildlife and should relocate, arguing the property is intended for public recreation.
“We coexist with the birds and the butterflies. We maintain the airfield … our planes have takeoff and landing requirements because they’re remote-controlled, and we stay out of the bobolink fields,” he said.
Many of the letters read that evening shared a similar sentiment: a desire for everyone to coexist with the farm.

Birders gathered at Frederick White Farm in Durham to observe bobolinks during the Connecticut Bobolink and Wildlife Festival last July. Credit: Courtesy of Annyta Vizard

Residents remained confused why the mowing was done so early this year, though some speculated that the town may have been trying to spend money before the end of the fiscal year.
In a statement to the Connecticut Mirror, Phil Augur, chair of the Durham Conservation Commission, said the decision to mow was “an effort to get back to grasslands.” He added that the mowed section “had started being overtaken by woody growth creating unfavorable conditions.”
Augur deferred further comments to the commission’s September meeting. 

The fields at Frederick White Farm in Durham on July 30. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

The purchase of White Farm
Durham had a long-term vision when it acquired Frederick White Farm from the White family in the mid-1960s with federal and state assistance. As the town’s population grew, town officials saw open spaces as long-term investments for Durham’s future. In a 1965 letter, the Conservation Commission wrote, “The need for water supplies, open spaces for recreation and wildlife preservation will become increasingly important to the life of the town.”
Since then, the town has preserved the farm as open space while leasing portions of it to local farmers for haying.
Although Durham does not have a formal written mowing policy, the town’s 2019 lease agreement for White Farm stated that “harvesting cannot occur prior to July 15th each year.” Residents said that the rule has been followed in previous years, but this year, the property was not leased. 
“I just want to see a written policy and regulations. … Because whenever they want to mow, it’s not against policy. It’s not an ordinance,” Vizard said. 
Augur, the Conservation Commission chair, did not address questions from the CT Mirror about town policies or rules regarding the July 15 date.
Joe Greenbacker, a 77-year-old farmer who has lived in Durham for 40 years, said the town first needs to “decide what they’re going to do with the property and stick to it,” whether that means managing it as a wildlife sanctuary or an agricultural operation.
He agreed that delaying mowing could discourage farmers from harvesting the hay.
“If they put restrictions on when anybody could mow it, it’s fine with me. But don’t expect they’re going to have farmers willing to come in there and make the hay, because it just won’t be worth it,” he said, adding that hay loses nutrient value as it ripens.
There is another factor that also influences mowing decisions: unpredictable weather.
According to Greenbacker, farmers need three consecutive dry days to make hay, and rainy weather can delay that process.
“Weather plays a big role in what we can and can’t do,” he said.

Grass grows on a field recently mowed by the city of Durham at Frederick White Farm.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Finding a balance
The debate in Durham reflects a broader challenge for the town as it grapples with how to balance wildlife preservation with agricultural needs. 
One organization that seeks to strike that balance is the Bobolink Project, a conservation program that pays farmers in parts of New England to adopt bird-friendly haying practices. According to its guidelines, the delayed first cut option recommends no cutting until July 15, while the delayed second cut allows for an early cut in May followed by a delay until July 24, giving the bobolinks enough time to renest. 
Hyla Howe, a grassland bird biologist at Mass Audubon and program manager for the Bobolink Project, said that mowing should be “an adaptive process where you’re watching what’s happening in the field, seeing if the numbers of birds are declining or increasing.”
While delayed mowing can protect the birds, which breed and build nests in the grass, repeated delayed haying without proper soil care can reduce a field’s quality over time, Howe said. She suggested testing the soil every two years to check nutrient levels, then following recommendations for maintenance of either warm-season or cool-season grasses.
Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection has its own mowing guidelines for state lands, which include parks, forests, wildlife management areas and natural area preserves. According to DEEP, mowing decisions are made individually to ensure that management practices align with the purpose and intended use of the property. 
“In wildlife management areas that are managed for grassland birds, we typically do not mow until Sept. 1 or later. In general, we follow the guidelines published by Mass Audubon,” Bill Flood, a spokesman for DEEP, said in an emailed statement.
Similar tensions have emerged in other Connecticut towns over mowing. 
In neighboring Middlefield, residents have expressed continued concerns about the mowing at Strickland Farm, a town-owned property that it leases to the Durham Fair Association for parking during the annual September fair.
“With the aggressive mowing that’s been done two to three times a year in the last six or seven years, they have completely wiped out the bobolinks at that location,” resident Christopher Grice said. 
According to the fair association’s attorney, John Corona, the demanded changes are “inherently inconsistent” with what he described as a “mutually beneficial, almost symbiotic relationship between the fair and the town’s open space property.”
He added that the lease allows the property to remain open and mowed year-round, which would otherwise be costly to the town. 
This year, the town of Middlefield established mowing recommendations that call for delaying the first cut at several town-owned fields until after July 15. However, Grice said a large section of town-owned Coginchaug Greenway was still mowed in June.
At the Phillips Farm Preserve in Southbury, the Southbury Land Trust restricted dog walkers’ access to a field where woodcocks nest and asked the farmers to not maintain field edges until fall. The farmers complied. However, unlike White Farm, the property is privately managed by the land trust.
“It’s tricky,” said Pat Monahan, stewardship director of the Southbury Land Trust. “You’re always trying to maintain a relationship with a busy farmer and manage the land for lots of different uses and what people think you use it for.
In Wallingford, a similar case emerged in which its Conservation Commission asked a farmer to delay mowing of a town-owned field after noticing bobolinks nesting in the area. Jeffrey Kohan, vice chair of Wallingford’s Planning and Zoning Committee, said the farmer was “amendable to the delaying of [mowing] this part of the field.”
Kohan added that there was no opposition from residents because the field is not as heavily used for recreation as White Farm.

Frederick White Farm in Durham on July 30. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley meets voters in Madison with five days until Election Day
description: Peggy Hedberg, a Madison resident, recently switched her support in the Democratic primary for governor from state Sen. Kelda Roys (D-Madison) to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley — a decision she said she has made because “pragmatically” she wants to vote for someone to win. Roys has been polling in the single digits. Hedberg said […]
text:
When Crowley entered his campaign’s new office on East Washington Avenue in Madison at mid-day on Wednesday, he made a circuit of the room, greeting attendees individually with a huge grin and firm handshakes. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Peggy Hedberg, a Madison resident, recently switched her support in the Democratic primary for governor from state Sen. Kelda Roys (D-Madison) to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley — a decision she said she has made because “pragmatically” she wants to vote for someone to win. Roys has been polling in the single digits.
Hedberg said it was Crowley’s energy that won her over.
“I felt like he had the strength to carry us,” she said, noting that it was hard for her to switch. She said she cares about electing women, especially as abortion access is one of the most important issues to her, but she also cares about having a candidate who can work with the Legislature to get things done. “I had to make a decision, and that was hard, but I felt that with Evers’ backing and other factors that this would be a better way for us to move forward.” 
Hedberg was at a meet and greet with Crowley on Wednesday afternoon in downtown Madison. Crowley is looking to win over voters like Hedberg with just five days until Election Day. 
Crowley told reporters that he is focusing on consolidating votes from people who are undecided. According to the last Marquette Law School poll, 34% of likely Democratic primary voters had not yet made up their minds. 
Crowley’s campaign ended in July, then restarted at the end of the month following the implosion of Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez’s campaign. In his second launch, Crowley entered with the endorsement of Gov. Tony Evers, triggering accusations that he is the candidate of the Democratic “establishment.” He said Wednesday that “when people try to call me the establishment, I look at that as a slur, particularly as an African American candidate.” Describing his background as a child of parents who struggled with addiction, mental illness and serial evictions, he said he has always represented the people, not the powerful.
When Crowley entered his campaign’s new office on East Washington Avenue in Madison at mid-day on Wednesday, he made a circuit of the room, greeting attendees individually with a huge grin and firm handshakes. Crowley told reporters that six days is “absolutely” enough time to get voters acquainted with him. 
The stop is one of several Crowley is making this week as he crisscrosses the state in an attempt to introduce himself to voters and win enough support to overcome state Rep. Francesca Hong’s substantial lead in recent polls. Election Day is Tuesday.
Crowley told one group of attendees that “there are Democrats everywhere,” describing his campaign stops in Wausau, Rhinelander, Hudson, Superior and Green Bay. At a recent stop in Baraboo he took pictures at the Clown Museum.
Crowley said he was trying “to see if we could find Tom Tiffany.”
Crowley told one group of attendees that “there are Democrats everywhere,” describing his campaign stops in Wausau, Rhinelander, Hudson, Superior and Green Bay. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
This week, Crowley campaigned in Appleton with Gov. Evers and won the endorsement of U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore, the Congressional Black Caucus PAC and state legislators including Legislative Black Caucus Chair Sen. Dora Drake and Rep. Lisa Subeck, who spoke at the Madison event.
“There is something magnetic about him. I think about some of the things that I have loved about Gov. Tony Evers — he is a good guy, he is a good person who leads with his head and with his heart — and I think David holds many of those same qualities,” Subeck told the crowd.
Crowley and Subeck served in the Legislature while Democrats were in the minority. Subeck said Crowley had a “particular talent for not only standing up for our core values, but for also working across the aisle without compromising our values” when he served in the Legislature.
Crowley told attendees that the biggest problem facing Democrats is that “all we’ve been doing is responding and reacting to Donald Trump and Republicans.”
“As long as we do that, guess who’s defining us for us? They are,” Crowley said. “So, it’s time for us to get off the sidelines and stop playing defense and get on the offense. This is the time where we not only need a Democratic governor, but we need to make sure that we’re flipping the state Senate, flipping the state Assembly, because none of these policies that I’m about to rattle off becomes a reality unless we’re in charge.” 
Crowley spoke about capping the cost of childcare at 7%, fixing the school funding formula and boosting the state’s share of special education costs to 90% as well as supporting unions by repealing the union-busting law Act 10.
At one point, Crowley took issue with a proposed moratorium on AI data centers, which Hong has made a key point in her campaign. He said that he is frustrated that the Republican-led Legislature finished its work this year without establishing any regulation on the constructions of them. 
“People may talk about a moratorium, but what is that moratorium going to do about the data centers that are currently being built or are operating right now? It’s short-term thinking but it doesn’t address the long-term concerns we all have in this state,” Crowley said, adding that data centers need to “pay their own way.”
Crowley said that implementing a ban on non-disclosure agreements between local governments and big tech companies building data centers, requiring union labor and having companies pay for their own clean energy is essential. 
Crowley also challenged predictions based on polling ahead of Election Day, especially after the results of Michigan’s U.S. Senate race. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, defeated U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens by about 1 point, after polls showed him leading the race by more than 10 points. 
Hong has been polling 20 points or more ahead of Crowley. 
The Crowley campaign released a memo on Wednesday that said “results in Michigan Tuesday night showed polling that failed to appropriately capture and reflect the primary electorate and well overstated the position of the race frontrunner. Democrats are in the driver’s seat in Wisconsin to choose David Crowley and have the best fighting chance against Tom Tiffany in November.”
The memo found that in the four-person primary for governor, Hong led Crowley 42% to 24% while Roys and former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan were still polling in the single digits. 
Asked about whether he thinks the other candidates could cut into his margins and propel Hong to the nomination, Crowley told reporters that his job is to “convince as many voters as possible why we’re the winning candidate.” 
“With it being almost a clear race between two particular candidates, those voters and those candidates, they’re going to have to make their own decisions,” Crowley said. He also said that he would never tell a candidate to drop out.
The Crowley campaign’s internal poll found Hong up 53% to 33% against Crowley in a head-to-head race. Once those being polled were informed of both candidates’ positions, Hong led Crowley 47% to 38%
Young people make up a large share of Hong’s base, but Evan Natzke, an 18-year-old who recently graduated from Milton High School south of Madison, enthusiastically greeted Crowley at the event. He told the Examiner that he met Crowley before and he appreciated that he seems like a “super genuine person.”
“I just love his energy. I feel like he’s just so charismatic,” Natzke said. 
Natzke said Hong has good ideas, but he is concerned about how she’ll do in the general election, saying that Republicans “are going to be able to paint this picture of her being this super crazy radical person.”
“I just don’t think that a normal voter is going to really like that image that is painted of her,” Natzke said. “And along with that, I’m also unsure if her policies will be able to work at the state level.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Witless whining on social media confirms that Kansas Republicans can’t take ‘no’ for an answer
description: Four years ago, Kansans said “hell no” to a constitutional amendment clearing the way for extremists to ban abortion. On Tuesday, Kansans said “hell no” again, this time to a constitutional amendment clearing the way for a conservative revamp of the state Supreme Court — banning abortion and gutting public education. Somehow, that message hasn’t […]
text:
Residents vote in Lawrence on Aug. 4, 2026. Kansans overwhelmingly rejected a constitutional amendment revamping how state Supreme Court justices were selected.(Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)Four years ago, Kansans said “hell no” to a constitutional amendment clearing the way for extremists to ban abortion.
On Tuesday, Kansans said “hell no” again, this time to a constitutional amendment clearing the way for a conservative revamp of the state Supreme Court — banning abortion and gutting public education.
Somehow, that message hasn’t been received.
Browsing social media on Tuesday night and Wednesday turned into a surreal experience for this journalist, as I watched Republicans grappling with a 22-percentage-point rejection of their agenda. Four years ago, the same voices were stunned by the state’s solidly pro-choice majority, and I poked good-natured fun at their incomprehension at the time.
Some of these commenters hide behind pseudonyms. Others serve in public-facing roles. Regardless, they all want you to know that conservative Republicans were the real victims here.

Kansas is going to be a blue state in the next 4 years.
I am so disappointed in this state.
— Governor Dill (@TheGreenOldDill) August 5, 2026

Let me go out on a not-very-long limb here and say that this Tweet is not true.
As much as I might wish it, and as much as some advocates may hope, Republican roots run deep in this state. That doesn’t mean residents love rightwing orthodoxy, just that they love voting for the GOP.
As I wrote yesterday, amazing things happen in Kansas when party labels aren’t affixed to elections. Voters were free to make a choice without the baggage of partisanship. This, incidentally, is why the Kansas Legislature will never create a citizen initiative or direct democracy process.
They don’t want to deal with what Kansas voters actually want.

Republicans in Kansas have now twice stupidly tried to pass constitutional amendments during primary elections when low turnout allows democrats to swamp the voting and defeat the amendments.
The best chance for amendments is in the general election of a presidential cycle!
—  (@FreeStateWill) August 5, 2026

I’ve seen a couple of posts make this point, and they misunderstand the situation completely.
Republicans may have been stupid. But they had a plan. Kansas has nearly twice as many registered Republicans as registered Democrats, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. Back in 2022, and this year, they placed constitutional amendments on midterm primary ballots in hopes of rigging the outcomes.
Democrats usually don’t face contested primary races. Independents don’t have anything to vote for at all. That means Republicans, and Republicans alone, have been trained to show up for primaries.
GOP leaders thought they could choose those casting ballots, rather than making a case to the entire state. That was the plan.

One of the worldwide trends in the rise of the authoritarian judge, jumping into leftist political causes with no accountability. Every new conservative leader sees this as a major threat but no one has been able to tame it. Even in my home state of Kansas an amendment lost. Bad.
— Matt Schlapp (@mschlapp) August 5, 2026

“Bad” indeed, Mr. Schlapp. You might know him as chairman of the American Conservative Union, which holds the annual Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC. He has also been accused, multiple times, of being a sex pest.
But hey, let’s watch out for those authoritarian judges here in the Sunflower State, with their seditious ideas that women have control over their own bodies and children have a right to education.

Kansans voted to turn down the opportunity to vote for their Supreme Court justices, so lib donor lawyers can keep selecting them, all in the name of “preserving abortion rights.” The Abortion Capital of the Midwest has a huge issue with: 1. lack of Republican voter turnout;…
— Victory or Death  (@IncognitoMeems) August 5, 2026

The good people of Johnson County will be surprised to learn that, in the words of Mr./Ms. Victory or Death, that they are “commie libs.”
In the old days, we called them moderate Republicans and they voted for Bill Graves. You know, the same two-term Republican governor who co-wrote an op-ed for Kansas Reflector about the importance of an independent judiciary.
But Kansas Republicans no longer nominate candidates like Graves. They turned up their noses at moderate Vicki Schmidt on primary night. So Johnson County voters have decided to vote — and change their voter registrations — accordingly.


Finally, Rep. Blake Carpenter, R-Derby, made clear on Facebook that as much as Kansans might want to move on to other issues, Republicans won’t be satisfied after Tuesday’s walloping.
“I know there will be people who say this debate is over and that those of us who support reform should simply move on,” he wrote in a remarkably dyspeptic dispatch. “I disagree. If we believe the current system is unaccountable, then we have a responsibility to continue advocating for something better.”
Earlier in the message, Carpenter advocates “a system more like the federal model, or at least adopt a commission where citizens hold the majority instead of attorneys.”
He won’t take “no” for an answer.
So after a day or two of rest, progressive advocates will take a deep breath, roll up their sleeves, and go back to work. For Kansans who want to preserve our shared rights and freedoms, no single win at the ballot box will ever be enough.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore: New deal allows state to direct the future of Preakness
description: The Preakness has a new, later race day and a new television contract, the latest in a week of rapid-fire developments that saw the state buy the Preakness away from Churchill Downs, which responded by excluding Maryland from its new, national racing series.
text:
Jon Miller, president of acquisitions and partnerships at NBC Sports, and Gov. Wes Moore (D) announce a new six-year network television deal to broadcast the Preakness and other thoroughbred horse racing in Maryland.  (Photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Changes lie ahead for Maryland’s signature thoroughbred horse race, including a new, later race day and a new, expanded network television contract.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) announced the changes Wednesday to the Preakness Stakes, historically the second event in racing’s Triple Crown. It was the latest in a week of rapid-fire developments that saw the state buy rights to the Preakness away from Kentucky Derby owner Churchill Downs, which responded by announcing a new national thoroughbred racing series that excludes the Preakness.
Wednesday’s changes mean that a race always run on the third Saturday of May — two weeks after the Kentucky Derby — will happen a week later. And on a Sunday. As part of expanded television coverage for a planned Memorial Day weekend of racing, with the state-owned Black-Eyed Susan Stakes being run on Saturday.
Moore said the new television deal and race day changes are meant to ensure the growth of the taxpayer-owned Preakness, the thoroughbred racing industry in the state and the neighboring Park Heights Community.
“Because I will always bet on Maryland, today, this Preakness deal joins the list of things that will not just grow our economy, but continue to show that in Maryland, we control our own destinies, and we don’t need others’ help to do it,” Moore said. “The Preakness can and will remain the second jewel of the Triple Crown, and nothing will change that.”
The changes will start with the 2027 Preakness.
Preakness, Pimlico left out of new race series by Churchill Downs, Belmont

Moving the Preakness back a week was seen as important because trainers of horses that run in the Kentucky Derby — including winners — have sometimes decided to skip the race in Baltimore to rest their horses for the longer Belmont Stakes in New York, the third leg of the Triple Crown. Doing so eliminates the potential for a Triple Crown winner and the public attention that comes with that possibility.
“The Triple Crown will continue to be one of the marquee sports events of the year, and we’ll continue having Preakness be at the center,” Moore told reporters.
NBC and the Maryland Jockey Club reached an agreement on a new six-year deal that includes coverage of the Preakness as well as the Black-Eyed Susan stakes and two other races — Preakness Preview Day in April and Maryland Million Day in October.
Maryland Jockey Club President and General Manager Bill Knauf said the focus is on showcasing the Preakness.
“Triple Crown has been going for 100 years, and it’s going to be around for 100 more, and it will always run through Pimlico,” he said.
The network, Maryland Jockey Club and Moore declined to provide financial details of the agreement.
Jon Miller, president of acquisitions and partnerships at NBC Sport, suggested the deal could include some sort of incentives possibly tied to viewership. NBC had long sought moving the race back a week in hopes of luring Kentucky Derby champions to the second jewel of the Triple Crown.
“When this process began, we showed them not only the benefits of obviously getting more horses in, but also the increased ratings,” Miller said. “Increased ratings create more revenue opportunities for us. More revenue opportunities for us gives us more money that we can turn around and pay the Preakness and the State of Maryland. So it works out.”
The announcement was applauded by Mark Anthony Thomas, president of the Greater Baltimore Committee.
“Ten years from now, we’re going to look back at this moment and this will be one of the smartest investments Maryland has made in one of its most prominent assets,” Thomas said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Moore’s announcement follows a flurry of activity in which the state announced the purchase of the intellectual property rights for the race.
“You cannot control your future if you do not own it,” Moore said. “You do not control what the future brings if you aren’t the ones making the decision about what the future brings. Maryland now owns the rights. Marylanders now own the assets. Marylanders will make the decisions.”
Ownership came with a cost. The purchase of two racetracks, the ill-fated purchase of a Carroll County farm meant to be a training center and $85 million for the intellectual property rights for the Preakness and Black-Eyed Susan. All in an industry that has its share of struggles as it tries to reinvent itself and attract new fans.
Maryland now effectively owns and controls the thoroughbred racing industry in the state.
“The Governor stated Maryland controls its own destiny,” said Senate Minority Leader Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore). “Maryland controls the Preakness. It doesn’t control Churchill Downs. It doesn’t control NYRA (New York Racing Association). And it doesn’t control where the nation’s best horses choose to run.”
Churchill Downs had offered $85 million to buy the intellectual property rights to the Preakness and Black-Eyed Susan Stakes from 1/ST Racing, but the state had a right to match that offer and it did, closing the sale last week. Days later, Churchill Downs and the New York Racing Authority, which owns the Belmont, announced a championship race series. The first two races in the six-race series are the Derby and the Belmont Stakes — the bookends of thoroughbred racing’s Triple Crown.
Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City), speaking Tuesday, had not been briefed on Moore’s announcement but said the Churchill Downs announcement was worrisome.
State finalizes deal to buy rights to Preakness for $85 million

“I don’t think the timing is a coincidence,” Ferguson said.
When asked if it was meant to be punitive, Ferguson said: “It’s not for me to say, but the timing certainly is. It appears to be quite highly correlated.”
Ferguson and other officials have questioned the state’s continued and deepening involvement in thoroughbred racing. The Preakness being left off the championship schedule has not diminished those concerns.
“My first read is this isn’t good, but I’m waiting for details to make sure that we’re not making decisions out of haste,” Ferguson said.
The exclusion raises questions about the fate of the Triple Crown and how that might affect the Preakness.
“The Thoroughbred Championship Series is designed around horses progressing from the Kentucky Derby to the Belmont Stakes and then through the rest of the championship season,” said Hershey. “If trainers are pursuing points in the Thoroughbred Championship Series, what incentive do they, other than the Derby winner, have to interrupt a five-week preparation for the Belmont Stakes by running in the Preakness two weeks earlier?”
Moore told reporters he is open to further discussions with Churchill Downs.
“You know we’re eager to continue conversations with Churchill Downs, but we’re also just very clear that maintaining the ownership of the Preakness is important to Maryland,” Moore said.
“Maintaining ownership of the assets connected to Preakness is important to Maryland. Making sure that we’re investing in not just the track but also our communities is important to Maryland,” he said. “So we’re always looking to partner with anybody to include Churchill Downs, but we’re also very clear about what the terms of those conversations are.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: For more than 100,000 Ohio Medicaid recipients, worries build about the future of home care
description: DAYTON — Few nonresidents of nursing homes know more about what they’re like than Dorothy Valentine. For decades, she worked in them, caring for “her” residents. Despite the hard work, weird hours, and low pay, it was her favorite job, she said. “I loved my residents,” Valentine said. “I always spoiled them. I almost got […]
text:
Dorothy Valentine, 80, of Dayton. (Photo by Marty Schladen, Ohio Capital Journal.)DAYTON — Few nonresidents of nursing homes know more about what they’re like than Dorothy Valentine. For decades, she worked in them, caring for “her” residents.
Despite the hard work, weird hours, and low pay, it was her favorite job, she said.
“I loved my residents,” Valentine said. “I always spoiled them. I almost got fired for spoiling my residents. I love people.”
Valentine, 80, spoke last week surrounded by medicines and medical devices in the living room of her modest duplex just west of downtown Dayton. 
She said that as much as she loved caring for people in nursing homes in Ohio and Texas, she dreads being in one herself because she knows how the quality of care can slip.
So, suffering from several serious infirmities, Valentine hopes to spend the rest of her days at home, with a son caring for her full-time and receiving other services as needed.
But, along with the rest of the nearly 140,000 Ohioans getting Medicaid-supported community care, she faces uncertainty. 
Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year cut nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid over 10 years. 
The most drastic provisions take effect Jan. 1. Before they do, Republican officials are highlighting what they say is rampant fraud in Medicaid-supported home care programs.
So, forced to find savings, those programs might seem a likely place for state Medicaid officials to start, which is what is worrying residents of their own homes like Valentine.
Polling shows that 62% of Americans think Medicare, the federal retirement program, pays for long-term nursing-home care, but it doesn’t. Medicaid does.
That’s why millions of American families with loved ones in the nursing home are forced to spend down their wealth until they qualify for Medicaid and then the federal-state health program foots the bill. 
Care for seniors is sucking wealth out of families — especially in Ohio

The University of Pennsylvania’s Leonard Davis Institute of Health Economics in July reported that it is mandatory for states receiving Medicaid dollars to finance nursing-home care, but not in-home care. 
Home-based care has become increasingly popular in recent decades. In 2022 it represented 65% of all Medicaid expenditures on long-term care, the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services reported.
“Either more people are going to go into nursing homes, which may not be consistent with their preferences, or people who stay at home may have to get their needs met by their family members or close friends who don’t get paid to do it,” the University of Pennsylvania quoted Rachel M. Werner, executive director of its Institute for Health Economics, as saying.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In addition to not being preferred by some seniors, nursing-home care is significantly more expensive than home-based care. 
A Place for Mom, a care-referral company based in New York, estimates that a semi-private room in a nursing home is 48% more expensive than the median cost of full-time, home-based care.
Even if it is more expensive and she doesn’t want to be there, nursing homes might be where people like Valentine are headed.
“I don’t want to be in no nursing home because of the way they treat you,” she said. “They don’t change you. I used to change my patients every two hours whether they needed it or not. I always cleaned them up.”
As it is now, her 63-year-old son Clifford lives with her and provides around-the-clock care. His mother’s respiratory and heart problems are acute enough that even trips to the store have to be kept brief as possible because he doesn’t want his mother to be alone, he said.
Ohio provides support through Medicaid waivers for family members who care for their loved ones. But Clifford hasn’t applied for it out of fear that household income will exceed limits for other benefits such as his mother’s Social Security or federal food assistance.
The Roosevelt Institute in April published a report saying that such unpaid caregivers provided $600 billion worth of services in 2021 and stunted their own economic prospects in the process.
Clifford Valentine said he nursed his wife through a terminal illness before caring for his mother.
“It’s kind of rough, but I’ve always done it,” he said.
Feds, Ohio Republicans focus on individual cases of Medicaid fraud, but what about corporations?

Some Republican political leaders say Medicaid programs for home care are the object of rampant fraud. In June, acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and other cabinet officials came to Ohio to highlight what they said was massive fraud in Medicaid generally.
And in a May radio interview, Ohio Auditor and state AG nominee Keith Faber said massive Medicaid home-care fraud isn’t being detected because “grandma’s never going to rat out” relatives who are being paid to care for her but are neglecting her instead. His campaign didn’t respond when asked to document an instance in which that actually happened.
With all the politics around the issue, people receiving and providing Medicaid support for home-based care are keeping their heads down.
In Dorothy Valentine’s case, she has Cityblock coordinating care on behalf of Molina Healthcare, which operates managed-care programs for Medicaid patients and those who, like Valentine, are eligible for both Medicaid and Medicare. 
Cityblock is paid a flat, per-member fee to coordinate services with an eye toward limiting costs through things like keeping them healthy enough to avoid hospital stays. The more savings it creates, the more money it makes.
Jenny Edelston, a spokeswoman, said policymakers should think hard about what might be lost by cutting funding for such programs. They help keep people out of hospitals and nursing homes, she said.
“Without particular attention to the impact of cuts on high-value (home-and community-based) health services, reduced funding can lead to short term pressure on Medicaid (managed-care organizations) — which may in turn cause (the care organizations) to pull back on investing in partnerships that leverage (home-and-community-based services) to avoid acute care down the line,” Edelston said in an email.
For Valentine, it’s a question of where she’ll spend her remaining days.
“This is where I want to be,” she said. “If it wasn’t for Cityblock, I don’t know what I’d do.”

title: Ohio sees second week of ‘significant’ increases in cyclosporiasis cases
description: Ohio has seen its second straight week of “significant increases” in cases of cyclosporiasis, the parasite that has been connected to leafy greens, and to severe diarrhea throughout the U.S, according to the state’s health director. The Ohio Department of Health shows the state has seen nearly 4,000 cases since June 1. The highest numbers […]
text:
Salad greens for sale at a bodega in Astoria, New York. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/ Stateline)Ohio has seen its second straight week of “significant increases” in cases of cyclosporiasis, the parasite that has been connected to leafy greens, and to severe diarrhea throughout the U.S, according to the state’s health director.
The Ohio Department of Health shows the state has seen nearly 4,000 cases since June 1.
The highest numbers come out of Lucas County, which has 553 cases to date since the beginning of the summer. Cuyahoga County has a reported 457 cases, and Wood County comes in third with 446 cases since June 1.
While Ohio hasn’t caught up to the numbers seen in Michigan, considered one of the biggest states in the cyclosporiasis outbreak, the numbers are getting close, according to the state’s health director, Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff.
“We have just seen over the course of the last couple of months a fairly steady and alarming increase in the number of cases,” Vanderhoff said in a Tuesday press conference.
“What it is telling us is that we have reason for continued concern about the risk people face from cyclosporiasis.”
Vanderhoff encouraged anyone who has been sick to respond to calls from health departments seeking to interview those who have been infected.
“These interviews provide crucial data … and help find commonalities among those who have been sick,” Vanderhoff said.
While the state is deferring to the FDA and the CDC to identify potential sources of the outbreak, the state has been collecting information they’ve passed on to federal agencies, according to Vanderhoff.
The CDC has traced infections back to iceberg lettuce in nine states including Ohio, and produce company Taylor Farms has recalled iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico, according to the federal agency.
The investigation into the outbreak is still ongoing, as the CDC is also investigating other cases it says are unrelated to the outbreak hitting Ohio and surrounding states.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Ohio health director dismissed ideas that fresh produce should be avoided entirely, pushing for more diligent cleaning practices instead.
“Prevention really begins not with avoiding … things our bodies need, but taking a sound approach to how we prepare fruits and vegetables every single day,” he said.
Proper washing of produce includes a thorough rinse under running water, and scrubbing fruits and vegetables with tougher skins with a brush.
Dr. Robert Frenck, a pediatrician and director of the Vaccine Research Center at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital, was mainly on the press conference to discuss child vaccines as a new school year approaches, but also served to dissuade ideas that cyclosporiasis is bigger than it is.
“In the greater scheme of things, it’s still a rather unusual infection,” Frenck said, adding that norovirus sees far more incidence rates annually than the parasitic infection that’s covering major news headlines this year.
The hallmark of cyclosporiasis is the lasting effects, Frenck said, with symptoms like diarrhea lasting weeks, sometimes months.
Treatment is possible through antibiotics, but Frenck said it’s important to know when to alert the doctor (after about a week of symptoms), and for physicians to make sure lab tests look for the parasite. Routine lab work wouldn’t normally cover that type of infection, according to the pediatrician.
Both Frenck and Vanderhoff said deaths are not typical from the infection.
Reported deaths in Michigan were connected to individuals with unrelated significant health problems, but Vanderhoff said that does give reason for immunocompromised, elderly, or very young individuals to keep medical professionals involved in their care.
“The caution that I would remind people about is if you’re vulnerable because your immune system is not working optimally … and you develop diarrhea, you should be reaching out to your provider immediately for guidance and direction,” Vanderhoff said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio General Assembly members propose sweeping bill to regulate data center development
description: Last week, a group of legislators in the Ohio House of Representatives introduced a far-reaching bill to regulate data center development across the state of Ohio. In the face of concerns about the environmental, aesthetic, and public finance ramifications of Ohio’s rapid growth in data center development, Ohio House Bill 983 introduces a range of […]
text:
An Amazon Web Services data center is shown situated near single-family homes. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)Last week, a group of legislators in the Ohio House of Representatives introduced a far-reaching bill to regulate data center development across the state of Ohio.
In the face of concerns about the environmental, aesthetic, and public finance ramifications of Ohio’s rapid growth in data center development, Ohio House Bill 983 introduces a range of interventions designed to insert the public into data center development decisions.
The bill will require voter approval for every new construction or expansion of a data center with peak electric load over one megawatt for every municipality and township within five miles of the project. 
Permits issued without voter approval would be considered void.
It would also impose new air emission and water discharge standards on a range of substances including PFAS, glycols, metals, and other organic compounds. These standards would apply to existing data centers after eighteen months. 
Owners of data centers would also be held financially responsible for water supply and water pressure impacts associated with their centers.
On the fiscal side, the legislation would ban local governments from offering property tax incentives for data centers and power plants associated with them. It would also require public disclosure of all data center agreements associated with development and supply.
This legislation would significantly slow down the development of data centers in Ohio, if not stop it altogether. 
The voter approval requirement in particular could lead to dozens of required communitywide votes across the country to authorize data center developments.
This would have a substantial impact on Ohio’s economy. 
Developers are set to invest $40 billion in data centers across the state of Ohio over the next four years. While this legislation would prevent some wasteful incentive spending, it would also likely cost the state economy tens of billions of dollars in investment.
One of the major concerns people have with data center development in Ohio is strain on public utilities, particularly electricity and water. 
If data center development drives up demand for each of these, it could drive prices for electricity and water up for local residents. 
This could fall more heavily on low-income residents because they spend more of their income on utilities than high-income residents. This bill’s proposed interventions could mitigate some of these cost concerns.
There are other spillover effects people worry about with data center developments. 
Will incentives leave less money available for schools? Will data centers lead to wastewater, air emissions, and noise pollution? 
These are concerns that could be bluntly dealt with through bans on incentives and community votes, which are likely to torpedo most projects.
Overall, though, it seems like this bill is a hammer for an issue that likely needs a scalpel. 
Communitywide votes to authorize new developments would likely be tantamount to a total ban of data center development across the state. This could slow Ohio’s economy to the tune of tens of billions of dollars over the next few years. 
Making sure that Ohio’s electricity and water systems keep up with new development could probably be achieved with less economic pain than a de facto permanent ban on development would create.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Legislative committee puts new Maryland building code on hold amid environmental concerns
description: A Maryland legislative committee is holding up a new building code regulation amid concerns that it is less environmentally stringent than the national code, which Maryland is supposed to adhere to.
text:
A joint House-Senate committee granted a request from Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) to put a hold on proposed new building code regulations in Maryland, amid concerns they may be too lax environmentally. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)A Maryland legislative committee is holding up a new building code regulation amid concerns that it is less environmentally stringent than the national code, which Maryland is supposed to adhere to.
In a letter Tuesday to Gov. Wes Moore (D), the House and Senate co-chairs of the Joint Committee on Administrative, Executive and Legislative Review signaled their intent to “conduct a more detailed study of this regulation and to ask that the board delay final adoption.”
During a July public hearing about the regulation, environmental organizations and energy think tanks such as the Chesapeake Climate Action Network and the Rocky Mountain Institute expressed frustration that Maryland’s version of the code for large commercial buildings allowed far more flexibility on energy efficiency measures than the International Energy Conservation Code, or IECC.
The IECC, for example, requires that newly constructed large buildings, including warehouses and apartment towers, generate a small amount of renewable energy on-site. But Maryland omitted that requirement, and also allowed builders to double-count certain energy efficiency measures.
Climate groups concerned by proposed Maryland building code

In a statement, Maryland Department of Labor spokesperson Dinah Winnick said that the agency is “taking this time to analyze all the comments received during the public comment period as well as consider the input received thus far from members of the General Assembly.”
“We welcome this opportunity to engage further with the AELR Committee and stakeholders on this important topic,” her statement said.
The hold was requested by committee member Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery), a leading voice on energy and environmental issues in the General Assembly.
“I respect her judgment,” said Del. Sandy Rosenberg (D-Baltimore City), a co-chair of the committee.
It isn’t just that the rules allow more flexibility to buildings, reducing their climate obligations compared to the national code, Charkoudian said. The rule may also flout state law.
“It appears to violate Maryland law, which requires that our building codes be at least consistent with, if not stronger than, the international standard,” Charkoudian said in an interview prior to the hold.
The AELR Committee consists of 10 delegates and 10 senators, and has the power to review regulations promulgated by state agencies in the Maryland Register, to ensure they match the intent of relevant laws passed by the General Assembly. the building code rules were published in the register on June 26, and a public comment period ended July 27.
If the committee doesn’t reach an agreement during the hold period, the agency can give notice that it plans to move forward with the regulations anyway. At that point, the hold can end on the 30th day after the agency gives notice or 105 days after the regulation was first published in the Register, whichever is later. But if the committee votes to oppose the regulation, it needs the governor’s OK before it can take effect.
