outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Price tag for Trump's D.C. deployment of National Guard: $1.4B more through 2029
text: WASHINGTON — The deployment of National Guard troops hailing from all across the country to Washington, D.C. is expected to cost taxpayers more than $1.4 billion in additional funds through 2029. The estimate from Jules Hurst III, President Donald Trump’s nominee to be the Pentagon’s comptroller, came in response to a series of questions from Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., as a part of Hurt’s confirmation process. “While American families are getting flattened by skyrocketing costs, Donald Trump is spending $1.4 billion to keep troops on the streets in Washington for years on end. The National Guard are not pawns and taxpayer dollars are not a piggy bank for Trump’s political stunts,” Warren wrote in a statement.According to the information provided by Hurst, the National Guard deployment is planned to continue until January 2029, the end of Trump’s second term. D.C. missionUnder Trump’s requested budget for the next fiscal year, his Make DC Safe and Beautiful mission — which has led renovation efforts of many of the city’s iconic landmarks and sought to reduce crime —  would receive $605 million in funding. That would include more $375 million for payroll expenses and travel allowances and nearly $230 million for operational expenses, such as housing and meals. Trump first deployed around 800 National Guard troops in Washington in August 2025, an effort to tackle what he called a “crime emergency” in the city. The move came after similar deployments in many Democratic-led cities across the country, including in Los Angeles and Chicago. He also sought to federalize and deploy troops in Portland, Oregon, but was later blocked in the federal courts. He threatened similar actions in locations including New York and Baltimore, often following with political battles with those states' Democratic leaders. National Guard deployments across the country cost nearly $500 million in 2025, according to the Congressional Budget Office.  In general, the office estimated, deploying 1,000 National Guard troops to a U.S. city costs between $18 million and $21 million each month. D.C. deployment grows The initial deployment in Washington has since grown, with thousands of troops from states all across the country now deployed in the nation’s capital.As of Aug. 1, there are more than 4,600 National Guard members deployed in Washington. About 680 of those guardsmen are from the District itself, while most are predominantly from the South. Georgia, South Carolina and Missisppi have sent the most guard members. But that total headcount has risen as many states and territories sent additional troops to help support events as part of the Trump-led Freedom250 celebration of the nation’s semiquincentennial in July. For some states, their National Guard members have been deployed quietly to the nation’s capital, including in Idaho, where the state made no formal announcement of the move. The Department of Defense’s budget estimates for fiscal years 2028 and 2029 assume a total headcount of approximately 2,500 National Guard personnel in Washington through January 2029. Future funding includes a planned $625.8 million for fiscal 2028 and $198.3 million for fiscal 2029.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s housing crisis isn’t one problem: it’s three
description:
Short-term rentals, an aging workforce and depopulation hit Vermont towns differently, and Montpelier lawmakers aren't tackling any of them head-on.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s housing crisis isn’t one problem: it’s three.
text:
This commentary is by Bryan Sell, who teaches in Vermont State University’s Resort and Hospitality Management program. 
Vermont’s housing debate is mostly treated as a problem of not enough units, with capitalist bogeymen feasting on the stock — outsiders hoarding homes, or investors gouging rents. These arguments resurrect Vermont’s old flatlander/woodchuck divide, sometimes said out loud in public forums. But look closer, and the conflict splits again: workers demanding reasonable rents versus investors seeking returns in some towns, blighted properties, affordability and absentee landlords in others. Three different fights, dressed up as one.
You’d be forgiven for thinking any one of these is the root cause, because in your town, it might be the only one. In the next town over, two entirely different causes may need to be addressed. In another town yet, there’s no cause for alarm at all.
The truth is that the housing crisis debate is complicated by three different causes that register differently between Vermont towns. Choosing a one-size-fits-all approach will never work.
The first is the short-term rental capturing existing housing stock: residential renters excluded for the sake of higher-paying vacationers. The second is an aging workforce that cannot meet the demand of a housing build-out. The third is a steady depopulation trend: birth rates dropping and Vermonters leaving the state.
Long-term rentals are converting to short-term rentals at alarming rates, but only in a narrow set of Vermont tourist towns — landlords see a bigger profit and take it. 
In ski towns like Killington, the conversion is nearly complete, evidenced by the highest home vacancy rate of any Vermont town with a real year-round population: 83.4% of its housing stock. The housing debate is framed around where the workers will live. The resort itself has addressed this by converting hotels into worker housing for its foreign J-1 and H-2B workforce. Ski resorts brought people back to places hollowed out during the farm-abandonment period of more than 100 years ago, helped by the state’s own funded campaign advertising those vacant properties to outsiders.
In Manchester, the conversion rate is far lower at 32.7%, but long-term residents worry about their cultural center being destroyed by seasonally vacant homes. And rightly so; Manchester has always sat in prime farm country and has never suffered the kind of population collapse that emptied towns like Killington.
Both towns show the second problem: an aging labor force. The state has about 15,000 workers who could build these homes, but many are expected to retire within the next few years. Neither town can build its way out of its housing problem with Vermont labor alone.
Some towns have very low vacancy rates — almost no second homes — and clearly show the third problem: depopulation, driven by low birth rates and Vermonters leaving the state. No amount of new housing changes that.
And yet state legislators are preparing housing bills for none of these problems. They generate tax revenue and increase supply, which is fine, but we shouldn’t pretend housing woes are being adequately addressed.
Montpelier occupies a unique spot in this debate, with the state’s tightest housing market. Housing is a real concern there. Just a handful of short-term rentals entering the mix could meaningfully raise rents and shrink availability.
Montpelier’s situation is oddly disconnected from what’s actually happening at the State House. Lawmakers have leaned on Act 181 and Act 69, both pieces of legislation aimed at supply. Neither touches worker-home conversion, and both ignore labor and demographics entirely. The one bill that would have addressed conversion directly, H.242, never advanced out of committee. It’s dead.
The real path forward is for towns to decide which of the three problems is their priority. If your town has a stable population, like East Montpelier or Westford, your primary problem is the aging workforce entering retirement. Who’s left to build affordable homes and who services them once built?
Maybe your town is like Montpelier or Randolph, where the market is tight, and vacancy is already low. Post-industrial towns like Barre City and Rutland City face depopulation and disinvestment directly — Vermonters leaving properties blighted. Short-term rentals aren’t the threat there, and tourism isn’t strong enough to be one.
Many tourist towns have already been fully captured by short-term rentals. But these towns have been seasonal with strong tourism for a very long time. Workers have certainly been displaced — but in Killington’s case, the resort answered by converting hotels into housing for a seasonal foreign workforce.
If you think this is too complicated, consider that some towns, such as Mendon, are geographically split: short-term rental pressure on one side, stable owner-occupied housing on the other, blighted properties in between. That calls for a zoning committee, not a town-wide ordinance.

READ MORE

None of this supports a scapegoat. Blaming outsiders won’t preserve your town’s cultural identity, and taxing one group over another won’t either. Likewise, retroactively restricting short-term rentals has already proven not to work elsewhere. Nor is the answer simply building more units. We don’t have the people to build them, and building housing in towns that have been depopulating for decades solves nothing.
The real solutions start with identifying the problem specific to your town, not reaching for one-size-fits-all fixes. Each town needs a sober look at tourism pressure, working-age structure, and demographics. We all need to appreciate that Vermont is more socioeconomically diverse than the proposed solutions assume.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s GOP primary for U.S. House pits 2 different personalities against each other
description:
Gerald Malloy and Mark Coester have run for Congress before, but this year they’re squaring off against each other in a bid to unseat U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s GOP primary for U.S. House pits 2 different personalities against each other.
text:
Gerald Malloy, left, and Mark Coester, Republican primary challengers for Vermont’s U.S. House of Representatives seat. Photos by Glenn Russell/VTDigger and VTDigger Editor

In the Republican primary this year for Vermont’s sole seat in the U.S. House, two candidates who have run for Congress before are on the ballot again. 
But other than the fact they’ve both sought federal office — and lost by large margins each time — Gerald Malloy and Mark Coester see differences in the approach they’d bring to the job, and even in their personalities.
“We’re miles apart in terms of, frankly, character and experience and platform,” Malloy said in a Vermont Public interview last month.
Malloy, who lives in Weathersfield, spent decades serving in the U.S. Army and more recently worked federal contract jobs in the defense industry, including with major firms such as Raytheon and Lockheed Martin. He moved to Vermont in 2020 and also owns property in Baltimore, Maryland, according to a federal financial disclosure report.
He’s made the case that his military service, which brought him around the world including to posts in the Middle East, positions him well to tackle some of the country’s biggest issues in Congress. His contracting work, he told Vermont Public, means he already has experience “supporting many, many, many government agencies.”
In 2022, Malloy ran what was his first campaign for office against then-U.S. Rep. Peter Welch, D-Vt., for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by former Sen. Patrick Leahy. He scored 28% of the vote to Welch’s 69%. Two years later, he challenged incumbent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., losing with 32% to Sanders’ 63%. 
Coester lives in Westminster and has operated small businesses in the logging, fishing and maple sugaring industries, among others, according to his campaign website. He has lived in the state for five decades, a video on his site says. He’s positioned himself as an anti-establishment candidate who can connect with working-class voters.
“Mark’s like you. He’s not some out-of-touch career politician,” the video states, urging voters to “send a logger to Congress.”
Coester ran against U.S. Rep. Becca Balint two years ago, scoring 30% of the vote to Balint’s 62%. Coester had both the Republican and Libertarian party nominations. 
Whoever wins this month’s GOP House primary will face Balint, who is seeking a third term in office, in the November general election. 
Both Malloy and Coester are critical of Balint’s record and her handling of the job, which they say focuses too much on criticizing the Trump administration rather than looking for ways to collaborate with it. But Coester has taken by far the more aggressive tack, sharing several videos to his social media feeds in recent weeks that appear to have been created with artificial intelligence and depict Balint in unflattering ways.
Coester was in the headlines earlier this year after one of those videos, which depicted him dropping Balint into a dumpster using an excavator, prompted the Vermont Attorney General’s Office to investigate the content creator who first shared it over concerns the video could have violated a new state law regulating AI-generated political media.

READ MORE

Coester did not make the video but told Seven Days he thought it was “hilarious” and posted it to his own feed. In that story, the newspaper quoted him calling a reporter who asked about his connection to the content creator, Hank Poitras, a “libtard fuck.”
Malloy has since seized on that comment, telling Vermont Public last month that it was an example of how Coester does not have the right temperament for public office. 
“I’ve known Mark for several years now. I’ve seen how he operates. He’s got a kind of a self-control issue,” Malloy said.
Coester did not respond to a request for comment for this story. In an interview published Monday that was conducted by Poitras, who goes by the moniker Planet Hank, Coester framed himself as someone who is open to hearing anyone’s perspective.
“I promise to be honest with people and listen to them,” he told Poitras. “If they want to be a jerk, fine. Maybe I won’t talk to them next time. But I’m willing to listen to anybody that wants civil discourse.”
Malloy’s campaign did not make him available for an interview ahead of this story’s publication. In past remarks, he has said he’d focus on advancing the same policy goals in Congress that Republican Gov. Phil Scott supports at the state level, including making Vermont more affordable and reducing regulatory barriers to new development. 
He told Vermont Public he is “completely on board with the governor’s vision”. He pointed as an example to the executive order Scott signed last month that included a slate of measures to decrease health insurance regulations in an effort to lower costs, including implementing age-based insurance premiums. He said that, broadly, the governor’s beliefs on reducing regulations need stronger support in Congress.
Malloy has also been tempered, on the campaign trail, in his support for President Trump.
He said he supports the U.S. and Israel’s war in Iran but does not think Trump did a good enough job justifying the need for that military intervention to the public. He thinks Trump “should just leave Canada alone,” he told Vermont Public, and “I don’t like him getting into a tiff with the Pope.” 
Malloy also said he does not think it’s in the country’s best interest “to try to track down every possible single person in the U.S. that might not be fully documented,” describing it as a poor use of resources.
Coester said his top priority once elected would be “to listen to Vermonters” as opposed to lobbyists and campaign donors. He gave Poitras an example of getting approached by a lobbyist “for Israel and Turkey and Iran,” but said that he would tell them, “Excuse me, sir, I’ve got to take a phone call from somebody back home.”
He also said the state is not affordable for many working-class people and thinks part of the reason why is that rampant use of illegal drugs has driven away people who would otherwise stay and contribute to the economy. His campaign has also focused on ending human trafficking, an issue he told WCAX does not get enough attention. 
“We’ve got serious problems in Vermont. Affordability, there’s no question about it,” he told Poitras. “Like, everybody’s broke.”
In addition to his 2024 bid for Congress, Coester ran in 2022 for one of two seats in the Vermont Senate representing Windham County. He won that year’s Republican primary but in the general election finished a distant sixth. 
Ahead of the 2022 election, Coester faced criticism from some over a float he used in a parade in Colchester that included a depiction of a symbol associated with the Spanish authoritarian dictator Francisco Franco as well as a drawing of “Pepe the Frog,” a cartoon character often linked to various far-right and white nationalist groups.
With just weeks to go until election day, Malloy has raised more money for his campaign than Coester, according to flings with the Federal Election Commission. Malloy has brought in $58,280, while Coester has raised $36,039, filings show.
Notably, just shy of 60% of Coester’s fundraising — $20,897 — has come from his own pockets. In comparison, about 9% of Malloy’s fundraising is from himself. 
Malloy’s campaign has been drawing more momentum with voters, too, according to a poll released last month. The University of New Hampshire survey found that among likely GOP primary voters, 58% would vote for Malloy but just 6% would vote for Coester, while another 32% were undecided. 
Vermont’s primary election is on Aug. 11.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s GOP primary for U.S. House pits 2 different personalities against each other.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas mother and son file suit accusing police department of illegal detention
description: Two Benton County residents who are U.S. citizens are suing Centerton police for detaining them at the request of federal immigration officers even though they showed valid identification.  In a federal lawsuit filed last week, Maria Guadalupe Rodriguez and her adult son, Jose Ricardo Munoz, argue three Centerton police officers violated their constitutional[...]
text:
(Getty Images)Two Benton County residents who are U.S. citizens are suing Centerton police for detaining them at the request of federal immigration officers even though they showed valid identification. 
In a federal lawsuit filed last week, Maria Guadalupe Rodriguez and her adult son, Jose Ricardo Munoz, argue three Centerton police officers violated their constitutional rights during a traffic stop in March 2025. The Fourth Amendment of the Constitution protects people against unreasonable searches and seizures. 
Rodriguez is the legal guardian of Munoz, who is incapacitated, the complaint said. 
Chief of Police Cody Harper did not immediately return a request for comment Wednesday. Harper is a defendant in the case along with officers William McCain, Larry McConnell and Joan Mosquera.
According to the complaint, McCain stopped Rodriguez for a minor traffic violation. She denies committing any traffic violations that supported the initial stop. 
McCain determined Rodriguez was driving on a valid Arkansas driver’s license after running her personal information through the Arkansas Criminal Information Center. Munoz produced a valid Arkansas identification card and McCain confirmed he was not wanted for any criminal violations. 
All three officers searched, handcuffed and arrested Rodriguez and her son for suspicion of being in the United States without proper documents or authorization, according to the complaint. They were taken to the Centerton Police Department where it was determined they were U.S. citizens and they were released without any traffic or criminal charges.
McCain’s police report indicates the arrest was made at the behest of federal Immigration Customs and Enforcement agents. It appears they were attempting to serve an “Immigration Administrative Arrest Warrant” on Rodriguez, but they took the wrong person into custody, according to the complaint. 
“Even if Centerton police officers had found and detained the correct person in Ms. Rodriguez, they had zero authority to violate the rights of Mr. Munoz, who was an innocent passenger in a car,” the complaint said. “In America, guilt by association is not a crime and will not support a reasonable suspicion or probable cause for a detention, search, or arrest.”
Traffic stops and the detention of U.S. citizens have become a flashpoint during the Trump administration’s national crackdown on immigration. 
Federal immigration officers have shot 22 people and killed six, including three U.S. citizens, since January 2025. Most shootings have stemmed from traffic stops. 
In Arkansas, ICE interactions can originate from traffic stops, in part due to a 2025 state law that requires Division of Correction and county sheriffs to participate in the model of the federal 287(g) program that permits local law enforcement to serve administrative warrants on immigrants in their custody. 
The federal program, which has three models, allows state and local law enforcement to perform specific immigration duties. Forty-four Arkansas municipalities have opted into the 287(g) program. Centerton is not one of them, according to ICE’s website.
The complaint also argues Centerton’s policy concerning the impoundment, towing and inventory searches of vehicles violates the Fourth Amendment because it allows for the seizure of a vehicle even when the detention and arrest of the suspect lacks sufficient reasonable suspicion or probable cause that they’ve committed a criminal offense. 
During Rodriguez’ traffic stop, police prevented her adult daughter, a U.S. citizen with a valid Arkansas driver’s license, from taking the car, and the impoundment cost around $300, according to the complaint. 
Rodriguez and her son are seeking monetary damages for violating their rights and a jury trial on all issues.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bottoms, Jackson offer competing visions on data centers, Medicaid expansion at business luncheon
description: ATHENS, Ga. – Data centers and Medicaid expansion were on the menu as Georgia’s candidates for governor made their pitches to the state’s business leaders Wednesday at an annual luncheon hosted by the Georgia Chamber of Commerce. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson took the stage at an Athens event center to pitch […]
text:
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderATHENS, Ga. – Data centers and Medicaid expansion were on the menu as Georgia’s candidates for governor made their pitches to the state’s business leaders Wednesday at an annual luncheon hosted by the Georgia Chamber of Commerce.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson took the stage at an Athens event center to pitch their policies to a crowd of over 1,000 members of the state’s business community.
“Small businesses in this state are seeing the same impacts from high inflation rates, affordability issues — they’re seeing that too, and so they want to hear what these two candidates have to offer,” Georgia Chamber President and CEO Chris Clark said after the luncheon.
“They also want to know that we’re going to have a chief executive that’s going to continue to help grow the state, grow the state’s economy in a quality way for jobs, not just in Atlanta or not just in Macon or Savannah, but in our most rural communities too,” he added.
Data centers
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lane Bottoms at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Georgia has seen its share of large data center proposals, and opposition to the energy-hungry server houses has echoed in city halls up and down the state.
The 2026 legislative session saw a number of bills with bipartisan support aimed at reining in new data center proposals, but none made it to the governor’s desk before the session ended.
Bottoms, who previously served as Atlanta mayor, said if elected governor, she will support a temporary pause on data center construction.
“I just want us to pause,” she told reporters. “I want us to gather all the information, factual information, and then make a determination on how we move forward. I can tell you when I’m moving around the state, a lot of people are concerned about the environmental impact. They’re also concerned about the rising cost of utility bills.”
But Bottoms indicated she would not support a permanent halt of the projects.
“I’ve also talked with some leaders, especially in our rural communities, who are saying that having data centers there helps them balance their budget,” she added. “So I am respectful of everyone’s thoughts on it, but at the end of the day, we’ve got to separate fact from fiction, and we don’t have enough facts on data centers to make an informed decision on how we move forward. We need a pause.”
Gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Jackson, who is invested in a data center in Texas, was more supportive of the technology hubs, arguing that they could make economic sense in more remote parts of the state.
“First of all, every community needs to have control of whether they have a data center or not, full stop,” Jackson said.
Jackson said data center projects could eliminate property taxes in some Georgia counties.
“No property taxes for the data center, or don’t have one. It’s totally up to them,” Jackson told reporters. “As a business person, I just want to give them that option so that they know both sides of the street.”
Medicaid expansion 
Gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and Gov. Brian Kemp at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Bottoms said if elected, she plans to eliminate Georgia Pathways, the state’s partial Medicaid expansion program created under Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. She said she would instead fully expand Medicaid.
Georgia is one of 10 states that have not fully expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act.
“There’s not a single community that you go into in this state that hasn’t been touched by our refusal to expand Medicaid, from hospitals in the metro area to hospitals in our rural communities,” she said. “And it weakens our entire healthcare system when we don’t expand Medicaid. And the irony of it is we are paying into a system that’s helping fund healthcare in states throughout the United States. We just haven’t done it in Georgia.”
Bottoms said she is optimistic that Democrats will flip the state House this year, but she said she thinks she can convince Republicans to support Medicaid expansion even if they continue to control the Legislature.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lane Bottoms at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“This is one of these issues that I believe can get bipartisan support,” she said. “It’s had bipartisan support before, but people have made it difficult for those across the aisle who want to support Medicaid expansion to get it done without money being put in races to run against them.”
But Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive, is not behind traditional Medicaid expansion.
“I understand how Medicaid works from a healthcare standpoint, and I do believe in an intelligent Medicaid expansion,” Jackson said.
Jackson said that will involve emphasizing work requirements and instituting fixed federal block grants rather than open-ended matching funds.
“I want to be able to give the opportunity to every Medicaid recipient to be able to be trained and at least get a job and get off of Medicaid,” he said. “I’m not going to measure our state by how many people are on Medicaid. I want to measure how many people are on commercial insurance, and the way to do that is reduce the cost of commercial insurance, and that’s what I want to do.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Todd Blanche still thinks he’s Trump’s lawyer, which means he can’t be our lawyer
description: Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general and nominee to be attorney general of the United States, slipped up during his Senate confirmation hearings when asked about his relationship with President Donald Trump.   “I’m his lawyer. Was his lawyer.” Oopsies. The attorney general is the lawyer for the United States government — we the people — and his […]
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the media as he arrives with his attorney Todd Blanche, right, in court for opening statements in his trial for allegedly covering up hush money payments at Manhattan Criminal Court on April 22, 2024, in New York City. Trump was convicted of falsifying business records in the first of his criminal cases to go to trial. Since his election, he's nominated Blanche to be attorney general of the United States. (Photo by Yuki Iwamura-Pool/Getty Images)Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general and nominee to be attorney general of the United States, slipped up during his Senate confirmation hearings when asked about his relationship with President Donald Trump.  
“I’m his lawyer. Was his lawyer.”
Oopsies. The attorney general is the lawyer for the United States government — we the people — and his obligation is to the law and the U.S. Constitution, not his former client’s lawless whims.    
We’ve become all too aware of his misplaced priorities and allegiances in Minnesota. More on that in a bit, but let us remember — so much has happened! — Blanche was Trump’s criminal lawyer when the then-ex-president was charged and convicted in the porn star payoff coverup; charged in the attempt to overturn the 2020 election; and charged with stealing classified documents and storing them in a Mar-a-Lago bathroom and other unsecured locations. 
Everyone deserves a criminal defense, but the American people deserve better than Blanche.
Last month, a federal judge in Florida released a scathing order — and referred Blanche to the New York State Bar Association for potential discipline — over the Trump slush fund episode, during which Blanche “negotiated” a deal between Trump, i.e., his boss, and the government, i.e., his client. 
“The Court determines that Plaintiffs improperly employed this lawsuit to justify a particular award in this matter — access to taxpayer funds and exemption from audits and other investigations — which was accomplished by leveraging control over Defendants,” she wrote.
In other words: A sleazy deal. 
In addition to money for cop-beating Jan. 6 insurrectionists, the deal would provide the president with immunity from the IRS. 
Great lawyering for Trump — but less so for us. 
Let’s turn closer to home, because Minnesota has much at stake in the next leader of the Department of Justice. 
Blanche has been attorney general and deputy attorney general as the Department of Justice has failed to bring charges against any of the men responsible for the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, and the shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis. 
Until last month, DOJ was sitting on evidence in the cases, forcing Minnesota to sue the feds in a shocking departure from the tradition of collaboration on important investigations.
“Without a public commitment by federal authorities to cooperate with the state, it is difficult – if not, impossible – to pursue justice that holds the individuals accountable for Alex’s death,” the Pretti family attorney Steve Schleicher said in a statement.
But at least the DOJ was chasing the, uh, real criminals, like Minnesota elected officials, including Gov. Tim Walz, Attorney General Keith Ellison and Mayor Jacob Frey, whose offices were sent wide-ranging subpoenas in an apparent criminal inquiry, which was promptly leaked by the feds in an obvious effort to strongarm the people we elected. 
A federal judge — appointed by President George W. Bush — quashed the subpoenas, with gusto: “Initiating a criminal investigation in order to harass political opponents or to coerce them into taking official action — particularly official action that the federal government cannot directly require those political opponents to take — is a blatantly unlawful and unethical use of the grand-jury process,” wrote Judge Patrick Schiltz. 
The DOJ has pursued a bevy of similarly fantastical investigations that have illustrated Blanche’s total lack of independence from his former client — and drawn the mockery they deserve: a sandwich thrower, an Olympian pool vandal, the former head of the FBI and – in Minnesota – journalists covering a protest, Renee Good’s wife, and 15 anti-ICE activists not accused of violence beyond kicking a car and knocking an agent’s notes out of his hand. 
In that instance, Schiltz, the same Bush-appointed judge, said he “inferred not every bit of evidence was necessarily gathered pursuant to a warrant.”
This sounds like Blanche’s people cut corners and violated the rights of American citizens. 
Partly in response, the once-esteemed Office of U.S. Attorney in Minnesota has emptied out, as prosecutors have left in disgust at the corrupt direction set by Blanche. 
The DOJ’s open hostility toward Minnesota extends to our institutions, as well. The feds have sued Minnesota and other states for refusing to hand over unredacted voter rolls, which would be a violation of our own state law guarding the privacy of voters.
As ProPublica reported recently, federal judges across the country have called Trump’s Justice Department at various times “unlawful,” “unethical,” “unseemly” or otherwise dishonest. The article quotes a former federal judge, another Bush appointee: “I don’t think in the annals of the Department of Justice, in the history of jurisprudence in the United States, we’ve ever seen anything close to this.”
I suppose it’s fitting that in this administration, this common reprobate is up for a promotion.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawrence faults Barrett over Medicaid cuts, renews Medicare for All push
description: Just over 12 hours after declaring victory in the Democratic primary, political organizer William Lawrence was back on the campaign trail, gathering outside of the University of Michigan Health – Sparrow Hospital in Lansing with healthcare providers and residents slated to feel the impact from changes to Medicaid through the federal One Big Beautiful Bill […[...]
text:
Political organizer and Democratic congressional candidate gathered with supporters outside University of Michigan Health - Sparrow Hospital, criticizing Republicans for cuts to Medicaid through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Aug. 5, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceJust over 12 hours after declaring victory in the Democratic primary, political organizer William Lawrence was back on the campaign trail, gathering outside of the University of Michigan Health – Sparrow Hospital in Lansing with healthcare providers and residents slated to feel the impact from changes to Medicaid through the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, individuals enrolled in Medicaid, which provides health coverage to people with limited income, will be required to provide proof of 80 hours per month of employment, community service, work program participation or at least half-time enrollment in education in order to receive benefits. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also requires Medicaid recipients to redetermine their eligibility every six months, rather than once a year.
The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimates that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, sponsored by congressional Republicans and signed by President Donald Trump in 2025, will increase the number of uninsured individuals in the U.S. by 10 million by 2034, with coverage losses from the work requirements accounting for 5.3 million of those losses.
The health professionals joining Lawrence at his Wednesday press conference warned that these restrictions would limit access for individuals who would otherwise be unable to obtain healthcare. 
Without this access Ashley Myers, a registered nurse who lives in Clinton County, warned that individuals would forgo care from their primary health provider, leading to increased visits to hospitals’ emergency departments, increasing costs on all patients, not just Medicaid recipients. 
Ashley Meyers, a registered nurse and supporter of Democratic congressional candidate Will Lawrence, speaks out against cuts to Medicaid through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Aug. 5, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Under the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, hospitals must provide emergency care to anyone, regardless of their ability to pay. However, increased instances of uninsured care lead to increased costs for hospitals and higher insurance premiums.
“Just over a year ago, in July of 2025, I watched along with everybody here as Tom Barrett and the Republican Party took an ax to our health care system, kicked millions of people off of their coverage, and raised prices for tens of millions more,” Lawrence said. “Then I saw the fear and the stress in the eyes of the people I began to meet on the campaign trail, wondering when the next shoe was going to drop and when their coverage was going to cut out, and what would happen to them and their families then.”
Lawrence, who is trying to unseat Congressman Barrett in November, noted his support for Medicare for All to address these concerns. 
“Every other wealthy nation on this planet guarantees health care to every man, woman, and child.” Lawrence said. “In the richest country in the world, here in the United States, there is no reason why we should have health insurance CEOs making millions, in some cases billions of dollars, while ordinary people are going into medical debt just to stay alive and care for their families.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
However, Barrett criticized Lawrence’s approach in a statement, arguing it would only serve to drive up health costs, pointing to his own legislative proposals to improve health access.
“In Congress, I have fought the big insurance companies who are putting profits and executive bonuses over their patients,” Barrett said, noting that he had also introduced legislation to improve drug price transparency and a bill to codify President Donald Trump’s executive order requiring pharmaceutical companies to sell drugs in the U.S. at prices comparable to those in other countries.
Lawrence countered that the One Big Beautiful Bill and Republicans’ decision not to renew tax credits on Affordable Care Act premiums have already increased health costs. 
According to KFF, premium payments for those with insurance through the Affordable Care Act Marketplace have increased by an average of 58% per month, with the average deductible increasing by 37%. 
“Barrett has no ground to speak about the interests of the district when it comes to health care policy because all people have seen is their bills increase and their health care become less secure under his term in office,” Lawrence said.

description: Grinnell College will use grant funding to connect its areas of arts education with emerging technologies through new campus space, programming and more. text:
Grinnell College received a $600,000 to create a new arts space on campus and support faculty development of curriculum and student opportunities. (Photo courtesy of Grinnell College)Grinnell College will use grant funding to connect its areas of arts education with emerging technologies through new campus space, programming and more.
The Grinnell private college announced in a news release it received $600,000 from the Sherman Fairchild Foundation to implement a four-year initiative that will involve the creation of an “intermedia space” as well as courses, faculty development and collaboration opportunities and student experiences to help them thrive in an artistic world increasingly influenced by technology.
“The liberal arts encourage students to ask bold questions, explore new ideas, and dynamically connect knowledge across disciplines,” Grinnell College President Anne Harris said in the release. “This generous support from the Sherman Fairchild Foundation allows us to build on those strengths by creating new opportunities for students and faculty to experiment and collaborate at the intersection of technology and the arts. We’re grateful for the Foundation’s investment in Grinnell’s students and in the future of creative learning.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The new space will support teaching and experimentation with technology alongside events and project installations, according to the release. Artists will visit Grinnell through the initiative as well, and students will have travel opportunities to experience art being created off campus.
Grant funding will also support faculty work and collaboration in redesigning existing courses and developing new interdisciplinary programs, the release stated, and will help faculty in their own technology training. Students and faculty, as well as artists and academics, will showcase the work made through the grant in “two public symposia,” the release stated.
Professor Craig Quintero, who will oversee the initiative in its first year, said in the release the college will hold an informational session in September to “provide details about the funding parameters” while getting community feedback on how art and technology at the college should work together.
Grinnell faculty are already looking into innovations in areas like digital music, virtual reality and more, Quintero said in the release, and funding from the grant will allow them to both deepen and expand their research.
“The grant is an amazing acknowledgement of the innovative work already being created in the arts at the College, while also providing funding to enable faculty to explore new digital mediums and add more technology-based projects to the curriculum,” Quintero said in the release.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Stitt selects Lindel Fields to serve as Cabinet secretary
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Rather than choosing a new education secretary for the final five months of his term, Gov. Kevin Stitt announced Wednesday he tapped Oklahoma’s state superintendent to serve as his top adviser on school policy. Lindel Fields will hold both positions, Stitt said, following Education Secretary Dan Hamlin’s recent departure. Oklahoma’s next gove[...]
text:
Gov. Kevin Stitt, right, stands with state Superintendent Lindel Fields during an Oklahoma State Board of Education meeting May 21 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Rather than choosing a new education secretary for the final five months of his term, Gov. Kevin Stitt announced Wednesday he tapped Oklahoma’s state superintendent to serve as his top adviser on school policy.
Lindel Fields will hold both positions, Stitt said, following Education Secretary Dan Hamlin’s recent departure. Oklahoma’s next governor, who would choose his or her own Cabinet officials, will take office in January, as will the next elected state superintendent.
Stitt will reach his term limit of eight years in office after 2026. Fields is not running in this year’s elections to stay in office.
“Lindel has already shown strong, steady leadership, and I am confident he will continue serving Oklahoma students and families with focus and integrity in this expanded role,” Stitt said in a statement.
The governor appointed Fields in October to the state superintendent post, which leads the Oklahoma State Department of Education and the state Board of Education. The appointment became necessary after former state Superintendent Ryan Walters resigned from office with more than a year left in his term.
Walters briefly held both positions of education secretary and state superintendent in 2023. He stepped down from the governor’s Cabinet after Attorney General Gentner Drummond wrote a letter objecting to the arrangement.
Serving in both positions violated laws against dual office holding, Drummond wrote at the time. The attorney general later issued a formal opinion that state agency heads cannot also sit on the governor’s Cabinet, which impacted several of Stitt’s secretaries’ ability to serve.
The Oklahoma Supreme Court struck down Drummond’s opinion, siding with members of Stitt’s Cabinet who sued the Attorney General’s Office.
The opinion reflected the office’s “good-faith reading of the law at the time, but the Court has now resolved the matter, and that resolution governs going forward,” spokesperson Carrie Burkhart said Wednesday.
Stitt’s most recent education secretary, Hamlin, who wasn’t involved in the lawsuit, departed in June after accepting a position at the University of Texas.
Fields said he is “humbled and honored” to be selected for both positions.
“My goal is simple: finish strong, build momentum, and leave Oklahoma’s education system stronger than I found it,” he said in a statement.

title: Board suspends administrator’s license, for undisclosed reasons, to ‘protect the public’
description: State regulators have suspended, without explanation, a nursing home administrator’s license to practice in Iowa. The Iowa Board of Nursing Home Administrators says that in April 2025, it received a complaint against the licensee Marcy Louise Martin, 51, concerning the “management of facility funds and documentation.” The board says the allegations, which it[...]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing administers and oversees many of Iowa's state licensing boards. (Photo courtesy of Getty Images; logo courtesy the State of Iowa)State regulators have suspended, without explanation, a nursing home administrator’s license to practice in Iowa.
The Iowa Board of Nursing Home Administrators says that in April 2025, it received a complaint against the licensee Marcy Louise Martin, 51, concerning the “management of facility funds and documentation.”
The board says the allegations, which it did not disclose, “remain disputed and unadjudicated,” and says no final findings of fact or conclusions of law have been reached. Martin, the board says, admits no wrongdoing.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
However, the board says, in order to “meet the board’s interest in protecting the public” Martin and the board have agreed that Martin shall not practice as a nursing home administrator or engage in any conduct that requires a license to practice as a nursing home administrator in Iowa.
As a result, the board says, the status of Martin’s license is being changed to “suspended.”
The action is being taken without any formal statement of charges being filed against Martin, and without her agreeing to surrender her license. It’s an unusual move for a state licensing board, which typically files formal charges against a licensee, which are then made public, before any sanctions such as a license suspension are imposed.
Stat records indicate Martin was first licensed by the board in May 2017, and that she has worked as a nursing home administrator at the Sunrise Hill Care Center in Traer.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Martin for comment. Board records indicate she now lives in Stewartville, Minnesota.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Legal battle over Jewish charter school begins in Oklahoma City federal court
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A second attempt to open the nation’s first publicly funded religious charter school landed in an Oklahoma courtroom on Wednesday in what could be another step toward returning the issue to the U.S. Supreme Court. At issue Wednesday was whether the Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board acted constitutionally when it twice denied […]
text:
Daniel Chen, counsel for the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, speaks to news reporters after a hearing Wednesday in Oklahoma City federal court on Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School, which he represents. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A second attempt to open the nation’s first publicly funded religious charter school landed in an Oklahoma courtroom on Wednesday in what could be another step toward returning the issue to the U.S. Supreme Court.
At issue Wednesday was whether the Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board acted constitutionally when it twice denied Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School’s request to open and operate using taxpayer funds.
Board members said a 2024 Oklahoma Supreme Court decision rejecting a similar request from a Catholic charter school prevented them from approving the religious school, which intends to provide a state-funded education that includes the teachings of the Jewish faith.
The school’s founders sued the board in Oklahoma City federal court over the denial. Their attorneys told a federal judge on Wednesday that the Oklahoma Supreme Court decision violated the free exercise the school’s religion. But Oklahoma families and taxpayers, who intervened in the case, argued that charter schools are an arm of the government and therefore must be nonsectarian.
Federal District Judge David L. Russell will decide in the coming weeks or months whether to grant the school’s request for a preliminary injunction, which would allow the school to establish a charter contract with the state and proceed toward opening.
Attorneys on multiple sides of the case agreed Russell’s decision is a likely starting point for appeals that could ultimately land the issue before the nation’s highest court again.
Members of the Statewide Charter School Board attend a meeting March 9 at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments on the Oklahoma Catholic charter school case last year with Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused. The remaining justices split 4-4 on the case, which allowed the Oklahoma Supreme Court ruling to stand.
“The case that’s before your honor today seems to be aimed squarely at returning to the (U.S.) Supreme Court,” said Alex Luchenitser, an attorney representing some of the Oklahomans opposing the school, during Wednesday’s hearing.
Russell’s decision on the preliminary injunction could be appealed to the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals. 
The appeals process will continue “probably all the way up until we break the 4-4 tie at the Supreme Court,” said Hiram Sasser, an attorney representing the Statewide Charter School Board, after the hearing.
Attorneys for the state board argued Wednesday in support of the Jewish school. They said the Oklahoma Supreme Court’s decision forced the board to commit “religious exclusion” and deny the school’s application to open.
The school’s founders, led by former Florida U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, applied to the board for approval to establish an online charter school in Oklahoma for students in grades K-12. The board voted to reject the school in February and March, citing its religious component both times.
Deutsch also founded a network of non-religious Hebrew-English charter schools in Florida that share the name Ben Gamla.
“My clients have looked at the Oklahoma charter school program and believe that it is really an excellent program and would offer the benefits for the type of education that they want to offer,” said Daniel Chen, an attorney representing Deutsch and the school, after the hearing.
Ben Gamla Charter Schools founder and former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch speaks to the Statewide Charter School Board on Jan. 12 in Oklahoma City to present an application to open an online Jewish charter school in Oklahoma. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
In the courtroom, Chen contended his clients’ constitutional rights were violated when they were denied the chance to access state charter school funding solely because of the school’s religious character. 
Although charter schools have long been considered public, he said they’re actually privately operated entities contracting with the state to provide educational services to families who freely choose to enroll. Other private schools or private entities are allowed to benefit from public programs without having to give up their religious objectives, he and other attorneys said.
But a group of mostly Jewish Oklahomans, who oppose the school, and their attorneys contended that charter schools are state actors because they are deeply “entwined” with government control and carry out an exclusively governmental function of free, public education.
Russell, the federal judge, acknowledged the public or private nature of a charter school is a core issue to the case.
“Right now, Ben Gamla is private,” the judge said during the hearing. “The question is whether it will become public by becoming a charter school.”
Multiple Jewish organizations and synagogues in Oklahoma have raised concerns that Ben Gamla’s founders failed to meaningfully consult the local Jewish community before attempting to open the school. 
Had they done so, they “would have been made aware that Oklahoma is already home to many Jewish educational opportunities,” the local groups said in a January joint statement.

title: Indiana Medicaid ‘back in black’
description: The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration returned $310 million to the state’s general fund this year, a dramatic turnaround for an agency once staring down a $1 billion deficit for Medicaid. FSSA Secretary Mitch Roob credited the reversal to a series of reforms the agency enacted during his tenure: regular financial reviews, must-return mailers,[...]
text:
Indiana Family & Social Services Administration Secretary Mitch Roob pictured in an AC/DC-inspired hat commemorating the agency's budget turnaround. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration returned $310 million to the state’s general fund this year, a dramatic turnaround for an agency once staring down a $1 billion deficit for Medicaid.
FSSA Secretary Mitch Roob credited the reversal to a series of reforms the agency enacted during his tenure: regular financial reviews, must-return mailers, stricter oversight of Applied Behavioral Analysis therapy and urging senior Medicaid members to enter into dual enrollment with Medicare — without any changes to eligibility.
Roob offered his outlook on Medicaid Wednesday during FSSA’s quarterly financial review to close out fiscal year 2026.
While he channeled optimism — entering the Indiana Government Center auditorium to the sound of AC/DC’s “Back in Black”— Roob warned the reversal does not mean the state has fixed its “unsustainable” Medicaid cost trajectory.
“Medicaid is a fiscal chronic illness,” he said, “and like a chronic illness, oversight of the Medicaid budget requires constant management, not a one-time cure. We are no longer drowning in death. Our head is above water. The question is: Can we keep it there?”
Coverage shifts to sickest Hoosiers
FSSA reported a 23% decline in Medicaid enrollment since Gov. Mike Braun took office last January, but overall expenditures fell by just 2%.


Childcare update
Indiana’s waitlist for child care vouchers is down to 29,814, according to an update from Adam Alson, director of the Office of Early Childhood and Out-of-School Learning for FSSA Wednesday morning.
The agency invited 9,000 low-income Hoosier families with young children to apply for the vouchers this summer after Braun asked the State Budget Committee to divert $200 million from the general fund to another account.
The waitlist had grown to nearly 35,400 as of February.


The Indiana Capital Chronicle this week found procedural closures exceeded determinations that benefit recipients were no longer eligible for coverage, with thousands of Hoosiers eventually returning to Medicaid.
The average cost per member is rising as coverage shifts to the sickest Hoosiers, with the greatest enrollment declines recorded in lower-cost programs like the Healthy Indiana Plan, otherwise known as the Medicaid expansion population.
On Wednesday, Roob referenced a report from Paragon Health Institute finding Indiana ranked third in the nation for improper Medicaid expansion enrollments.
FSSA spent an average of $513 per member each month for HIP members who exited the program in 2025 — far below the $885 average monthly cost per HIP member who maintained their coverage and the $710 monthly cost for new entrants, according to data released Wednesday.
“We had every expectation that this would happen,” Roob said, though he said historically, costs associated with new entrants declined as members started maintenance medications.
‘Unsustainable’ growth
State and federal spending on HIP grew from $2.9 billion in 2017 to an estimated $6.4 billion in fiscal year 2027, according to FSSA projections.
Costs are climbing for other Medicaid programs too.
The state and federal government spent $3.1 billion on Hoosier Care Connect and Hoosier HealthWise, the Medicaid programs for pregnant women, children and disabled adults, in 2017. Those costs are projected to rise to $4.3 billion, despite a decline in enrollment.
Meanwhile, the annual cost for Medicaid waivers and PathWays for Aging, which covers long-term and in-home care for older Hoosiers, is projected to rise from $4.2 billion to $10.9 billion in fiscal year 2027.
Screenshot courtesy of the Indiana Family & Social Services Administration
Roob set a target of 2% growth to stabilize Medicaid spending to mirror General Fund growth.
“Every dollar we give to a hospital is a dollar we don’t give to a school,” he said.
FSSA saved the state $24 million by moving nearly 3,200 Medicare-eligible Medicaid members to dual-enrollment status. The agency intends to urge more senior members to do the same to further mitigate costs.
The agency is also working with the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid and tech company Oracle to use artificial intelligence software to analyze Medicaid claims for suspect billing patterns, and will soon roll out work requirements for HIP members.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

text:
Rows of carts await shoppers at an Oklahoma business on Sunday, March 16, 2025. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Bargain hunters are expected to hit the stores this weekend to take advantage of Oklahoma’s sales tax holiday.
The three-day annual event, during which clothing and footwear priced less than $100  are exempted from state and local sales taxes, starts at 12:01 a.m. Friday and ends at midnight Sunday.
Last year, the state reimbursed cities slightly more than $3.7 million for lost sales tax revenue. The state also reimbursed counties $628,403, said Emily Haxton, Oklahoma Tax Commission spokesperson.
Accessories, such as purses, jewelry, special clothing or footwear used for athletic events and school supplies are not subject to the sales tax holiday.
While many parents will be flocking to malls and other outlets to take advantage of the savings, Sen. Carri Hicks, D-Oklahoma City, will sit it out.
“It’s too much for me personally,” said Hicks, the mother of three children who range in age from 8 to 12. 
While the event poses a “huge opportunity for families,” it is not worth fighting the crowds with three kids, she said. 
Retail outlets aren’t the only ones that benefit from the event.
“As shoppers head out to prepare for the new school year, many also stop to dine at local restaurants,” said James Leewright, president and CEO of the Oklahoma Restaurant  Association. “That added traffic provides a welcome boost for restaurants and their employees while keeping more dollars circulating in Oklahoma communities.”
The state sales tax is 4.5%, according to the Sales Tax Handbook. Local sales taxes vary. The combined state and average local sales tax rate is 9.06%, according to the Tax Foundation, which ranked Oklahoma sixth in the nation for the highest combined state and average local sales tax rate.
Diane Yetter, president and founder of the Sales Tax Institute, said states offer a variety of sales tax holidays. 
Some include clothing while others include energy efficient appliances and items used in bad weather, such as generators.
Oklahoma has held its sales tax holiday since 2007.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. House Democrats introduce measure to bar corporations from political contributions
description: A new legislative proposal would bar corporations from contributing to political campaigns in Pennsylvania.
text:
Reps. Paul Friel (D-Chester), Joe Webster (D-Montgomery), and Tarik Khan (D-Philadelphia) introduced legislation that would bar corporations from political contributions at a press conference on Aug. 5, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star.
A new legislative proposal would bar corporations from contributing to political campaigns in Pennsylvania as Democratic state lawmakers work to enact campaign finance reforms. 
The measure would rewrite the state’s corporate charter to ensure corporations do not have “any power to directly or indirectly engage in election activity or ballot question activity.” Under the proposal, any corporation that does engage in election activity would be stripped of its charter and business privileges. It would also face civil action from the state Attorney General. 
Rep. Joe Webster (D-Montgomery), the legislation’s primary sponsor, said the measure  is a response to a spike in corporate spending after the 2010 Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission Supreme Court decision. That ruling struck down existing campaign finance restrictions and allowed corporations to pour unlimited funds and resources into political efforts. 
“In 2024, all by itself, one year, federal elections saw over $4 billion in outside spending, and that’s nearly 12 times the number prior to Citizens United,” he said at a press conference Wednesday. “The power of that money diminishes the power of the Pennsylvania voter.”  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Reps. Tarik Khan (D-Philadelphia), Paul Friel (D-Chester), and Ben Waxman (D-Philadelphia) are co-sponsoring the bill, which has been referred to the House State Government Committee. 
“I’m not a lawyer … But I know that corporations should not be racing to buy politicians,” Khan said. “We need common sense. We need to protect our politics. We need to protect our institutions. We need to make sure that corporations are not in a race to buy politicians to prevent action on issues that are important to the public.”
In May, Hawaii became the first state to sign a bill barring corporations from political expenditures into law. Webster said Montana and Minnesota are “on the same track” to limit corporations’ influence over politics. 
And earlier this summer, the state House passed legislation — which Webster also sponsored — that would prohibit corporations with foreign ownership from using their money to influence state elections with bipartisan support. It hasn’t advanced out of the Senate’s State Government Committee. 
The co-sponsors emphasized that campaign finance reform should not be a partisan issue, with Webster noting that this is just one of “100 or more” issues that the legislature could be working on.  
Webster added that he expects the measure to have enough support to pass the House. However, he acknowledged that doesn’t mean the bill will reach Gov. Josh Shapiro’s desk this year. 
“We tee this up now. We make sure it’s an issue. We’re going to see the influence of money in the election by November,” he said. “Then we come back in ’27 and get this done.”

title: Election Day 2026: Congressional primaries give way to general election challenges
description: Several of Michigan’s incumbent representatives have identified their opponent for the coming months, as Democrats and Republicans solidified their nominees across the state’s 13 congressional districts.  When polls closed at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, results began pouring in from clerks’ offices across the state. text:
iQoncept/Getty ImagesSeveral of Michigan’s incumbent representatives have identified their opponent for the coming months, as Democrats and Republicans solidified their nominees across the state’s 13 congressional districts. 
When polls closed at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, results began pouring in from clerks’ offices across the state. While most races have since been called, the Democratic challenger slated to face the incumbent in Michigan’s 2nd Congressional District has yet to be determined.
 
1st Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) and attorney Callie Barr are slated for a rematch come November, with unofficial results showing the Republican incumbent and the Democratic challenger taking home their party’s nomination.
Bergman faced off against healthcare executive Matthew DenOtter and Army veteran Justin Michal, receiving 74.3% of the vote, per preliminary results shared by the Associated Press at 3:19 p.m. Wednesday. 
Barr received 58.4% of the vote in the Democratic primary where she faced Iron Mountain Mayor Pro Tem Kyle Blomquist and industrial design firm owner Wayne Stiles.
 
2nd Congressional District
While U.S. Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Caledonia) was unopposed in the Republican primary, the Democratic contest remained too close to call Wednesday afternoon. 
U.S. Marine Corps Veteran Ben Ambrose, Physician Assistant Jamie Hill and Lake County Commissioner Clyde Welford, are each seeking to oppose Moolenaar in the general election.
 
3rd Congressional District
Former TV Meteorologist Terri DeBoer will challenge U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids) in the general election, securing 78.6% of the vote in the Republican Primary as of 3:20 p.m. Wednesday according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press. Michigan National Guard Veteran Ryan Cushman received 21.4%.
Scholten was unopposed in the Democratic primary.
 
4th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township) staved off a challenge from former Holland Mayor Phil Tanis, with unofficial results showing Huizenga with 85% percent of the vote at 3:20 p.m. Wednesday.
In the Democratic primary, state Sen. Sean McCann of Kalamazoo defeated former congressional staffer Diop Harris, securing 65.7% of the vote according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press.
 
5th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Tim Walberg of Tipton was unopposed in the Republican primary, with Democrat Christian Vukasovich similarly unopposed.
 
6th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Ann Arbor was unopposed in the Democratic primary, as was Republican Heather Smiley.
 
7th Congressional District
Lansing-area political organizer William Lawrence won the Democratic nomination for the mid-Michigan district, receiving 43.7% of the vote, easily defeating former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, who received 28.8% while retired Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam received 27.6%
Lawrence is now slated to face the incumbent, U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), in the November general election.
 
8th Congressional District
Republican voters in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District rejected Amir Hassan, the candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump, for the GOP nomination, choosing instead Thomas Smith, even though Smith suspended his campaign on July 16.
The district, which includes the tri-cities of Saginaw, Midland and Bay City, as well as the Flint area, is currently represented by U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City), who was first elected in 2024 and is seeking re-election. She ran unopposed in the Democratic primary.
 
9th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township) will face CNC machinist Ray Pooley in the general election, with both McClain and Pooley unopposed in their primary elections.
 
10th Congressional District
The matchup for November in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District will feature the Republican nominee, U.S. Army Captain Michael Bouchard Jr., and the Democratic nominee, attorney Christina Hines, who each secured their respective party’s nominations in Tuesday’s primary election. 
 
11th Congressional District
State Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield) emerged victorious in a four-person race for the Democratic nomination to this Oakland County-based district. The heavily Democratic seat means Moss is likely to fill U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ empty congressional seat come 2027, although he’ll have to get by Troy Mayor Ethan Baker, the sole Republican candidate on the ballot.  
 
12th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit) defeated challengers Shanelle Jackson and Byron Nolen, receiving 73.9% of the vote as of 11:49 a.m. Wednesday according to unofficial results.
Republican James Hooper was unopposed in the primary.
 
13th Congressional District
Michigan State Rep. Donavan McKinney emerged victorious in the race for Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, lodging a successful challenge against incumbent U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit).
McKinney is almost assured to be elected to Congress in the reliably Democratic district. The only Republican candidate, T.P. Nykoriak, was sentenced in 2016 to 16 months in federal prison for stealing U.S. savings bonds from a church.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: ‘You have a choice on how you respond.’ Kelly Brush on thriving after a life-altering accident
description:
Brush is a leader of a national movement to empower people with spinal cord injuries, and
her foundation grants about $1 million per year to help people with disabilities purchase adaptive sports equipment and maintain an active lifestyle.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘You have a choice on how you respond.’ Kelly Brush on thriving[...]
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Kelly Brush riding an adaptive mountain bike during the 2025 Kelly Brush Foundation bike camp. Courtesy photo
Few people have turned adversity into opportunity as dramatically as Kelly Brush.
Brush was on the Middlebury College ski team when she was paralyzed in a ski racing accident in 2006. Twenty years later, Brush is a leader of a national movement to empower people with spinal cord injuries.
“I’m so glad that I’m able to do that and support … thousands of other people that I don’t even know and their families and create things that just feel a little bit better,” Brush told me.
I asked Brush what enabled her to stay positive following her accident.
“Whenever something happens in life, you have a choice on how you respond,” she replied. “Even when there’s things that are really hard or really sad, you feel that, and then you make the choice to move you forward in a good direction.”

Kelly Brush is the founder and spokesperson for the Kelly Brush Foundation. Courtesy photo

Brush has mixed feelings about people calling her an inspiration. If “an understanding of who I am and what I’ve done creates inspiration, that’s great. But not the inspiration that comes just because I exist and I’m in a wheelchair.”
Brush is concerned about how people with disabilities are especially vulnerable to delays or cutbacks in health care. She has personal experience of this: she recently had to undergo major back surgery and had to seek care in an emergency room when her primary care provider couldn’t see her for several weeks.
“People with disabilities have greater health care needs,” she said. “When the health care system isn’t set up well, we are then paying more for those greater needs. I see it time and again with complications that come from spinal cord injuries.”
Brush, who recently turned 40, is the founder and spokesperson for the Kelly Brush Foundation, which grants about $1 million per year to people with spinal cord injuries to purchase adaptive sports equipment and maintain an active lifestyle. Its best known fundraiser is the annual Kelly Brush Ride, which draws nearly 1,000 bike riders and will take place this year on Sept. 12 in Middlebury. There are also Kelly Brush Rides in Park City, Utah, and the Bay Area.
Brush is especially proud of the community that she and her foundation have helped build. “When I got hurt, I didn’t know anybody else with a spinal cord injury,” she said. Now her foundation connects people with spinal cord injuries with one another. 
“There’s something really different about being able to build community with people who are doing things similarly to you, as well as just the ability to feel seen and be seen by other people who are living a similar life to you outside of adaptive sports.”
Brush lives in Charlotte with her two young daughters. She worked for 10 years as a pediatric nurse practitioner, but is taking a break from that to lead her foundation and look after her children.

Kelly Brush using a sit-ski on a snowy mountain slope. Courtesy photo

I asked Brush what she hopes people take away from her story.
“To be excited about the fact that I’ve been able to live such a full life and continue to have all the same highs and lows that so many people have and I do it from my wheelchair,” she replied.
“I definitely have some more struggles than others. But my life is awesome and really fun. I hope people can see that and see the beauty in life, no matter what comes up and what happens, and find and follow that.”
